How to read these pages

Maths is not read in a straight line, so the pages are built for jumping around. Every mention of a numbered result, like Theorem 1.11, is a link. Hover over it to read the statement where you are, click to go there, and use the ↩ back button that appears bottom-left to return. The small ⇥ on a hover card opens the result in a panel beside the text instead, which is handy when a proof keeps leaning on it. On a phone, tap once to preview and again to go.

The contents of the chapter you are in sit on the left, with the section you are reading marked, and a thin bar shows how far through you are. Under each section heading is a rough reading time, what the section contains, and two small gauges: how hard it is, and how much the rest of the course relies on it. They are guesses, made by someone who has read ahead.

The small labels in the left margin say what a stretch of text is for: the question sets up a problem, intuition gives the picture to keep in mind, motivation explains why the next definition is needed, in words restates a result, technique marks a trick that will come back, careful flags a pitfall, and connection links to another part of the course. A thin line beside the text shows how far each label reaches. On the right, a miniature of the whole chapter shows where you are; drag the outlined box, or click anywhere on it, to move.

Numbering follows the lecture notes, and the small page numbers in the margin point into them. Grey Background boxes explain material the notes take from elsewhere. Exercise boxes show only a name until you open them, and the answer stays folded until you ask for it. When enough has been covered for a problem-sheet question, a pencilled note says so.

To find anything in any course, press / (or ⌘K / Ctrl-K, or the search button). It looks through results, section titles, figures, exercises, sheet questions and the running text, and takes you straight to the spot.

0.1Backgroundp. 1

≈ 2 min·difficulty ●○○·importance ★★☆
roadmapwhat the course is for

In the last fifty years probability theory has emerged both as a core mathematical discipline, alongside geometry, algebra and analysis, and as a fundamental way of thinking about the world. It gives a rigorous framework for modelling the randomness around us, and it has become an indispensable tool everywhere from physics and neuroscience to genetics, communication networks and mathematical finance. Probabilistic arguments have also become important inside mathematics itself, from number theory to partial differential equations.

The course has two halves. The first (Chapters 1–3) builds measure theory: what it means to assign probabilities to events, and to integrate. The notes build on Part A Integration; this version explains everything it borrows. The second half (Chapters 4–7) uses that foundation to define conditional expectation properly and then to study martingales, a class of random processes with remarkable properties.The nearest thing to a course text is David Williams, Probability with Martingales (CUP). The notes also recommend Durrett’s Probability: Theory and Examples, Capiński and Kopp’s Measure, Integral and Probability (gentle), Meyer’s Probability and Potentials and Varadhan’s Probability Theory (“not for the faint-hearted”). This chapter shows three places martingales turn up, without any of the machinery. Read it for the ideas; every step marked as informal here is made rigorous later.

0.3Example 1: Simple Symmetric Random Walkp. 4

≈ 7 min·1 figure, 1 exercise·difficulty ●○○·importance ★★★

Consider a sequence of independent random variables \((X_n)_{n\ge1}\), all with the same distribution

\[\PP(X_n=-1)=\PP(X_n=1)=\tfrac12.\]

Note that \(\E[X_n]=0\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(X_n)=\E[X_n^2]=1\). Let \(S_0=0\) and

\[S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nX_k,\qquad n\ge1,\]

be their cumulative sums. Think of a walker who tosses a fair coin each second and steps left or right. This process is the simple symmetric random walk (SSRW).

intuitiona first glimpse of a martingale

Suppose we have watched the walk up to time \(n-1\) and want to predict \(S_n\). Since \(S_n=S_{n-1}+X_n\), and \(X_n\) is independent of everything so far and has mean 0, our best guess is

\[\E[S_n\mid S_{n-1},\dots,S_0]=\E[S_n\mid S_{n-1}]=S_{n-1}+\E[X_n]=S_{n-1}.\]

Here \(\E[\,\cdot\mid S_{n-1},\dots,S_0]\) means "the expectation, given the values of \(S_0,\dots,S_{n-1}\)", which you can compute with the conditional probabilities from Prelims because everything is discrete. Making this notion precise in general is the job of Chapter 4.

This property captures something essential about the process \((S_n)_n\): the current value is the best prediction of the next one, given the whole history. A process with this property is called a martingale,The name has tangled origins. A martingale was a gambling system (double your stake after every loss), and also a strap in a horse’s harness; the word may come from the town of Martigues. The notes call these “weird historical reasons”, which is fair. and we'll define it properly in Chapter 6. It is not surprising that such processes turn up in many applications: fair games, prices in efficient markets and suitably normalised population sizes all have this property.

the questionhow far does the walk wander?

There are many questions one could ask about the walk. One of the first is its long-time behaviour. From the weak law of large numbers we know that \(S_n/n\to0\) in probability, that is, \(\PP(|S_n/n|>\eps)\to0\) for every \(\eps>0\). Later (Chapter 7) we will show that this convergence actually takes place almost surely: with probability one, the sequence of numbers \(S_n/n\) tends to 0. This is a non-trivial extension; it took mathematicians over 200 years to prove it.

You have also seen (the central limit theorem) that the size of \(S_n\) is about \(\sqrt n\):

\[\frac{S_n}{\sqrt n}\dto N(0,1),\]

meaning \(\PP(S_n/\sqrt n\le x)\to\Phi(x)\), the standard normal distribution function. Put differently, if I run 100 simulations of the walk and plot \(S_n/\sqrt n\) for a large \(n\), I expect only about 2 paths to be outside the interval \((-2.326,2.326)\), since \(\PP(|Z|>2.326)\approx0.02\) for \(Z\sim N(0,1)\).

So what about those rare paths? How far do they get? This is governed by the law of the iterated logarithm: almost surely,

\[\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{S_n}{\sqrt{n\log\log n}}=\sqrt2\qquad\text{and}\qquad\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{S_n}{\sqrt{n\log\log n}}=-\sqrt2.\]

Every path eventually stays inside \(\pm(1+\eps)\sqrt{2n\log\log n}\), but keeps poking out past \(\pm(1-\eps)\sqrt{2n\log\log n}\) forever. Although the walk evolves completely at random, these results pin down its shape remarkably precisely.

Background · lim sup and lim inf

For a sequence of real numbers \((x_n)\),

\[\limsup_{n\to\infty}x_n=\lim_{n\to\infty}\Big(\sup_{m\ge n}x_m\Big),\qquad\liminf_{n\to\infty}x_n=\lim_{n\to\infty}\Big(\inf_{m\ge n}x_m\Big).\]

The tail suprema \(\sup_{m\ge n}x_m\) can only decrease as \(n\) grows, so the first limit always exists in \([-\infty,\infty]\); similarly for the second. The lim sup is the largest value the sequence keeps coming back near, the lim inf the smallest. A sequence converges exactly when the two agree (and are finite). For example \(x_n=(-1)^n(1+\frac1n)\) has lim sup \(1\) and lim inf \(-1\).

ExerciseBack to the origin
For the simple symmetric random walk, what are \(\PP[S_2=0]\) and \(\PP[S_4=0]\)?
show answer

After two steps the walk is back at 0 exactly when one step went up and one went down: the paths \(+-\) and \(-+\), two of the four equally likely paths. So \(\PP[S_2=0]=\frac24=\frac12\). After four steps it needs two ups and two downs, and there are \(\binom42=6\) such paths among \(2^4=16\), so \(\PP[S_4=0]=\frac6{16}=\frac38\). In general \(\PP[S_{2n}=0]=\binom{2n}{n}2^{-2n}\), which shrinks roughly like \(1/\sqrt{\pi n}\): returns get rarer, but slowly enough that the walk still comes back infinitely often.

0.4Example 2: Mathematical Financep. 4

≈ 7 min·1 result, 1 figure·difficulty ●●○·importance ★☆☆
set-upa one-stock market

Suppose \((S_n)_{n\ge0}\) models the price of a risky asset, a share, at times \(n=0,1,2,\dots\) A trader buys and sells the share. At time \(n\) they have wealth \(V_n\) and decide to hold \(H_n=H_n(S_0,S_1,\dots,S_n)\) shares; the notation says the decision may use the prices seen so far, but not future ones. The rest of their wealth, \(V_n-H_nS_n\) (negative if they borrowed), sits in a bank account earning interest at rate \(r\) per period. At time \(n+1\) they therefore have

\[\begin{aligned}V_{n+1}&=H_nS_{n+1}+(V_n-H_nS_n)(1+r)\\&=H_n\big(S_{n+1}-(1+r)S_n\big)+V_n(1+r).\end{aligned}\]

Money at different times is easier to compare after removing the interest. Introduce discounted quantities \(\tilde V_n:=(1+r)^{-n}V_n\) and \(\tilde S_n:=(1+r)^{-n}S_n\). Dividing the last equation by \((1+r)^{n+1}\) gives

\[\tilde V_{n+1}=H_n(\tilde S_{n+1}-\tilde S_n)+\tilde V_n=\dots=V_0+\sum_{t=0}^{n}H_t(\tilde S_{t+1}-\tilde S_t).\]

The trader's discounted wealth is their starting capital plus, at each step, (number of shares held) × (change in discounted price). We will meet this object again under the name discrete stochastic integral or martingale transform (Chapter 6).

Now suppose that at time \(0\) someone wants to buy from the trader a financial product which, at time \(N\), pays \(f(S_0,S_1,\dots,S_N)\); for example a call option paying \(\max(S_N-K,0)\). What price should the trader set? If they can find a trading strategy \(H\) such that \(V_N=f\) no matter how prices move, then \(V_0\) is the fair price: by trading, the trader reproduces (hedges) the payoff exactly, so they bear no risk. But when is this possible, and how do we find \(V_0\)? One case where it works is the binomial model.

Proposition 0.1 (Binomial model pricing).p. 6 Suppose there exist two constants \(u,d\) such that \(0<1-d<1<1+r<1+u\) and \(S_{n+1}\in\{(1+u)S_n,(1-d)S_n\}\) a.s., for all \(n\ge0\). Then for any \(f\), there exist \(V_0,H\) such that \(f=V_N\) a.s. In addition, there exists a unique probability measure \(\mathbb Q\) such that \((\tilde S_n)_{n\ge0}\) is a \(\mathbb Q\)-martingale and

\[V_0=(1+r)^{-N}\E_{\mathbb Q}[f(S_0,\dots,S_N)].\]
in wordsProposition 0.1

Here "a.s." (almost surely) means "with probability one", and \(\E_{\mathbb Q}\) is expectation computed with the probabilities \(\mathbb Q\) rather than the real-world ones.

Why it works (one step, then induction). Take one period, starting from a node where the price is \(s\), and suppose the claim pays \(v_u\) if the price goes up and \(v_d\) if it goes down. We want a holding \(H\) of stock and a starting value \(V\) that reproduce both outcomes:

\[\begin{aligned}H(1+u)s+(V-Hs)(1+r)&=v_u,\\H(1-d)s+(V-Hs)(1+r)&=v_d.\end{aligned}\]

Subtracting the two equations kills \(V\) and gives

\[H=\frac{v_u-v_d}{(u+d)s}.\]

Substituting back,

\[V=\frac{1}{1+r}\big(q\,v_u+(1-q)\,v_d\big),\qquad q=\frac{r+d}{u+d}.\]

The condition \(1-d<1+r<1+u\) is exactly \(0<q<1\). So \(V\) is a discounted average of the two outcomes, weighted by \(q\) instead of the true probability.

Call \(\mathbb Q\) the measure under which each step goes up with probability \(q\), independently. Under \(\mathbb Q\), the expected next discounted price is

\[\frac{q(1+u)s+(1-q)(1-d)s}{(1+r)^{n+1}}=\frac{s}{(1+r)^n},\]

which is the martingale property; and \(q\) is the only up-probability that gives it.

Finally, work backwards from time \(N\), one period at a time. This builds \(V_0\) and the whole strategy \(H\), and unwinding the averages gives

\[V_0=(1+r)^{-N}\E_{\mathbb Q}[f].\]
∎
intuitionwhy real-world odds drop out

Notice what is missing from the formula: the real-world probability that the price goes up. Two traders who disagree completely about where the market is heading must still agree on the price of the option, or one of them can make risk-free money from the other.

connectionprices become martingales

The take-away message is that although the original process (the price) need not be a martingale, after a transformation (discounting, and a change of measure) it turns into one. This is useful because it lets us use martingale theory to study the original process. This is not special to finance: in many applications there is a martingale lurking somewhere.

0.5Example 3: The Galton–Watson Branching Processp. 6

≈ 11 min·3 results, 1 figure, 1 exercise·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★☆
history

In spite of earlier work by Bienaymé, the branching process is attributed to the polymath Sir Francis Galton and the Revd Henry Watson. Like many Victorians, Galton was worried about the demise of English family names. He posed a question in the Educational Times of 1873:

The decay of the families of men who have occupied conspicuous positions in past times has been a subject of frequent remark, and has given rise to various conjectures. The instances are very numerous in which surnames that were once common have become scarce or wholly disappeared. The tendency is universal, and, in explanation of it, the conclusion has hastily been drawn that a rise in physical comfort and intellectual capacity is necessarily accompanied by a diminution in ‘fertility’…

He went on to ask "What is the probability that a name dies out by the ‘ordinary law of chances’?" Watson sent a solution, which they published jointly the following year. The first step was to distil the problem into a workable model.

Definition 0.2 (Galton–Watson branching process).p. 6 Let \((X_{n,r})_{n,r\ge1}\) be an infinite array of independent identically distributed random variables, each with the same distribution as \(X\), where \(\PP[X=k]=p_k\) for \(k=0,1,2,\dots\) The sequence \((Z_n)_{n\ge0}\) defined by

  1. \(Z_0=1\),
  2. \(Z_n=X_{n,1}+\dots+X_{n,Z_{n-1}}\) for \(n\ge1\)

is the Galton–Watson branching process (started from a single ancestor) with offspring distribution \(X\).

in wordsDefinition 0.2

In words: generation \(n-1\) has \(Z_{n-1}\) individuals; the \(r\)-th of them has \(X_{n,r}\) children, independently of everyone else; and \(Z_n\) counts all the children. (If \(Z_{n-1}=0\) the sum is empty and \(Z_n=0\): once extinct, always extinct.) In the original setting \(Z_n\) counted the male descendants of a single male ancestor after \(n\) generations. It is also a crude model for the spread of a virus, with each generation lasting a couple of weeks and each infected person independently infecting a random number of others.

set-upmean and generating function

Two quantities control the process: the mean offspring \(m=\E[X]=\sum_kkp_k\), which we assume finite, and the probability generating function (pgf)

\[f(\theta)=\E[\theta^X]=\sum_{k=0}^\infty p_k\theta^k,\qquad0\le\theta\le1.\]

The pgf encodes the whole distribution: \(f(0)=p_0\), \(f(1)=1\), and \(f'(1)=m\).

Claim 0.3.p. 7 Let \(f_n(\theta)=\E[\theta^{Z_n}]\). Then \(f_n\) is the \(n\)-fold composition of \(f\) with itself (where by convention a 0-fold composition is the identity).

‘Proof’ (informal). We proceed by induction. For the base case, \(f_0(\theta)=\E[\theta^1]=\theta\), the identity. Now assume \(n\ge1\) and that \(f_{n-1}\) is the \((n-1)\)-fold composition.

Suppose we know that \(Z_{n-1}=k\). Then \(Z_n\) is a sum of \(k\) independent copies of \(X\), so

\[\begin{aligned}\E\big[\theta^{Z_n}\,\big|\,Z_{n-1}=k\big]&=\E\big[\theta^{X_{n,1}+\dots+X_{n,k}}\big]\\&=\E\big[\theta^{X_{n,1}}\big]\cdots\E\big[\theta^{X_{n,k}}\big]&&\why{by independence}\\&=f(\theta)^k.\end{aligned}\]

The middle step uses the fact that the expectation of a product of independent variables is the product of their expectations.

Writing this for all \(k\) at once:

\[\E\big[\theta^{Z_n}\,\big|\,Z_{n-1}\big]=f(\theta)^{Z_{n-1}}.\](1)

This is our first example of a conditional expectation that is itself a random variable: its value depends on the random \(Z_{n-1}\).

Averaging over \(Z_{n-1}\),

\[\begin{aligned}f_n(\theta)=\E\big[\theta^{Z_n}\big]&=\E\Big[\E\big[\theta^{Z_n}\,\big|\,Z_{n-1}\big]\Big]\\&=\E\big[f(\theta)^{Z_{n-1}}\big]=f_{n-1}\big(f(\theta)\big),\end{aligned}\](2)

and the claim follows by induction.∎

techniquethe tower property, met properly in Chapter 4

In (2) we used the tower property: averaging the conditional averages gives the overall average. Here it is just the partition theorem from Prelims,

\[\E[Y]=\sum_k\E[Y\mid Z_{n-1}=k]\,\PP(Z_{n-1}=k),\]

which applies because the events \(\{Z_{n-1}=k\}\) form a countable partition of the sample space. In the general theory we will need something that works when conditioning on a continuous random variable, where every single value has probability zero (Chapter 4).

Watson wanted the extinction probability, the probability that \(Z_n=0\) for some \(n\).

Claim 0.4.p. 7 Let \(q=\PP[Z_n=0\text{ for some }n]\). Then \(q\) is the smallest root in \([0,1]\) of the equation \(\theta=f(\theta)\). In particular, assuming \(p_1=\PP[X=1]<1\),

  • if \(m=\E[X]\le1\), then \(q=1\),
  • if \(m=\E[X]>1\), then \(q<1\).

‘Proof’ (informal). Step 1: \(q\) is a root of \(f(\theta)=\theta\). Let \(q_n=\PP[Z_n=0]=f_n(0)\). Since \(\{Z_n=0\}\subseteq\{Z_{n+1}=0\}\) (once the family dies out it stays dead), \(q_n\) increases with \(n\), and

\[q=\lim_{n\to\infty}q_n=\lim_{n\to\infty}f_n(0).\](3)

This is Lemma 1.4: the events \(\{Z_n=0\}\) increase to \(\{Z_n=0\text{ for some }n\}\).

Now \(f_{n+1}(0)=f(f_n(0))\), that is, \(q_{n+1}=f(q_n)\). Since \(f\) is continuous, letting \(n\to\infty\) on both sides shows that

\[q=f(q).\]

Step 2: what the roots look like. The function \(f\) is convex on \([0,1]\): its second derivative

\[f''(\theta)=\sum_kk(k-1)p_k\theta^{k-2}\]

is \(\ge0\), so its graph bends upwards. Also \(f(1)=1\). So only two things can happen, depending on the slope \(m=f'(1)\) at \(1\).

  • If \(m\le1\), the graph of \(f\) stays above the diagonal on \([0,1)\), and the only root is \(\theta=1\).
  • If \(m>1\), the graph crosses the diagonal once more, at some \(\theta_0<1\).

Step 3: which root. In the second case we must check that \(q\) is the smaller root \(\theta_0\). The function \(f\) is increasing, and \(q_0=0\le\theta_0\), so by induction

\[q_{n+1}=f(q_n)\le f(\theta_0)=\theta_0\qquad\text{for all }n.\]

Letting \(n\to\infty\) gives \(q\le\theta_0\).∎

intuition

1">

It's not hard to guess the result for \(m>1\) and \(m<1\), but the case \(m=1\) is far from obvious: on average each person has exactly one child, yet the family dies out with probability one.

ExerciseTwo children or none
Each individual has no children with probability \(\frac14\) and two children with probability \(\frac34\). What is the extinction probability?
show answer

The generating function is \(f(\theta)=\frac14+\frac34\theta^2\). Solving \(\theta=f(\theta)\) means

\[3\theta^2-4\theta+1=0,\qquad\text{that is}\qquad(3\theta-1)(\theta-1)=0,\]

with roots \(\frac13\) and \(1\). The smallest is \(q=\frac13\).

This fits the picture above: the mean number of children is \(\frac34\cdot2=\frac32>1\), so extinction is not certain.

One check you can do in your head: the first individual's line dies out if it has no children (probability \(\frac14\)), or if it has two and both their lines die out (probability \(\frac34q^2\)). With \(q=\frac13\) that is

\[\tfrac14+\tfrac34\cdot\tfrac19=\tfrac14+\tfrac1{12}=\tfrac13.\]
connectionyet another martingale

The extinction probability is only one statistic we might care about. Can we say anything about how the population grows or declines? Consider

\[\E[Z_{n+1}\mid Z_n=k]=\E[X_{n+1,1}+\dots+X_{n+1,k}]=km\](4)

by linearity of expectation. In other words \(\E[Z_{n+1}\mid Z_n]=mZ_n\), another conditional expectation that is a random variable. Now rescale: write

\[M_n=\frac{Z_n}{m^n}.\]

Then \(\E[M_{n+1}\mid M_n]=M_n\). In fact more is true, \(\E[M_{n+1}\mid M_0,M_1,\dots,M_n]=M_n\): again we encounter a martingale!

carefullimits and expectations need not commute

It is natural to ask whether \(M_n\) has a limit as \(n\to\infty\) and, if so, what we can say about it. We are going to develop the tools to answer this (Chapter 6). For now, notice that for \(m\le1\) we have "proved" that the population dies out with probability one, so \(M_\infty=\lim_nM_n=0\) with probability one, while \(\E[M_n]=1\) for every \(n\). So

\[0=\E[M_\infty]\ne\lim_{n\to\infty}\E[M_n]=1.\](5)

Taking expectations and taking limits do not commute here. We will need to be careful when passing to limits; (5) is our first meeting with the phenomenon behind Fatou's Lemma (Theorem 2.12) and uniform integrability (Chapter 6).

roadmapwhat the course will make precise

One of the main aims of the course is to provide the tools to make arguments like these precise. Another is to make sense of martingales in much more general settings, which requires defining conditional expectation when conditioning on a continuous random variable. That starts with measure theory, in Chapter 1.

Chapter 1

Measure spaces

Which sets deserve a size, and how should sizes add? This chapter builds the machinery that answers both questions, then shows that on the real line all of it comes down to one increasing function.

Sizes that add upp. 8

≈ 7 min·1 result, 1 figure, 1 exercise·difficulty ●○○·importance ★★★
the questionwhich sets deserve a size?

We want to assign a mass, or size, to subsets of a space in a consistent way. For us the subsets will be events, collections of outcomes in a sample space \(\Omega\), and the mass will be a probability: a number saying how likely the event is to occur.

motivationwhy not measure every subset?

The obvious wish is to give every subset a size. Write \(\Pow(\Omega)\) for the power set of \(\Omega\), the set of all its subsets. For a finite or countable \(\Omega\) the wish can be granted (Example 1.6). For \(\Omega=\R\) it can't. There is no way to give every subset of \(\R\) a "length" that is translation invariant (sliding a set along doesn't change its length) and countably additive (the length of a countable union of disjoint pieces is the sum of their lengths). The background box below explains why. So we settle for less: we pick out a collection of well-behaved subsets, and ask only that it be closed under the operations we actually perform on events, namely complements ("not \(A\)") and unions ("\(A\) or \(B\)").

Background · Why not every subset of ℝ can have a length

Suppose \(\lambda\) gave every subset of \(\R\) a length, countably additive and unchanged by translation, with \(\lambda([0,1])=1\). Call \(x,y\in[0,1)\) equivalent if \(x-y\) is rational. The equivalence classes split \([0,1)\) into pieces; choose one point from each piece and call the resulting set \(V\) (this choice needs the axiom of choice).

For each rational \(q\in[0,1)\) let \(V_q\) be \(V\) shifted by \(q\), wrapping around modulo 1. Two facts: the \(V_q\) are disjoint (if \(V_q\) and \(V_{q'}\) shared a point, two different chosen points would differ by a rational), and together they cover \([0,1)\) (every \(x\) is equivalent to some chosen point \(v\), and \(x=v+q\) mod 1 for a rational \(q\)). By translation invariance every \(V_q\) has the same length \(c=\lambda(V)\). Countable additivity then says \(1=\sum_{q}c\), a countable sum of one constant. That sum is \(0\) if \(c=0\) and \(\infty\) if \(c>0\). Neither is \(1\), so \(\lambda\) cannot exist.Vitali, 1905. The axiom of choice is genuinely needed: Solovay showed in 1970 that, if a certain large-cardinal axiom is consistent, so is a version of set theory without full choice in which every subset of \(\R\) has a Lebesgue measure. This is an aside from logic, and nothing in the course depends on it.

Definition 1.1 (Algebras and σ-algebras).p. 9 Let \(\Omega\) be a set and let \(\A\subseteq\Pow(\Omega)\) be a collection of subsets of \(\Omega\).

  1. \(\A\) is an algebra (on \(\Omega\)) if \(\emptyset\in\A\) and for all \(A,B\in\A\), \(A^c=\Omega\setminus A\in\A\) and \(A\cup B\in\A\).
  2. \(\A\) is a σ-algebra (on \(\Omega\)) if \(\emptyset\in\A\), \(A\in\A\) implies \(A^c\in\A\), and for all sequences \((A_n)_{n\ge1}\) of elements of \(\A\), \(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n\in\A\).
in wordsDefinition 1.1

Since \(A\cap B=(A^c\cup B^c)^c\) (De Morgan), an algebra is also closed under intersections and differences: it is closed under finite set operations. A σ-algebraThe σ is for German Summe: unions used to be called sums. The same letter turns up in \(F_\sigma\), a countable union of closed sets, beside \(G_\delta\), with δ for Durchschnitt, intersection. is closed under countable ones, for example \(\bigcap_n A_n=\big(\bigcup_n A_n^c\big)^c\). We tend to write \(\F\) for a σ-algebra; some people say σ-field. Note that \(A^c\) only makes sense once we know which \(\Omega\) we are in.

Every σ-algebra is an algebra: to get \(A\cup B\), use the sequence \(A,B,\emptyset,\emptyset,\dots\). On a finite set the converse holds too, because a sequence of subsets of a finite set contains only finitely many different sets. The two notions only come apart on infinite sets, and here is the standard example.

ExerciseFinite or cofinite
Check that this \(\A\) really is an algebra.
show answer

\(\emptyset\) is finite. Taking complements swaps "finite" and "cofinite" (a set is cofinite if its complement is finite). If \(A\) and \(B\) are both finite, so is \(A\cup B\); if one of them, say \(B\), is cofinite, then \((A\cup B)^c\subseteq B^c\) is finite. So \(\A\) is an algebra, and Figure 1.1 shows that it is not a σ-algebra.

Weighing setsp. 9

≈ 13 min·5 results, 2 figures, 2 exercises·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★★

Definition 1.2 (Set functions).p. 9 Let \(\A\) be any set of subsets of \(\Omega\) containing \(\emptyset\). A set function on \(\A\) is a function \(\mu:\A\to[0,\infty]\) with \(\mu(\emptyset)=0\). We say that \(\mu\) is

  1. increasing if \(\mu(A)\le\mu(B)\) for all \(A,B\in\A\) with \(A\subseteq B\);
  2. additive if \(\mu(A\cup B)=\mu(A)+\mu(B)\) for all disjoint \(A,B\in\A\) with \(A\cup B\in\A\);
  3. countably additive, or σ-additive, if for all sequences \((A_n)\) of disjoint sets in \(\A\) with \(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n\in\A\),
    \[\mu\Big(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n\Big)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\mu(A_n).\]
in wordsDefinition 1.2

Two small points about the definition. First, the values live in \([0,\infty]\): a set may have infinite size, with the conventions \(a+\infty=\infty\) and \(\infty+\infty=\infty\). A sum of non-negative terms always makes sense in \([0,\infty]\) and doesn't depend on the order of the terms, so the right-hand side above is never ambiguous. Second, the clause "with \(A\cup B\in\A\)" is there because \(\A\) is an arbitrary collection. The union may simply not be in it, and then \(\mu\) has nothing to say about it.This matters in the proof of Theorem 1.15, where \(\mu_0\) lives on an algebra that is not a σ-algebra. Countable additivity is only demanded when the countable union happens to land back in the algebra. A measure space is then a set with a σ-algebra and a countably additive set function on it.

Definition 1.3 (Measure spaces).p. 9 A measurable space is a pair \((\Omega,\F)\) where \(\F\) is a σ-algebra on \(\Omega\). A measure space is a triple \((\Omega,\F,\mu)\) where \(\Omega\) is a set, \(\F\) is a σ-algebra on \(\Omega\) and \(\mu:\F\to[0,\infty]\) is a countably additive set function. We call \(\mu\) a measure on \((\Omega,\F)\) and say that \(\mu\) is

  1. finite if \(\mu(\Omega)<\infty\);
  2. σ-finite if there is a sequence \((E_n)_{n\ge1}\) of sets from \(\F\) with \(\mu(E_n)<\infty\) for all \(n\) and \(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty E_n=\Omega\);
  3. a probability measure if \(\mu(\Omega)=1\).
set-upvocabulary for Definition 1.3

The sets in \(\F\) are called measurable sets; they are the ones \(\mu\) is defined on. If \(\mu\) is a probability measure we call \((\Omega,\F,\mu)\) a probability space and usually write \(\PP\) instead of \(\mu\). A few specimens, to calibrate the words. (Lebesgue measure, the second one, is the measure that gives each interval its length; we construct it properly in Corollary 1.13, and until then you can use it with that one property in mind.)

  • A fair die: \(\mu(A)=|A|/6\) on \(\Pow(\{1,\dots,6\})\)probability
  • Lebesgue measure on \(\R\): infinite, but the sets \(E_n=[-n,n]\) have finite measure \(2n\) and exhaust \(\R\)σ-finite
  • Counting measure \(\mu(A)=|A|\) (the number of elements, possibly \(\infty\)) on \(\Pow(\N)\): take \(E_n=\{1,\dots,n\}\)σ-finite
  • Counting measure on \(\Pow(\R)\)not σ-finite
ExerciseCounting is not σ-finite
Why is counting measure on \(\R\) not σ-finite?
show answer

A set has finite counting measure only if it is finite, and a countable union of finite sets is countable. \(\R\) is not.

connectionfrom additivity to monotone limits

Every measure is additive (pad the pair \(A,B\) out with empty sets and use countable additivity) and increasing (if \(A\subseteq B\) then \(\mu(B)=\mu(A)+\mu(B\setminus A)\ge\mu(A)\)). Measures also respect monotone limits of sets. For a sequence of sets, \(F_n\uparrow F\) means \(F_n\subseteq F_{n+1}\) for all \(n\) and \(\bigcup_n F_n=F\): the sets grow and fill out \(F\). Similarly \(G_n\downarrow G\) means \(G_n\supseteq G_{n+1}\) for all \(n\) and \(\bigcap_n G_n=G\): the sets shrink down to \(G\).

Lemma 1.4 (Monotone convergence properties).p. 9 Let \((\Omega,\F,\mu)\) be a measure space.

  1. If \((F_n)_{n\ge1}\) is a sequence of sets from \(\F\) with \(F_n\uparrow F\), then \(\mu(F_n)\uparrow\mu(F)\) as \(n\to\infty\).
  2. If \((G_n)_{n\ge1}\) is a sequence of sets from \(\F\) with \(G_n\downarrow G\), and \(\mu(G_k)<\infty\) for some \(k\in\N\), then \(\mu(G_n)\downarrow\mu(G)\) as \(n\to\infty\).

Proof (the notes defer this to Part A). Part (1). Cut \(F\) into disjoint rings. Writing \(F_0=\emptyset\),

\[F=F_1\cup(F_2\setminus F_1)\cup(F_3\setminus F_2)\cup\cdots.\]

These rings are disjoint and in \(\F\), so countable additivity gives

\[\mu(F)=\sum_{k\ge1}\mu(F_k\setminus F_{k-1}).\]

The \(n\)-th partial sum of this series is \(\mu(F_n)\), because the first \(n\) rings make up \(F_n\). A series of non-negative terms converges to its sum through increasing partial sums, so \(\mu(F_n)\uparrow\mu(F)\).

Part (2). Consider only \(n\ge k\). The sets \(G_k\setminus G_n\) increase to \(G_k\setminus G\), so by part (1),

\[\mu(G_k\setminus G_n)\uparrow\mu(G_k\setminus G).\]

Since \(\mu(G_k)<\infty\), all the sets involved have finite measure, and additivity gives

\[\mu(G_k\setminus G_n)=\mu(G_k)-\mu(G_n),\qquad\mu(G_k\setminus G)=\mu(G_k)-\mu(G).\]

Subtracting from the finite number \(\mu(G_k)\) gives \(\mu(G_n)\downarrow\mu(G)\).

Notice where finiteness was used: with \(\mu(G_k)=\infty\) the subtraction would read \(\infty-\infty\), which is meaningless.∎

carefulthe finiteness in Lemma 1.4 (2)

The condition \(\mu(G_k)<\infty\) in (2) is essential. Take \(G_n=(n,\infty)\subseteq\R\) with Lebesgue measure: the third mode below.

roadmapwhy Lemma 1.5 matters: Theorem 1.15

The following partial converse is sometimes useful. We will lean on it in the proof of Theorem 1.15.

Lemma 1.5.p. 10 Let \(\mu:\A\to[0,\infty)\) be an additive set function on an algebra \(\A\) taking only finite values. Then \(\mu\) is countably additive if and only if for every sequence \((A_n)\) of sets in \(\A\) with \(A_n\downarrow\emptyset\) we have \(\mu(A_n)\to0\).

in wordsLemma 1.5

In words: to check countable additivity, it is enough to check that sets shrinking to nothing have measures shrinking to zero.

ExerciseContinuity at the empty set
Prove Lemma 1.5.
show answer

(⇒) Suppose \(A_n\downarrow\emptyset\). Every point of \(A_n\) leaves the sequence at some finite stage, so \(A_n\) is the disjoint union of the sets \(A_k\setminus A_{k+1}\), \(k\ge n\), all of which lie in \(\A\). Countable additivity gives

\[\mu(A_n)=\sum_{k\ge n}\mu(A_k\setminus A_{k+1}).\]

For \(n=1\) this series converges (to \(\mu(A_1)<\infty\)), and \(\mu(A_n)\) is its tail, so \(\mu(A_n)\to0\).

(⇐) Let \(A_1,A_2,\dots\in\A\) be disjoint with \(A=\bigcup_nA_n\in\A\), and put

\[R_N=A\setminus(A_1\cup\dots\cup A_N).\]

Then \(R_N\in\A\) because \(\A\) is an algebra, and \(R_N\downarrow\emptyset\). Finite additivity gives

\[\mu(A)=\sum_{n\le N}\mu(A_n)+\mu(R_N),\]

and \(\mu(R_N)\to0\), so letting \(N\to\infty\) gives \(\mu(A)=\sum_n\mu(A_n)\).

✎Now try question B3 of Problem Sheet 1. You have just seen one solution; try writing it out without looking.

There are lots of measure spaces out there, several of which you already know. The simplest are the discrete ones.

Example 1.6 (Discrete measure theory).p. 10 Let \(\Omega\) be a countable set. A mass function on \(\Omega\) is any function \(\bar\mu:\Omega\to[0,\infty]\). Given such a \(\bar\mu\) we can define a measure on \((\Omega,\Pow(\Omega))\) by setting \(\mu(A)=\sum_{x\in A}\bar\mu(x)\). Equally, given a measure \(\mu\) on \((\Omega,\Pow(\Omega))\) we can define a corresponding mass function by \(\bar\mu(x)=\mu(\{x\})\). For countable \(\Omega\) there is a one-to-one correspondence between measures on \((\Omega,\Pow(\Omega))\) and mass functions.

✎Now try questions A1, A3, B1, B6 of Problem Sheet 1. They need nothing beyond σ-algebras and measures.
intuitiondiscrete measures as the toy model

Countable additivity is what makes the correspondence one-to-one: every \(A\subseteq\Omega\) is the countable disjoint union of its singletons, so \(\mu(A)\) is forced to equal \(\sum_{x\in A}\mu(\{x\})\). A probability mass function from Prelims is exactly a mass function with total mass 1.

Discrete measure spaces are a toy version of the general theory, and essentially the only setting in which a measure can be written down explicitly. In general σ-algebras have no explicit description, and, as we saw, not every subset can be given a measure. So the strategy is to specify the measure on a smaller class of sets that generates the σ-algebra, the way singletons did in Example 1.6, and then extend. That raises two problems.

roadmapuniqueness, then existence

The construction problem is usually handled by Carathéodory’s Extension Theorem (Theorem 1.12). The uniqueness problem can usually be settled by a corollary of Dynkin’s π-system Lemma (Theorem 1.11). First we need more vocabulary.

Generating σ-algebrasp. 10

≈ 11 min·4 results, 2 figures, 1 exercise·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★★

Definition 1.7 (Generated σ-algebras).p. 10 Let \(\A\) be a collection of subsets of \(\Omega\). Define

\[\sigma(\A)=\{A\subseteq\Omega : A\in\F\text{ for all }\sigma\text{-algebras }\F\text{ on }\Omega\text{ containing }\A\}.\]

Then \(\sigma(\A)\) is a σ-algebra (exercise), called the σ-algebra generated by \(\A\). It is the smallest σ-algebra containing \(\A\): if \(\F\supseteq\A\) is a σ-algebra then \(\F\supseteq\sigma(\A)\).

intuitiontop-down versus bottom-up

This definition works from the top down: intersect everything that could possibly qualify. On a finite \(\Omega\) you can also work from the bottom up, applying complements and unions until nothing new appears.On infinite sets the bottom-up route is treacherous. Start from the open subsets of \(\R\), apply countable unions and complements, and repeat: after any countable number of rounds you still have not reached every Borel set. (You need \(\omega_1\) rounds, where \(\omega_1\) is the first uncountable ordinal. This is an aside; safe to skip.) The top-down definition sidesteps all of that. Either way the answer has a simple shape. Call two outcomes inseparable if every generating set contains both or neither. The classes of inseparable outcomes are the atoms, and \(\sigma(\A)\) is exactly the collection of unions of atoms. With \(k\) atoms that makes \(2^k\) sets.

ExerciseThe smallest σ-algebra
Why is \(\sigma(\A)\) a σ-algebra, and why the smallest one containing \(\A\)?
show answer

The family of σ-algebras containing \(\A\) is non-empty, since \(\Pow(\Omega)\) belongs to it. Each defining property survives intersection: \(\emptyset\) lies in every member; if \(A\) lies in every member, so does \(A^c\); if every \(A_n\) lies in every member, so does \(\bigcup_nA_n\). So \(\sigma(\A)\) is a σ-algebra and it contains \(\A\). If \(\F\supseteq\A\) is any σ-algebra, it is one of the sets being intersected, so \(\F\supseteq\sigma(\A)\).

The most important generated σ-algebra is built from the open sets of a space.

Background · Open sets and topologies

A set \(U\subseteq\R\) is open if around each of its points there is a little interval still inside \(U\): for every \(x\in U\) there is \(r>0\) with \((x-r,x+r)\subseteq U\). Open intervals \((a,b)\) are open, and so are unions of them; \([0,1]\) is not open, since no interval around \(0\) fits inside it. A set is closed if its complement is open: \([a,b]\), single points and \((-\infty,x]\) are closed.

The same idea works in \(\R^d\) with balls in place of intervals. In general, a topology on a set \(\Omega\) is just a collection \(\T\) of subsets, declared to be the open sets, that contains \(\emptyset\) and \(\Omega\) and is closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections. A topological space is a set with a topology. For this course you only need the open sets of \(\R\) and \(\R^d\).

Definition 1.8 (Borel σ-algebra, Borel measure).p. 10 Let \(\Omega\) be a topological space with topology (that is, set of open sets) \(\T\). Then the Borel σ-algebra on \(\Omega\) is the σ-algebra generated by the open sets, \(\B(\Omega)=\sigma(\T)\). A measure \(\mu\) on \((\Omega,\B(\Omega))\) is called a Borel measure on \(\Omega\).

in wordsDefinition 1.8

\(\B(\Omega)\) depends on the topology as well as on the set. Usually the topology is understood; on \(\R\) we always mean the usual one from the box above. Sets in \(\B(\R)\) are called Borel sets. Nearly every set you can describe explicitly is Borel: open and closed sets, intervals of every kind, countable sets, and anything built from these by countably many complements, unions and intersections.

Definition 1.9 (π-system).p. 10 Let \(\I\) be a collection of subsets of \(\Omega\). We say that \(\I\) is a π-system if \(A,B\in\I\) implies \(A\cap B\in\I\).

intuitionhow weak a π-system is

An algebra is automatically a π-system. A π-system is a much weaker thing than an algebra: no complements, no unions, just intersections.

Example 1.10.p. 11 The collection \(\pi(\R)=\{(-\infty,x] : x\in\R\}\) forms a π-system, and \(\sigma(\pi(\R))\), the σ-algebra it generates, is \(\B(\R)\), the σ-algebra of all Borel subsets of \(\R\) (exercise).

examplewhat rays generate

Rays are about the dullest sets imaginable, so it is worth seeing how much they generate. Figure 1.5 works through the exercise.

Uniqueness, and why intersections matterp. 11

≈ 5 min·1 result, 1 figure·difficulty ●●●·importance ★★☆

Here's why we care about π-systems.

Theorem 1.11 (Uniqueness of extension).p. 11 Let \(\mu_1\) and \(\mu_2\) be measures on the same measurable space \((\Omega,\F)\), and let \(\I\subseteq\F\) be a π-system. If \(\mu_1(\Omega)=\mu_2(\Omega)<\infty\) and \(\mu_1=\mu_2\) on \(\I\), then \(\mu_1=\mu_2\) on \(\sigma(\I)\).

✎Now try questions B2, B4, C3 of Problem Sheet 1.
in wordsTheorem 1.11

We will often apply the theorem to a π-system with \(\sigma(\I)=\F\), and then \(\mu_1\) and \(\mu_2\) agree everywhere. A very important special case: if two probability measures agree on a π-system, they agree on the σ-algebra it generates. The notes refer to Williams, Appendix A.1 for the proof; here is how it goes.

Proof sketch. Let

\[\D=\{A\in\F:\mu_1(A)=\mu_2(A)\},\]

the sets on which the two measures agree. Because \(\mu_1\) and \(\mu_2\) are finite with equal total mass, \(\D\) has three properties:

  1. \(\Omega\in\D\);
  2. if \(A\subseteq B\) are both in \(\D\) then \(B\setminus A\in\D\), since \(\mu_i(B\setminus A)=\mu_i(B)-\mu_i(A)\) is a subtraction of finite numbers;
  3. if \(A_n\in\D\) with \(A_n\uparrow A\) then \(A\in\D\), by Lemma 1.4.

A collection with these three properties is called a d-system (or λ-system).

Dynkin's lemma says: a d-system that contains a π-system \(\I\) contains all of \(\sigma(\I)\). (The proof shows that the smallest d-system containing \(\I\) is also closed under intersections, and a d-system closed under intersections is a σ-algebra.)

Our \(\D\) contains \(\I\), so it contains \(\sigma(\I)\), which is the claim.∎

motivationwhy intersections?

Why should closure under intersection be the hypothesis? Because knowing \(\mu(A)\) and \(\mu(B)\) tells you nothing about \(\mu(A\cap B)\). A collection that generates everything can still leave the measure badly underdetermined.

connectionFigure 1.6 and Dynkin’s lemma

The six sets on which the two measures in Figure 1.6 agree form a d-system that is not closed under intersection, which is exactly the gap Dynkin's lemma needs a π-system to close.

carefulfiniteness can’t be dropped

The finiteness condition can't be dropped either. On \(\R\), let \(\mu_1(A)\) count the rationals in \(A\) and let \(\mu_2=2\mu_1\). Both give every interval \((a,b]\) with \(a<b\) measure \(\infty\) (each such interval contains infinitely many rationals), so they agree on the π-system of such intervals together with \(\emptyset\), which generates \(\B(\R)\). And \(\mu_1(\R)=\mu_2(\R)=\infty\). Yet \(\mu_1(\{0\})=1\ne2=\mu_2(\{0\})\). In the proof above, the step \(B\setminus A\in\D\) needed to subtract, and \(\infty-\infty\) is meaningless.

Existence: Carathéodoryp. 11

≈ 8 min·2 results, 1 figure·difficulty ●●●·importance ★★☆

That deals with uniqueness. What about existence?

Theorem 1.12 (Carathéodory Extension Theorem).p. 11 Let \(\Omega\) be a set and \(\A\) an algebra on \(\Omega\), and let \(\F=\sigma(\A)\). Let \(\mu_0:\A\to[0,\infty]\) be a countably additive set function. Then there exists a measure \(\mu\) on \((\Omega,\F)\) such that \(\mu=\mu_0\) on \(\A\).

in wordsTheorem 1.12

Remark. If \(\mu_0(\Omega)<\infty\), Theorem 1.11 tells us that \(\mu\) is unique, since an algebra is certainly a π-system.

The theorem doesn't hand out measures for free. It reduces constructing a measure on a σ-algebra, where we can't even list the sets, to constructing a countably additive set function on an algebra, where we usually can. We will use it to describe every probability measure on \((\R,\B(\R))\).

intuitionouter measure as cheapest cover

The proof is not examinable, but the idea is worth having. Think of \(\mu_0\) as a price list for the sets in the algebra. To measure an arbitrary set \(B\), buy a countable collection of sets from the list that covers \(B\), as cheaply as possible. That cheapest price is the outer measure of \(B\):

\[\mu^*(B)=\inf\Big\{\sum_{j=1}^\infty\mu_0(A_j) : A_j\in\A,\ \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty A_j\supseteq B\Big\}.\]

Every set gets an outer measure, but outer measure is not additive on all sets (Vitali's set again). So call \(B\) measurable if it splits every set \(E\) cleanly, \(\mu^*(E)=\mu^*(E\cap B)+\mu^*(E\cap B^c)\). (If \(\mu_0(\Omega)\) is finite, one can instead call \(B\) measurable if \(\mu^*(B)+\mu^*(B^c)=\mu_0(\Omega)\): \(B\) and its complement can both be covered efficiently.) One then checks that the measurable sets form a σ-algebra containing \(\A\), and that \(\mu^*\) restricted to them is countably additive and agrees with \(\mu_0\) on \(\A\). For details see Appendix A.1 of Williams, or Varadhan.

The infimum runs over countable covers, and that one word does a lot of work.

carefulcountable covers are subtle

Watch the red part as the number of intervals grows. Each rational is eventually covered, yet the uncovered length never drops below \(1-\eps\). In the limit the red part is a closed set of positive length that contains no rational at all.Covering by finitely many intervals is the older idea of Jordan content. Under it \(\Q\cap[0,1]\) has outer content 1 and inner content 0, so it has no content at all. Lebesgue’s move to countable covers is what repairs this.

Corollary 1.13.p. 11 There exists a unique Borel measure \(\mu\) on \(\R\) such that for all \(a,b\in\R\) with \(a<b\), \(\mu((a,b])=b-a\). The measure \(\mu\) is the Lebesgue measure on \(\B(\R)\).

✎Now try question B5 of Problem Sheet 1.
roadmapwhere the hard part is done

The proof is an exercise. The hard part is checking countable additivity on a suitable algebra, and the proof of Theorem 1.15 below does exactly this in a closely related case (take \(F(x)=x\) there, ignoring that it isn't bounded). Uniqueness needs an extra step since \(\mu(\R)=\infty\): for each \(n\) the restriction \(\mu_n(A)=\mu(A\cap(-n,n])\) is a finite measure, two candidates' restrictions agree on intervals and hence everywhere by Theorem 1.11, and \(\mu(A)=\lim_n\mu_n(A)\) by Lemma 1.4.

From Part A · Null sets, and the Lebesgue σ-algebra

A set \(N\) with \(\mu(N)=0\) is a null set (for \(\mu\)). Countable sets are Lebesgue-null: cover the \(j\)-th point by an interval of length \(\eps/2^j\), as in Figure 1.7. Null sets are everywhere in what follows, because the integral can't see them (Chapter 2).

In Part A Integration, Lebesgue measure was defined on a σ-algebra \(\M_{\mathrm{Leb}}\) of "Lebesgue measurable sets", built with the outer measure above, which contains \(\B(\R)\) but is strictly larger. It turns out (exercise) that \(\M_{\mathrm{Leb}}\) consists of all sets that differ from a Borel set by a subset of a null set.

asidewhy Borel, not Lebesgue sets

Remark. In this course we work with \(\B(\R)\) rather than \(\M_{\mathrm{Leb}}\). The Borel σ-algebra is large enough for us, and its definition doesn't depend on a measure, whereas which sets are null does.Most Lebesgue measurable sets are not Borel. There are only as many Borel sets as real numbers. But the Cantor set (see below) is null and has as many points as \(\R\), so every one of its subsets is null, hence Lebesgue measurable, and there are strictly more of those than there are real numbers. (This changes later, when studying continuous-time martingales.)

Measures on the line are increasing functionsp. 12

≈ 16 min·2 results, 3 figures·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★★

In discrete measure theory there was a one-to-one correspondence between measures and mass functions. Is there something similar for Borel measures on \(\R\), that is, measures on \((\R,\B(\R))\)?

Definition 1.14.p. 12 Let \(\mu\) be a Borel probability measure on \(\R\). The distribution function of \(\mu\) is the function \(F:\R\to\R\) defined by \(F(x)=\mu((-\infty,x])\).

in wordsDefinition 1.14

This is the cumulative distribution function from Prelims, now defined for any probability measure on \(\R\). Any distribution function \(F\) has the following properties:

  1. \(F\) is (weakly) increasing: \(x<y\) implies \(F(x)\le F(y)\);
  2. \(F(x)\to0\) as \(x\to-\infty\) and \(F(x)\to1\) as \(x\to\infty\);
  3. \(F\) is right continuous: \(y\downarrow x\) implies \(F(y)\to F(x)\).
techniqueLemma 1.4 at work

The first holds because \(\mu\) is increasing. For the second, \((-\infty,-n]\downarrow\emptyset\) and \((-\infty,n]\uparrow\R\), so Lemma 1.4 gives \(F(-n)\to0\) and \(F(n)\to1\) (and \(F\) is monotone, so the limit along integers is the full limit). For the third, suppose that \(y_n\downarrow x\) and let \(A_n=(-\infty,y_n]\). Then \(A_n\downarrow A=(-\infty,x]\), so by Lemma 1.4, \(F(y_n)=\mu(A_n)\downarrow\mu(A)=F(x)\). We often write \(F(-\infty)=0\) and \(F(\infty)=1\) as shorthand for the second property.

Left limits behave differently. If \(y_n\uparrow x\) with every \(y_n<x\), then \((-\infty,y_n]\uparrow(-\infty,x)\), which is missing the point \(x\) itself. So the left limit \(F(x-)=\lim_{y\uparrow x}F(y)\) equals \(\mu((-\infty,x))\), and the jump \(F(x)-F(x-)\) is exactly \(\mu(\{x\})\).Some texts, notably in the Russian tradition, define \(F(x)=\PP(X<x)\) instead. That \(F\) is left continuous and pairs naturally with intervals \([a,b)\). Nothing deep changes: the filled dots in Figure 1.8 would move to the bottom of each jump.

roadmapbuilding every measure on ℝ

Using the Carathéodory Extension Theorem we can construct all Borel probability measures on \(\R\): there is one for each distribution function. Since finite measures can all be obtained from probability measures by multiplying by a constant, this describes all finite measures on \(\B(\R)\) as well.

Theorem 1.15 (Lebesgue).p. 12 Let \(F:\R\to\R\) be an increasing, right continuous function with \(F(-\infty)=0\) and \(F(\infty)=1\). Then there is a unique Borel probability measure \(\mu=\mu_F\) on \(\R\) such that \(\mu((-\infty,x])=F(x)\) for every \(x\). Every Borel probability measure \(\mu\) on \(\R\) arises in this way.

in wordsTheorem 1.15

In other words, there is a one-to-one correspondence between distribution functions and Borel probability measures on \(\R\). The measure of a half-open interval is the rise of \(F\) across it: \(\mu((a,b])=F(b)-F(a)\), since \((a,b]=(-\infty,b]\setminus(-\infty,a]\).

Proof of Theorem 1.15: uniqueness and ‘every µ arises’. Suppose for the moment that the existence statement holds.

Uniqueness. The collection

\[\pi(\R)=\{(-\infty,x]:x\in\R\}\]

is a π-system which generates \(\B(\R)\) (Example 1.10). Two probability measures with the same distribution function \(F\) agree on every ray \((-\infty,x]\), so by Theorem 1.11 they agree on all of \(\B(\R)\).

Every \(\mu\) arises. Let \(\mu\) be any Borel probability measure on \(\R\) and let \(F\) be its distribution function. Then \(F\) has the properties required in the first part of the theorem, so we obtain a measure \(\mu_F\). By uniqueness, \(\mu_F\) is the measure \(\mu\) we started with.∎

set-upan algebra of intervals

For existence we apply Theorem 1.12, so first we need a suitable algebra. For \(-\infty\le a\le b<\infty\), let \(I_{a,b}=(a,b]=\{x\in\R:a<x\le b\}\), and set \(I_{a,\infty}=(a,\infty)\). Let \(\I=\{I_{a,b}:-\infty\le a\le b\le\infty\}\) be the collection of intervals open on the left and closed on the right. Let \(\A\) be the set of finite disjoint unions of elements of \(\I\). Then \(\A\) is an algebra (the complement of a finite union of such intervals is again one, and so is the union of two), and \(\sigma(\A)=\sigma(\I)=\B(\R)\).

Define a set function \(\mu_0\) on \(\A\) by

\[\mu_0(I_{a,b})=F(b)-F(a)\]

for intervals (with \(F(\pm\infty)\) read as the limits \(1\) and \(0\)), extended to \(\A\) by adding over disjoint unions.

It is an easy exercise to show that \(\mu_0\) is well defined and finitely additive. (A set in \(\A\) can be cut into intervals in many ways, but the sums agree, because \(F(b)-F(a)=\big(F(b)-F(c)\big)+\big(F(c)-F(a)\big)\).)

Carathéodory's Extension Theorem then gives a probability measure on \(\B(\R)\) extending \(\mu_0\), provided \(\mu_0\) is countably additive on \(\A\). Proving this is slightly tricky, and right continuity has to be used at some point. Since \(\mu_0\) is finite and additive on \(\A\), Lemma 1.5 says it is countably additive if and only if

\[\mu_0(A_n)\to0\qquad\text{for every sequence }(A_n)\text{ in }\A\text{ with }A_n\downarrow\emptyset.\]

Here is what goes wrong without right continuity.

techniqueproof by compactness

Now the argument. Suppose, for a contradiction, that \(F\) has the stated properties but there exist \(A_1,A_2,\ldots\in\A\) with \(A_n\downarrow\emptyset\) and \(\mu_0(A_n)\not\to0\). Since \(\mu_0(A_n)\) is a decreasing sequence, it has a limit, and that limit is some \(\delta>0\); so \(\mu_0(A_n)\ge\delta\) for all \(n\). We look for a descending sequence of non-empty compact sets inside the \(A_n\), because the intersection of such a sequence is never empty.

Background · Compact sets, and why nested ones never vanish

In \(\R\), a set is compact if it is closed and bounded (this is the Heine–Borel theorem; it can be taken as the definition here). Finite unions of closed bounded intervals, like \([0,1]\cup[2,3]\), are compact.

Fact. If \(E_1\supseteq E_2\supseteq\cdots\) are non-empty compact sets, then \(\bigcap_nE_n\ne\emptyset\). Proof: pick \(x_n\in E_n\). All the \(x_n\) lie in the bounded set \(E_1\), so by Bolzano–Weierstrass some subsequence converges, say to \(x\). For each fixed \(m\), the terms of the subsequence from index \(m\) on lie in \(E_m\) (the sets are nested), and \(E_m\) is closed, so the limit \(x\) is in \(E_m\). This holds for every \(m\).

Both hypotheses matter. The sets \((0,\frac1n]\) are nested and non-empty but not closed, and their intersection is empty: the point \(0\) they crowd towards is never included. The sets \([n,\infty)\) are closed but not bounded, and their intersection is empty too.

intuitiontrading intervals for compact sets

The sets in \(\A\) are unions of half-open intervals, which are not compact. The proof trades them for closed, bounded ones, losing only a little mass at each step. Step through it below.

A zoo of distribution functionsp. 13

≈ 4 min·1 exercise·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★☆

The integral \(\int f\,d\mu\) against a general measure is built in Chapter 2. For this section, read \(\int_A f(x)\,dx\) as the familiar integral of \(f\) over \(A\); for continuous \(f\) and intervals \(A\) it is the Riemann integral from Prelims.

exampledensities and point masses

When \(F\) is continuously differentiable, say, it is precisely the cumulative distribution function of a continuous random variable with probability density function \(f(x)=F'(x)\), as in Prelims. More generally, if \(f\ge0\) is measurable and Lebesgue integrable with \(\int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x)\,dx=1\) (both words are defined in Chapter 2), we can use \(f\) as a density to construct a measure \(\mu\) on \((\R,\B(\R))\) by setting

\[\mu(A)=\int_Af(x)\,dx.\]

This measure has distribution function \(F(x)=\int_{-\infty}^xf(y)\,dy\). It is not necessarily true that \(F'(x)=f(x)\) for all \(x\), but it holds for almost all \(x\), meaning for all \(x\) outside a Lebesgue-null set.Changing \(f\) on a null set, for instance at the two endpoints of \([0,1]\), changes nothing about \(\mu\). So no statement about \(F'=f\) at individual points can be expected. For example, taking \(f=1\) on \((0,1)\), or on \([0,1]\), and \(f=0\) otherwise, gives \(F(x)=0\) for \(x<0\), \(F(x)=x\) for \(0\le x\le1\) and \(F(x)=1\) for \(x>1\): the uniform distribution on \([0,1]\). (In Figure 1.8: Uniform, Normal, Exponential.)

For a very different example, take a sequence of points \(x_1,x_2,\ldots\) (for example the non-negative integers) with probabilities \(p_n>0\) at these points and \(\sum_np_n=1\). The discrete probability measure and its distribution function are

\[\mu(A)=\sum_{n\,:\,x_n\in A}p_n,\qquad F(x)=\sum_{n\,:\,x_n\le x}p_n,\]

so \(F\) increases by jumps, the jump at \(x_n\) being of height \(p_n\) (Fair die, Poisson). The picture can be complicated, for example if there is a jump at every rational.

ExerciseCounting the jumps
Why can a distribution function have at most countably many jumps?
show answer

The jump at \(x\) is \(\mu(\{x\})\), and singletons are disjoint, so the jumps share a total mass of at most 1. If \(F\) had \(n\) jumps of height greater than \(\frac1n\), their total would exceed 1. So for each \(n\) there are fewer than \(n\) such jumps, and the set of all jumps is a countable union of finite sets.

carefulneither density nor jumps

There are also continuous distribution functions that don't come from any density.

Background · The Cantor set and the Devil’s staircase

Start with \([0,1]\). Remove the open middle third \((\frac13,\frac23)\), leaving two intervals of length \(\frac13\). Remove the middle third of each, leaving four of length \(\frac19\), and so on. What survives every step is the Cantor set \(C\). After \(n\) steps the remaining length is \((\frac23)^n\to0\), so \(C\) is Lebesgue-null. Yet \(C\) is uncountable: its points are exactly the numbers with a ternary expansion using only the digits 0 and 2, and swapping 2s for 1s turns these into all binary expansions of \([0,1]\).

That swap defines the Cantor function or Devil's staircase \(F\): on \(C\), read the ternary digits, replace each 2 by 1, and read the result in binary; on each removed gap, \(F\) is constant. \(F\) is continuous and increasing from \(0\) to \(1\), so by Theorem 1.15 it is the distribution function of a probability measure. That measure has no atoms (\(F\) is continuous) but no density either: \(F'=0\) on every gap, so off the null set \(C\), and a density would have to be \(0\) almost everywhere. All its mass lives on the null set \(C\), spread "uniformly" in the sense that each surviving interval at step \(n\) gets mass \(2^{-n}\).

payoffthe Devil’s staircase

So the Devil’s staircase corresponds, roughly speaking, to the uniform distribution on the Cantor set (Devil's staircase in Figure 1.8). The measures \(\mu\) described in this chapter are sometimes called Lebesgue–Stieltjes measures; we will return to them a little later.These three kinds are all there is. Every distribution function is a mixture \(\alpha F_{\mathrm{ac}}+\beta F_{\mathrm d}+\gamma F_{\mathrm{sc}}\) of an absolutely continuous one (with a density), a discrete one (pure jumps) and a singular continuous one (like the staircase): the Lebesgue decomposition. The Mixture preset has one of each.

What we now have

≈ 2 min·difficulty ●○○·importance ★★☆
  1. A measure space \((\Omega,\F,\mu)\): a σ-algebra of events, closed under countable operations, and a countably additive way of weighing them (Definition 1.3).
  2. Uniqueness needs only a π-system: finite measures with the same total mass that agree on \(\I\) agree on \(\sigma(\I)\) (Theorem 1.11).
  3. Existence needs only an algebra: a countably additive \(\mu_0\) on \(\A\) extends to \(\sigma(\A)\) (Theorem 1.12).
  4. On \(\R\) the two combine. Borel probability measures correspond exactly to increasing, right continuous \(F\) with \(F(-\infty)=0\) and \(F(\infty)=1\) (Theorem 1.15).
roadmapon to integration

With a rich supply of measures in hand, Chapter 2 builds integration against any of them, from scratch.

Chapter 2

Integration

Chapter 1 gave us measures. Here we learn to integrate against any of them, which turns probabilities into expectations, and prove the three theorems that let limits pass through integrals. The notes cite Part A for most of this; here it is built from the ground up.
