roadmapwhy build the integral from scratch

We now have a very rich class of measures to work with. Part A Integration builds a theory of integration for Lebesgue measure on \(\R\). The notes observe that the same definitions and proofs work for any measure space, and state the results. Since you haven't seen Part A, this chapter gives the construction and the key proofs in full. None of it is long, and the ideas are used constantly afterwards.

2.1Measurable functions and the definition of the integralp. 14

≈ 20 min·11 results, 1 figure, 3 exercises·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★★
motivationwhy measurable functions

To integrate a function \(f\) against \(\mu\) we will need to measure sets like \(\{\omega: f(\omega)>t\}\). So we first restrict to functions for which these sets are in \(\F\).

Definition 2.1 (Measurable function).p. 14 Let \((\Omega,\F)\) and \((\Lambda,\G)\) be measurable spaces. A function \(f:\Omega\to\Lambda\) is measurable (with respect to \(\F,\G\)) if

\[A\in\G\implies f^{-1}(A)\in\F.\]
in wordsDefinition 2.1

Here \(f^{-1}(A)=\{\omega\in\Omega:f(\omega)\in A\}\) is the preimage of \(A\), the set of points that \(f\) sends into \(A\); \(f\) need not be invertible. In probability language: \(f\) is measurable if every question "is \(f(\omega)\) in \(A\)?" (for \(A\in\G\)) is an event. This is the same idea as continuity in topology (preimages of open sets are open), with "measurable set" in place of "open set".

Usually \(\Lambda=\R\) or \(\Rbar=[-\infty,\infty]\), the extended real line. In that case we always take \(\G\) to consist of the Borel sets, \(\G=\B(\R)\) or \(\B(\Rbar)\), and omit it from the notation.\(\B(\Rbar)\) is generated by the sets \([-\infty,t]\); equivalently it consists of the sets \(B\), \(B\cup\{\infty\}\), \(B\cup\{-\infty\}\), \(B\cup\{\pm\infty\}\) with \(B\) Borel in \(\R\). On \(\Rbar\) we use the conventions \(a+\infty=\infty\) for \(a>-\infty\), \(a\cdot\infty=\infty\) for \(a>0\), and \(0\cdot\infty=0\); the expression \(\infty-\infty\) is left undefined. This contrasts with functions from \(\R\), where different σ-algebras get used in different circumstances (sometimes including \(\M_{\mathrm{Leb}}\) from Chapter 1, though not in this course).

Proposition 2.2.p. 14 A function \(f:\Omega\to\R\) or \(f:\Omega\to\Rbar\) is measurable with respect to \(\F\) (and \(\B(\R)\) or \(\B(\Rbar)\)) if and only if \(\{x : f(x)\le t\}\in\F\) for every \(t\in\R\).

Proof. (⇒) We have \(\{f\le t\}=f^{-1}((-\infty,t])\), and \((-\infty,t]\) is a Borel set.

(⇐) This uses a trick worth naming, the good sets principle. Let

\[\G=\{A\subseteq\R : f^{-1}(A)\in\F\}\]

be the collection of "good" sets. Preimages commute with every set operation:

\[f^{-1}(\emptyset)=\emptyset,\qquad f^{-1}(A^c)=f^{-1}(A)^c,\qquad f^{-1}\Big(\bigcup_nA_n\Big)=\bigcup_nf^{-1}(A_n).\]

Since \(\F\) is a σ-algebra, it follows that \(\G\) is a σ-algebra.

By hypothesis \(\G\) contains every ray \((-\infty,t]\), so it contains the σ-algebra they generate, which is \(\B(\R)\) by Example 1.10. That is exactly measurability.

For \(f:\Omega\to\Rbar\) the proof is the same, using that \(\B(\Rbar)\) is generated by \(\{[-\infty,t]:t\in\R\}\).∎

✎Now try question A2 of Problem Sheet 1.
techniquethe good-sets principle

The pattern of this proof (to show something holds for every set in \(\sigma(\C)\), show that the sets where it holds form a σ-algebra containing \(\C\)) will appear again and again. Similar arguments show that \(\{f<t\}\), \(\{f\ge t\}\) or \(\{f>t\}\) for all \(t\) would do equally well.

set-updefault conventions

Unless otherwise stated, measurable functions map to \(\R\) with the Borel σ-algebra. Thus a measurable function on \((\Omega,\F)\) means a function \(\Omega\to\R\) that is \((\F,\B(\R))\)-measurable.

intuitionfunctions generalise sets

Remark. Real-valued functions on \(\Omega\) generalise subsets of \(\Omega\) in a natural way: the subset \(A\) corresponds to its indicator function \(\ind_A\), equal to \(1\) on \(A\) and \(0\) off it. As a sanity check, \(\ind_A\) is a measurable function if and only if \(A\) is a measurable set: \(\{\ind_A\le t\}\) is \(\emptyset\), \(A^c\) or \(\Omega\) depending on \(t\).

recaplim sup for functions

Recall (see the background box on lim sup) that

\[\limsup_{n\to\infty}x_n=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sup_{m\ge n}x_m\qquad\text{and}\qquad\liminf_{n\to\infty}x_n=\lim_{n\to\infty}\inf_{m\ge n}x_m.\]

For functions these are taken pointwise: \((\limsup_nf_n)(\omega)=\limsup_nf_n(\omega)\). The following result says that measurability survives everything we will ever do to functions.

Lemma 2.3.p. 14 Let \((f_n)\) be a sequence of measurable functions on \((\Omega,\F)\) taking values in \(\Rbar\), and let \(h:\R\to\R\) be continuous. Then, whenever they make sense (for example, \(\infty-\infty\) is not defined), the following are also measurable functions on \((\Omega,\F)\):

\[f_1+f_2,\quad f_1f_2,\quad\max\{f_1,f_2\},\quad\min\{f_1,f_2\},\quad f_1/f_2,\quad h\circ f_1,\]
\[\sup_nf_n,\quad\inf_nf_n,\quad\limsup_{n\to\infty}f_n,\quad\liminf_{n\to\infty}f_n.\]

Proof sketch (from Part A). By Proposition 2.2 (and the remark after it) we just need to check that suitable level sets are events.

Suprema and infima. Both are countable set operations on level sets:

\[\Big\{\sup_nf_n\le t\Big\}=\bigcap_n\{f_n\le t\},\qquad\Big\{\inf_nf_n<t\Big\}=\bigcup_n\{f_n<t\}.\]

Then lim sup and lim inf are built from these:

\[\limsup_nf_n=\inf_n\Big(\sup_{m\ge n}f_m\Big),\qquad\liminf_nf_n=\sup_n\Big(\inf_{m\ge n}f_m\Big).\]

Sums. We have \(f_1(\omega)+f_2(\omega)>t\) exactly when there is a rational \(q\) with \(f_1(\omega)>q\) and \(f_2(\omega)>t-q\). So

\[\{f_1+f_2>t\}=\bigcup_{q\in\Q}\big(\{f_1>q\}\cap\{f_2>t-q\}\big),\]

a countable union. (Using rationals is what keeps it countable.)

Continuous functions. If \(U\subseteq\R\) is open then \(h^{-1}(U)\) is open, by continuity, so it is Borel, and

\[(h\circ f)^{-1}(U)=f^{-1}(h^{-1}(U))\in\F.\]

The open sets generate \(\B(\R)\), so the good sets principle finishes the job.

The rest follow from these, with some care about infinite values. For example, using \(h(x)=x^2\),

\[f_1f_2=\tfrac14\big((f_1+f_2)^2-(f_1-f_2)^2\big),\qquad\max\{f_1,f_2\}=\tfrac12\big(f_1+f_2+|f_1-f_2|\big).\]
∎
roadmapthree steps to the integral

Let \((\Omega,\F,\mu)\) be a measure space. Given a measurable function \(f:\Omega\to\Rbar\), we want to define, where possible, the integral of \(f\) with respect to \(\mu\). There are many notations:

\[\int f\,d\mu=\int_\Omega f\,d\mu=\mu(f)=\int_{x\in\Omega}f(x)\,d\mu(x)=\int f(x)\,\mu(dx).\]

The dummy variable (here \(x\)) is needed when, for example, \(f(x,y)\) has two variables and we integrate \(x\mapsto f(x,y)\) with \(y\) fixed.

The plan has three steps: first functions taking finitely many values, then non-negative functions by approximation from below, then general functions by splitting into positive and negative parts.

Definition 2.4.p. 15 A simple function \(\varphi\) on a measure space \((\Omega,\F,\mu)\) is a function \(\varphi:\Omega\to\R\) that may be written as a finite sum

\[\varphi=\sum_{k=1}^na_k\ind_{E_k}\](6)

where each \(E_k\in\F\) and each \(a_k\in\R\). The canonical form of \(\varphi\) is the unique decomposition as in (6) where the numbers \(a_k\) are distinct and non-zero and the sets \(E_k\) are disjoint and non-empty.

in wordsDefinition 2.4

A simple function is a measurable function that takes only finitely many values; its canonical form lists the non-zero values \(a_k\) and the sets \(E_k=\{\varphi=a_k\}\) where they are taken. For example, \(3\ind_{[0,2]}+\ind_{[1,3]}\) on \(\R\) is simple, with canonical form \(3\ind_{[0,1)}+4\ind_{[1,2]}+\ind_{(2,3]}\).

The following definitions were given in Part A for Lebesgue measure, and extend with no change to a general measure space.

Definition 2.5.p. 15 If \(\varphi\) is a non-negative simple function with canonical form (6), then we define the integral of \(\varphi\) with respect to \(\mu\) as

\[\int\varphi\,d\mu=\sum_{k=1}^na_k\,\mu(E_k).\]
intuitionheight times base

This is "height times base" summed over the steps, with \(\mu\) measuring the bases. The formula also applies (exercise) whenever \(\varphi\) is written as in (6), even if not in canonical form, as long as we avoid \(\infty-\infty\), for example by taking all \(a_k\ge0\). In the example above, with \(\lambda\) Lebesgue measure,

\[3\cdot\lambda([0,2])+1\cdot\lambda([1,3])=8=3\cdot1+4\cdot1+1\cdot1.\]

Definition 2.6.p. 15 For a non-negative measurable function \(f\) on \((\Omega,\F,\mu)\) we define the integral

\[\int f\,d\mu=\sup\Big\{\int\varphi\,d\mu : \varphi\text{ simple},\ 0\le\varphi\le f\Big\}.\]

Note that the supremum may be equal to \(+\infty\).

in wordsDefinition 2.6

So the integral of \(f\ge0\) is the best lower estimate by staircases. Two immediate consequences: if \(0\le f\le g\) then \(\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu\) (every staircase under \(f\) is under \(g\)), and for simple \(f\) Definition 2.6 agrees with Definition 2.5.

intuitionchop the range, not the domain

The essential difference from the Riemann integral is which axis is chopped up. Riemann cuts the domain into intervals and asks how high \(f\) is on each. Lebesgue cuts the range into levels and asks how big (in \(\mu\)-measure) the set where \(f\) lies between two levels is. That set can be scattered all over the place, which is no problem for a measure but would be fatal for Riemann. The standard staircases are

\[\varphi_n=\min\Big(n,\ 2^{-n}\big\lfloor2^nf\big\rfloor\Big),\]

which round \(f\) down to the grid of multiples of \(2^{-n}\), capped at height \(n\).

ExerciseStaircases
Show that the staircases \(\varphi_n\) are simple, increase with \(n\), and converge to \(f\) pointwise.
show answer

Simple. \(\varphi_n\) takes only the values \(k2^{-n}\) for \(0\le k\le n2^n\), on the sets

\[\{k2^{-n}\le f<(k+1)2^{-n}\}\qquad\text{(and }\{f\ge n\}\text{ for the top value)},\]

which are in \(\F\) because \(f\) is measurable. So \(\varphi_n\) is simple.

Increasing. Passing from \(n\) to \(n+1\) halves the grid spacing and raises the cap. Rounding down to a finer grid can only give a larger or equal value, so \(\varphi_n\le\varphi_{n+1}\).

Converging. If \(f(\omega)<\infty\), then once \(n>f(\omega)\) we have

\[0\le f(\omega)-\varphi_n(\omega)<2^{-n}.\]

If \(f(\omega)=\infty\), then \(\varphi_n(\omega)=n\to\infty\). Either way \(\varphi_n(\omega)\uparrow f(\omega)\).

connectionstaircases + MCT, used everywhere

The fact that every measurable \(f\ge0\) is an increasing limit of simple functions is the workhorse of the theory. Combined with the Monotone Convergence Theorem below it shows that \(\int f\,d\mu=\lim_n\int\varphi_n\,d\mu\): you can compute the integral along any increasing sequence of staircases, not just by taking a supremum.

Definition 2.7.p. 15 We say that a measurable function \(f\) on \((\Omega,\F,\mu)\) is integrable if \(\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty\). If \(f\) is integrable, its integral is defined to be

\[\int f\,d\mu=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu,\]

where \(f^+=\max(f,0)\) and \(f^-=\max(-f,0)\) are the positive and negative parts of \(f\).

in wordsDefinition 2.7

Note that \(f=f^+-f^-\) and \(|f|=f^++f^-\), and both parts are non-negative and measurable (Lemma 2.3), so their integrals are defined by Definition 2.6. A very important point: if \(f\) is measurable, then \(\int f\,d\mu\) is defined either if \(f\) is non-negative (when \(\infty\) is a possible value) or if \(f\) is integrable (when it is a finite number). For other \(f\) we would risk \(\infty-\infty\) and leave it undefined.

There are other possible sequences of steps to defining the integral, giving the same result. The integral has the basic properties you would expect. For example, if \(f\) and \(g\) are measurable functions on \((\Omega,\F,\mu)\) that are either both non-negative or both integrable, and \(c\in\R\) (with \(c\ge0\) in the non-negative case), then

\[\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu,\qquad\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu.\]
Proof sketchLinearity
Why is the integral linear?
show answer

For simple functions it is bookkeeping: write \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) over a common partition of \(\Omega\) into finitely many sets, on each of which both are constant. For \(f,g\ge0\), take simple \(\varphi_n\uparrow f\) and \(\psi_n\uparrow g\); then \(\varphi_n+\psi_n\) are simple and increase to \(f+g\), so the Monotone Convergence Theorem (Theorem 2.13) applied three times gives

\[\int(f+g)=\lim\int(\varphi_n+\psi_n)=\lim\int\varphi_n+\lim\int\psi_n=\int f+\int g.\]

For integrable \(f,g\), put \(h=f+g\). From \(h^+-h^-=f^+-f^-+g^+-g^-\) we get \(h^++f^-+g^-=h^-+f^++g^+\), all terms non-negative; integrate both sides using the non-negative case, then rearrange (everything is finite).

set-upintegrating over a set

We have defined integrals only over the whole space, and that is all we need. If \(f\) is a measurable function on \((\Omega,\F,\mu)\) and \(A\in\F\), then we define

\[\int_Af\,d\mu=\int f\ind_A\,d\mu,\]

that is, we integrate (over the whole space) the function that agrees with \(f\) on \(A\) and is \(0\) outside \(A\).

What the integral looks like for familiar measures

exampleLebesgue and discrete measures

If \(\mu\) is Lebesgue measure on \((\R,\B(\R))\), we have just defined the Lebesgue integral, as in Part A. For a nice function on an interval, say continuous on \([a,b]\), it agrees with the Riemann integral, so all the integrals you know how to compute still give the same answers.

For a very different example, suppose that \(\mu\) is a discrete measure with mass \(p_i\) at the point \(x_i\), for a finite or countably infinite sequence \(x_1,x_2,\dots\) Then

\[\int f\,d\mu=\sum_if(x_i)\,p_i\]

whenever \(f\ge0\) (where \(+\infty\) is allowed as the answer) or the sum converges absolutely. So sums are integrals too, with respect to a discrete measure. For another example, suppose that \(\mu\) has distribution function \(F(x)=\int_{-\infty}^xg(y)\,dy\), a density \(g\) as in Chapter 1. Then

\[\int f\,d\mu=\int f(x)g(x)\,dx,\]

where the second integral is with respect to Lebesgue measure.

techniquethe standard machine

In proving statements like these it helps to work in four stages: first \(f=\ind_E\), then simple \(f\) (by linearity), then non-negative measurable \(f\) (by approximating with simple \(f_n\uparrow f\) and the Monotone Convergence Theorem), and finally general \(f\) (by splitting into \(f^+\) and \(f^-\)). This is sometimes called the standard machine. For the discrete example: for \(f=\ind_E\) both sides are \(\mu(E)=\sum_{x_i\in E}p_i\), and the machine does the rest.

Remark 2.8.p. 16 For \(f\ge0\), \(\int f\,d\mu\) is determined by the numbers \(\mu(\{x:f(x)\ge t\})\) for \(t\ge0\) (exercise). Hence, for general \(f\), \(\int f\,d\mu\) is determined by the numbers

\[\mu(\{x:f(x)\ge t\})\text{ for }t\ge0\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mu(\{x:f(x)\le t\})\text{ for }t\le0.\]

Since \(\{x:f(x)\ge t\}\) is the complement of the union of the sets \(\{x:f(x)\le s\}\), \(s<t\), on a probability space \(\int f\,d\mu\) is determined by the numbers \(\mu(\{x:f(x)\le t\})\), \(t\in\R\).

This holds even across probability spaces: if \(f_i\) is a measurable function on the probability space \((\Omega_i,\F_i,\mu_i)\) for \(i=1,2\) and

\[\mu_1(\{f_1\le t\})=\mu_2(\{f_2\le t\})\qquad\text{for every }t\in\R,\]

then \(\int f_1\,d\mu_1=\int f_2\,d\mu_2\), or both are undefined.

in wordsRemark 2.8

Why: the staircase \(\varphi_n\) for \(f\ge0\) has integral

\[\int\varphi_n\,d\mu=\sum_k k2^{-n}\mu\big(k2^{-n}\le f<(k+1)2^{-n}\big)+n\,\mu(f\ge n),\]

and each of these measures is a difference of numbers \(\mu(f\ge t)\). Then \(\int f\,d\mu=\lim_n\int\varphi_n\,d\mu\). In probability language: the expectation of a random variable depends only on its distribution, which is what lets us compute expectations from distribution functions.

Definition 2.9 (µ-almost everywhere).p. 16 Let \((\Omega,\F,\mu)\) be a measure space. We say that a property holds µ-almost everywhere, or µ-a.e., if it holds except on a set of µ-measure zero. If \(\mu\) is a probability measure, we often say almost surely or a.s. instead. Thus an event \(A\) holds almost surely if \(\PP[A]=1\). This does not imply that \(A=\Omega\).

examplewhat almost sure means

For example, a uniformly random point of \([0,1]\) is irrational almost surely, even though rational points exist. An important property of integration is that

\[f=g\ \ \mu\text{-a.e.}\implies\int f\,d\mu=\int g\,d\mu.\]

(For \(f\ge0\) and a null set \(N\): any simple \(\varphi\le f\ind_N\) has \(\int\varphi\,d\mu=\sum_ka_k\mu(E_k\cap N)=0\), so \(\int f\ind_N\,d\mu=0\), and therefore \(\int f\,d\mu=\int f\ind_{N^c}\,d\mu\); the rest follows by splitting into positive and negative parts.) Generally speaking, we don't care what happens on sets of measure zero. It is vital to remember that notions of almost everywhere depend on the underlying measure \(\mu\).

The measurable functions that interest us most are random variables.

Definition 2.10 (Random variable).p. 16 In the special case when \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\) is a probability space, we call a measurable function \(X:\Omega\to\R\) a (real-valued) random variable. Sometimes we consider \(X:\Omega\to\Rbar\) instead.

intuitionrandom variables as observations

As in Prelims, think of \(\Omega\) as the set of possible outcomes of an experiment, and of \(X\) as something you observe or measure. Measurability says that "\(X\le t\)" is an event, so it has a probability. What is the integral of \(X\)?

Definition 2.11 (Expectation).p. 16 The expectation of a random variable \(X\) defined on \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\) is

\[\E[X]=\int X\,d\PP=\int_\Omega X(\omega)\,d\PP(\omega).\]
✎Now try question B3 of Problem Sheet 2. It needs Lebesgue measure from Chapter 1 and random variables from this section.
connectionexpectation and the law of X

It is defined when \(X\ge0\), or when \(\E|X|<\infty\), in which case we say \(X\) is integrable. A random variable \(X\) induces a probability measure \(\mu_X\) on \(\R\), its law or distribution, via

\[\mu_X(A)=\PP[X^{-1}(A)]=\PP[X\in A]\qquad\text{for }A\in\B(\R).\]

(It is countably additive because preimages of disjoint sets are disjoint.) In particular \(F_X(x)=\mu_X((-\infty,x])\) is the distribution function of \(X\), in the sense of Definition 1.14. Since \(\{(-\infty,x]:x\in\R\}\) is a π-system, the distribution function uniquely determines \(\mu_X\) (Theorem 1.11). From Remark 2.8,

\[\E[X]=\int_\Omega X(\omega)\,d\PP(\omega)=\int_\R x\,d\mu_X(x).\]

More generally \(\E[g(X)]=\int_\R g(x)\,d\mu_X(x)\) for measurable \(g\ge0\) (by the standard machine: for \(g=\ind_A\) both sides are \(\PP(X\in A)\)). With the two examples above, this gives back the Prelims formulas \(\E[g(X)]=\sum_xg(x)\PP(X=x)\) and \(\E[g(X)]=\int g(x)f_X(x)\,dx\). Very often in applications we suppress the sample space \(\Omega\) and work directly with \(\mu_X\).

ExerciseThe function Riemann couldn’t integrate
Let \(\lambda\) be Lebesgue measure on \([0,1]\) and \(f=\ind_{\Q\cap[0,1]}\), which is 1 on rationals and 0 elsewhere. What is \(\int f\,d\lambda\)?
show answer

\(f\) is the indicator of the set \(A=\Q\cap[0,1]\), so it is simple and \(\int f\,d\lambda=\lambda(A)\). Each single point has measure zero, because \(\{x\}\subseteq(x-\eps,x]\) and \(\lambda((x-\eps,x])=\eps\) for every \(\eps>0\). \(A\) is countable, so countable additivity gives \(\lambda(A)=\sum_{q\in A}\lambda(\{q\})=0\). So the integral is \(0\). Riemann's approach fails here because every interval, however short, contains both rationals and irrationals, so upper sums are always 1 and lower sums always 0. Lebesgue's integral never chops up the \(x\)-axis, so it doesn't care.

2.2The Convergence Theoremsp. 17

≈ 8 min·4 results, 1 figure·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★★
the questioncan limits pass through integrals?

The central question of this section: if \(f_n\to f\), does \(\int f_n\,d\mu\to\int f\,d\mu\)? Not always. Here is the basic failure, which you have already seen as equation (5) in Chapter 0: on \([0,1]\) with Lebesgue measure, \(f_n=n\ind_{(0,1/n)}\) tends to 0 at every point, yet \(\int f_n=1\) for every \(n\). The mass doesn't disappear; it concentrates into a spike of width \(\frac1n\) and height \(n\), and in the limit it falls through the cracks. The three theorems below say exactly when this can and can't happen. The notes cite Part A for the proofs; here they are.

Theorem 2.13 (Monotone Convergence Theorem).p. 17 Let \((f_n)\) be a sequence of non-negative measurable functions on \((\Omega,\F,\mu)\). Then

\[f_n\uparrow f\implies\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.\]
in wordsTheorem 2.13

Note that we are not excluding \(\int f\,d\mu=\infty\). Also, we could just as well write \(f_n\uparrow f\) µ-almost everywhere. (The notes state Fatou's Lemma first; we prove MCT first because Fatou's proof uses it.)

Proof of Theorem 2.13. The easy inequality. The limit \(f=\sup_nf_n\) is measurable by Lemma 2.3. Since \(f_n\le f_{n+1}\le f\), monotonicity of the integral gives

\[\int f_n\le\int f_{n+1}\le\int f,\]

so \(\ell=\lim_n\int f_n\) exists and \(\ell\le\int f\).

The reverse inequality. Fix a simple function \(\varphi=\sum_ka_k\ind_{E_k}\) (in canonical form, with \(a_k>0\)) with \(0\le\varphi\le f\), and fix a number \(c\in(0,1)\). The idea is to wait until \(f_n\) has caught up with a slightly shrunk copy \(c\varphi\) of \(\varphi\). Let

\[A_n=\{f_n\ge c\varphi\}\in\F.\]

These sets increase with \(n\), and their union is \(\Omega\):

  • where \(\varphi=0\), every \(A_n\) contains the point;
  • where \(\varphi>0\), we have \(f\ge\varphi>c\varphi\), so \(f_n\ge c\varphi\) for large \(n\).

Now \(f_n\ge c\varphi\ind_{A_n}\), which is simple, so

\[\int f_n\,d\mu\ge c\sum_ka_k\,\mu(E_k\cap A_n).\]

As \(n\to\infty\), \(E_k\cap A_n\uparrow E_k\), so \(\mu(E_k\cap A_n)\uparrow\mu(E_k)\) by Lemma 1.4. Hence

\[\ell\ge c\int\varphi\,d\mu.\]

Finally let \(c\uparrow1\), then take the supremum over all such \(\varphi\). By Definition 2.6 this gives \(\ell\ge\int f\,d\mu\).∎

techniquethe factor c < 1

The factor \(c<1\) is a small trick: we can't expect \(f_n\ge\varphi\) eventually (e.g. if \(f_n\uparrow f=\varphi\) strictly from below), but we can expect \(f_n\ge c\varphi\). Equivalently, considering partial sums, the Monotone Convergence Theorem says that for any sequence \((f_n)\) of non-negative measurable functions,

\[\int\sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n\,d\mu=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\int f_n\,d\mu.\]

Non-negative series can always be integrated term by term.

Theorem 2.12 (Fatou’s Lemma).p. 17 Let \((f_n)\) be a sequence of non-negative measurable functions on \((\Omega,\F,\mu)\). Then

\[\int\liminf_{n\to\infty}f_n\,d\mu\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int f_n\,d\mu.\]

Proof. Let

\[g_n=\inf_{m\ge n}f_m.\]

Then \(g_n\ge0\) is measurable, and \(g_n\uparrow\liminf_mf_m\) by the definition of lim inf.

For every \(m\ge n\) we have \(g_n\le f_m\), so \(\int g_n\le\int f_m\). Taking the infimum over \(m\ge n\),

\[\int g_n\le\inf_{m\ge n}\int f_m.\]

Now let \(n\to\infty\). The left side tends to \(\int\liminf f_n\) by the Monotone Convergence Theorem, and the right side tends to \(\liminf\int f_n\).∎

in wordsTheorem 2.12

Fatou's Lemma says mass can be lost in the limit but never created. The spike \(n\ind_{(0,1/n)}\) shows the inequality can be strict: \(0<1\).

set-uppointwise convergence

Recall that \((f_n)\) converges pointwise to \(f\) if, for every \(x\in\Omega\), \(f_n(x)\to f(x)\) as \(n\to\infty\).

Theorem 2.14 (Dominated Convergence Theorem).p. 17 Let \((f_n)\) be a sequence of measurable functions on \((\Omega,\F,\mu)\) with \(f_n\to f\) pointwise. Suppose that for some integrable function \(g\), \(|f_n|\le g\) for all \(n\). Then \(f\) is integrable and

\[\int f_n\,d\mu\to\int f\,d\mu\quad\text{as }n\to\infty.\]

Proof. Letting \(n\to\infty\) in \(|f_n|\le g\) gives \(|f|\le g\), so \(f\) is integrable.

From below. Now \(g+f_n\ge0\) and \(g+f_n\to g+f\), so Fatou's Lemma gives

\[\int(g+f)\le\liminf_n\int(g+f_n)=\int g+\liminf_n\int f_n.\]

Since \(\int g<\infty\) we can subtract it from both sides:

\[\int f\le\liminf_n\int f_n.\]

From above. Applying the same argument to \(g-f_n\ge0\) gives

\[-\int f\le\liminf_n\Big(-\int f_n\Big)=-\limsup_n\int f_n.\]

Together,

\[\limsup_n\int f_n\le\int f\le\liminf_n\int f_n,\]

so the limit exists and equals \(\int f\).∎

✎Now try questions A1, A4, B2 of Problem Sheet 2.
in wordsTheorem 2.14

Again, convergence almost everywhere is enough. The dominating function \(g\) is a fixed integrable roof that every \(f_n\) fits under. It rules out the escaping spike: any roof over all the spikes \(n\ind_{(0,1/n)}\) must be at least about \(1/x\) near \(0\), which is not integrable.

We will also use the following less standard result.

Lemma 2.15 (Reverse Fatou Lemma).p. 17 Let \((f_n)\) be a sequence of non-negative, measurable functions. Assume that there exists an integrable function \(g\) such that \(f_n\le g\) for all \(n\). Then

\[\int\limsup_{n\to\infty}f_n\,d\mu\ge\limsup_{n\to\infty}\int f_n\,d\mu.\]

Proof. Apply Fatou to \(h_n=g-f_n\ge0\):

\[\int\liminf_n(g-f_n)\le\liminf_n\int(g-f_n),\]

that is,

\[\int g-\int\limsup_nf_n\le\int g-\limsup_n\int f_n.\]

Now cancel \(\int g\), which is allowed because \(\int g\,d\mu<\infty\).∎

2.3Product Spaces and Independencep. 18

≈ 25 min·17 results, 2 figures, 1 exercise·difficulty ●●●·importance ★★★
the questionwhat is independence, measure-theoretically?

Independence is about two experiments that don't influence each other, and the natural model for that is a product: the outcome of the joint experiment is a pair \((\omega_1,\omega_2)\), and probabilities of "box-shaped" events multiply.

Definition 2.16 (Product σ-algebras).p. 18 Given two sets \(\Omega_1\) and \(\Omega_2\), the Cartesian product \(\Omega=\Omega_1\times\Omega_2\) is the set of pairs \((\omega_1,\omega_2)\) with \(\omega_1\in\Omega_1\) and \(\omega_2\in\Omega_2\).

If \(\F_i\) is a σ-algebra on \(\Omega_i\), then a measurable rectangle in \(\Omega=\Omega_1\times\Omega_2\) is a set of the form \(A_1\times A_2\) with \(A_1\in\F_1\) and \(A_2\in\F_2\). The product σ-algebra \(\F=\F_1\times\F_2\) is the σ-algebra on \(\Omega\) generated by the set of all measurable rectangles. (Note that \(\F\) is not the Cartesian product of \(\F_1\) and \(\F_2\).)

examplerectangles can be scattered

The "rectangles" can be very scattered: \(A_1\) and \(A_2\) are any measurable sets. A disc in \(\R^2\) is not a rectangle, but it is in \(\B(\R)\times\B(\R)\), as a countable union of small squares (in fact \(\B(\R)\times\B(\R)=\B(\R^2)\)).

roadmapproduct measure: uniqueness first

Given two probability measures \(\PP_1\) and \(\PP_2\) on \((\Omega_1,\F_1)\) and \((\Omega_2,\F_2)\) respectively, we'd like to define a probability measure on \((\Omega,\F)\) by setting

\[\PP[A_1\times A_2]=\PP_1[A_1]\,\PP_2[A_2]\](7)

for each measurable rectangle and extending it to the whole of \(\F\). Note that the set \(\I\) of measurable rectangles is a π-system, since

\[(A_1\times A_2)\cap(B_1\times B_2)=(A_1\cap B_1)\times(A_2\cap B_2),\]

and, by definition, \(\sigma(\I)=\F\). So if such a probability measure on \((\Omega,\F)\) exists, it is unique by Theorem 1.11.

set-upan algebra of rectangles

For existence, first extend \(\PP\) to the algebra \(\A\) consisting of all finite disjoint unions of measurable rectangles, by setting

\[\PP[R_1\cup\dots\cup R_n]=\sum_{i=1}^n\PP[R_i]\](8)

when \(R_1,\dots,R_n\in\I\) are disjoint. It is a tedious but straightforward exercise to check that this is well defined, that is, independent of how a set is cut into rectangles. (It also follows from the proof of the next lemma.) To extend \(\PP\) to the whole of \(\F=\sigma(\A)\) by Carathéodory's Extension Theorem, we need to check that \(\PP\) defined by (7) and (8) is countably additive on \(\A\).

Lemma 2.17.p. 18 The set function \(\PP\) defined on \(\A\) through (7) and (8) is countably additive on \(\A\).

Proof. Measure as an integral of slices. For any \(A\in\A\) and \(\omega_2\in\Omega_2\), define the section

\[A_{\omega_2}=\{\omega_1:(\omega_1,\omega_2)\in A\}\subseteq\Omega_1,\]

the horizontal slice of \(A\) at height \(\omega_2\). Let \(f(\omega_2)=\PP_1[A_{\omega_2}]\), the size of that slice. Then \(f\) is a simple function on \(\Omega_2\) (consider first the case \(A=A_1\times A_2\), where \(f=\PP_1[A_1]\ind_{A_2}\)), and

\[\PP[A]=\int f(\omega_2)\,d\PP_2.\]

This is "area = integral of slice lengths", Cavalieri's principle. Check it on a rectangle:

\[\int\PP_1[A_1]\ind_{A_2}\,d\PP_2=\PP_1[A_1]\PP_2[A_2].\]

Countable additivity. Now let \(A_n\in\A\) be disjoint sets with union \(A\in\A\). Let \(A_{n,\omega_2}=\{\omega_1:(\omega_1,\omega_2)\in A_n\}\) and \(f_n(\omega_2)=\PP_1[A_{n,\omega_2}]\), so (as above) \(\PP[A_n]=\int f_n\,d\PP_2\).

For each \(\omega_2\in\Omega_2\), the slices \(A_{n,\omega_2}\) are disjoint, with union \(A_{\omega_2}\). Hence, since \(\PP_1\) is a measure,

\[\PP_1[A_{\omega_2}]=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\PP_1[A_{n,\omega_2}],\qquad\text{that is,}\qquad f=\sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n.\]

Since the \(f_n\) are non-negative, the Monotone Convergence Theorem (applied on \((\Omega_2,\F_2,\PP_2)\)) gives

\[\PP[A]=\int f\,d\PP_2=\sum_n\int f_n\,d\PP_2=\sum_n\PP[A_n].\]

Extension. By Carathéodory's Extension Theorem (Theorem 1.12) and Theorem 1.11, \(\PP\) extends uniquely to a probability measure on \(\sigma(\A)=\F\).∎

✎Now try questions A2, A3 of Problem Sheet 2.

Definition 2.18 (Product measure).p. 18 The measure \(\PP\) defined through (7) is called the product measure on \((\Omega,\F)\), and denoted \(\PP_1\times\PP_2\). The probability space \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\) is the product probability space \((\Omega_1\times\Omega_2,\F_1\times\F_2,\PP_1\times\PP_2)\).

connectionfinitely many factors

The definitions extend easily to the product \(\F_1\times\dots\times\F_k\) of \(k\) σ-algebras, and the product \(\PP_1\times\dots\times\PP_k\) of \(k\) probability measures. These product operations behave as you expect: for example, \((\PP_1\times\PP_2)\times\PP_3=\PP_1\times\PP_2\times\PP_3\). (It is not true in general that \(\PP_1\times\PP_2=\PP_2\times\PP_1\): if \(\Omega_1\ne\Omega_2\) these measures aren't even defined on the same space.)

Definition 2.19.p. 19 Let \((\Omega_i,\F_i)_{i\ge1}\) be a sequence of measurable spaces. The product σ-algebra \(\F=\prod_{i=1}^\infty\F_i\) on \(\Omega=\prod_{i=1}^\infty\Omega_i\) is the σ-algebra generated by all sets of the form

\[\prod_{i=1}^nA_i\times\prod_{i=n+1}^\infty\Omega_i,\qquad A_i\in\F_i,\]

i.e., by all finite-dimensional measurable rectangles.

intuitionpoints as infinite sequences

A point of \(\prod_i\Omega_i\) is an infinite sequence \((\omega_1,\omega_2,\dots)\), for example the outcomes of infinitely many coin tosses. The generating sets constrain only finitely many coordinates: "the first toss is heads and the third is tails".

Remark 2.20 (Countable products of probability measures).p. 19 Given a sequence of probability spaces, one can define a product probability measure on the product σ-algebra with the expected properties. One way to do this is to apply Theorem 1.12 directly as in the proof of Lemma 2.17, but the condition is quite tricky to verify. It also follows by taking a suitable ‘limit’ of finite products using the Kolmogorov Consistency Theorem.The Kolmogorov Consistency (or Extension) Theorem says: if you specify, for every \(n\), a probability measure for the first \(n\) coordinates, and these specifications are consistent (forgetting the \(n\)-th coordinate of the \(n\)-dimensional one gives the \((n-1)\)-dimensional one), then there is a measure on infinite sequences with all of them as its finite-dimensional pieces. It needs some regularity, which \(\R\) has. An alternative approach for Borel measures on \(\R\) is outlined on the problem sheets.

payoffindependent sequences exist

This is what makes "let \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) be independent coin tosses" a legitimate sentence. The most familiar example of a product measure is Lebesgue measure on \(\R^2\) (area), or more generally on \(\R^d\), built the same way.

motivationwhy Fubini–Tonelli

Our integration theory was valid for any measure space. But as you know from \(\R^2\), to calculate the integral of a function of two variables it is convenient to proceed in stages and calculate a repeated integral: if \(f\) is integrable with respect to Lebesgue measure on \(\R^2\), then

\[\int_{\R^2}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy=\int\Big(\int f(x,y)\,dx\Big)dy=\int\Big(\int f(x,y)\,dy\Big)dx.\]

This result (Fubini's Theorem) applies just as well to the product of general probability measures.

Integrating one coordinate at a time

Theorem 2.21 (Fubini + Tonelli).p. 19 Let \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\) be the product of the probability spaces \((\Omega_i,\F_i,\PP_i)\), \(i=1,2\), and let \(f(\omega)=f(\omega_1,\omega_2)\) be a bounded, measurable function on \((\Omega,\F)\). The functions

\[x\mapsto\int_{\Omega_2}f(x,y)\,d\PP_2(y),\qquad y\mapsto\int_{\Omega_1}f(x,y)\,d\PP_1(x)\]

are \(\F_1\)-, \(\F_2\)-measurable respectively. Suppose either (i) that \(f\) is integrable on \(\Omega\) or (ii) that \(f\ge0\). Then

\[\begin{aligned}\int_\Omega f\,d\PP&=\int_{\Omega_2}\Big(\int_{\Omega_1}f(x,y)\,d\PP_1(x)\Big)d\PP_2(y)\\&=\int_{\Omega_1}\Big(\int_{\Omega_2}f(x,y)\,d\PP_2(y)\Big)d\PP_1(x),\end{aligned}\]

where in case (ii) the common value may be \(\infty\).

techniquethe standard machine again

Case (ii) is usually called Tonelli's theorem and case (i) Fubini's. The proof is the standard machine: for \(f=\ind_{A_1\times A_2}\) both repeated integrals are \(\PP_1[A_1]\PP_2[A_2]\); the good sets principle (with a d-system argument as in Theorem 1.11) extends this to all \(f=\ind_A\), \(A\in\F\); then simple functions, monotone limits and positive/negative parts.

carefulintegrability is needed

Warning. For \(f\) to be integrable we require \(\int|f|\,d\PP<\infty\). If we drop the assumption that \(f\) is integrable or non-negative, it is not hard to cook up examples where both repeated integrals exist but their values differ. Here is one with sums in place of integrals (counting measure on \(\N\times\N\); sums are integrals against counting measure, as we saw above).

roadmapindependence through products

One of the central ideas in probability theory is independence, and it is intricately linked with product measure. Intuitively, two events are independent if they have no influence on each other: knowing that one has happened tells us nothing about the chance that the other has happened. More formally:

Independence

Definition 2.22 (Independence).p. 19 Let \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\) be a probability space. Let \(I\) be a finite or countably infinite set. We say that the events \((A_i)_{i\in I}\), where each \(A_i\in\F\), are independent if for all finite subsets \(J\subseteq I\),

\[\PP\Big[\bigcap_{i\in J}A_i\Big]=\prod_{i\in J}\PP[A_i].\]

Sub σ-algebras \(\G_1,\G_2,\dots\) of \(\F\) are called independent if whenever \(A_i\in\G_i\) and \(i_1,i_2,\dots,i_n\) are distinct, then

\[\PP[A_{i_1}\cap\dots\cap A_{i_n}]=\prod_{k=1}^n\PP[A_{i_k}].\]
intuitionsub σ-algebras as information

A sub σ-algebra of \(\F\) is a σ-algebra \(\G\subseteq\F\) on the same \(\Omega\); think of it as a body of information (as in Figure 1.4). Note that we impose these conditions for finite subsets only, but they then also hold for countable subsets, using Lemma 1.4 (intersect more and more of the sets). They also hold after complementing some or all of the \(A_i\) (exercise).

ExercisePairs are not enough
Why insist on all finite subsets, rather than just pairs?
show answer

Pairwise independence is genuinely weaker. Toss two fair coins; let \(A\) = "first is heads", \(B\) = "second is heads", \(C\) = "the two tosses agree". Each has probability \(\frac12\), and each pair is independent (for instance \(\PP[A\cap C]=\PP[\text{HH}]=\frac14\)). But \(\PP[A\cap B\cap C]=\frac14\ne\frac18\): knowing \(A\) and \(B\) determines \(C\).

connectionback to Prelims

How does this fit in with our notion of independence from Prelims? We need to relate random variables to σ-algebras.

Definition 2.23 (σ-algebra generated by a random variable).p. 20 Let \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\) be a probability space and let \(X\) be a real-valued random variable on \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\). The σ-algebra generated by \(X\) is

\[\sigma(X)=\{X^{-1}(A):A\in\B(\R)\}.\]
intuitionσ(X) is what X tells you

\(\sigma(X)\) is the collection of events of the form "\(X\in A\)": the information you have if you are told the value of \(X\) and nothing else. It is easy to check that \(\sigma(X)\) is a σ-algebra (preimages commute with set operations, as in the proof of Proposition 2.2), and by definition of a random variable we have \(\sigma(X)\subseteq\F\). Moreover,

\[\sigma(X)=\sigma\big(\{\{X\le t\}:t\in\R\}\big),\]

where \(\{X\le t\}=\{\omega:X(\omega)\le t\}\) (again, compare Proposition 2.2).

Definition 2.24 (σ-algebra generated by a sequence of random variables).p. 20 More generally, if \((X_n)\) is a finite or infinite sequence of random variables on \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\), then

\[\sigma(X_1,X_2,\dots)=\sigma\Big(\bigcup_n\sigma(X_n)\Big)=\sigma\big(\{\{X_n\le t\}:n\ge1,t\in\R\}\big).\]

Definition 2.25.p. 20 Let \(X\) be a random variable on a probability space \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\), and let \(\G\subseteq\F\) be a σ-algebra. Then \(X\) is called \(\G\)-measurable if \(X\) is measurable as a function on \((\Omega,\G)\).

in wordsDefinition 2.25

In other words, \(X\) is \(\G\)-measurable if and only if \(\sigma(X)\subseteq\G\). Thus \(\sigma(X)\) is the smallest σ-algebra with respect to which \(X\) is measurable. It is easy to check that \(X\) is \(\G\)-measurable if and only if \(\{X\le t\}\in\G\) for every \(t\in\R\). Read "\(X\) is \(\G\)-measurable" as "the information in \(\G\) is enough to determine the value of \(X\)". On the die of Figure 1.4 with \(\G\) generated by the evens, the indicator of "even" is \(\G\)-measurable, but the roll itself is not.

To understand what these definitions mean, note that a random variable \(Y\) is \(\sigma(X)\)-measurable if and only if \(Y=f(X)\) for some measurable function \(f:\R\to\R\): knowing \(X\) determines \(Y\) exactly when \(Y\) is a function of \(X\).The direction “\(Y=f(X)\) implies \(\sigma(Y)\subseteq\sigma(X)\)” is just \(Y^{-1}(A)=X^{-1}(f^{-1}(A))\). The converse is the Doob–Dynkin lemma, proved by the standard machine: start with \(Y=\ind_{X^{-1}(B)}=\ind_B(X)\). Similarly, \(Y\) is \(\sigma(X_1,X_2,\dots)\)-measurable if and only if \(Y=f(X_1,X_2,\dots)\) for some measurable function \(f\) on the countable product of \((\R,\B(\R))\) with itself.

Definition 2.26 (Independent random variables).p. 20 Random variables \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) are called independent if the σ-algebras \(\sigma(X_1),\sigma(X_2),\dots\) are independent.

connectionthe Prelims version

In more familiar language, \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent if for each pair \(A,B\) of Borel subsets of \(\R\),

\[\PP[X\in A,Y\in B]=\PP[X\in A]\,\PP[Y\in B].\]

Any measurable function \(f\) from a probability space \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\) to a measurable space \((\Lambda,\G)\) induces a probability measure \(\mu_f=\PP\circ f^{-1}\) on \((\Lambda,\G)\), defined by \(\mu_f(A)=\PP[f\in A]=\PP[f^{-1}(A)]\): the push-forward of \(\PP\) by \(f\). The following result is easy to check.

Lemma 2.27.p. 20 Two random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) on the probability space \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\) are independent if and only if the measure \(\mu_{X,Y}\) induced on \(\R^2\) by \((X,Y)\) is the product measure \(\mu_X\times\mu_Y\), where \(\mu_X\) and \(\mu_Y\) are the measures on \(\R\) induced by \(X\) and \(Y\) respectively.

connectionjoint densities

(Both measures agree on rectangles \(A\times B\) exactly when \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, and rectangles form a π-system generating \(\B(\R^2)\).) This generalises what you learned in Prelims and Part A: two continuous random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent if and only if their joint density factorises as \(f_{X,Y}(x,y)=f_X(x)f_Y(y)\).

motivationwhy Theorem 2.28 is needed

Of course the conditions of Definition 2.26 would be impossible to check in general: we don't have a nice explicit description of the σ-algebras \(\sigma(X_i)\). But we can use Theorem 1.11 (uniqueness of extension) to reduce them to something manageable.

Theorem 2.28.p. 21 Let \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\) be a probability space. Suppose that \(\G\) and \(\H\) are sub σ-algebras of \(\F\) and that \(\G_0\) and \(\H_0\) are π-systems with \(\sigma(\G_0)=\G\) and \(\sigma(\H_0)=\H\). Then \(\G\) and \(\H\) are independent iff \(\G_0\) and \(\H_0\) are independent, i.e. \(\PP[G\cap H]=\PP[G]\PP[H]\) whenever \(G\in\G_0\), \(H\in\H_0\).

Proof. One direction is trivial. For the other, we upgrade one side at a time.

Step 1: upgrade \(\H_0\) to \(\H\). Fix \(G\in\G_0\). The two functions

\[H\mapsto\PP[G\cap H]\qquad\text{and}\qquad H\mapsto\PP[G]\PP[H]\]

define measures on \((\Omega,\H)\). (Check: both give \(\emptyset\) measure 0, and both are countably additive, the first because \(G\cap\bigcup_nH_n=\bigcup_n(G\cap H_n)\) is a disjoint union when the \(H_n\) are disjoint.)

They have the same total mass \(\PP[G]\), and they agree on the π-system \(\H_0\). So by Theorem 1.11 they agree on \(\sigma(\H_0)=\H\). Hence

\[\PP[G\cap H]=\PP[G]\PP[H]\qquad\text{for }G\in\G_0,\ H\in\H.\]

Step 2: upgrade \(\G_0\) to \(\G\). Now fix \(H\in\H\) and repeat the argument with the two measures \(G\mapsto\PP[G\cap H]\) and \(G\mapsto\PP[G]\PP[H]\) on \((\Omega,\G)\), which agree on \(\G_0\) by Step 1.∎

in wordsbeyond two σ-algebras

This extends easily to \(n\) σ-algebras and hence (since independence is defined by looking at finitely many at a time) to a sequence of σ-algebras.

Corollary 2.29.p. 21 A sequence \((X_n)_{n\ge1}\) of real-valued random variables on \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\) is independent iff for all \(n\ge1\) and all \(x_1,\dots,x_n\in\R\) (or \(\Rbar\)),

\[\PP[X_1\le x_1,\dots,X_n\le x_n]=\PP[X_1\le x_1]\cdots\PP[X_n\le x_n].\]
✎Now try questions B1, C2, C3 of Problem Sheet 2.
in wordsCorollary 2.29

The sets \(\{X_i\le x\}\), \(x\in\R\), form a π-system generating \(\sigma(X_i)\); allowing \(x=\infty\) lets us leave some variables unconstrained, and Theorem 2.28 (extended to \(n\) σ-algebras) does the rest. So independence of random variables is the familiar statement that the joint distribution function factorises.

payoffi.i.d. sequences exist

The existence of countable product spaces (Remark 2.20) tells us that, given Borel probability measures \(\mu_1,\mu_2,\dots\) on \(\R\), there is a probability space on which there are independent random variables \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) with \(\mu_{X_i}=\mu_i\): take \(\Omega=\R^\N\) with the product measure and let \(X_i\) be the \(i\)-th coordinate.

The tail σ-algebra and Kolmogorov's 0-1 law

roadmaptail events

We finish this section with one of the most beautiful results in probability theory, concerning "tail events" associated with sequences of independent random variables.

Definition 2.30 (Tail σ-algebra).p. 21 For a sequence of random variables \((X_n)_{n\ge1}\) define

\[\T_n=\sigma(X_{n+1},X_{n+2},\dots)\qquad\text{and}\qquad\T=\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty\T_n.\]

Then \(\T\) is called the tail σ-algebra of the sequence \((X_n)_{n\ge1}\).

in wordsDefinition 2.30

\(\T_n\) is the information in the sequence from time \(n+1\) on; \(\T\) is what you can still determine if you are allowed to ignore any finite number of initial terms. (An intersection of σ-algebras is a σ-algebra, as in the proof that \(\sigma(\A)\) is one.) Roughly speaking, any event \(A\) such that (a) whether \(A\) holds is determined by the sequence \((X_n)\), but (b) changing finitely many of the values does not affect whether \(A\) holds, is in the tail σ-algebra. These conditions sound impossible to meet together, but many events involving limits satisfy them. For example, \(A=\{(X_n)\text{ converges}\}\) is a tail event: just check that \(A\in\T_n\) for each \(n\), which holds because whether a sequence converges doesn't depend on its first \(n\) terms. So is \(\{\sum_nX_n\text{ converges}\}\). But \(\{X_1>0\}\) is not, and neither is \(\{\sum_nX_n>0\}\).

Theorem 2.31 (Kolmogorov’s 0-1 law).p. 21 Let \((X_n)\) be a sequence of independent random variables. Then the tail σ-algebra \(\T\) of \((X_n)\) contains only events of probability 0 or 1. Moreover, any \(\T\)-measurable random variable is almost surely constant.

Proof. Step 1: the past is independent of the future. Let \(\F_n=\sigma(X_1,\dots,X_n)\). Note that \(\F_n\) is generated by the π-system of events

\[\A=\big\{\{X_1\le x_1,\dots,X_n\le x_n\}:x_1,\dots,x_n\in\R\big\},\]

and \(\T_n\) is generated by the π-system of events

\[\B=\big\{\{X_{n+1}\le x_{n+1},\dots,X_{n+k}\le x_{n+k}\}:k\ge1,\ x_{n+1},\dots,x_{n+k}\in\R\big\}.\]

For any \(A\in\A\) and \(B\in\B\), the independence of the random variables \((X_n)\) gives \(\PP[A\cap B]=\PP[A]\PP[B]\). So by Theorem 2.28 the σ-algebras \(\sigma(\A)=\F_n\) and \(\sigma(\B)=\T_n\) are independent.

Step 2: the tail is independent of everything. Since \(\T\subseteq\T_n\), we conclude that \(\F_n\) and \(\T\) are independent, for every \(n\). Hence \(\bigcup_{n\ge1}\F_n\) and \(\T\) are independent.

Now \(\bigcup_{n\ge1}\F_n\) is a π-system (although not in general a σ-algebra) generating the σ-algebra \(\F_\infty=\sigma((X_n)_{n\ge1})\). So, applying Theorem 2.28 again, \(\F_\infty\) and \(\T\) are independent.

Step 3: so the tail is independent of itself. But \(\T\subseteq\F_\infty\), so if \(A\in\T\) then \(A\) is independent of itself:

\[\PP[A]=\PP[A\cap A]=\PP[A]^2,\]

and so \(\PP[A]=0\) or \(\PP[A]=1\).

Random variables. Now suppose that \(Y\) is any real-valued \(\T\)-measurable random variable. Its distribution function \(F_Y(y)=\PP[Y\le y]\) is increasing, right continuous, and takes only values in \(\{0,1\}\). So

\[\PP[Y=c]=1,\qquad\text{where }c=\inf\{y:F_Y(y)=1\}.\]

This extends easily to the extended-real-valued case.∎

payoff0 or 1, never in between

The punchline: if the \(X_n\) are independent, then the probability that \(\sum_nX_n\) converges, or that \(X_n\to0\), is either 0 or 1. It is never \(\frac12\). The theorem doesn't say which; that takes other arguments.

Example 2.32.p. 22 Let \((X_n)_{n\ge1}\) be a sequence of independent, identically distributed (i.i.d.) random variables and let \(S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nX_k\). Consider \(L=\limsup_{n\to\infty}S_n/n\). Then \(L\) is a tail random variable and so almost surely constant. We’ll prove later in the course that, under weak assumptions, \(L=\E[X_1]\) almost surely.

intuitionwhy L is a tail variable

Why is \(L\) a tail random variable? For fixed \(k\),

\[\frac{S_n}{n}=\frac{X_1+\dots+X_k}{n}+\frac{X_{k+1}+\dots+X_n}{n},\]

and the first term tends to 0 as \(n\to\infty\). So

\[L=\limsup_n\frac1n\sum_{j=k+1}^nX_j,\]

which is \(\T_k\)-measurable, for every \(k\). The "later" is Chapter 7, where the strong law of large numbers is proved with martingales.

Chapter 3

Modes of convergence

“Random variables converge” can mean four different things. This chapter sorts them out, with two lemmas that decide whether events happen infinitely often, a handful of inequalities that do most of the day-to-day work, and the spaces Lp.
