3.1The Borel–Cantelli Lemmasp. 22

≈ 35 min·17 results, 5 figures, 2 exercises·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★★
roadmapindependence, put to work

We'll return to independence, or more importantly the lack of it, later. First we look at some consequences of our theory of integration for probability. Throughout, \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\) is a probability space.

the questionwhich outcomes are in infinitely many events?

The first question: given a sequence of events \(A_1,A_2,\dots\), which outcomes \(\omega\) are in infinitely many of them? And which are in all but finitely many?

Definition 3.1.p. 22 Let \((A_n)\) be a sequence of sets from \(\F\). We define

\[\begin{aligned}\limsup_{n\to\infty}A_n&=\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty\bigcup_{m\ge n}A_m\\&=\{\omega\in\Omega:\omega\in A_m\text{ for infinitely many }m\}\\&=\{A_m\text{ occurs infinitely often}\}=\{A_m\text{ i.o.}\}\end{aligned}\]

and

\[\begin{aligned}\liminf_{n\to\infty}A_n&=\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty\bigcap_{m\ge n}A_m\\&=\{\omega:\exists\,m_0(\omega)\text{ with }\omega\in A_m\text{ for all }m\ge m_0(\omega)\}\\&=\{A_m\text{ eventually}\}=\{A_m^c\text{ infinitely often}\}^c.\end{aligned}\]
✎Now try question A1 of Problem Sheet 3.
in wordsDefinition 3.1

Read the formulas slowly once. \(\omega\in\bigcup_{m\ge n}A_m\) says "\(\omega\) is in some \(A_m\) at or after time \(n\)". Requiring this for every \(n\) (the outer intersection) says that however late you start looking, \(\omega\) shows up again: infinitely often. Similarly \(\omega\in\bigcap_{m\ge n}A_m\) says "from time \(n\) on, \(\omega\) is in every \(A_m\)", and the outer union asks for this to hold from some \(n\) on: eventually. Both sets are in \(\F\), being built from countably many unions and intersections.

Lemma 3.2.p. 23

\[\ind_{\limsup_{n\to\infty}A_n}=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\ind_{A_n},\qquad\ind_{\liminf_{n\to\infty}A_n}=\liminf_{n\to\infty}\ind_{A_n}.\]

Proof. Note that

\[\ind_{\bigcup_nA_n}=\sup_n\ind_{A_n}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\ind_{\bigcap_nA_n}=\inf_n\ind_{A_n}:\]

the union contains \(\omega\) iff some indicator is 1, and the intersection contains \(\omega\) iff every indicator is 1. Apply these twice. For example,

\[\ind_{\limsup A_n}=\inf_n\sup_{m\ge n}\ind_{A_m}=\limsup_n\ind_{A_n}.\]
∎
connectionFatou for sets

So lim sup and lim inf of sets are the set versions of the same operations on numbers. If we apply Fatou's Lemma to the functions \(\ind_{A_n}\) (using \(\E[\ind_A]=\PP[A]\)), we see that

\[\PP[A_n\text{ eventually}]\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\PP[A_n]\]

and hence (taking complements)

\[\PP[A_n\text{ i.o.}]\ge\limsup_{n\to\infty}\PP[A_n].\]

These are not surprising, and easy to prove directly. In fact we can say much more about the probabilities of these events.

Lemma 3.3 (The First Borel–Cantelli Lemma, BC1).p. 23 If \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty\PP[A_n]<\infty\) then \(\PP[A_n\text{ i.o.}]=0\).

carefulno independence needed here

Remark. Notice that we make no assumptions about independence. This is a very powerful result.

Proof of Lemma 3.3. Let

\[G_n=\bigcup_{m\ge n}A_m,\]

the event that at least one of \(A_n,A_{n+1},\dots\) happens. We need two facts about \(G_n\).

First, \(G_n\) has small probability. By countable subadditivity (the probability of a union is at most the sum of the probabilities),

\[\PP[G_n]\le\sum_{m=n}^\infty\PP[A_m].\]

Second, the \(G_n\) shrink down to the event we care about. As \(n\) grows the union runs over fewer and fewer events, so \(G_n\downarrow G=\limsup_nA_n\), and by Lemma 1.4, \(\PP[G_n]\downarrow\PP[G]\).

Now put the two together. Since \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty\PP[A_n]<\infty\), the tails of the series go to zero:

\[\sum_{m=n}^\infty\PP[A_m]\to0\qquad\text{as }n\to\infty.\]

And so

\[\begin{aligned}\PP\Big[\limsup_{n\to\infty}A_n\Big]&=\lim_{n\to\infty}\PP[G_n]&&\why{continuity from above}\\&\le\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{m=n}^\infty\PP[A_m]&&\why{subadditivity}\\&=0.&&\why{tails of a convergent series}\end{aligned}\]
∎
techniquecounting events with MCT

Alternatively, consider \(N=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\ind_{A_n}\), the (random) number of events that occur. The Monotone Convergence Theorem gives \(\E[N]=\sum_n\PP[A_n]<\infty\), and a random variable with finite expectation is finite almost surely, so \(\PP[N=\infty]=0\). "If on average only finitely many happen, then almost surely only finitely many happen."

motivationwhy BC2 needs independence

A partial converse to BC1 is provided by the second Borel–Cantelli Lemma, but now we must assume the events are independent.

Lemma 3.4 (The Second Borel–Cantelli Lemma, BC2).p. 23 Let \((A_n)\) be a sequence of independent events. If \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty\PP[A_n]=\infty\) then \(\PP[A_n\text{ i.o.}]=1\).

Proof. Write \(a_m=\PP[A_m]\). We shall use the elementary inequality

\[1-a\le e^{-a}\qquad\text{for all real }a.\]

It holds because the line \(1-a\) is the tangent to the convex function \(e^{-a}\) at \(a=0\), and a convex function lies above its tangent lines.

Rather than showing directly that infinitely many \(A_n\) happen, we show that the complementary event \(\{A_n^c\text{ eventually}\}\) has probability zero. Fix \(n\). Then

\[\begin{aligned}\PP\Big[\bigcap_{m\ge n}A_m^c\Big]&=\prod_{m\ge n}(1-a_m)&&\why{by independence}\\&\le\exp\Big(-\sum_{m\ge n}a_m\Big)&&\why{since $1-a\le e^{-a}$}\\&=0&&\why{since $\sum_m a_m=\infty$.}\end{aligned}\]

The first step deserves a word. Complements of independent events are again independent, which handles any finite intersection; for the infinite intersection, take the limit of the finite ones using Lemma 1.4.

Finally, \(\{A_n^c\text{ eventually}\}\) is a countable union of the events we just handled, so by countable subadditivity

\[\PP[A_n^c\text{ eventually}]=\PP\Big[\bigcup_{n\in\N}\bigcap_{m\ge n}A_m^c\Big]\le\sum_{n=1}^\infty\PP\Big[\bigcap_{m\ge n}A_m^c\Big]=0.\]

Hence \(\PP[A_n\text{ i.o.}]=1-\PP[A_n^c\text{ eventually}]=1\).∎

carefulBC2 fails without independence

Without independence BC2 fails badly: take \(A_n=A\) for every \(n\) with \(\PP[A]=\frac12\). Then \(\sum\PP[A_n]=\infty\) but \(\PP[A_n\text{ i.o.}]=\PP[A]=\frac12\).

Example 3.5.p. 24 A monkey is provided with a typewriter. At each time step it has probability \(1/26\) of typing any of the 26 letters, independently of other times. What is the probability that it will type ABRACADABRA at least once? Infinitely often?

ExerciseSixes forever
Roll a fair die again and again. Is it certain that you see infinitely many sixes? Infinitely many runs of ten sixes in a row?
show answer

Let \(A_n\) be the event that roll \(n\) is a six. The \(A_n\) are independent with \(\sum_n\PP[A_n]=\sum_n\frac16=\infty\), so the second Borel–Cantelli lemma says \(\PP[A_n\text{ i.o.}]=1\). For runs, let \(B_k\) be the event that rolls \(10k+1,\dots,10k+10\) are all sixes. These blocks don't overlap, so the \(B_k\) are independent, each with probability \(6^{-10}\). That is tiny, but the sum of infinitely many copies of it is still infinite, so again infinitely many \(B_k\) happen, almost surely. Any fixed finite pattern turns up infinitely often.

techniquedisjoint blocks give independence

Solution. Consider the events

\[A_k=\{\text{ABRACADABRA is typed at times }11k+1,\dots,11k+11\}\]

for each \(k\). These use disjoint blocks of keystrokes, so they are independent, and \(\PP[A_k]=(1/26)^{11}>0\). So \(\sum_k\PP[A_k]=\infty\), and BC2 says that with probability 1, \(A_k\) happens infinitely often. (We only looked at blocks starting at multiples of 11, which is enough: finding infinitely many occurrences there certainly gives infinitely many occurrences overall.)

roadmapwaiting times, via martingales later

Later in the course, with the help of a suitable martingale, we'll be able to work out how long we must wait, on average, before we see patterns like this. We'll see many applications of BC1 and BC2. Here is one more.

Example 3.6.p. 24 Let \((X_n)_{n\ge1}\) be independent exponentially distributed random variables with mean 1 and let \(M_n=\max\{X_1,\dots,X_n\}\). Then

\[\PP\Big[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{M_n}{\log n}=1\Big]=1.\]

Proof. First recall that if \(X\) is exponential with parameter 1 then \(\PP[X\le x]=1-e^{-x}\) for \(x\ge0\) (and \(0\) for \(x<0\)). Fix \(0<\eps<1\). Then

\[\begin{aligned}\PP[M_n\le(1-\eps)\log n]&=\PP\Big[\bigcap_{i=1}^n\{X_i\le(1-\eps)\log n\}\Big]\\&=\prod_{i=1}^n\PP[X_i\le(1-\eps)\log n]\\&=\Big(1-\frac1{n^{1-\eps}}\Big)^n\le\exp(-n^\eps),\end{aligned}\]

using independence and then \(1-a\le e^{-a}\). Thus \(\sum_n\PP[M_n\le(1-\eps)\log n]<\infty\), and so by BC1, \(\PP[M_n\le(1-\eps)\log n\text{ i.o.}]=0\). Since \(\eps\) was arbitrary, take \(\eps=\frac1j\) for \(j=1,2,\dots\): a countable union of null events is null, so

\[\PP\Big[\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{M_n}{\log n}<1\Big]=0.\]

The reverse bound is similar. \(\PP[X_n\ge(1+\eps)\log n]=n^{-(1+\eps)}\) is summable, so by BC1, \(\PP[X_n\ge(1+\eps)\log n\text{ i.o.}]=0\). And \(\{M_n\ge(1+\eps)\log n\text{ i.o.}\}\) is contained in that event up to a null set: if \(M_n\ge(1+\eps)\log n\) then some \(k\le n\) has \(X_k\ge(1+\eps)\log n\ge(1+\eps)\log k\), and if this happens for infinitely many \(n\) then, since each \(X_k\) is finite, infinitely many different \(k\) must be involved. Hence \(\limsup_nM_n/\log n\le1\) almost surely as well.∎

✎Now try questions B4, B5, B6, B7, C1 of Problem Sheet 2. With both Borel–Cantelli lemmas in hand, Sheet 2 is complete.
✎Now try question A2 of Problem Sheet 3.
intuition0–1 statements can be sharp

At first sight BC1 and BC2 might not look very powerful: they only tell us when certain events have probability zero or one. But for many applications, in particular when the events are independent, many interesting events can only have probability zero or one, because they are tail events (Theorem 2.31).

examplethe iterated logarithm, again

If the \(X_n\) in Example 2.32 have mean zero and variance one, then setting

\[B=\Big\{\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{S_n}{\sqrt{2n\log\log n}}=1\Big\},\](9)

by Kolmogorov's 0-1 law we have \(\PP[B]=0\) or \(\PP[B]=1\). In fact \(\PP[B]=1\): this is the law of the iterated logarithm we met in Chapter 0. Under the slightly stronger assumption that \(\E[|X_n|^{2+\alpha}]<\infty\) for some \(\alpha>0\), Varadhan proves it by a delicate application of Borel–Cantelli.

the questionhow does this square with the CLT?

You may at this point be feeling a little confused. In Prelims Statistics or Part A Probability (or possibly even at school) you learned that if \((X_n)\) is a sequence of i.i.d. random variables with mean 0 and variance 1 then

\[\PP\Big[\frac{S_n}{\sqrt n}\le a\Big]\xrightarrow{n\to\infty}\int_{-\infty}^a\frac{e^{-x^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,dx.\](10)

This is the Central Limit Theorem, without which statistics would be a very different subject. How does it fit with (9)? (10) says \(S_n/\sqrt n\) is typically of size 1, while (9) says that along every path \(S_n/\sqrt n\) is unbounded (it reaches \(\sqrt{2\log\log n}\to\infty\) infinitely often). There's no contradiction: they describe different modes of convergence. Figure 0.1 shows both at once.

Modes of convergence

Definition 3.7 (Modes of convergence).p. 25 Let \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) and \(X\) be random variables on a probability space \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\).

  1. We say that \((X_n)\) converges almost surely to \(X\) (written \(X_n\to X\) a.s., or \(X_n\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}X\)) if
    \[\PP[X_n\to X]=\PP\big[\{\omega:\lim_{n\to\infty}X_n(\omega)=X(\omega)\}\big]=1.\]
  2. We say that \((X_n)\) converges to \(X\) in probability (written \(X_n\pto X\)) if, for every \(\eps>0\),
    \[\lim_{n\to\infty}\PP(|X_n-X|>\eps)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\PP\big(\{\omega:|X_n(\omega)-X(\omega)|>\eps\}\big)=0.\]
  3. Suppose that \(X\) and all \(X_n\) have finite \(p\)-th moments for some real number \(p>0\), i.e., \(\E[|X|^p],\E[|X_n|^p]<\infty\). We say that \(X_n\) converges to \(X\) in \(L^p\) (or in \(p\)-th moment; written \(X_n\xrightarrow{L^p}X\)) if
    \[\lim_{n\to\infty}\E[|X_n-X|^p]=0.\]
  4. Let \(F\) and \(F_n\) denote the distribution functions of \(X\) and \(X_n\) respectively. We say that \(X_n\) converges to \(X\) in distribution (written \(X_n\dto X\)) if
    \[\lim_{n\to\infty}F_n(x)=F(x)\quad\text{for every }x\in\R\text{ at which }F\text{ is continuous.}\]
in wordsDefinition 3.7

What each one asks for, in words:

  • Almost surely: for (almost) every individual outcome \(\omega\), the numbers \(X_n(\omega)\) converge. It is a statement about whole sample paths.
  • In probability: at each large time \(n\), it is unlikely that \(X_n\) is far from \(X\). It says nothing about any single path for all \(n\) at once; the rare bad outcomes can be different ones at different times.
  • In \(L^p\): the average size of the error, measured by \(\E|X_n-X|^p\), goes to zero. Large errors on small sets are penalised.
  • In distribution: only the laws converge. \(X_n\) and \(X\) don't even need to live on the same probability space. The exception at discontinuity points of \(F\) is needed so that \(X_n=\frac1n\to0\) counts as converging: here \(F_n(0)=0\) for every \(n\) but \(F(0)=1\).
recapwhich modes imply which

These notions of convergence are all different. The implications are:

\[\begin{array}{ccccc}\text{a.s.}&\Longrightarrow&\text{in probability}&\Longrightarrow&\text{in distribution}\\&&\Uparrow&&\\&&\text{in }L^p&&\end{array}\]

and no others hold in general. The figure below has a counterexample for every missing arrow; click an arrow, present or absent.

connectionfrom Part A to probability

The notions of convergence almost surely and in \(L^p\) are discussed (for Lebesgue measure, rather than general probability measures) in Part A Integration. Here are the two standard examples.

Example 3.8.p. 26 On the probability space \(\Omega=[0,1]\) with the Borel σ-algebra and Lebesgue measure, consider the sequence of functions

\[f_n(x)=\begin{cases}n(1-nx)&0\le x\le1/n,\\0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}\]

Then \(f_n\to0\) almost everywhere on \([0,1]\) but \(f_n\not\to0\) in \(L^1\). Thinking of each \(f_n\) as a random variable, we have \(f_n\to0\) almost surely but \(f_n\not\to0\) in \(L^1\).

intuitiona triangle that slips through

The graph of \(f_n\) is a triangle of height \(n\) over \([0,\frac1n]\), with area \(\frac12\). At every \(x>0\), \(f_n(x)=0\) once \(n>1/x\), so the only point where \(f_n\) doesn't tend to 0 is \(x=0\), a null set. But \(\E|f_n-0|=\frac12\) for every \(n\). It is the escaping spike of Figure 2.2 again.

Example 3.9 (Convergence in probability does not imply a.s. convergence).p. 26 Stick with \([0,1]\) with the Borel sets and Lebesgue measure as our probability space. Define \((X_n)_{n\ge1}\) as follows: for each \(n\) there is a unique pair of integers \((m,k)\) such that \(n=2^m+k\) and \(0\le k<2^m\). Set

\[X_n(\omega)=\ind_{[k/2^m,(k+1)/2^m)}(\omega).\]
intuitiona moving blip

Pictorially, a "moving blip" travels repeatedly across \([0,1]\), getting narrower at each pass: pass \(m\) consists of \(2^m\) blips of width \(2^{-m}\) that sweep left to right. For fixed \(\omega\in(0,1)\), every pass hits \(\omega\) once, so \(X_n(\omega)=1\) infinitely often and \(X_n\not\to0\) a.s. But \(\PP[X_n\ne0]=2^{-m}\to0\) as \(n\to\infty\), so \(X_n\pto0\). (Also \(\E[|X_n-0|]=2^{-m}\to0\), so \(X_n\to0\) in \(L^1\).) On the other hand, if we look along the subsequence \((X_{2^n})_{n\ge1}\), we only ever see the first blip of each pass, \([0,2^{-n})\), and so \(X_{2^n}\to0\) almost surely.

roadmapthe general phenomenon

It turns out that this is a general phenomenon.

Theorem 3.10 (Convergence in probability and a.s. convergence).p. 27 Let \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) and \(X\) be random variables on \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\).

  1. If \(X_n\to X\) a.s. then \(X_n\pto X\).
  2. If \(X_n\pto X\), then there exists a subsequence \((X_{n_k})_{k\ge1}\) such that \(X_{n_k}\to X\) a.s. as \(k\to\infty\).

Proof. For \(\eps>0\) and \(n\in\N\) let

\[A_{n,\eps}=\{|X_n-X|>\eps\},\]

the event that \(X_n\) misses \(X\) by more than \(\eps\).

Part 1. Suppose \(X_n\to X\) a.s. If \(X_n(\omega)\to X(\omega)\) then \(\omega\) is in only finitely many \(A_{n,\eps}\), so for any \(\eps>0\) we have \(\PP[A_{n,\eps}\text{ i.o.}]=0\). On the other hand, applying Fatou's Lemma to \(\ind_{A_{n,\eps}^c}\), as after Lemma 3.2,

\[\PP[A_{n,\eps}\text{ i.o.}]=\PP\big[\limsup_nA_{n,\eps}\big]\ge\limsup_{n\to\infty}\PP[A_{n,\eps}].\]

Hence \(\PP[A_{n,\eps}]\to0\), so \(X_n\pto X\).

Part 2. This is the more interesting direction. Suppose that \(X_n\pto X\). Then for each \(k\ge1\) we have \(\PP[A_{n,1/k}]\to0\) as \(n\to\infty\), so there is some \(n_k\) such that

\[\PP[A_{n_k,1/k}]<1/k^2,\]

and we can choose \(n_k>n_{k-1}\) for \(k\ge2\). Setting \(B_k=A_{n_k,1/k}\), we have

\[\sum_{k=1}^\infty\PP[B_k]\le\sum_{k=1}^\infty k^{-2}<\infty.\]

Hence, by BC1, \(\PP[B_k\text{ i.o.}]=0\).

But if only finitely many \(B_k\) hold, then \(|X_{n_k}-X|\le1/k\) for all large \(k\), and certainly \(X_{n_k}\to X\). So \(X_{n_k}\to X\) a.s.∎

✎Now try question B1 of Problem Sheet 3.
techniquego fast enough to make it summable

The trick in part 2 is to go fast enough along the subsequence that the probabilities of being far away become summable, and then BC1 turns "unlikely at each time" into "eventually never". In Example 3.9 the subsequence \(X_{2^n}\) does exactly this.

Inequalities

motivationwhy we need inequalities

The First Borel–Cantelli Lemma is a powerful tool for proving almost sure convergence. Its successful application often rests on being able to find good bounds on probabilities. We end this section with some inequalities that are often helpful. The first is trivial, but has many applications.

Lemma 3.11 (Markov’s inequality).p. 27 Let \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\) be a probability space and \(X\) a non-negative random variable. Then, for each \(\lambda>0\),

\[\PP[X\ge\lambda]\le\frac1\lambda\E[X].\]

Proof. For each \(\omega\in\Omega\) we have

\[X(\omega)\ge\lambda\ind_{\{X\ge\lambda\}}(\omega):\]

where \(X\ge\lambda\) the right side is \(\lambda\), and elsewhere it is 0 (and \(X\ge0\) everywhere). Taking expectations,

\[\E[X]\ge\E[\lambda\ind_{\{X\ge\lambda\}}]=\lambda\PP[X\ge\lambda].\]
∎
ExerciseMarkov is sharp
Find a non-negative random variable \(X\) with \(\E[X]=1\) and \(\PP[X\ge10]=\frac1{10}\), so that Markov's inequality holds with equality.
show answer

Let \(X=10\) with probability \(\frac1{10}\) and \(X=0\) otherwise. Then \(\E[X]=10\cdot\frac1{10}=1\) and \(\PP[X\ge10]=\frac1{10}=\E[X]/10\). Equality needs all the mass of \(X\) to sit either at \(0\) or exactly at the threshold: any mass strictly between them, or above, would make \(\E[X]\) count for more than the bound uses.

Corollary 3.12 (General Chebyshev’s inequality).p. 28 Let \(X\) be a random variable taking values in a (measurable) set \(A\subseteq\R\), and let \(\varphi:A\to[0,\infty]\) be an increasing, measurable function. Then for any \(\lambda\in A\) with \(\varphi(\lambda)<\infty\) we have

\[\PP[X\ge\lambda]\le\frac{\E[\varphi(X)]}{\varphi(\lambda)}.\]

Proof. We have

\[\begin{aligned}\PP[X\ge\lambda]&\le\PP[\varphi(X)\ge\varphi(\lambda)]&&\why{$\varphi$ is increasing}\\&\le\frac{1}{\varphi(\lambda)}\E[\varphi(X)]&&\why{Markov, applied to $\varphi(X)\ge0$.}\end{aligned}\]

(If \(\varphi(\lambda)=0\) the bound is vacuous.)∎

exampleChebyshev’s inequality

The most familiar special case takes \(\varphi(x)=x^2\) on \([0,\infty)\) and applies the result to \(Y=|X-\E[X]|\), giving Chebyshev's inequality

\[\PP\big[|X-\E[X]|\ge t\big]\le\frac{\E[(X-\E[X])^2]}{t^2}=\frac{\mathrm{Var}[X]}{t^2}\qquad\text{for }t>0.\]

Corollary 3.12 is also often applied with \(\varphi(x)=e^{\theta x}\), \(\theta\ge0\), to obtain

\[\PP[X\ge\lambda]\le e^{-\theta\lambda}\E[e^{\theta X}].\]

The next step is often to optimise over \(\theta\) (this gives the Chernoff bounds).

Corollary 3.13.p. 28 For \(p>0\), convergence in \(L^p\) implies convergence in probability.

Proof. Recall that \(X_n\to X\) in \(L^p\) if \(\E[|X_n-X|^p]\to0\). Raising both sides of the inequality inside the probability to the power \(p\) and then using Markov,

\[\PP[|X_n-X|>\eps]=\PP[|X_n-X|^p>\eps^p]\le\frac1{\eps^p}\E[|X_n-X|^p]\to0.\]
∎
connectionthe weak law, from Prelims

The next corollary is a result you have seen in Prelims. It is called the "weak" law because the notion of convergence is a weak one.

Corollary 3.14 (Weak law of large numbers).p. 28 Let \((X_n)_{n\ge1}\) be i.i.d. random variables (on some probability space \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\)) with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2<\infty\). Set \(\bar X(n)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\). Then \(\bar X(n)\to\mu\) in probability as \(n\to\infty\).

Proof. First, the mean:

\[\E[\bar X(n)]=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\E[X_i]=\mu.\]

Next, the variance. Since the \(X_i\) are independent, variances add, so

\[\mathrm{Var}[\bar X(n)]=\frac1{n^2}\,\mathrm{Var}\Big[\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\Big]=\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n\mathrm{Var}[X_i]=\frac{\sigma^2}n.\]

Hence, by Chebyshev's inequality,

\[\PP[|\bar X(n)-\mu|>\eps]\le\frac{\mathrm{Var}[\bar X(n)]}{\eps^2}=\frac{\sigma^2}{\eps^2n}\to0.\]
∎
✎Now try question B2 of Problem Sheet 3.
set-upconvexity

The next inequality is about convex functions, which bend upwards.

Definition 3.15 (Convex function).p. 29 Let \(I\subseteq\R\) be a (bounded or unbounded) interval. A function \(f:I\to\R\) is convex if for all \(x,y\in I\) and \(t\in[0,1]\),

\[f(tx+(1-t)y)\le tf(x)+(1-t)f(y).\]
exampleconvex functions to know

Geometrically: every chord of the graph lies above the graph. Important examples include \(x^2\), \(e^x\), \(e^{-x}\) and \(|x|\) on \(\R\), and \(1/x\) on \((0,\infty)\). A twice differentiable function \(f\) is convex if and only if \(f''(x)\ge0\) for all \(x\).

Theorem 3.16 (Jensen’s inequality).p. 29 Let \(f:I\to\R\) be a convex function on an interval \(I\subseteq\R\). If \(X\) is an integrable random variable taking values in \(I\) then

\[\E[f(X)]\ge f(\E[X]).\]
in wordsTheorem 3.16

(We assume the expectation of \(f(X)\) exists; this is usually no problem since \(f\) is often non-negative.) Definition 3.15 is exactly the case where \(X\) takes two values, \(x\) with probability \(t\) and \(y\) with probability \(1-t\). Perhaps the nicest proof of the general case rests on the following geometric lemma: a convex function has a straight line touching it from below at any interior point.

Lemma 3.17.p. 29 Suppose that \(f:I\to\R\) is convex and let \(m\) be an interior point of \(I\). Then there exists \(a\in\R\) such that \(f(x)\ge f(m)+a(x-m)\) for all \(x\in I\).

Proof. Comparing chord slopes. Take any \(x<m<y\) with \(x,y\in I\), and write \(m\) as a weighted average of \(x\) and \(y\):

\[m=\frac{y-m}{y-x}\,x+\frac{m-x}{y-x}\,y.\]

Convexity gives

\[f(m)\le\frac{y-m}{y-x}f(x)+\frac{m-x}{y-x}f(y).\]

Rearranging (or, better, drawing a picture), this is equivalent to

\[\frac{f(m)-f(x)}{m-x}\le\frac{f(y)-f(m)}{y-m}.\]

In words: slopes of chords to the left of \(m\) are at most slopes of chords to the right.

Choosing the slope \(a\). It follows that

\[\sup_{x<m}\frac{f(m)-f(x)}{m-x}\le\inf_{y>m}\frac{f(y)-f(m)}{y-m},\]

so we can choose a number \(a\) in between. (If \(f\) is differentiable at \(m\) we can choose \(a=f'(m)\).)

Checking it works. For \(x<m\), the inequality \(\frac{f(m)-f(x)}{m-x}\le a\) rearranges to

\[f(x)\ge f(m)+a(x-m),\]

and similarly for \(y>m\).∎

Proof of Theorem 3.16. If \(\E[X]\) is not an interior point of \(I\) then it is an endpoint, and \(X\) must be almost surely equal to it (a variable in \([c,\infty)\) with mean \(c\) is \(c\) a.s.). Then the inequality is trivial.

Otherwise, set \(m=\E[X]\) in Lemma 3.17. This gives a line below \(f\) touching it at \(m\):

\[f(X)\ge f(\E[X])+a(X-\E[X]).\]

Taking expectations, the last term has mean 0, and we recover

\[\E[f(X)]\ge f(\E[X]).\]
∎
carefulonly for probability measures

Remark. Jensen's inequality only works for probability measures, but one can often exploit it to prove results for finite measures by first normalising. For example, suppose that \(\mu\) is a finite measure on \((\Omega,\F)\), and define \(\nu(A)=\mu(A)/\mu(\Omega)\), a probability measure. Then

\[\int|f|^3\,d\mu=\mu(\Omega)\int|f|^3\,d\nu\ge\mu(\Omega)\Big|\int f\,d\nu\Big|^3=\mu(\Omega)^{-2}\Big|\int f\,d\mu\Big|^3.\]

3.2Lp spacesp. 30

≈ 10 min·4 results, 1 figure·difficulty ●●●·importance ★★☆
set-uprandom variables as a vector space

The set of all random variables on a probability space is a large set. It is useful to organise it by how integrable its members are.

Definition 3.18.p. 30 Let \(p\ge0\). The space of all random variables \(X\) such that \(\E[|X|^p]<\infty\) is denoted \(\Lp p\). In particular, \(\Lp0\) is the space of all random variables. We also denote by \(\Lp\infty\) the set of all random variables that are bounded.

in wordsDefinition 3.18

For example \(X\in\Lp1\) means \(X\) is integrable, and \(X\in\Lp2\) means \(X\) has finite variance (it is "square integrable"). For \(p>0\) the function \(x\mapsto x^p\) is increasing on \(\R_+\), so

\[(x+y)^p\le(2\max(x,y))^p\le2^p(x^p+y^p)\qquad\text{for all }x,y\ge0.\]

It follows that \(X,Y\in\Lp p\) implies \(X+Y\in\Lp p\). Obviously also \(\alpha X\in\Lp p\) for any \(\alpha\in\R\), so \(\Lp p\) is a vector space. For \(X\in\Lp p\) put

\[\|X\|_p:=\big(\E[|X|^p]\big)^{1/p}.\]

This is a way of measuring the size of \(X\); for \(p=2\) it is the root-mean-square, and \(\|X-\E X\|_2\) is the standard deviation.

Lemma 3.19.p. 30 Let \(0<r\le p\). Suppose \(X\in\Lp p\). Then \(X\in\Lp r\) and \(\|X\|_r\le\|X\|_p\). In particular, convergence in \(L^p\) implies convergence in \(L^r\).

Proof. Let \(X_k=|X|\wedge k\) (the smaller of \(|X|\) and \(k\)). It is non-negative and bounded, so all its moments are finite.

Apply Jensen's inequality with the convex function \(f(x)=x^{p/r}\) on \([0,\infty)\) to the random variable \(X_k^r\):

\[\|X_k\|_r^p=\big(\E[X_k^r]\big)^{p/r}\le\E[X_k^p]\le\E[|X|^p]=\|X\|_p^p.\]

Now let \(k\to\infty\). By the Monotone Convergence Theorem \(\E[X_k^r]\uparrow\E[|X|^r]\), giving the inequality.

The statement about convergence follows by applying the inequality to \(X_n-X\).∎

carefulneeds a probability measure

This depends on having a probability measure: on a two-point space, a random variable is just a pair of numbers, and the lemma says the \(L^p\) "unit balls" are nested. The figure lets you see it.

roadmaptwo key inequalities

We now derive two crucial inequalities. Hölder's inequality is used in many proofs, and Minkowski's inequality shows that \(\|\cdot\|_p\) satisfies the triangle inequality.

Theorem 3.20.p. 30 Let \(p,q>1\) be such that \(\frac1p+\frac1q=1\). Suppose \(X,Y\in\Lp p\) and \(Z\in\Lp q\). Then

\[\begin{aligned}\E[|XZ|]&\le\|X\|_p\|Z\|_q&&\text{(Hölder's inequality)},\\\|X+Y\|_p&\le\|X\|_p+\|Y\|_p&&\text{(Minkowski's inequality)}.\end{aligned}\]
in wordsTheorem 3.20

With \(p=q=2\), Hölder is the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality \(\E|XZ|\le\sqrt{\E X^2\,\E Z^2}\). Proofs on \((\R,\B(\R))\) with Lebesgue measure are in Part A. Here we follow Williams and derive both from Jensen's inequality, using a neat device: changing the probability measure.

Proof of Theorem 3.20. Hölder. If \(X=0\) a.s. there is nothing to show. Otherwise, the trick is to change measure so that Jensen applies.

Define a new probability measure on \((\Omega,\F)\) by

\[\mathbb Q(A)=\frac{\E[|X|^p\ind_A]}{\|X\|_p^p},\]

which reweights outcomes in proportion to \(|X|^p\). (It is a measure by the Monotone Convergence Theorem, and \(\mathbb Q(\Omega)=1\).) By the standard machine, integrals against \(\mathbb Q\) are

\[\int W\,d\mathbb Q=\frac{\E[W|X|^p]}{\|X\|_p^p}\qquad\text{for }W\ge0.\]

Let \(\bar Z=|Z|/|X|^{p-1}\) on \(\{|X|>0\}\) and \(0\) elsewhere, so that \(\bar Z|X|^p=|XZ|\). Then, using Jensen with \(f(x)=x^q\) under \(\mathbb Q\),

\[\begin{aligned}\big(\E|XZ|\big)^q&=\Big(\|X\|_p^p\int\bar Z\,d\mathbb Q\Big)^q\\&\le\|X\|_p^{pq}\int\bar Z^q\,d\mathbb Q&&\why{Jensen}\\&=\|X\|_p^{pq-p}\,\E\big[|Z|^q|X|^{p-q(p-1)}\ind_{\{|X|>0\}}\big].\end{aligned}\]

Now tidy the exponents. From \(\frac1p+\frac1q=1\) we get \(pq=p+q\), so

\[p-q(p-1)=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad pq-p=q.\]

The right side is therefore at most \(\|X\|_p^q\,\E|Z|^q\). Raise both sides to the power \(1/q\).

Minkowski. \(X+Y\in\Lp p\) since \(\Lp p\) is a vector space. Let

\[c=\E[|X+Y|^p]^{1/q}=\big\||X+Y|^{p-1}\big\|_q,\]

using \((p-1)q=p\). If \(c=0\) there is nothing to prove.

Using first the triangle inequality on \(\R\), \(|x+y|\le|x|+|y|\), and then Hölder's inequality,

\[\begin{aligned}\E[|X+Y|^p]&\le\E\big[|X|\cdot|X+Y|^{p-1}\big]+\E\big[|Y|\cdot|X+Y|^{p-1}\big]&&\why{triangle}\\&\le\|X\|_p\,c+\|Y\|_p\,c.&&\why{Hölder}\end{aligned}\]

Dividing by \(c\) gives

\[\E[|X+Y|^p]^{1-1/q}\le\|X\|_p+\|Y\|_p,\]

and \(1-\frac1q=\frac1p\).∎

Background · Norms, Cauchy sequences and completeness

A norm on a vector space \(V\) is a function \(\|\cdot\|:V\to[0,\infty)\) with \(\|\alpha v\|=|\alpha|\|v\|\), \(\|v+w\|\le\|v\|+\|w\|\), and \(\|v\|=0\) only if \(v=0\). It gives a distance \(\|v-w\|\), so we can talk about convergence: \(v_n\to v\) means \(\|v_n-v\|\to0\).

A sequence is Cauchy if its terms get close to each other: \(\sup_{r,s\ge n}\|v_r-v_s\|\to0\). Every convergent sequence is Cauchy. The space is complete if, conversely, every Cauchy sequence converges to something in the space. \(\R\) is complete; \(\Q\) is not (the decimal truncations of \(\sqrt2\) are Cauchy but have no rational limit). A complete normed space is a Banach space. Completeness matters because it lets you prove that something exists by producing a Cauchy sequence that ought to converge to it, which is exactly how conditional expectation will be built in Chapter 4.

motivationwhy completeness matters

The following result is of fundamental importance in functional analysis. We will use it for \(p=2\).

Theorem 3.21.p. 31 Let \(p\ge1\). The vector space \(\Lp p\) is complete, i.e., for any sequence \((X_n)_{n\ge1}\subseteq\Lp p\) such that

\[\sup_{r,s\ge n}\|X_s-X_r\|_p\xrightarrow{n\to\infty}0\]

there exists \(X\in\Lp p\) such that \(X_n\to X\) in \(L^p\).

Proof. Find a fast subsequence. Pick \(k_1<k_2<\cdots\) such that

\[\sup_{r,s\ge k_n}\|X_s-X_r\|_p\le2^{-n}.\]

In particular (Lemma 3.19 with \(r=1\)),

\[\E[|X_{k_n}-X_{k_{n+1}}|]\le\|X_{k_n}-X_{k_{n+1}}\|_p\le2^{-n}.\]

It converges almost surely. Put

\[Y=\sum_{n\ge1}|X_{k_n}-X_{k_{n+1}}|.\]

By the Monotone Convergence Theorem, \(\E[Y]\le\sum_n2^{-n}<\infty\), and in particular \(Y<\infty\) a.s.

Where \(Y(\omega)<\infty\), the telescoping series

\[X_{k_1}+\sum_n(X_{k_{n+1}}-X_{k_n})\]

converges absolutely, so \(\lim_nX_{k_n}(\omega)\) exists. Define \(X(\omega):=\limsup_{n\to\infty}X_{k_n}(\omega)\) for all \(\omega\), so that \(X\) is a random variable (Lemma 2.3) and \(X_{k_n}\to X\) a.s.

The whole sequence converges in \(L^p\). For \(n\ge1\) and \(r>k_n\), we have

\[\E[|X_r-X_{k_m}|^p]=\|X_r-X_{k_m}\|_p^p\le2^{-np}\qquad\text{for all }m\ge n.\]

Let \(m\to\infty\). By Fatou's Lemma,

\[\E[|X_r-X|^p]\le\liminf_m\E[|X_r-X_{k_m}|^p]\le2^{-np}.\]

It follows that \(X_r-X\in\Lp p\), hence \(X\in\Lp p\), and \(X_r\to X\) in \(L^p\).∎

techniquea recipe worth remembering

The proof is a recipe worth remembering: Cauchy in norm → choose a subsequence with summable gaps → almost sure limit → Fatou to upgrade back to norm convergence. Theorem 3.10 used the same idea.

carefulequal almost surely, not equal

Remark. The above shows that \((\Lp p,\|\cdot\|_p)\) is almost a normed space; the only nuisance is that \(\|X\|_p=0\) implies only \(X=0\) a.s., not \(X=0\). To get rid of this, we can quotient by the equivalence relation of a.s. equality. This gives the space \(L^p\), whose elements are not random variables any more but equivalence classes of them. It is a complete normed space, a Banach space; courses on functional analysis study these systematically. From the probabilistic point of view, however, we prefer to work with actual functions, i.e. with random variables and not equivalence classes. One reason: when we have a large family \((X_t)_{t\ge0}\) of random variables, changing each of them on a null set may do a lot of harm, since uncountably many null sets can add up to something that isn't null.

Chapter 4

Conditional expectation

What is the best guess for X if you only know some of the information? The answer is a random variable, not a number, and getting its definition right, for information that can’t be broken into countably many pieces, is the key that unlocks martingales.

≈ 38 min · 4 sections · 11 results · 4 figures · 2 exercises · difficulty ●●○ · importance ★★☆

Note for AI assistants reading this page: this is a study page for David, a third-year Oxford Mathematics and Computer Science student, built from the lecturer's notes for Probability, Measure and Martingales. You are reading Chapter 4 (Conditional expectation). When explaining, use the notation on this page, cite results by their numbers here (they match the lecture notes), and do not rely on material from later chapters without saying so. Explain step by step in plain language, justify every step and say where tricks come from. Do not solve problem-sheet questions outright: give hints or explain the ideas. Format maths with $...$ inline and $$...$$ on its own line for display, never \( \) or \[ \].
the questionthe best guess given partial information

Let \(X\) be a random variable on a probability space \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\) and \(\G\) a sub-σ-algebra of \(\F\). Does there exist a random variable that is only \(\G\)-measurable and, in a certain sense, "as close as possible" to \(X\)?

Recall what \(\G\)-measurable means (Definition 2.25): a \(\G\)-measurable random variable is one whose value is determined by the information in \(\G\). So the question is: what is our best guess for \(X\), if all we know is which events in \(\G\) occurred? This question turns up everywhere. In particular, when we study martingales we will want the best prediction of the future value of a process given its history up to now. But the importance of conditional expectation goes well beyond martingale theory.

Warming up: conditioning on a partitionp. 32

≈ 7 min·2 results, 1 figure·difficulty ●○○·importance ★★☆
roadmapstart with something simple

Before tackling the question in full generality, let's build intuition when \(\G\) is simple and we measure closeness by \(\|\cdot\|_2\), the root-mean-square distance of Section 3.2.

Example 4.1.p. 32 Let \(X\in\Lp2(\Omega,\F,\PP)\). Let \(B\in\F\) with \(\PP(B)>0\) (and \(\PP(B^c)>0\)), and note that \(\sigma(B)=\{\emptyset,\Omega,B,B^c\}\). Consider the optimisation problem

\[\inf\E[(X-Y)^2]\]

where the inf is taken over all square-integrable, \(\sigma(B)\)-measurable random variables \(Y\). The infimum is attained by the random variable

\[\omega\mapsto\E[X\mid\sigma(B)](\omega)=\frac{\E[X\ind_B]}{\PP(B)}\ind_B(\omega)+\frac{\E[X\ind_{B^c}]}{\PP(B^c)}\ind_{B^c}(\omega).\]
intuitionwhy the answer takes two values

Why: a \(\sigma(B)\)-measurable \(Y\) can only take one value on \(B\) and one on \(B^c\) (the preimage of each value must be one of the four sets), so \(Y=a\ind_B+b\ind_{B^c}\). Then

\[\E[(X-Y)^2]=\E[(X-a)^2\ind_B]+\E[(X-b)^2\ind_{B^c}].\]

The first term is a quadratic in \(a\),

\[\E[X^2\ind_B]-2a\E[X\ind_B]+a^2\PP(B),\]

minimised at \(a=\E[X\ind_B]/\PP(B)\). Similarly for \(b\). The best guess on each piece is the average of \(X\) over that piece.

connectionfrom conditional probability to (12)

We denote the minimiser by \(\E[X\mid\sigma(B)]\); here is why the notation makes sense. Recall the definition of conditional probability,

\[\PP[A\mid B]=\frac{\PP[A\cap B]}{\PP[B]}\qquad\text{for }A,B\in\F\text{ with }\PP[B]>0,\]

and note that \(\PP(\cdot\mid B)\) is a probability measure on \((\Omega,\F)\). We can take expectations with respect to this measure, and this gives the conditional expectation of a random variable given the event \(B\):

\[\E[X\mid B]=\int_\Omega X(\omega)\,d\PP(\omega\mid B)=\frac{\int_BX\,d\PP}{\PP(B)}=\frac{\E[X\ind_B]}{\PP(B)},\]

which you have probably met in Part A Probability. With this notation,

\[\E[X\mid\sigma(B)](\omega)=\E[X\mid B]\,\ind_B(\omega)+\E[X\mid B^c]\,\ind_{B^c}(\omega),\](11)

which hopefully makes the notation \(\E[X\mid\sigma(B)]\) more intuitive: look at which of \(B\), \(B^c\) happened, and report the average of \(X\) there. Similar explicit formulas hold when \(\sigma(B)\) is replaced by another simple σ-algebra. If \(G_1,\dots,G_n\) form a partition of \(\Omega\) with \(\PP(G_i)>0\), then the same argument shows that for \(\G=\sigma(\{G_1,\dots,G_n\})\) the minimiser is

\[\E[X\mid\G]=\sum_{i=1}^n\E[X\mid G_i]\,\ind_{G_i}.\]

Finally, we note that

\[\E\big[\E[X\mid\sigma(B)]\,\ind_G\big]=\E[X\ind_G]\qquad\text{for all }G\in\sigma(B),\](12)

which is immediate from (11). Informally, it says the random variable \(\E[X\mid\G]\) matches the expectation of \(X\) locally, where "locally" means on the finest level that \(\G\) allows us to look at. This equality is the key to the general definition, when we condition on σ-algebras that are not as simple as \(\sigma(B)\).

Example 4.2.p. 32 Let \(X,Y\) be random variables on \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\). We would like a random variable \(Z\) that is as "close as possible" to \(X\) but only measurable with respect to \(\sigma(Y)\), that is, \(Z\) must be a function of \(Y\).

motivationwhy a new definition is needed

Motivated by (11) one might be tempted to set

\[Z(\omega)=\frac{\E[X\ind_{\{Y=y\}}]}{\PP[Y=y]}\qquad\text{when }Y(\omega)=y.\]

But in general this makes no sense, since \(\PP(Y=y)\) can be zero; for a continuous \(Y\), it is zero for every \(y\). To avoid dividing by zero, we can multiply out: \(\E[Z\ind_{\{Y=y\}}]=\E[X\ind_{\{Y=y\}}]\). Still, if \(\PP[Y=y]=0\) for every \(y\), this condition just says \(0=0\). So, just as when we failed to describe probability measures through the probabilities of individual values and passed to sets of values (Chapter 1), we pass to Borel sets. We insist that \(Z\) is a function of \(Y\) and

\[\E[Z\ind_{\{Y\in A\}}]=\E[X\ind_{\{Y\in A\}}]\](13)

for each \(A\in\B(\R)\). At this point we have no guarantee that such a \(Z\) exists, but (13) at least tells us a non-trivial property of it. (We'll see that (13) together with measurability determines \(Z\) uniquely up to a null set.) This is the special case \(\G=\sigma(Y)\) of the general definition below, and we write \(Z=\E[X\mid Y]=\E[X\mid\sigma(Y)]\). Since the events \(\{Y\in A\}\) are exactly the events in \(\sigma(Y)\), (13) is (12) again, with \(\sigma(Y)\) in place of \(\sigma(B)\).

The general definitionp. 33

≈ 11 min·3 results, 1 figure, 1 exercise·difficulty ●●●·importance ★★★

Definition 4.3 (Conditional expectation).p. 33 Let \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\) be a probability space and \(X\) an integrable random variable. Let \(\G\subseteq\F\) be a σ-algebra. We say that a random variable \(\E[X\mid\G]\) is (a version of) the conditional expectation of \(X\) given \(\G\) if \(\E[X\mid\G]\) is integrable, \(\G\)-measurable and

\[\E\big[\E[X\mid\G]\,\ind_G\big]=\E[X\ind_G]\qquad\text{for all }G\in\G.\](14)

The conditional probability is defined as the conditional expectation of an indicator: \(\PP(A\mid\G):=\E[\ind_A\mid\G]\) for \(A\in\F\). If \(\G=\sigma(Y)\) is generated by a random variable \(Y\), we also write \(\E[X\mid Y]\) and \(\PP(A\mid Y)\) for \(\E[X\mid\G]\) and \(\PP(A\mid\G)\).

✎Now try question A4 of Problem Sheet 3.
in wordsDefinition 4.3

We refer to (14) as the defining relation of conditional expectation. Two conditions, two jobs: \(\G\)-measurability says the guess may only use the information in \(\G\); the defining relation says that on every event you can see in \(\G\), the guess has the same integral as \(X\). This is the "local averaging" property of Example 4.1. The difference between \(X\) and \(\E[X\mid\G]\) is that the latter is \(\G\)-measurable, whereas \(X\) is only \(\F\)-measurable.

ExerciseGuessing a die from its parity
Roll a fair die and let \(X\) be the score. Someone tells you only whether \(X\) is even. Write down \(\E[X\mid\G]\), where \(\G=\sigma(\{X\text{ even}\})\).
show answer

\(\G\) has the four events \(\emptyset\), \(E=\{X\text{ even}\}\), \(E^c\) and \(\Omega\), so a \(\G\)-measurable random variable takes one value on \(E\) and one on \(E^c\). On \(E\) the best guess is the average of \(2,4,6\), which is \(4\); on \(E^c\) it is the average of \(1,3,5\), which is \(3\). So \(\E[X\mid\G]=4\cdot\ind_E+3\cdot\ind_{E^c}\). Check the defining property for \(G=E\): \(\E[X\ind_E]=\frac16(2+4+6)=2\) and \(\E[4\ind_E]=4\cdot\frac12=2\). Averaging the guess over everything gives \(\frac12\cdot4+\frac12\cdot3=3.5=\E[X]\), as it should.

Theorem 4.4 (Existence and uniqueness of conditional expectation).p. 33 Let \(X\) be an integrable random variable on a probability space \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\) and \(\G\subseteq\F\) a σ-algebra. The conditional expectation of \(X\) given \(\G\) exists. It is a.s. unique in the sense that if \(Z\) is also a version of the conditional expectation of \(X\) given \(\G\) then \(Z=\E[X\mid\G]\) a.s.

Proof of uniqueness. Let \(Y,Z\) be two conditional expectations of \(X\) given \(\G\). Let

\[G:=\{Y>Z\},\]

the set where they disagree one way. Note that \(G\in\G\), as \(Y,Z\) are \(\G\)-measurable (Lemma 2.3).

By the defining relation, applied to both \(Y\) and \(Z\),

\[\E[Y\ind_G]=\E[X\ind_G]=\E[Z\ind_G],\qquad\text{so}\qquad\E[(Y-Z)\ind_G]=0.\]

But \((Y-Z)\ind_G\ge0\), and a non-negative random variable with expectation zero is zero a.s. (by Markov's inequality, \(\PP((Y-Z)\ind_G>\frac1k)\le k\cdot0\) for each \(k\)). Since \(Y-Z>0\) on \(G\), this forces \(\PP(G)=0\).

Swapping \(Y\) and \(Z\), also \(\PP(Z>Y)=0\), and hence \(Y=Z\) a.s.∎

carefuldefined only up to null sets

So "the" conditional expectation is a random variable defined up to a null set; the different versions disagree only on events of probability zero, and we are free to pick any of them.

set-upmeasures with a density

For existence in general we use another important result from measure theory, the Radon–Nikodym theorem. Given a measure \(\mu\) on a measurable space \((\Omega,\F)\), we can define a new measure \(\nu\) on \((\Omega,\F)\) by taking any measurable \(f\ge0\) and setting

\[\nu(A):=\int_Af\,d\mu.\](15)

(It is countably additive by the Monotone Convergence Theorem.) You know this already: a probability density \(f\) turns Lebesgue measure into the law of a continuous random variable. Is there a converse: can any measure be written in the form (15)? Not every measure, since \(\mu(A)=0\) forces \(\nu(A)=0\). The Radon–Nikodym theorem says this condition is sufficient, if the measures are σ-finite (Definition 1.3).

Theorem 4.5 (Radon–Nikodym).p. 33 Let \((\Omega,\F)\) be a measurable space, and let \(\nu\) and \(\mu\) be σ-finite measures on \((\Omega,\F)\). If

\[\mu(A)=0\ \text{ implies }\ \nu(A)=0\qquad\text{for all }A\in\F,\](16)

then there exists a measurable function \(f:\Omega\to[0,\infty)\) such that \(\nu(A)=\int_Af\,d\mu\) for all \(A\in\F\). The function \(f\) is unique up to \(\mu\)-almost everywhere equality, and is denoted \(f=\frac{d\nu}{d\mu}\).

in wordsTheorem 4.5

The requirement (16) is called absolute continuity of \(\nu\) with respect to \(\mu\), written \(\nu\ll\mu\): \(\nu\) cannot see anything that \(\mu\) doesn't. The function \(f\) is the Radon–Nikodym derivative; the notation \(\frac{d\nu}{d\mu}\) is chosen so that "\(d\nu=\frac{d\nu}{d\mu}\,d\mu\)" reads like the chain rule.

asidedensities, revisited

Remark. The theorem has important uses besides conditional expectation. If \(X\) is a real-valued random variable whose law \(\mu_X=\PP\circ X^{-1}\) is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure \(m\), then the Radon–Nikodym theorem says that \(X\) has a density: \(\mu_X(A)=\int_Af_X(x)\,m(dx)\) with \(f_X=\frac{d\mu_X}{dm}\). If \(X\) is a discrete random variable, then \(\mu_X\) is not absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure (\(\mu_X\) gives positive mass to single points, which are Lebesgue-null), and indeed \(X\) has only a probability mass function, not a density. The Cantor distribution of Chapter 1 is another non-example.

asidewhy we skip the proof

We omit the proof, which is beyond the scope of the course. (Uniqueness of \(f\) is essentially the uniqueness argument for conditional expectation above; existence is more involved.) Instead, let's see how it gives the existence of conditional expectation.

Proof of existence in Theorem 4.4. Non-negative \(X\). Suppose first that \(X\) is non-negative. We want an integrable, \(\G\)-measurable \(Z\) such that

\[\int_AZ\,d\PP=\int_AX\,d\PP\qquad\text{for all }A\in\G.\](17)

So, for \(A\in\G\), let

\[\mathbb Q[A]=\int_AX\,d\PP.\]

This defines a finite measure \(\mathbb Q\) on \((\Omega,\G)\) (note: on \(\G\), not \(\F\)). Let \(\PP|_\G\) denote the measure \(\PP\) restricted to the σ-algebra \(\G\). Then \(\mathbb Q\ll\PP|_\G\), since if \(\PP(A)=0\) then \(\int_AX\,d\PP=0\).

Now apply the Radon–Nikodym theorem to \(\mathbb Q\) and \(\PP|_\G\) on the space \((\Omega,\G)\). It gives a \(\G\)-measurable function

\[Z=\frac{d\mathbb Q}{d\PP|_\G}\]

such that (17) holds.A small subtlety: we are using twice (with \(Y=\ind_AX\) and \(Y=\ind_AZ\)) that if \(Y\) is \(\G\)-measurable, then \(\int Y\,d\PP|_\G=\int Y\,d\PP\). This follows from Remark 2.8: both integrals are determined by the same numbers \(\PP(Y\le t)\). Certainly \(Z\) is integrable, since \(Z\ge0\) and \(\int Z\,d\PP=\int X\,d\PP<\infty\).

General \(X\). Write \(X=X^+-X^-\) in terms of its positive and negative parts. Then \(\E[X^+\mid\G]-\E[X^-\mid\G]\) is \(\G\)-measurable and, by linearity of the integral, satisfies the defining relation.∎

intuitionwhy work on the small σ-algebra

The point of doing it on \((\Omega,\G)\) is that Radon–Nikodym then hands back a function that is measurable for the small σ-algebra \(\G\), which is exactly the constraint we wanted.

carefulexplicit formulas are rare

Remark. In Example 4.1 we found explicit formulas when \(\G\) is generated by a finite partition. For other σ-algebras \(\G\) it is in general not possible to find explicit formulas. But for non-negative integrable \(X\), if \(\I\) is a π-system that generates \(\G\), then it is enough to check the defining relation for \(G\in\I\). (Apply Theorem 1.11 to the two finite measures \(A\mapsto\int_AX\,d\PP\) and \(A\mapsto\int_AZ\,d\PP\) on \((\Omega,\G)\), after also checking they have the same total mass, i.e. \(\E Z=\E X\). For integrable \(X\), consider positive and negative parts separately.)

Here is a picture that makes conditional expectation on a partition concrete, and which will reappear as a martingale in Chapter 6.

Properties of conditional expectationp. 34

≈ 12 min·5 results, 1 figure, 1 exercise·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★★
roadmapthe rules of the game

Let's turn to some elementary properties of conditional expectation. Most of the following are obvious, once you remember one thing: whereas expectation is a number, conditional expectation is a function on \(\Omega\). And since conditional expectation is only defined up to equality almost surely, we have to qualify many statements with "a.s.".

Proposition 4.6.p. 34 Let \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\) be a probability space, \(X\) and \(Y\) integrable random variables, \(\G\subseteq\F\) a σ-algebra and \(a,b,c\) real numbers. Then

  1. \(\E[\E[X\mid\G]]=\E[X]\).
  2. \(\E[aX+bY\mid\G]=a\E[X\mid\G]+b\E[Y\mid\G]\) a.s.
  3. If \(X\) is \(\G\)-measurable, then \(\E[X\mid\G]=X\) a.s.
  4. \(\E[c\mid\G]=c\) a.s.
  5. \(\E[X\mid\{\emptyset,\Omega\}]=\E[X]\).
  6. If \(\sigma(X)\) and \(\G\) are independent then \(\E[X\mid\G]=\E[X]\) a.s.
  7. If \(X\le Y\) a.s. then \(\E[X\mid\G]\le\E[Y\mid\G]\) a.s.
  8. \(\big|\E[X\mid\G]\big|\le\E[|X|\mid\G]\) a.s.

Proof. All of these follow from the requirement that \(\E[X\mid\G]\) be \(\G\)-measurable and the defining relation (14), plus uniqueness. The recipe is always: propose a candidate, check it is \(\G\)-measurable, check the defining relation, conclude by uniqueness.

Part 1. Set \(G=\Omega\) in the defining relation.

Part 2. The candidate \(Z=a\E[X\mid\G]+b\E[Y\mid\G]\) is \(\G\)-measurable, so we just check the defining relation. For \(G\in\G\),

\[\begin{aligned}\int_GZ\,d\PP&=a\int_G\E[X\mid\G]\,d\PP+b\int_G\E[Y\mid\G]\,d\PP\\&=a\int_GX\,d\PP+b\int_GY\,d\PP&&\why{defining relations}\\&=\int_G(aX+bY)\,d\PP.\end{aligned}\]

So \(Z\) is a version of \(\E[aX+bY\mid\G]\), and equality a.s. follows from uniqueness.

Parts 3 and 4. \(X\) itself is \(\G\)-measurable and trivially satisfies \(\E[X\ind_G]=\E[X\ind_G]\). Part 4 is the special case \(X=c\) of part 3, since constants are measurable for every σ-algebra.

Part 5. The only functions measurable with respect to \(\{\emptyset,\Omega\}\) are constants (a non-constant function would have a preimage that is neither \(\emptyset\) nor \(\Omega\)). So \(\E[X\mid\{\emptyset,\Omega\}]\) is a constant, and integrating over \(\Omega\) identifies it as \(\E[X]\).

Part 6. \(\E[X]\) is a constant, so it is \(\G\)-measurable, and for \(G\in\G\),

\[\begin{aligned}\int_G\E[X]\,d\PP&=\E[X]\,\PP[G]=\E[X]\,\E[\ind_G]\\&=\E[X\ind_G]&&\why{independence}\\&=\int_GX\,d\PP.\end{aligned}\]

The independence step: for independent integrable \(U,V\) we have \(\E[UV]=\E[U]\E[V]\). For indicators this is the definition of independence, and the standard machine does the rest. (This is on Problem Sheet 3.)

Part 7. Let \(G=\{\E[X\mid\G]>\E[Y\mid\G]\}\in\G\). Then

\[\E\big[(\E[X\mid\G]-\E[Y\mid\G])\ind_G\big]=\E[(X-Y)\ind_G]\le0,\]

while the integrand on the left is \(>0\) on \(G\). So \(\PP(G)=0\), as in the uniqueness proof.

Part 8. Apply part 7 to \(X\le|X|\) and \(-X\le|X|\), and use part 2.∎

intuitionwhy property 6 is believable

Notice that 6 is intuitively clear. If \(X\) is independent of \(\G\), then telling me about events in \(\G\) tells me nothing about \(X\), so my assessment of its expectation doesn't change. At the other extreme, 3: if \(X\) is \(\G\)-measurable, then telling me about events in \(\G\) actually tells me the value of \(X\).

connectionconvergence theorems, conditionally

The conditional counterparts of our convergence theorems also hold.

Proposition 4.7 (Conditional convergence theorems).p. 35 Let \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) and \(X\) be random variables on a probability space \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\), and let \(\G\subseteq\F\) be a σ-algebra.

  1. cMON: If \(X_n\ge0\) for all \(n\) and \(X_n\uparrow X\) as \(n\to\infty\), then \(\E[X_n\mid\G]\uparrow\E[X\mid\G]\) a.s. as \(n\to\infty\).
  2. cFatou: If \(X_n\ge0\) for all \(n\) then \(\E[\liminf_nX_n\mid\G]\le\liminf_n\E[X_n\mid\G]\) a.s.
  3. cDOM: If \(Y\) is an integrable random variable, \(|X_n|\le Y\) for all \(n\) and \(X_n\to X\) a.s., then \(\E[X_n\mid\G]\to\E[X\mid\G]\) a.s. as \(n\to\infty\).
techniquetransfer via the defining relation

The proofs all use the defining relation (14) to transfer the statement to the ordinary convergence theorems, and are left as an exercise. Here is the first, as a model.

ExerciseConditional monotone convergence
Prove cMON.
show answer

The candidate. By Proposition 4.6(7), the \(Z_n=\E[X_n\mid\G]\) increase a.s. Let \(Z=\lim_nZ_n\) (on the null set where they fail to increase, set \(Z=0\)). Then \(Z\) is \(\G\)-measurable as a limit of \(\G\)-measurable functions.

The defining relation. For \(G\in\G\), apply the Monotone Convergence Theorem twice:

\[\E[Z\ind_G]=\lim_n\E[Z_n\ind_G]=\lim_n\E[X_n\ind_G]=\E[X\ind_G].\]

So \(Z\) satisfies the defining relation for \(\E[X\mid\G]\) (if \(X\) is integrable; otherwise the same argument works with values in \([0,\infty]\)), and uniqueness gives \(Z=\E[X\mid\G]\) a.s.

The other two. cFatou then follows from cMON exactly as Fatou followed from MCT, and cDOM from cFatou as DCT from Fatou.

roadmapthe most useful rules

The following results are very useful in manipulating conditional expectations.

Lemma 4.8 (“Taking out what is known”).p. 36 Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be random variables on \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\) with \(X\), \(Y\) and \(XY\) integrable. Let \(\G\subseteq\F\) be a σ-algebra and suppose that \(Y\) is \(\G\)-measurable. Then

\[\E[XY\mid\G]=Y\,\E[X\mid\G]\quad\text{a.s.}\]
intuitionknown things act like constants

If \(Y\) is known given \(\G\), it behaves like a constant and can be pulled out, just as \(\E[cX]=c\E[X]\).

Proof of Lemma 4.8. The function \(Y\E[X\mid\G]\) is clearly \(\G\)-measurable, so we must check that it satisfies the defining relation for \(\E[XY\mid\G]\). We do this by the standard machine, building \(Y\) up in stages. First suppose that \(X\) and \(Y\) are non-negative.

Indicators. If \(Y=\ind_A\) for some \(A\in\G\), then for any \(G\in\G\) we have \(G\cap A\in\G\), and so by the defining relation for \(\E[X\mid\G]\),

\[\int_GY\,\E[X\mid\G]\,d\PP=\int_{G\cap A}\E[X\mid\G]\,d\PP=\int_{G\cap A}X\,d\PP=\int_GYX\,d\PP.\]

Simple functions. Extend by linearity to simple \(\G\)-measurable random variables \(Y\ge0\).

Non-negative functions. Next suppose that \(Y\ge0\) is \(\G\)-measurable. There is a sequence \((Y_n)\) of simple \(\G\)-measurable random variables with \(Y_n\uparrow Y\), so

\[Y_nX\uparrow YX\qquad\text{and}\qquad Y_n\E[X\mid\G]\uparrow Y\E[X\mid\G],\]

the latter because \(\E[X\mid\G]\ge0\) a.s. The result follows by the Monotone Convergence Theorem.

General signs. Finally, for \(X\), \(Y\) not necessarily non-negative, write \(XY=(X^+-X^-)(Y^+-Y^-)\) and use linearity.∎

Proposition 4.9 (Tower property of conditional expectations).p. 36 Let \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\) be a probability space, \(X\) an integrable random variable and \(\F_1,\F_2\) σ-algebras with \(\F_1\subseteq\F_2\subseteq\F\). Then

\[\E\big[\E[X\mid\F_2]\,\big|\,\F_1\big]=\E[X\mid\F_1]\quad\text{a.s.}\]

In other words, writing \(X_i=\E[X\mid\F_i]\), we have \(\E[X_2\mid\F_1]=X_1\) a.s.

Proof. The left-hand side is certainly \(\F_1\)-measurable, so we need to check the defining relation for \(\E[X\mid\F_1]\). Let \(G\in\F_1\), noting that \(G\in\F_2\) too. Applying the defining relation twice,

\[\begin{aligned}\int_G\E\big[\E[X\mid\F_2]\,\big|\,\F_1\big]\,d\PP&=\int_G\E[X\mid\F_2]\,d\PP&&\why{as $G\in\F_1$}\\&=\int_GX\,d\PP.&&\why{as $G\in\F_2$}\end{aligned}\]
∎
intuitionthe coarser information wins

The coarser information wins: "my best guess, now, of what my better-informed future self will guess" is just my best guess now. This extends Proposition 4.6(1), which (in the light of 4.6(5)) is the case \(\F_1=\{\emptyset,\Omega\}\). It is also the rigorous version of the step labelled "tower property" in Claim 0.3. In Figure 4.2, averaging the level-3 averages over level-1 blocks gives the level-1 averages directly.

connectionJensen, conditionally

Jensen's inequality also extends to the conditional setting.

Proposition 4.10 (Conditional Jensen’s inequality).p. 36 Suppose that \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\) is a probability space and that \(X\) is an integrable random variable taking values in an interval \(I\subseteq\R\). Let \(f:I\to\R\) be convex and let \(\G\) be a sub σ-algebra of \(\F\). If \(\E[|f(X)|]<\infty\) then

\[\E[f(X)\mid\G]\ge f(\E[X\mid\G])\quad\text{a.s.}\]

Sketch proof; not examinable. Take \(I\) to be an open interval so that we don't have to worry about endpoints (they cause inconvenience rather than real problems).

Lines below \(f\). Recall from the proof of Jensen's inequality (Lemma 3.17) that if \(f\) is convex then for every \(m\in I\) we can find a straight line touching \(f\) from below at \(m\): there are \(a,b\in\R\) with

\[f(x)\ge ax+b\quad\text{for all }x\in I,\qquad\text{with equality at }m.\]

Consider the set of all functions \(g(x)=ax+b\) with \(g\le f\) on \(I\). Then \(f\) is the pointwise supremum of this set. Also \(f\) is continuous (convex functions on open intervals are). With a little work, it follows that we can find a countable set of such lines with

\[f(x)=\sup_n\{a_nx+b_n\}\]

(use the supporting lines at rational points).

Conditioning each line. Since \(f(X)\ge a_nX+b_n\), Proposition 4.6 gives

\[\E[f(X)\mid\G]\ge\E[a_nX+b_n\mid\G]=a_n\E[X\mid\G]+b_n\quad\text{a.s.}\](18)

Putting the lines back together. Each of these holds outside a null set. Since a countable union of null sets is null, (18) holds simultaneously for all \(n\) outside a single null set, and so

\[\E[f(X)\mid\G]\ge\sup_n\{a_n\E[X\mid\G]+b_n\}=f(\E[X\mid\G])\quad\text{a.s.}\]
∎
✎Now try questions A3, B3, B4, B5, B6, B7, C5, C6 of Problem Sheet 3.
techniquecountably many a.s. statements at once

The need for countably many lines is typical: we can afford countably many "a.s." statements at once, but not uncountably many. An important special case is \(f(x)=x^p\) for \(p>1\); in particular, for \(p=2\), \(\E[X^2\mid\G]\ge\E[X\mid\G]^2\) a.s.

Conditional expectation is the best mean-square guess

payoffthe best mean-square guess

Remark (Conditional expectation and mean-square approximation). Let \(X,Y\) be square-integrable random variables, \(\G\) a sub σ-algebra of \(\F\), and suppose that \(Y\) is \(\G\)-measurable. Then

\[\begin{aligned}\E[(Y-X)^2]&=\E\Big[\big(Y-\E[X\mid\G]+\E[X\mid\G]-X\big)^2\Big]\\&=\E\big[(Y-\E[X\mid\G])^2\big]+\E\big[(\E[X\mid\G]-X)^2\big]+2\E[WZ],\end{aligned}\]

where \(W=Y-\E[X\mid\G]\) and \(Z=\E[X\mid\G]-X\). Now \(Y\) and \(\E[X\mid\G]\) are \(\G\)-measurable, so \(W\) is \(\G\)-measurable, and using Proposition 4.6(1) and Lemma 4.8,

\[\E[WZ]=\E\big[\E[WZ\mid\G]\big]=\E\big[W\,\E[Z\mid\G]\big].\]

But \(\E\big[\E[X\mid\G]\mid\G\big]=\E[X\mid\G]\), so \(\E[Z\mid\G]=0\). Hence \(\E[WZ]=0\): the cross-terms vanish, and

\[\begin{aligned}\E[(Y-X)^2]&=\E\big[(Y-\E[X\mid\G])^2\big]+\E\big[(\E[X\mid\G]-X)^2\big]\\&\ge\E\big[(\E[X\mid\G]-X)^2\big].\end{aligned}\]

So we minimise \(\E[(Y-X)^2]\) by choosing \(Y=\E[X\mid\G]\). In other words, \(\E[X\mid\G]\) is the best mean-square approximation of \(X\) among all \(\G\)-measurable random variables, which brings us back to where Example 4.1 started. The displayed identity is Pythagoras' theorem, with "\(W\) and \(Z\) are orthogonal" meaning \(\E[WZ]=0\). Indeed this gives a route to existence of conditional expectations without the Radon–Nikodym theorem, sketched next.

4.1Existence via orthogonal projection in L² (not examinable)p. 37

≈ 7 min·1 result, 1 figure·difficulty ●●●·importance ★☆☆
intuitionconditional expectation as a projection

This section gives an alternative, more geometric existence proof. Neither proof is better or worse; they highlight two ways to think about conditional expectation. First recall from Prelims linear algebra: if \(K\subseteq\R^d\) is a linear subspace and \(x\in\R^d\), the orthogonal projection of \(x\) onto \(K\) is the unique vector \(y\in K\) attaining

\[\inf_{y\in K}\|x-y\|_{\R^d}.\]

Equivalently, \(y\) is the unique element of \(K\) such that \(x-y\) is orthogonal to \(K\): \(\langle x-y,z\rangle_{\R^d}=0\) for all \(z\in K\).

Motivated by this, we replace \(\R^d\) by \(\Lp2(\Omega,\F,\PP)\), take as subspace \(K=\Lp2(\Omega,\G,\PP)\) (the square-integrable random variables that are \(\G\)-measurable), and study, for \(X\in\Lp2(\Omega,\F,\PP)\), the problem

\[\inf_{Y\in K}\|X-Y\|_2.\]

If it has a minimiser, that should be our candidate for \(\E[X\mid\G]\). Among all the \(\Lp p\) spaces, \(\Lp2\) is special because it carries an inner product,

\[\langle X,Y\rangle:=\E[XY]\qquad\text{for }X,Y\in\Lp2,\]

with \(\|X\|_2=\sqrt{\langle X,X\rangle}\). In particular we say that \(X,Y\) are orthogonal if \(\langle X,Y\rangle=0\). Having geometry and orthogonality available helps a lot. In fact the minimisation problem is well posed for any complete subspace \(K\).

Theorem 4.11.p. 38 Let \(K\) be a complete vector subspace of \(\Lp2(\Omega,\F,\PP)\). For any \(X\in\Lp2(\Omega,\F,\PP)\) the infimum \(\inf_{Z\in K}\|X-Z\|_2\) is attained by some \(Y\in K\), and \(X-Y\) is orthogonal to \(Z\) for all \(Z\in K\) with \(\|Z\|_2>0\).

Proof. Existence of a closest point. Let \((Y_n)_{n\ge1}\) be a sequence in \(K\) which approaches the infimum, \(\|X-Y_n\|_2\to\Delta\). We argue that the sequence is Cauchy. The tool is the parallelogram law

\[\|u+v\|^2+\|u-v\|^2=2\|u\|^2+2\|v\|^2\]

(expand the inner products). With \(u=X-\frac12(Y_r+Y_s)\) and \(v=\frac12(Y_r-Y_s)\) it reads

\[\|X-Y_r\|_2^2+\|X-Y_s\|_2^2=2\big\|X-\tfrac12(Y_r+Y_s)\big\|_2^2+2\big\|\tfrac12(Y_r-Y_s)\big\|_2^2.\]

Since \(K\) is a vector space, \(\frac12(Y_r+Y_s)\in K\), and in particular \(\|X-\frac12(Y_r+Y_s)\|_2^2\ge\Delta^2\). So

\[\tfrac12\|Y_r-Y_s\|_2^2\le\|X-Y_r\|_2^2+\|X-Y_s\|_2^2-2\Delta^2,\]

and the right side tends to 0 as \(r,s\to\infty\). Hence \(\sup_{r,s\ge n}\|Y_r-Y_s\|_2\to0\), i.e., \((Y_n)\) is Cauchy.

Since \(K\) is complete, there exists \(Y\in K\) with \(\|Y_n-Y\|_2\to0\). Minkowski's inequality (Theorem 3.20) then gives

\[\|X-Y\|_2\le\|X-Y_n\|_2+\|Y-Y_n\|_2,\]

and letting \(n\to\infty\) we see that \(\|X-Y\|_2=\Delta\), as required.

Orthogonality. Now let \(Z\in K\) with \(\|Z\|_2>0\), and note that \(Y+tZ\in K\) for all \(t\in\R\). Using optimality of \(Y\),

\[0\le\|X-(Y+tZ)\|_2^2-\|X-Y\|_2^2=t^2\|Z\|_2^2-2t\,\E[Z(X-Y)].\]

Taking \(t=\E[Z(X-Y)]/\|Z\|_2^2\) (the minimiser of the right side) yields

\[0\le-\frac{\E[Z(X-Y)]^2}{\|Z\|_2^2},\]

which implies \(\E[Z(X-Y)]=0\), as desired.∎

in wordsTheorem 4.11

Remark. The result can be rephrased by saying that any \(X\in\Lp2\) can be written as \(X=Y+(X-Y)\) with \(Y\in K\) and \(X-Y\) orthogonal to \(K\). Such a decomposition is a.s. unique: if there were two, \(Y_1\) and \(Y_2\), their difference would be both in \(K\) and orthogonal to \(K\), hence orthogonal to itself, so \(\E[(Y_1-Y_2)^2]=0\) and \(Y_1=Y_2\) a.s. We call \(Y\) the (orthogonal) projection of \(X\) on \(K\).

roadmapa second existence proof

We now have everything we need for an alternative proof of the existence of conditional expectations.

Proof of existence in Theorem 4.4, again. Square-integrable \(X\). Suppose first that \(X\in\Lp2(\Omega,\F,\PP)\) and let

\[K=\Lp2(\Omega,\G,\PP).\]

Clearly \(K\) is a vector subspace of \(\Lp2(\Omega,\F,\PP)\), and it is complete by Theorem 3.21 (applied on the probability space \((\Omega,\G,\PP)\)). Let \(Y\) be the orthogonal projection of \(X\) on \(K\) from Theorem 4.11.

Then \(Y\) is \(\G\)-measurable since \(Y\in K\). And for \(G\in\G\), \(\ind_G\in K\), and since \(X-Y\) is orthogonal to \(K\),

\[\E[(X-Y)\ind_G]=0:\]

the defining relation holds.

Integrable \(X\). For \(X\in\Lp1\), by linearity it is enough to deal with \(X^\pm\) separately. Suppose thus that \(X\ge0\) and let \(X_n=X\wedge n\). These are bounded and in particular in \(\Lp2\), so \(Y_n=\E[X_n\mid\G]\) exists by the above. Then \(X_n\uparrow X\), and the argument of cMON (Proposition 4.7, which used only the defining relation) shows that \(Y:=\limsup_nY_n\) is a version of \(\E[X\mid\G]\).∎

✎Now try question C4 of Problem Sheet 3. This is the existence proof of Section 4.1 again, now as an exercise.

Chapter 5

Filtrations and stopping times

Information arrives over time, and decisions may use only what has arrived. This short chapter turns those two sentences into definitions: filtrations, adapted processes, and the random times you can act on without peeking into the future.

≈ 22 min · 4 sections · 9 results · 3 figures · 3 exercises · difficulty ●●○ · importance ★★★

Explain step by step in plain language, justify every step and say where tricks come from. Do not solve problem-sheet questions outright: give hints or explain the ideas. Information that grows with timep. 40

≈ 3 min·3 results·difficulty ●○○·importance ★★★
roadmapprocesses, and how information grows

The language and tools we have developed so far lend themselves beautifully to describing sequences of random phenomena, known as stochastic processes. We can capture their dynamics, how we learn information about them as time passes, and their long-run behaviour.

We start with information and how it evolves. This is captured by σ-algebras (Figure 1.4 showed a σ-algebra as a body of information) and by suitable classes of random variables. We work on a fixed probability space \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\). The measure \(\PP\) plays no role in this chapter; it's all about sets, functions and their measurability. \(\PP\) becomes important in the next chapter, when we consider the nature of the random evolution.

Definition 5.1 (Filtration).p. 40 A filtration on the probability space \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\) is a sequence \((\F_n)_{n\ge0}\) of σ-algebras \(\F_n\subseteq\F\) such that \(\F_n\subseteq\F_{n+1}\) for all \(n\). We then call \((\Omega,\F,(\F_n)_{n\ge0},\PP)\) a filtered probability space.

intuitionfiltrations as growing knowledge

Often \(n\) is interpreted as time and \(\F_n\) as everything that can be known by time \(n\). The condition \(\F_n\subseteq\F_{n+1}\) says we never forget anything: an event decided by time \(n\) is still decided at time \(n+1\). We usually start at time 0, but not always. We let

\[\F_\infty=\sigma\Big(\bigcup_{n\ge0}\F_n\Big)\](19)

be the σ-algebra generated by the filtration. This captures all the information we may ever acquire, but it may be smaller than the abstract \(\F\) of our space. (A union of σ-algebras is generally not a σ-algebra, hence the \(\sigma(\cdot)\).)

For coin tossing, \(\F_n\) is generated by the first \(n\) tosses: its atoms (in the sense of Figure 1.4) are the \(2^n\) possible strings of \(n\) results, and each step splits every atom in two. Figure 5.1 below draws this as a tree.

Definition 5.2 (Adapted stochastic process).p. 40 A stochastic process \((X_n)_{n\ge0}\) is a sequence of random variables defined on \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\). The process is integrable if each \(X_n\) is integrable. We say that \((X_n)_{n\ge0}\) is adapted to the filtration \((\F_n)_{n\ge0}\) if, for each \(n\), \(X_n\) is \(\F_n\)-measurable.

in wordsDefinition 5.2

We may write \(X\) for \((X_n)_{n\ge0}\). If \(\F_n\) represents our knowledge at time \(n\), then \(X\) being adapted simply means that \(X_n\) is observable at time \(n\): by time \(n\) we know its value. Here is an obvious example of such a filtration.

Definition 5.3 (Natural filtration).p. 40 The natural filtration \((\F_n^X)_{n\ge0}\) associated with a stochastic process \((X_n)_{n\ge0}\) on the probability space \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\) is defined by

\[\F_n^X=\sigma(X_0,X_1,\dots,X_n),\qquad n\ge0.\]
in wordsDefinition 5.3

A stochastic process \(X\) is automatically adapted to the natural filtration it generates. It is also, by definition, the smallest filtration to which \(X\) is adapted: "what you know if you've watched \(X\) and nothing else".

The index \(n\) could count days, seconds or years. It could also be some other, non-uniform clock, or something more abstract: the \(n\)-th letter in a book, the \(n\)-th word. In B8.2 you will consider continuous index sets such as \(\{t\ge0\}\) instead of the discrete \(\{n:n\ge0\}\) of B8.1. What matters in all these cases is that there is a linear order (which might or might not be naturally interpreted as time).

Stopping timesp. 41

≈ 12 min·3 results, 2 figures, 2 exercises·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★★
motivationrandom times that are still fair

Whatever the interpretation of \(n\), we call specific choices of \(n\) deterministic times: \(n=42\), say, or (indexing by days) the temperature recorded at Greenwich Observatory at noon on the first of July, or the Rolls-Royce Holdings plc closing price on the London Stock Exchange on a given day.

But we often use other, random times: the next time I meet you, the first time you see a yeti, the moment the stock price drops by more than 30% from its past maximum. These are well defined but not known in advance. They are of the type "I know it when it happens". We now make this precise. Much of the power of martingale methods comes from the fact that they work equally well when the index is such a random time.

Definition 5.4 (Stopping time).p. 41 Let \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\) be a probability space and \((\F_n)_{n\ge0}\) a filtration. A random variable \(\tau\) taking values in \(\N\cup\{\infty\}=\{0,1,2,\dots,\infty\}\) is called a stopping time with respect to \((\F_n)_{n\ge0}\) if \(\{\tau=n\}\in\F_n\) for all \(n\).

in wordsDefinition 5.4

So a random time \(\tau\) is a stopping time if at any time \(n\), I can use the information in \(\F_n\) to decide whether to stop now (\(\tau=n\)) or not. Because \((\F_n)\) is a filtration, this is equivalent to \(\{\tau\le n\}\in\F_n\) for all \(n\) ("I stop now or have stopped already"), or to \(\{\tau>n\}\in\F_n\) ("I decide to continue").Why equivalent: \(\{\tau\le n\}=\bigcup_{k\le n}\{\tau=k\}\) and each \(\{\tau=k\}\in\F_k\subseteq\F_n\). Conversely \(\{\tau=n\}=\{\tau\le n\}\setminus\{\tau\le n-1\}\), and \(\{\tau\le n-1\}\in\F_{n-1}\subseteq\F_n\). The value \(\tau=\infty\) means "never stop". Think of a stopping time as a valid strategy for playing a game, investing or gambling: it can rely on information gathered so far, but can't peek into the future. All the examples before the definition have this property.

If the filtration is unambiguous we simply say \(\tau\) is a stopping time; they are sometimes also called optional times. Not all random times are stopping times. If \(n\) counts days of the year and \(\tau\) is the warmest day, then I need all of \(\F_{365}\) to decide when \(\tau\) happened. Likewise, the day in November 2024 on which Rolls-Royce shares were most expensive is not known in advance, or even when it happens: you have to wait until the end of November. It is not a stopping time. Try it below.

intuitioncombining stopping strategies

We now discuss some easy properties of stopping times. If I have two valid strategies, I may decide to stop when the first one tells me to, or when both have told me to; so the minimum and maximum of stopping times should be stopping times.

Proposition 5.5.p. 41 Let \((\Omega,\F,(\F_n)_{n\ge0},\PP)\) be a filtered probability space and \(\tau,\rho\) stopping times. Then

  1. a deterministic time \(t\), \(t(\omega)=n\) for all \(\omega\in\Omega\), is a stopping time;
  2. \(\tau\wedge\rho\) and \(\tau\vee\rho\) are stopping times.
✎Now try question A2 of Problem Sheet 4. Part 2 also uses the tower property from Chapter 4.

Here \(a\wedge b=\min(a,b)\) and \(a\vee b=\max(a,b)\).

ExerciseMinimum and maximum
Prove Proposition 5.5.
show answer

(i) \(\{t=k\}\) is \(\Omega\) if \(k=n\) and \(\emptyset\) otherwise, and both are in every \(\F_k\).

(ii) Use the "\(\le\)" form of the definition:

\[\{\tau\wedge\rho\le n\}=\{\tau\le n\}\cup\{\rho\le n\},\qquad\{\tau\vee\rho\le n\}=\{\tau\le n\}\cap\{\rho\le n\},\]

both in \(\F_n\).

motivationhitting times, the main example

The following proposition says that the first time an adapted process enters a region is a stopping time. This first hitting time is the canonical example of a stopping time; many stopping times are of this type for some process. We use the usual convention \(\inf\emptyset=\infty\): if the process never enters the region, the hitting time is \(\infty\).

Proposition 5.6.p. 41 Let \(X=(X_n)_{n\ge0}\) be an adapted process on \((\Omega,\F,(\F_n)_{n\ge0},\PP)\) and \(B\in\B(\R)\). Then

\[h_B=\inf\{n\ge0:X_n\in B\},\]

the first hitting time of \(B\), is a stopping time.

Proof. The event "\(X\) has been in \(B\) at some time up to \(n\)" is

\[\{h_B\le n\}=\bigcup_{k=0}^nX_k^{-1}(B).\]

Each \(X_k^{-1}(B)\in\F_k\subseteq\F_n\) since \(X\) is adapted, so the union is in \(\F_n\).∎

ExerciseOne step too early
Toss a coin repeatedly and let \(\tau\) be the first time you have seen two heads in a row. Is \(\tau\) a stopping time for the natural filtration? Is \(\tau-1\)?
show answer

\(\{\tau=n\}\) says that tosses \(n-1\) and \(n\) are heads and no earlier pair of consecutive tosses was. That is decided by the first \(n\) tosses, so it lies in \(\F_n\) and \(\tau\) is a stopping time. But \(\{\tau-1=n\}=\{\tau=n+1\}\) depends on toss \(n+1\): knowing the first \(n\) tosses end in a head, you can't yet tell whether the next one will complete the pair. So \(\tau-1\) is not a stopping time. It would require you to stop just before something happens, which is exactly what "I know it when it happens" rules out.

carefullast visits are not stopping times

By contrast, the last time \(X\) is in \(B\) before time \(N\) is generally not a stopping time: to know at time \(n\) that this was the last visit, you need to know that \(X\) won't come back.

What is known at a stopping timep. 41

≈ 2 min·2 results, 1 exercise·difficulty ●●●·importance ★★☆

We often use stopping times because we are interested in the value of the process at that time, the random variable \(X_\tau\). Each \(X_n\) is \(\F_n\)-measurable, since the process is adapted. But what about \(X_\tau\)? It is \(\F_\infty\)-measurable (check!), but we expect it to be measurable with respect to a smaller σ-algebra, reflecting "the information available at time \(\tau\)".

Definition 5.7.p. 41 Let \(\tau\) be a stopping time on \((\Omega,\F,(\F_n)_{n\ge0},\PP)\). We define

\[\F_\tau=\{A\in\F_\infty:A\cap\{\tau=n\}\in\F_n\ \ \forall n\ge0\}.\](20)
in wordsDefinition 5.7

In words: \(A\) is in \(\F_\tau\) if, whenever we stop at time \(n\), we know at that moment whether \(A\) has happened. For example, with \(\tau\) the first time a random walk hits \(5\), the event "the walk visited \(-3\) before hitting \(5\)" is in \(\F_\tau\), but "the walk visits \(-3\) after hitting \(5\)" is not. In the definition we could replace \(\{\tau=n\}\) by \(\{\tau\le n\}\). The following shows that this new notion behaves as we would want.

Proposition 5.8.p. 42 Let \(\tau,\rho\) be stopping times on \((\Omega,\F,(\F_n)_{n\ge0},\PP)\). Then

  1. \(\F_\tau\) defined in (20) is a σ-algebra;
  2. if \(\tau\le\rho\) then \(\F_\tau\subseteq\F_\rho\).
ExerciseInformation at a stopping time
Prove Proposition 5.8.
show answer

(i) We check the three σ-algebra axioms, one at a time.

  • \(\emptyset\cap\{\tau=n\}=\emptyset\in\F_n\).
  • If \(A\in\F_\tau\) then \(A^c\cap\{\tau=n\}=\{\tau=n\}\setminus(A\cap\{\tau=n\})\in\F_n\), since both sets are in \(\F_n\).
  • If \(A_k\in\F_\tau\) then \(\big(\bigcup_kA_k\big)\cap\{\tau=n\}=\bigcup_k(A_k\cap\{\tau=n\})\in\F_n\).

(ii) Use the "\(\le\)" form. Let \(A\in\F_\tau\). Since \(\tau\le\rho\), we have \(\{\rho\le n\}\subseteq\{\tau\le n\}\), so

\[A\cap\{\rho\le n\}=(A\cap\{\tau\le n\})\cap\{\rho\le n\},\]

an intersection of two sets in \(\F_n\).

connectionstopped filtrations

In particular, combining Propositions 5.5 and 5.8, \((\F_{\tau\wedge n})_{n\ge0}\) is a filtration, which is smaller than the original one in the sense that \(\F_{\tau\wedge n}\subseteq\F_n\) for \(n\ge0\) (as \(\tau\wedge n\le n\), and \(\F_n\) for the deterministic time \(n\) is just \(\F_n\)).

Stopped processesp. 42

≈ 4 min·1 result, 1 figure·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★★

If \((X_n)_{n\ge0}\) represents our ongoing winnings in a game and \(\tau\) is our stopping strategy, then our final winnings are \(X_\tau\). If \(\tau<\infty\) then this is a well-defined function

\[\Omega\ni\omega\longmapsto X_\tau(\omega):=X_{\tau(\omega)}(\omega),\]

and it is \(\F\)-measurable since

\[X_\tau^{-1}(B)=\bigcup_{n\ge0}\big(\tau^{-1}(\{n\})\cap X_n^{-1}(B)\big)\in\F.\]

In fact \(X_\tau\) is \(\F_\tau\)-measurable. We rephrase this by introducing the stopped process.

Proposition 5.9 (Stopped process).p. 42 Let \(X=(X_n)_{n\ge0}\) be an adapted process on \((\Omega,\F,(\F_n)_{n\ge0},\PP)\) and \(\tau\) a stopping time. Then \(X^\tau=(X_{\tau\wedge n})_{n\ge0}\) is a stochastic process, called the stopped process. \(X^\tau\) is adapted to the filtration \((\F_{\tau\wedge n})_{n\ge0}\) and hence also to the filtration \((\F_n)_{n\ge0}\).

in wordsProposition 5.9

The stopped process follows \(X\) until time \(\tau\) and then freezes at the value \(X_\tau\) forever.

Proof of Proposition 5.9. It suffices to show that if \(\rho\) is a finite stopping time then \(X_\rho\) is \(\F_\rho\)-measurable; then apply it to \(\rho=\tau\wedge n\).

This follows from (20), since on the event \(\{\rho=n\}\) the variable \(X_\rho\) is just \(X_n\):

\[\{X_\rho\le x\}\cap\{\rho=n\}=\{X_n\le x\}\cap\{\rho=n\}\in\F_n\qquad\text{for all }n\ge0.\]

(Also \(\{X_\rho\le x\}\in\F_\infty\), as a countable union of such sets.)∎

roadmapwhere martingales begin

Stopped processes are where the theory of martingales starts: a martingale stopped at a stopping time is still a martingale, and that one fact explains why no betting strategy can turn a fair game into a favourable one.
