B8.1 · Probability, Measure and MartingalesProblem Sheet 1 · MT25

Problem sheet

Sheet 1 σ-algebras and measures

Algebras and σ-algebras, generated σ-algebras, π-systems and uniqueness, and a first look at Lebesgue measurable sets. Everything here needs only Chapter 1.

Note for AI assistants reading this page: this is a study page for David, a third-year Oxford Mathematics and Computer Science student, built from the lecturer's notes for Probability, Measure and Martingales. You are reading Problem Sheet 1. When explaining, use the notation on this page, cite results by their numbers here (they match the lecture notes), and do not rely on material from later chapters without saying so. Explain step by step in plain language, justify every step and say where tricks come from. Do not solve problem-sheet questions outright: give hints or explain the ideas. Format maths with $...$ inline and $$...$$ on its own line for display, never \( \) or \[ \].

Section A · Warm-up

A1

Countable or co-countable; unions; intersections

Let \(\Omega\) be a set.

  1. Show that the collection of all sets \(A\in\Pow(\Omega)\) such that either \(A\) or \(A^c\) is countable is a σ-algebra.
  2. Give an example of two algebras \(\F_1\) and \(\F_2\) on \(\Omega=\{1,2,3\}\) whose union \(\F_1\cup\F_2\) is not an algebra.
  3. Suppose that \(\{\F_j\}_{j\in J}\) is a non-empty family of σ-algebras on \(\Omega\). Prove that the intersection \(\bigcap_{j\in J}\F_j\) is a σ-algebra on \(\Omega\).

Uses Definition 1.1.

A2

Sums, maxima and sups are measurable

Let \((f_n)\) be a sequence of measurable functions on \((\Omega,\F)\) taking values in \(\R\). Show that \(f_1+f_2\), \(\max\{f_1,f_2\}\) and \(\sup_nf_n\) are all measurable functions.

Uses Definition 2.1 and Proposition 2.2, so this one is best left until Chapter 2.

A3

A 0-1 measure on co-countable sets

On \(\R\) consider the σ-algebra \(\A\) of sets which are either countable or have a countable complement. Let \(\mu(A)=0\) for countable \(A\) and \(\mu(A)=1\) otherwise, for \(A\in\A\). Show that \(\mu\) is a probability measure on \(\A\).

Uses Definition 1.3 and part 1 of question A1.

Section B · To be handed in

B1

σ-algebras from partitions

Let \(P=\{P_j\}_{j\in J}\) be a partition of a set \(\Omega\) (a collection of disjoint non-empty sets with union \(\Omega\)). Show that the set \(U(P)\) consisting of all possible unions of sets \(P_j\) is a σ-algebra on \(\Omega\). Conversely, show that any σ-algebra \(\F\) on a countable set \(\Omega\) is of the form \(U(P)\) for some partition \(P\) of \(\Omega\). [Warning: the converse is very far from true when \(\Omega\) is uncountable.]

B2

Rays generate the Borel sets

Let \(\T\) be the set of all open subsets of \(\R\), and let \(\pi(\R)\) be the π-system

\[\pi(\R):=\{(-\infty,x]:x\in\R\}.\]

Prove that \(\B(\R)\) (defined to be \(\sigma(\T)\)) is equal to \(\sigma(\pi(\R))\). [Hint: recall that every open subset of \(\R\) is a countable disjoint union of (finite or infinite) open intervals.]

This is the exercise left open in Example 1.10.

B3

Continuity at ∅ and countable additivity

Let \(\mu:\A\to[0,\infty)\) be an additive set function on an algebra \(\A\) taking only finite values. Show that \(\mu\) is countably additive if and only if for every sequence \((A_n)\) of sets in \(\A\) with \(A_n\downarrow\emptyset\) we have \(\mu(A_n)\to0\).

This is Lemma 1.5.

B4

Uniqueness fails without a π-system

Let \(\Omega\) be a set and \(\I\) a π-system on \(\Omega\). Let \(\F=\sigma(\I)\). Suppose that \(\mu_1\) and \(\mu_2\) are two measures on \((\Omega,\F)\) with \(\mu_1(\Omega)=\mu_2(\Omega)<\infty\) and \(\mu_1=\mu_2\) on \(\I\). Then a theorem in lectures shows that \(\mu_1=\mu_2\) on \(\F\). Find an example on \(\Omega=\{1,2,3,4\}\) where this fails if we drop the assumption that \(\I\) is a π-system.

The theorem is Theorem 1.11.

B5

Lebesgue sets are Borel up to null sets

Revise the definition of Lebesgue outer measure \(m^*(A)\) and the σ-algebra \(\M_{\mathrm{Leb}}\) of Lebesgue-measurable sets. (The Lebesgue outer measure of any \(A\subseteq\R\) is \(m^*(A)=\inf\{\sum_{i\ge1}|J_i|: J_1,J_2,\dots\text{ intervals with }\bigcup_iJ_i\supseteq A\}\), and \(A\) is Lebesgue measurable if \(m^*(F\cap A)+m^*(F\cap A^c)=m^*(F)\) for every \(F\subseteq\R\).) Show that \(A\subseteq[0,1]\) is Lebesgue measurable if and only if there exist a Borel set \(B\) and a null set \(N\) such that \(A=B\,\Delta\,N\), where \(\Delta\) denotes symmetric difference. Extend this to any \(A\subseteq\R\).

The outer measure is the one sketched after Theorem 1.12, and the aside after Corollary 1.13 compares \(\M_{\mathrm{Leb}}\) with \(\B(\R)\).

B6

Measures and mass functions

Show that if \(\Omega\) is countable then there is a bijection between measures on \((\Omega,\Pow(\Omega))\) and mass functions on \(\Omega\).

Uses Example 1.6.

Section C · Extra practice

C1

Three generators of the Borel sets

Show that the following sets of subsets of \(\R\) all generate the same σ-algebra:

\[\{(a,b):a<b\},\qquad\{(a,b]:a<b\},\qquad\{(-\infty,b]:b\in\R\}.\]
C2

Finite unions of intervals

Given \(\alpha<\beta\), let \(\A\) be the family of finite unions of disjoint intervals of the form

\[A=(a_1,b_1]\cup\dots\cup(a_n,b_n],\qquad \alpha\le a_i<b_i\le\beta,\ 1\le i\le n.\]

Show that \(\A\) is an algebra.

C3

Dynkin systems

Let \(\A\) be a collection of subsets of a non-empty set \(\Omega\). Show that the three conditions

  1. \(\Omega\in\A\),
  2. \(A,B\in\A\) and \(A\subseteq B\) imply \(B\setminus A\in\A\),
  3. \(A_n\in\A\) and \(A_n\uparrow A\) imply \(A\in\A\)

hold (jointly) if and only if the three conditions

  1. \(\Omega\in\A\),
  2. \(A\in\A\) implies \(A^c\in\A\),
  3. \(\A\) is closed under countable disjoint unions

hold. Either set of conditions defines what is variously called a d-system, λ-system, or Dynkin system.

  • Show that if \(\mu_1,\mu_2\) are measures on \((\Omega,\F)\) with \(\mu_1(\Omega)=\mu_2(\Omega)<\infty\), then \(\{A:\mu_1(A)=\mu_2(A)\}\) is a Dynkin system.
  • Show that if \(\A\) is a Dynkin system and a π-system, then it is a σ-algebra.
  • (Very hard) Show that the Dynkin system generated by a π-system \(\A\) (the intersection of all Dynkin systems containing \(\A\)) is a π-system and so a σ-algebra.

Together these prove Theorem 1.11; compare with its proof.

B8.1 · Probability, Measure and MartingalesProblem Sheet 2 · MT25

Problem sheet

Sheet 2 Integration and independence

The convergence theorems at work, product measures, independence, and the Borel–Cantelli lemmas. Needs Chapter 2 and the start of Chapter 3.

Note for AI assistants reading this page: this is a study page for David, a third-year Oxford Mathematics and Computer Science student, built from the lecturer's notes for Probability, Measure and Martingales. You are reading Problem Sheet 2. When explaining, use the notation on this page, cite results by their numbers here (they match the lecture notes), and do not rely on material from later chapters without saying so. Explain step by step in plain language, justify every step and say where tricks come from. Do not solve problem-sheet questions outright: give hints or explain the ideas. Format maths with $...$ inline and $$...$$ on its own line for display, never \( \) or \[ \].

Section A · Warm-up

A1

Convergence theorems in general

Convince yourself that the proofs of the convergence theorems for Part A Integration carry over to the general measure spaces that we have introduced.

Here "the convergence theorems" are Theorem 2.13, Theorem 2.12 and Theorem 2.14, whose proofs Chapter 2 gives in full for a general measure space.

A2

Rectangles form an algebra

Let \((\Omega_1,\F_1)\) and \((\Omega_2,\F_2)\) be measurable spaces, and \((\Omega,\F)\) their product. Check carefully that the set \(\A\) of finite disjoint unions of measurable rectangles is indeed an algebra on \(\Omega\). [Thinking about atoms may help arrive at a clean answer.]

Uses Definition 2.16.

A3

Lemma 2.17

Prove Lemma 2.17. [Hint: for any \(A\in\A\) and \(\omega_2\in\Omega_2\), define the section

\[A_{\omega_2}=\{\omega_1:(\omega_1,\omega_2)\in A\}\subseteq\Omega_1,\]

and consider \(f(\omega_2)=\PP_1[A_{\omega_2}]\).]

A4

Linearity of the integral

Show that if \(f\) and \(g\) are measurable functions on \((\Omega,\F,\mu)\) that are either both non-negative or both integrable, and \(c\in\R\), then

\[\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu,\qquad \int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu.\]

[Hint: use the MCT.]

Uses Definition 2.6, Definition 2.7 and Theorem 2.13.

Section B · To be handed in

B1

Independence with complements

Let \((A_n)\) be a sequence of independent events. Show that if \(I,J\) are disjoint (finite or countable) sets of indices, then

\[\PP\Big[\bigcap_{i\in I}A_i\cap\bigcap_{j\in J}A_j^c\Big]=\prod_{i\in I}\PP[A_i]\prod_{j\in J}\big(1-\PP[A_j]\big).\]

(You may wish to use induction on \(|J|\).)

Uses Definition 2.22 and Lemma 1.4.

B2

Scheffé’s lemma

Prove Scheffé's Lemma: let \((f_n)\) be a sequence of non-negative integrable functions on \((\Omega,\F,\mu)\) and suppose that \(f_n(x)\to f(x)\) for \(\mu\)-almost every \(x\in\Omega\), where \(f\) is also integrable. Then

\[\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\to0\quad\text{if and only if}\quad\int f_n\,d\mu\to\int f\,d\mu.\]

One direction is a one-liner; for the other, \((f-f_n)^+\le f\) and Theorem 2.14 do the work.

B3

Quantile functions build every distribution

Let \(F:\R\to[0,1]\) be an increasing, right-continuous function with \(\lim_{x\to\infty}F(x)=1\) and \(\lim_{x\to-\infty}F(x)=0\). The goal of this exercise is to give an alternative proof that there exists a unique probability measure \(\mu\) on \((\R,\B(\R))\) such that, for all \(x\),

\[\mu((-\infty,x])=F(x).\]

  1. Show that, if \(\mu\) exists, it is unique.
  2. Define \(G:(0,1)\to\R\) by \(G(y):=\inf\{x\in\R:F(x)\ge y\}\). Show that \(G\) is increasing, that \(F(x)\ge y\iff x\ge G(y)\), and deduce that \(G\) is left-continuous (\(G(y)\to G(x)\) as \(y\uparrow x\)).
  3. Let \(\Omega:=(0,1)\), \(\F:=\B((0,1))\) the Borel σ-algebra on \((0,1)\), and \(\PP\) the restriction of Lebesgue measure to \(\F\). Show that \(X:=G\) is a random variable on \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\), and that the induced measure \(\mu_X:=\PP\circ X^{-1}\) satisfies \(\mu_X((-\infty,x])=\PP[X\le x]=F(x)\).

This reproves Theorem 1.15; part 1 is Theorem 1.11 again.

B4

Records and double records

Let \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) be independent random variables, each uniformly distributed on \([0,1]\). Let \(A_n\) be the event that a record occurs at time \(n\):

\[A_n=\{X_n>X_m\text{ for all }m<n\}.\]

Find the probability of \(A_n\) and show that \(A_1,A_2,\dots\) are independent. Deduce that, with probability one, infinitely many records occur. Now consider double records, that is, two records in a row. What is the probability of infinitely many double records?

Uses Lemma 3.3 and Lemma 3.4.

B5

A biased walk returns finitely often

Let \((X_n)_{n\ge1}\) be independent, identically distributed random variables with \(\PP[X_n=1]=p\) and \(\PP[X_n=-1]=1-p\), where \(p\neq\frac12\). Let \(S_0:=0\) and \(S_n:=\sum_{k=1}^nX_k\) for \(n\ge1\). Show that \(\PP[S_n=0\text{ i.o.}]=0\). [You might, or might not, find Stirling's formula useful: \(n!\sim\sqrt{2\pi n}\,n^ne^{-n}\).]

Uses Lemma 3.3. Compare Section 0.3, where \(p=\frac12\).

B6

The symmetric walk visits every integer

Let \((X_n)_{n\ge1}\) be independent with \(\PP[X_n=1]=\PP[X_n=-1]=\frac12\). Let \(S_0:=0\) and \(S_n:=\sum_{k=1}^nX_k\). For \(x\in\Z\) let \(A_x:=\{S_n=x\text{ for infinitely many }n\}\), and

\[B_-:=\Big\{\liminf_{n\to\infty}S_n=-\infty\Big\},\qquad B_+:=\Big\{\limsup_{n\to\infty}S_n=\infty\Big\}.\]

  1. Using Kolmogorov's 0-1 law, prove that \(\PP[B_-]\in\{0,1\}\) and \(\PP[B_+]\in\{0,1\}\).
  2. Prove that \(\PP[B_-]=\PP[B_+]\).
  3. Using a Borel–Cantelli lemma, show that for all \(k\ge1\), \(\limsup_{n\to\infty}(S_{n+k}-S_n)=k\) almost surely.
  4. Deduce from part 3 that \(\PP[B_-^c\cap B_+^c]=0\), and therefore that \(\PP[B_-]=\PP[B_+]=1\). Conclude that \(\PP[A_x]=1\) for all \(x\in\Z\).

Uses Theorem 2.31 and Lemma 3.4.

B7

Tails, sums and maxima

Let \(Z\) be a random variable taking non-negative integer values. Show that \(\E[Z]=\sum_{n\ge1}\PP[Z\ge n]\).

Let \(X\) be an integrable random variable (\(\E[|X|]<\infty\)). Show that for any \(\eps>0\),

\[\sum_{n=1}^\infty\PP[|X|\ge\eps n]<\infty.\]

Now let \((X_i)_{i\ge1}\) be identically distributed random variables and let \(M_n=\max\{|X_j|:1\le j\le n\}\). If \(\E[|X_1|^\alpha]<\infty\) for some \(\alpha\in(0,\infty)\), show that \(M_n/n^{1/\alpha}\to0\) with probability 1. [Hint: fix \(\eps>0\), let \(A_n=\{|X_n|\ge\eps n^{1/\alpha}\}\) and apply the first Borel–Cantelli lemma.]

Section C · Extra practice

C1

No one-colour progressions

Let \((X_n)\) be independent, identically distributed random variables taking values in \(\{R,G\}\) (red and green), with \(\PP[X_n=R]=1-\PP[X_n=G]=\alpha\) for some \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). Show that, almost surely, the sequence has no one-colour arithmetic subsequence: for all \(a,b\in\N\) with \(a\neq0\), \(\{X_{an+b}:n\in\N\}=\{R,G\}\). Now find a deterministic sequence \((x_n)\) with the same property.

C2

Exponential spacings

Let \(X_1,X_2\) be independent exponential random variables with parameter one. Let \(Y_1=\min\{X_1,X_2\}\) and \(Y_2=\max\{X_1,X_2\}-Y_1\). Show that \(Y_1\) and \(Y_2\) are independent. Generalise to three independent exponential random variables with parameter one.

C3

Independent uniforms from binary digits

Let \(\Omega\) be the probability space \(([0,1],\B([0,1]),\PP)\), with \(\PP\) Lebesgue measure. Show that there is a sequence \((X_n)\) of independent random variables on \(\Omega\) with \(\PP[X_n=0]=\PP[X_n=1]=\frac12\) for every \(n\). Show also that for any such sequence on any probability space, \(Y=\sum_{n\ge1}X_n/2^n\) is uniformly distributed on \([0,1]\).

Deduce that there is a sequence \((Y_n)\) of independent random variables on \(\Omega\), each uniform on \([0,1]\). Hence show that there is a product probability measure \(\PP\) on the countable product of \(([0,1],\B([0,1]))\) with itself such that \(\PP[\omega_i\le x]=x\) for all \(i\ge1\) and \(x\in[0,1]\), where \(\omega_i\) is the \(i\)th coordinate of \(\omega=(\omega_i)_{i\ge1}\).

Compare Remark 2.20.

← ContentsPMM
B8.1 · Probability, Measure and MartingalesProblem Sheet 3 · MT25

Problem sheet

Sheet 3 Convergence and conditional expectation

Modes of convergence, the inequalities of Chapter 3, and practice with conditional expectation from Chapter 4.

Note for AI assistants reading this page: this is a study page for David, a third-year Oxford Mathematics and Computer Science student, built from the lecturer's notes for Probability, Measure and Martingales. You are reading Problem Sheet 3. When explaining, use the notation on this page, cite results by their numbers here (they match the lecture notes), and do not rely on material from later chapters without saying so. Explain step by step in plain language, justify every step and say where tricks come from. Do not solve problem-sheet questions outright: give hints or explain the ideas. Format maths with $...$ inline and $$...$$ on its own line for display, never \( \) or \[ \].

Section A · Warm-up

A1

Indicators of limsup and liminf

Show that \(\ind_{\limsup_nA_n}=\limsup_n\ind_{A_n}\) and \(\ind_{\liminf_nA_n}=\liminf_n\ind_{A_n}\).

Uses Definition 3.1.

A2

Maxima of exponentials

Let \((X_n)_{n\ge1}\) be independent exponential random variables with mean 1, and let \(M_n=\max\{X_1,\dots,X_n\}\). Show that

\[\PP\Big[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{M_n}{\log n}=1\Big]=1.\]

Uses Lemma 3.3 and Lemma 3.4.

A3

Where a conditional expectation is positive

Let \(X\ge0\) be a random variable on \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\), and let \(\G\subseteq\F\) be a σ-algebra. Show that \(\{X>0\}\subseteq\{\E[X\mid\G]>0\}\), up to an event of probability zero. Show also that \(\{\E[X\mid\G]>0\}\) is the smallest \(\G\)-measurable event containing \(\{X>0\}\), up to events of probability zero.

Uses Definition 4.3 and Proposition 4.6.

A4

Conditioning with a joint density

Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be bounded random variables on \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\) with joint density \(f(x,y)\), so that \(\PP[(X,Y)\in A]=\int_Af(x,y)\,dx\,dy\) for measurable \(A\subseteq\R^2\). Apply Fubini's theorem to show that

\[\E[X\mid\sigma(Y)]=\frac{\int xf(x,Y)\,dx}{\int f(x,Y)\,dx}.\]

In other words, \(\E[X\mid\sigma(Y)]=g(Y)\) where \(g(y)=\int xf(x,y)\,dx\big/\int f(x,y)\,dx\).

Uses Theorem 2.21 and Definition 4.3.

Section B · To be handed in

B1

Probability implies distribution

Show that convergence in probability implies convergence in distribution.

Uses Definition 3.7.

B2

In probability, not almost surely

Let \((X_n)_{n\ge2}\) be independent random variables with

\[\PP[X_n=n]=\PP[X_n=-n]=\frac1{2n\log n},\qquad\PP[X_n=0]=1-\frac1{n\log n}.\]

Let \(S_n=X_2+\dots+X_n\). Prove that \(S_n/n\to0\) in probability, but not almost surely. [Hint: compute the variance of \(S_n\) for the convergence in probability, and use a Borel–Cantelli lemma for the almost sure part.]

Uses Corollary 3.12 and Lemma 3.4.

B3

Independence, mean independence, uncorrelated

Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be bounded random variables on \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\). Show that each of the following statements implies the next, but that the reverse implications do not hold: (i) \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent; (ii) \(\E[X\mid Y]=\E[X]\) a.s.; (iii) \(\E[XY]=\E[X]\E[Y]\).

Uses Proposition 4.6 and Lemma 4.8.

B4

Each the conditional mean of the other

Suppose that \(X\) and \(Y\) are integrable random variables on \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\) with

\[\E[X\mid Y]=Y\text{ a.s.},\qquad\E[Y\mid X]=X\text{ a.s.}\]

Prove that \(\PP[X=Y]=1\). [Hint: the square-integrable case is immediate. In general, first show that \(\E[Xf(Y)]=\E[Yf(Y)]\) for any bounded measurable \(f\). Then take \(f=\ind_{[c,\infty)}\) and show that \(\E[(X-Y)\ind_{\{Y\ge c>X\}}]=0\) for every \(c\in\R\). Conclude.]

B5

σ(Y)-measurable means a function of Y

Let \(X\) be a \(\sigma(Y)\)-measurable random variable. Show that there is a measurable function \(f:\R\to\R\) such that \(X=f(Y)\). [Hint: first consider \(X=\ind_A\) for a suitable set \(A\).] What can you say when \(X\) is \(\sigma(Y,Z)\)-measurable?

Uses Definition 2.23 and the approximation by simple functions in Section 2.1.

B6

Conditional Markov inequality

Let \(X\) be an integrable random variable, \(\G\subseteq\F\) a σ-algebra, and \(Z\) a strictly positive, \(\G\)-measurable, integrable random variable. Show the conditional Markov inequality:

\[\E\big[\ind_{\{|X|\ge Z\}}\mid\G\big]\le\frac1Z\,\E\big[|X|\mid\G\big]\quad\text{a.s.}\]

Carefully state any properties of conditional expectation that you use.

Compare Lemma 3.11; uses Proposition 4.6 and Lemma 4.8.

B7

Conditioning on sums

Let \(X,Y\) be independent, identically distributed, integrable random variables. Calculate:

  1. \(\E[X\mid X,Y]\) and \(\E[X\mid Y]\);
  2. \(\E[X\mid X+Y]\) and \(\E[Y\mid X+Y]\);
  3. \(\E[h(X,Y)\mid X+Y,X-Y]\) for a bounded Borel measurable \(h:\R^2\to\R\).

Section C · Extra practice

C1

A maximal-type Lᵖ bound

Let \(X,Y\) be positive random variables such that \(x\,\PP(X\ge x)\le\E[Y\ind_{\{X\ge x\}}]\) for all \(x>0\). Prove that for \(p>1\) and \(q=p/(p-1)\), \(\|X\|_p\le q\|Y\|_p\).

C2

Covariance

For \(X,Y\in\Lp2(\Omega,\F,\PP)\) let \(\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=\E\big[(X-\E[X])(Y-\E[Y])\big]=\E[XY]-\E[X]\E[Y]\). Show that \(\mathrm{Cov}\) is bilinear and that \(\mathrm{Var}(X+Y)=\mathrm{Var}(X)+\mathrm{Var}(Y)\) if \(\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=0\). When \(\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=0\) we say \(X\) and \(Y\) are uncorrelated. Independent random variables are uncorrelated; show by a counterexample that the converse can fail.

C3

The parallelogram law

Define \(\langle X,Y\rangle:=\E[XY]\) for \(X,Y\in\Lp2(\Omega,\F,\PP)\); this is well defined because \(XY\in\Lp1\) by Hölder's inequality. Show that \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\) is bilinear and use it to prove the parallelogram law

\[\|X\|_2^2+\|Y\|_2^2=\tfrac12\big(\|X+Y\|_2^2+\|X-Y\|_2^2\big).\]
C4

Conditional expectation as projection

Let \(K\) be a complete vector subspace of \(\Lp2(\Omega,\F,\PP)\).

  1. Show that for any \(X\in\Lp2\) the infimum \(\inf_{Z\in K}\|X-Z\|_2\) is attained by some \(Y\in K\), and that \(X-Y\) is orthogonal to every \(Z\in K\).
  2. Let \(K\) be the space of almost surely constant random variables. Show that the projection of \(X\) onto \(K\) is \(\E[X]\).
  3. Let \(\G\) be a sub-σ-algebra of \(\F\) and \(K=\Lp2(\Omega,\G,\PP)\). Show that the minimiser \(Y\) is a version of \(\E[X\mid\G]\).
  4. Use these results to show that \(\E[X\mid\G]\) exists when we only assume \(X\in\Lp1(\Omega,\F,\PP)\).
This gives a proof of the existence of conditional expectation that avoids the Radon–Nikodym theorem.

This is the route of Section 4.1 and Theorem 4.11.

C5

cMON, cFatou, cDOM

Prove cMON, cFatou and cDOM.

These are the three parts of Proposition 4.7.

C6

Pythagoras for conditional expectations

  1. Show that if \(Y\) is a \(\G\)-measurable random variable, then \(\E\big[Y(X-\E[X\mid\G])\big]=0\) (when the expectations make sense).
  2. Suppose \(\H\subseteq\G\) are σ-algebras and \(\E[X^2]<\infty\). Show that
    \[\E\big[(X-\E[X\mid\G])^2\big]+\E\big[(\E[X\mid\G]-\E[X\mid\H])^2\big]=\E\big[(X-\E[X\mid\H])^2\big].\]

B8.1 · Probability, Measure and MartingalesProblem Sheet 4 · MT25

Problem sheet

Sheet 4 Martingales

Stopping times, optional stopping and martingale convergence. Question A2 needs only Chapter 5; the rest leans on the martingale chapters, which are not written here yet.

Note for AI assistants reading this page: this is a study page for David, a third-year Oxford Mathematics and Computer Science student, built from the lecturer's notes for Probability, Measure and Martingales. You are reading Problem Sheet 4. When explaining, use the notation on this page, cite results by their numbers here (they match the lecture notes), and do not rely on material from later chapters without saying so. Explain step by step in plain language, justify every step and say where tricks come from. Do not solve problem-sheet questions outright: give hints or explain the ideas. Format maths with $...$ inline and $$...$$ on its own line for display, never \( \) or \[ \].

Section A · Warm-up

A1

Martingale transforms

Let \((Y_n)_{n\ge0}\) be a supermartingale on a filtered probability space \((\Omega,\F,(\F_n)_{n\ge0},\PP)\), let \((V_n)_{n\ge1}\) be a non-negative predictable process, and let \(X_0=0\) and

\[X_n=\sum_{k=1}^nV_k(Y_k-Y_{k-1}),\qquad n\ge1.\]

Show that if each \(X_n\) is integrable, then \((X_n)_{n\ge0}\) is a supermartingale. What happens when \(V\) is negative? And/or \(Y\) is a submartingale?

A2

Operations on stopping times

Suppose \(\tau,\rho\) are stopping times on some \((\Omega,\F,(\F_n)_{n\ge0},\PP)\).

  1. Show that \(\tau+\rho\), \(\tau\wedge\rho\) and \(\tau\vee\rho\) are also stopping times. If \(\tau\le\rho\), is \(\rho-\tau\) a stopping time?
  2. Now suppose that for some \(K\ge1\) and some \(\eps>0\) we have, for every \(n\ge0\),

    \[\PP[\tau\le n+K\mid\F_n]\ge\eps\quad\text{a.s.}\]

    Prove that \(\PP[\tau>mK]\le(1-\eps)^m\) and deduce that \(\E[\tau]<\infty\).

Part 1 uses Definition 5.4 and Proposition 5.5; part 2 uses the tower property, Proposition 4.9.

A3

Martingales via stopping times

On a filtered probability space \((\Omega,\F,(\F_n)_{n\ge0},\PP)\), let \((M_n)_{n\ge0}\) be an adapted, integrable process. Show that \(M\) is a martingale if and only if \(\E[M_\tau]=\E[M_0]\) for all bounded stopping times \(\tau\). [Hint: consider \(A\in\F_n\) and the two stopping times \(\tau=n+1\) and \(\tau=n+\ind_{A^c}\).]

A4

What a martingale can and can’t do

Let \((M_n)_{n\ge0}\) be a martingale with \(M_0=0\). Which of the following are possible?

  1. For some \(n\), \(\E[M_n]>0\).
  2. For some almost surely finite stopping time \(\tau\), \(\E[M_\tau]>0\).
  3. \(M_n\to\infty\) as \(n\to\infty\) with probability 1.
What if, in addition, \(M\) is bounded in \(\Lp1\)? What if \(M\) is uniformly integrable?

Section B · To be handed in

B1

Wald’s equation

Suppose \(X_n\), \(n\ge1\), are i.i.d. with finite mean, and \(N\) is a stopping time for the natural filtration of \((X_n)_{n\ge1}\) with \(\E[N]<\infty\). Show Wald's equation:

\[\E\Big[\sum_{n=1}^NX_n\Big]=\E[N]\,\E[X_1].\]
B2

Kelly betting

(Martingale formulation of Bellman's optimality principle.) Your winnings per unit stake on a game are \(\eps_n\) in round \(n\), where \((\eps_n)_{n\ge1}\) are i.i.d. with \(\PP[\eps_n=+1]=p\), \(\PP[\eps_n=-1]=q\) and \(\frac12<p=1-q<1\). Let \(\F_n:=\sigma(\eps_1,\dots,\eps_n)\). Your stake \(V_n\) on game \(n\) is \(\F_{n-1}\)-measurable and lies strictly between 0 and \(Z_{n-1}\), your fortune at time \(n-1\). Assume \(\E[|\log Z_n|]<\infty\) for all \(n\ge0\). You want to maximise the expected "interest rate" \(\E[\log(Z_N/Z_0)]\) at a fixed horizon \(N\), given the constant \(Z_0>0\).

Prove that, if \(Z_n>0\),

\[\E\big[\log(Z_{n+1}/Z_n)\mid\F_n\big]=f(V_{n+1}/Z_n),\qquad f(x):=p\log(1+x)+q\log(1-x).\]

Deduce that for any predictable strategy \((V_n)\), the process \((\log Z_n-n\alpha)_{n\ge0}\) is a supermartingale, where \(\alpha:=p\log p+q\log q+\log2\) (sometimes called the "entropy"). Conclude that \(\E[\log(Z_N/Z_0)]\le N\alpha\). Describe explicitly the strategy for which \((\log Z_n-n\alpha)\) is a martingale and the inequality is an equality.

B3

Branching processes in L²

Let \((Z_n)\) be a Galton–Watson branching process with offspring distribution \(X\), with \(\mu=\E[X]>1\) and \(\sigma^2=\mathrm{Var}[X]<\infty\). Set \(\F_n=\sigma(Z_k:k\le n)\) and \(M_n=Z_n/\mu^n\), an \((\F_n)\)-martingale. Compute \(\E[Z_{n+1}^2\mid\F_n]\) (you may reason conditionally on \(\{Z_n=k\}\), since these events form a countable partition of \(\Omega\)). Using induction, find a formula for \(\E[Z_n^2]\) in terms of \(n\), \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\). Deduce that \((M_n)\) is bounded in \(\Lp2\), and converges in \(\Lp2\) and in \(\Lp1\).

The process is the one from Section 0.5; conditioning on a partition is Example 4.1.

B4

Discrete harmonic functions

Let \(A\subset\Z^2\) be a finite set of lattice points, and let \(B\) (the boundary of \(A\)) be the set of points of \(\Z^2\setminus A\) with at least one horizontal or vertical neighbour in \(A\). Given any \(g:B\to\R\), construct \(f:A\cup B\to\R\) with \(f|_B=g\) and, for every \(v\in A\),

\[f(v)=\frac14\sum_{w\sim v}f(w),\]

the sum running over the four neighbours of \(v\); \(f\) is a discrete harmonic function with boundary condition \(g\). Let \((X_n)_{n\ge0}\) be a simple symmetric random walk on \(\Z^2\) with \(X_0\in A\), and let \(h_B=\inf\{n\ge0:X_n\in B\}\). Show that \(f(X_{n\wedge h_B})\), \(n\ge0\), is a martingale for the natural filtration of \(X\). [Hint: for \(v\in A\), start a walk at \(v\) and consider \(g(X_{h_B})\).]

\(X_{n\wedge h_B}\) is the stopped process of Proposition 5.9.

B5

Gambler’s ruin

(Gambler's ruin.) Let \((X_n)_{n\ge1}\) be i.i.d. with \(\PP[X_1=1]=p\), \(\PP[X_1=-1]=q\), \(0<p=1-q<1\) and \(p\ne q\). For integers \(0<a<b\) define \(S_n:=a+X_1+\dots+X_n\) and \(\tau:=\inf\{n:S_n=0\text{ or }S_n=b\}\). Let \(\F_n:=\sigma(X_1,\dots,X_n)\) and check that \(\tau\) is a stopping time. Prove that

\[M_n:=\Big(\frac qp\Big)^{S_n}\quad\text{and}\quad N_n:=S_n-n(p-q)\]

are martingales for \((\F_n)\). Deduce the values of \(\PP[S_\tau=0]\) and \(\E[\tau]\). [Argue the use of the optional stopping theorem carefully: you could use \(\tau\wedge m\) and let \(m\to\infty\).]

That \(\tau\) is a stopping time follows from Definition 5.4; compare Figure 5.1.

B6

Likelihood ratios

Toss a coin repeatedly, with \(X_i\) the outcome of the \(i\)th toss, on a space \((\Omega,\F)\) carrying two probability measures \(\PP_A\) and \(\PP_B\): under hypothesis A the probability of heads is \(a\), under hypothesis B it is \(b\), for some \(a,b\in(0,1)\). Write \(\PP_A(x_1,\dots,x_n)=\PP_A(X_1=x_1,\dots,X_n=x_n)\), and similarly for \(\PP_B\). Show that

\[Z_n=\frac{\PP_A(X_1,\dots,X_n)}{\PP_B(X_1,\dots,X_n)}\]

is a martingale under \(\PP_B\) for the filtration \(\F_n=\sigma(X_k:k\le n)\). Conclude that \(Z_\infty:=\lim_nZ_n\) exists with probability 1. If \(b\ne a\), what is the distribution of \(Z_\infty\)? Deduce that \(1/Z_n\) is a \(\PP_A\)-martingale and comment on its convergence. (This is a special case of the consistency of the likelihood ratio test.)

B7

Pólya’s urn

(Pólya's urn.) At time 0 an urn holds one white ball and one black ball. At each step we draw a ball uniformly at random and return it together with another ball of the same colour. So at time \(n\) there are \(n+2\) balls, of which \(B_n\) are black and \(W_n=n+2-B_n\) white, with \(B_n\in\{1,\dots,n+1\}\). Show that \(\PP(B_n=k)=\frac1{n+1}\) for \(k=1,\dots,n+1\). Show that \(M_n=B_n/(n+2)\) is a martingale for a filtration you should specify. Conclude that \(M_n\) converges to some \(M_\infty\), say in what sense, and find the distribution of \(M_\infty\).

B8

Martingales bounded in L²

Let \((M_n)_{n\ge0}\) be a martingale on \((\Omega,\F,(\F_n)_{n\ge0},\PP)\).

  1. Show that \((M_n)\) is bounded in \(\Lp2\) if and only if

    \[\E[M_0^2]<\infty\quad\text{and}\quad\sum_{k\ge1}\E\big[(M_k-M_{k-1})^2\big]<\infty.\]

  2. Assume \((M_n)\) is bounded in \(\Lp2\). Show that there is a random variable \(M_\infty\) with \(M_n\to M_\infty\) a.s. and \(\lim_n\E[(M_n-M_\infty)^2]=0\), that is, \(M_n\to M_\infty\) in \(\Lp2\). [Hint: use Doob's forward convergence theorem for the a.s. limit and part 1 for the \(\Lp2\) convergence.]

Section C · Extra practice

C1

The extinction martingale

For a Galton–Watson process with offspring generating function \(f(\theta)=\E[\theta^X]\), show that \(W_n=q^{Z_n}\) is a martingale (specify the filtration), where \(q\) is the smallest root of \(\theta=f(\theta)\) in \([0,1]\).

C2

Waiting for HTHTHT

Flip a fair coin repeatedly. What is the expected number of tosses until the pattern HTHTHT first appears? What are the largest and smallest expected waiting times for patterns of length 6? Give a pattern attaining each.

C3

Pólya’s urn reaching 3/4

Show that the probability that the fraction of white balls in Pólya's urn is ever as large as \(3/4\) is at most \(2/3\). Is it equal to \(2/3\), or smaller?

C4

Conditional expectations along a filtration

Show that if \((\F_n)\) is a filtration with \(\F_\infty=\sigma\big(\bigcup_n\F_n\big)\) and \(Y_n\to Y\) in \(\Lp1\), then \(\E[Y_n\mid\F_n]\to\E[Y\mid\F_\infty]\) in \(\Lp1\).

C5

Exponential martingales

Let \((Y_n)_{n\ge1}\) be i.i.d. and \(t\in\R\) with \(\psi(t)=\E[e^{tY_1}]<\infty\). Let \(S_0=0\), \(S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nY_k\) and \(M_n=e^{tS_n}/\psi(t)^n\). Show that \((M_n)\) is a martingale (an exponential martingale). Must \(M_n\) converge as \(n\to\infty\)?

C6

Martingales of Markov chains

Let \((X_n)_{n\ge0}\) be a Markov chain on a finite state space \(S\), let \(g:S\to\R\) and \(M_n=g(X_n)\).

  1. If the chain is irreducible, show that \(M\) is a martingale only when \(g\) is constant.
  2. In general, which \(g\) give martingales? (Consider how \(g\) behaves on each closed communicating class.)
  3. Show that part 1 can fail on a countably infinite state space.

CS · MT26 · Computational Learning TheoryChapter 1 · notes pp. 1–19

Chapter 1

Probably approximately correct

A learner sees labelled examples and must guess the rule behind them. This chapter turns that into mathematics: what counts as success, what it may cost, and a first example of a rule that is easy to state but hard to learn.

≈ 47 min · 6 sections · 8 results · 5 figures · 3 exercises · difficulty ●●○ · importance ★★★

Note for AI assistants reading this page: this is a study page for David, a third-year Oxford Mathematics and Computer Science student, built from the lecturer's notes for Computational Learning Theory. You are reading Chapter 1 (Probably approximately correct learning). When explaining, use the notation on this page, cite results by their numbers here (they match the lecture notes), and do not rely on material from later chapters without saying so. Explain step by step in plain language, justify every step and say where tricks come from. Do not solve problem-sheet questions outright: give hints or explain the ideas. Format maths with $...$ inline and $$...$$ on its own line for display, never \( \) or \[ \].
roadmapwhy the definitions must be robust

This course asks what it means for a computer to learn from examples, and when learning is possible. The answers have to be robust. If a small change to the definitions turned a learnable problem into an unlearnable one, the definitions would be telling us about themselves rather than about learning. So we build the framework slowly, one choice at a time, and come back later to check that the choices didn't matter much.

1.1A Rectangle Learning Gamep. 1

≈ 11 min·1 figure, 1 exercise·difficulty ●○○·importance ★★★
set-upthe rectangle game

Here is a game. Some points in the plane are labelled positive (\(+\)) or negative (\(-\)). We are promised that there is an axis-aligned rectangle (one whose sides are horizontal and vertical) such that the points inside it are exactly the positive ones. The rectangle itself is hidden. Our task is to produce a rectangle that is "close" to the hidden one.

examplebananas

Why would anyone care? The notes suggest bananas. Measure each banana's curvature and length. A banana passes the regulations if both numbers are "medium", which means they lie between some lower and upper limits. The regulator knows the limits; we don't. We only see which of our bananas passed. From that we want a rule good enough to predict whether the next banana will pass.

Write \(R\) for the hidden rectangle and \(c_R:\R^2\to\{+,-\}\) for its labelling rule: \(c_R(x)=+\) if \(x\) lies in \(R\) and \(c_R(x)=-\) otherwise.[[A function whose range has at most two values is called boolean. Which two values doesn't matter, so the notes switch freely between \(\{+,-\}\), \(\{0,1\}\) and \(\{-1,+1\}\).]]

intuitionthe tightest fit

The obvious strategy is to draw the smallest axis-aligned rectangle containing every positive point. Call it \(R'\) and predict \(+\) inside it, \(-\) outside. This is the tightest fit algorithm.

carefulwhere it can go wrong

Since every positive point lies in \(R\), and \(R'\) is the smallest rectangle containing them, \(R'\) sits inside \(R\). So the tightest fit never calls a negative point positive. Its only mistakes are on the strip of \(R\) that \(R'\) doesn't reach. If the points we are asked about later tend to fall in that strip, we will do badly. That observation forces a choice: the data we learn from should look like the data we are tested on.

Measuring error with a distribution

set-uperror under a distribution

Let \(\D\) be a probability distribution on \(\R^2\). For now assume \(\D\) has a continuous density that is positive everywhere; Exercise 1.1 in the notes, and Sheet 1, remove this assumption. The training data are \(m\) points drawn independently from \(\D\), each labelled by \(c_R\). The error of a hypothesis \(h\) is the chance that it disagrees with the truth on a fresh point from the same distribution:

\[\err(h;c_R,\D)=\PP_{x\sim\D}\big[h(x)\neq c_R(x)\big].\](1.1)

When \(c_R\) and \(\D\) are clear we just write \(\err(h)\).

For machine learners · Training and test data

In applied machine learning the data are split into a training set, used to fit the model, and a test set, used to estimate its error. Done properly, the error on the test set is an unbiased estimate of \(\err(h)\) in (1.1). People also hold out a validation set to choose between several trained models. In this course choosing between models counts as part of the learning algorithm, so no separate validation set appears.

roadmapwhat we will prove

We now show that the tightest fit is good: for any target accuracy \(\eps>0\) and confidence \(1-\delta\), enough data makes \(\err(h_{R'})\le\eps\) with probability at least \(1-\delta\).

intuitionfour strips

The trick is to look at four strips \(T_1,T_2,T_3,T_4\) running along the inside of the four sides of \(R\), each chosen so that a point drawn from \(\D\) lands in it with probability exactly \(\eps/4\). (The continuous density guarantees that strips of exactly this mass exist.) The strips may overlap at the corners, which only helps.

Suppose the sample contains at least one point in each strip. Those points are positive, so \(R'\) must reach into every strip, and everything \(R'\) misses lies in \(T_1\cup T_2\cup T_3\cup T_4\). That union has probability at most \(\eps/4+\eps/4+\eps/4+\eps/4=\eps\), so \(\err(h_{R'})\le\eps\). Tick show strips in Figure 1.1 to watch this happen. When a strip is empty, the missed region can reach well beyond it, and its mass is no longer controlled.

Background · The union bound

For any events \(A_1,\dots,A_k\),

\[\PP[A_1\cup\dots\cup A_k]\le\PP[A_1]+\dots+\PP[A_k].\]

The right side counts outcomes in several \(A_i\) more than once, so it can only be too big. The bound needs no independence at all, which is why it appears in almost every proof in this course: when you want to show that none of several bad things happens, bound each one separately and add.

Background · The inequality \(1-x\le e^{-x}\)

The curve \(y=e^{-x}\) is convex and its tangent line at \(x=0\) is \(y=1-x\). A convex function lies above its tangent lines, so \(1-x\le e^{-x}\) for every real \(x\). Raising both sides to the power \(m\) (both are non-negative when \(0\le x\le1\)) gives \((1-x)^m\le e^{-mx}\). This turns "\(m\) independent misses" into an exponential that is easy to solve for \(m\).

techniqueunion bound, then 1 − x ≤ e^−x

So the only way to fail is to miss a strip entirely. Let \(A_i\) be the event that none of the \(m\) sample points lands in \(T_i\). One point misses \(T_1\) with probability \(1-\eps/4\), and the points are independent, so \(\PP[A_1]=(1-\eps/4)^m\), and the same holds for each \(A_i\). By the union bound,

\[\PP[A_1\cup A_2\cup A_3\cup A_4]\le4\Big(1-\frac\eps4\Big)^m\le4\exp\Big(-\frac{m\eps}4\Big).\](1.2)

The right side is at most \(\delta\) as soon as

\[m\ge\frac4\eps\log\frac4\delta.\](1.3)

With that many examples, the tightest fit has error at most \(\eps\) with probability at least \(1-\delta\). (Here and throughout, \(\log\) is the natural logarithm.)

in wordsaccuracy and confidence

Read \(\eps\) as an accuracy parameter and \(\delta\) as a confidence parameter. The bound (1.3) asks for more data as either gets smaller, which is reasonable, and the price is modest. Halving the error, from \(\eps=0.02\) to \(\eps=0.01\) say, only doubles the data the bound asks for, and the dependence on \(\delta\) is logarithmic.[[So far this is only an upper bound for one algorithm. Chapter 3 proves lower bounds that hold for every algorithm, and shows the \(1/\eps\) scaling can't be beaten.]]

ExerciseOne percent, ninety-nine times out of a hundred
How many examples does (1.3) ask for if we want error at most \(1\%\) with probability at least \(99\%\)?
show answer

Take \(\eps=\delta=0.01\). Then \(\frac4\eps=400\) and \(\log\frac4\delta=\log400\approx5.99\), so \(m\ge400\times5.99\approx2397\) examples suffice. Notice that \(\delta\) enters only through the logarithm: asking for \(99.99\%\) confidence instead would raise \(\log(4/\delta)\) to about \(10.6\), less than doubling the sample.

carefulcorner cases

One corner case: what if we see no positive points at all, or only one? Allow degenerate rectangles (the empty set, single points, and segments parallel to an axis). Then the tightest fit is always defined, and the argument above goes through unchanged. If after \(m\ge\frac4\eps\log\frac4\delta\) draws we have still seen no positive point, predicting "negative" everywhere has error at most \(\eps\) with probability at least \(1-\delta\). Later corner cases of this kind will be left to you.

✎Now try question 1 of Problem Sheet 1. The non-optional part needs only the argument above.

1.2Key Components of the PAC Learning Frameworkp. 4

≈ 13 min·3 results, 2 figures·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★★
roadmapfrom a game to a framework

The rectangle game already contains the main features of a mathematical theory of learning.

  1. The learner does not know the target, otherwise there would be nothing to learn. It does know the set of possible targets: in the game, the target is always an axis-aligned rectangle.
  2. The learner sees data drawn independently from a distribution \(\D\), and we assume nothing about \(\D\). Real environments are complicated, and pretending the data come from some tidy distribution would be unrealistic.
  3. The learner's output is judged on the same distribution \(\D\) that produced the training data.
  4. Learning should be efficient in two senses. It should be statistically efficient, needing few examples, and computationally efficient, running in reasonable time. Usually "efficient" will mean polynomial in the relevant size parameters.
set-upvocabulary

Here is the vocabulary that makes these precise.

The instance space \(\X\) is the set of possible inputs. In the game it was \(\R^2\). For image classification it might be arrays of pixel colours. In this course \(\X\) will almost always be \(\{0,1\}^n\) or \(\R^n\).

A concept over \(\X\) is a boolean function \(c:\X\to\{0,1\}\), and a concept class \(\C\) is a set of concepts. In the game, \(\C\) is the set of indicator functions of axis-aligned rectangles. The learner knows \(\C\) but not which \(c\in\C\) is labelling the data. A class that is too small may not describe the real process; one that is too large, such as all boolean functions, leaves no hope of efficient learning.

Data come from an example oracle \(\EX(c,\D)\). Each call draws \(x\sim\D\) independently and returns the labelled example \((x,c(x))\). Each call costs one unit of time.

1.2.1 PAC learning: take I

set-uphypotheses and their error

The function a learner outputs is called a hypothesis, to tell it apart from the target. Its error is defined just as in (1.1):

\[\err(h;c,\D)=\PP_{x\sim\D}\big[h(x)\neq c(x)\big].\](1.4)

Definition 1.1 (PAC learning, take I).p. 6 Let \(\C\) be a concept class over \(\X\). We say \(\C\) is PAC learnable (take I) if there is a learning algorithm \(L\) with the following property. For every concept \(c\in\C\), every distribution \(\D\) over \(\X\), and every \(0<\eps<\frac12\) and \(0<\delta<\frac12\), if \(L\) has access to \(\EX(c,\D)\) and is given \(\eps\) and \(\delta\), then with probability at least \(1-\delta\) it outputs a hypothesis \(h\in\C\) with \(\err(h)\le\eps\). The probability is over the random examples and any internal randomness of \(L\). The number of calls to \(\EX(c,\D)\), the sample complexity, must be bounded by a polynomial in \(1/\eps\) and \(1/\delta\).

If moreover the running time of \(L\) is polynomial in \(1/\eps\) and \(1/\delta\), then \(\C\) is efficiently PAC learnable (take I).

in wordsDefinition 1.1

PAC stands for probably approximately correct. "Approximately correct" because we only ask for error at most \(\eps\): two concepts may differ on a single point that \(\D\) almost never produces, and no finite sample can tell them apart. "Probably" because the sample might be unrepresentative, a rare but real possibility, and then the algorithm is allowed to fail.

Theorem 1.2.p. 6 The concept class of axis-aligned rectangles in \(\R^2\) is efficiently PAC learnable (take I).

connectionSection 1.1 is the proof

The proof is the analysis of Section 1.1: the tightest fit runs in time linear in \(m\), and (1.3) gives \(m\) polynomial in \(1/\eps\) and \(\log(1/\delta)\).

1.2.2 PAC learning: take II

motivationharder targets deserve more

Take I ignores how complicated the targets are. Learning a rectangle should be easier than learning a blobby region with a long wiggly boundary, and a fair definition should give the harder class more resources. A rectangle is described by four numbers; a complicated shape needs many more.

exampleone function, many descriptions

The point is clearest for boolean functions on the hypercube \(\{0,1\}^n\), the set of bit strings of length \(n\). One function can be written down in many ways: as its truth table with \(2^n\) entries, as a circuit of \(\wedge\) (and), \(\vee\) (or) and \(\neg\) (not) gates, or in disjunctive normal form (DNF), an "or" of "and"s of literals, like

\[(z_1\wedge\bit{z_3}\wedge z_7)\vee(z_2\wedge z_4\wedge\bit{z_8})\vee(z_1\wedge z_3).\]

Here \(\bit{z_3}\) means "not \(z_3\)". The choice can change the length of the description enormously: the parity function \(z_1\oplus\dots\oplus z_n\) has a circuit of size \(O(n)\) but needs at least \(2^{n-1}\) terms in DNF (Exercise 1.2 in the notes).

set-upsizes of concepts and instances

A representation scheme for \(\C\) is an onto map \(R:\Sigma^*\to\C\), where \(\Sigma\) is a finite alphabet and \(\Sigma^*\) is the set of finite strings over it. Any string \(\sigma\) with \(R(\sigma)=c\) is a representation of \(c\). A size function on strings then gives each concept a size,

\[\size(c)=\min\{\size(\sigma):R(\sigma)=c\},\]

the length of its shortest description.[[For classes like rectangles that need real numbers, allow strings over \(\Sigma\cup\R\), and count each real number as one unit of storage and each arithmetic operation on reals as one unit of time.]]

Instances have sizes too. A \(10\times10\) black-and-white image is 100 bits; a \(1024\times1024\) colour image is over three million numbers. Bigger instances should be allowed more time, if only to read them. So we let \(\X_n\) be \(\{0,1\}^n\) or \(\R^n\), let \(\C_n\) be a concept class over \(\X_n\), and consider all sizes at once: \(\X=\bigcup_{n\ge1}\X_n\) and \(\C=\bigcup_{n\ge1}\C_n\).

Definition 1.3 (PAC learning, take II).p. 8 For \(n\ge1\) let \(\C_n\) be a concept class over \(\X_n\), and let \(\C=\bigcup_n\C_n\) and \(\X=\bigcup_n\X_n\). We say \(\C\) is PAC learnable (take II) if there is an algorithm \(L\) such that for every \(n\), every \(c\in\C_n\), every distribution \(\D\) over \(\X_n\) and every \(0<\eps,\delta<\frac12\): given access to \(\EX(c,\D)\) and inputs \(n\), \(\size(c)\), \(\eps\) and \(\delta\), \(L\) outputs \(h\in\C_n\) that with probability at least \(1-\delta\) satisfies \(\err(h)\le\eps\). The sample complexity must be bounded by a polynomial in \(n\), \(\size(c)\), \(1/\eps\) and \(1/\delta\).

If moreover the running time is polynomial in \(n\), \(\size(c)\), \(1/\eps\) and \(1/\delta\), then \(\C\) is efficiently PAC learnable (take II).

carefulefficiency depends on representation

In most examples every \(c\in\C_n\) has size bounded by a fixed polynomial in \(n\), and then efficiency simply means polynomial in \(n\), \(1/\eps\) and \(1/\delta\). But the definition is sensitive to the representation. If every boolean function is written as a truth table, then \(\size(c)=2^n\) and the class of all boolean functions becomes "efficiently" learnable, because the algorithm is allowed time polynomial in \(2^n\). With decision trees, circuits or DNF formulas as the representation, it is widely believed that all boolean functions are not efficiently learnable, and later chapters give evidence from cryptography.

1.3Learning Conjunctionsp. 9

≈ 10 min·2 results, 1 figure, 1 exercise·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★★
set-upconjunctions

Our second problem is on the hypercube. An instance \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) is an assignment of values to \(n\) boolean variables \(z_1,\dots,z_n\). A literal is a variable \(z_i\) or its negation \(\bit{z_i}\). A conjunction (or term) is an "and" of literals, for instance with \(n=10\):

\[\varphi=z_1\wedge\bit{z_3}\wedge\bit{z_8}\wedge z_9.\](1.5)

So \(\varphi(x)=1\) exactly when \(x_1=1\), \(x_3=0\), \(x_8=0\) and \(x_9=1\); the other six bits are free. Formally a conjunction is given by two sets \(P,N\subseteq[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}\), the indices of its positive and negative literals:

\[\varphi_{P,N}=\bigwedge_{i\in P}z_i\wedge\bigwedge_{i\in N}\bit{z_i}.\](1.6)

We allow \(P\cap N\neq\emptyset\), so that \(z_1\wedge\bit{z_1}\), which is false everywhere, is a conjunction. With \(P=N=\emptyset\) we get the empty conjunction, true everywhere. Let \(\mathrm{CONJUNCTIONS}_n=\{\varphi_{P,N}:P,N\subseteq[n]\}\). Each of \(P\) and \(N\) is a bit string of length \(n\), so every conjunction has a representation of size \(2n\).

ExerciseHow many conjunctions?
How many different functions \(\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) are conjunctions?
show answer

A conjunction with \(P\cap N=\emptyset\) is determined by choosing, for each variable, whether it appears positively, negatively, or not at all, and different choices give different functions (each one has a different set of satisfying assignments, a "subcube"). That gives \(3^n\) functions. Every conjunction with \(P\cap N\neq\emptyset\) is the constant \(0\), which is one more function. So there are \(3^n+1\). In particular at least \(2^n\), so any representation needs at least \(n\) bits for some conjunctions, and \(2n\) is not wasteful.

intuitionstart cautious, delete what the data refute

The oracle \(\EX(c,\D)\) returns pairs \((x,y)\) with \(y=c(x)\): \(y=1\) when \(x\) satisfies the target conjunction \(c\). Algorithm 1.1 starts with the most cautious hypothesis, the conjunction of all \(2n\) literals, which is false everywhere. Every positive example then tells it some literals that cannot be in the target, and it deletes them. Negative examples are ignored.

Algorithm 1.1 CONJUNCTIONS learner
  1. Input: \(n\), \(m\), access to \(\EX(c,\D)\)
  2. set \(h=z_1\wedge\bit{z_1}\wedge z_2\wedge\bit{z_2}\wedge\dots\wedge z_n\wedge\bit{z_n}\) all \(2n\) literals
  3. for \(i=1,\dots,m\):
  4. draw \((x_i,y_i)\) from \(\EX(c,\D)\)
  5. if \(y_i=1\): ignore negative examples
  6. for \(j=1,\dots,n\):
  7. if \(x_{i,j}=0\), drop \(z_j\) from \(h\); else drop \(\bit{z_j}\) from \(h\)
  8. Output: \(h\)
in wordsAlgorithm 1.1

The output is the longest conjunction consistent with the data: a literal is removed only when some positive example proves it can't be in the target. In particular the literals of \(c\) are never removed, so \(h\) only ever says \(1\) where \(c\) does. Figure 1.4 lets you run it.

Theorem 1.4.p. 10 If \(m\ge\frac{2n}\eps\log\frac{2n}\delta\), Algorithm 1.1 efficiently PAC (take II) learns CONJUNCTIONS.

Proof. Setting up. Fix the target \(c\) and the distribution \(\D\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\). Think of a literal \(\ell\) as a one-literal conjunction, so \(\ell(x)=x_i\) if \(\ell=z_i\) and \(\ell(x)=1-x_i\) if \(\ell=\bit{z_i}\). Let

\[p(\ell)=\PP_{x\sim\D}\big[c(x)=1\text{ and }\ell(x)=0\big],\]

the chance that a fresh example would knock \(\ell\) out of \(h\). If \(p(\ell)>0\) then \(\ell\) is not in \(c\), since a literal of \(c\) is \(1\) wherever \(c\) is.

Harmful literals get removed. Call \(\ell\) harmful if \(p(\ell)\ge\eps/2n\). Harmful literals are the ones that would cost us if they survived, so we show that with high probability they all get removed.

Let \(A_\ell\) be the event that the harmful literal \(\ell\) survives all \(m\) draws. That needs every draw to avoid \(\{c=1,\ell=0\}\), so

\[\PP[A_\ell]\le(1-\eps/2n)^m.\]

There are at most \(2n\) harmful literals, so by the union bound the event \(E\) that some harmful literal survives has

\[\PP[E]\le2n\Big(1-\frac\eps{2n}\Big)^m\le2n\exp\Big(-\frac{m\eps}{2n}\Big),\]

which is at most \(\delta\) when \(m\ge\frac{2n}\eps\log\frac{2n}\delta\).

Harmless survivors cost little. Now suppose \(E\) does not happen, so every literal left in \(h\) is harmless. Since \(h\) is never \(1\) where \(c\) is \(0\), an error on \(x\) means \(c(x)=1\) and \(h(x)=0\), and then some literal \(\ell\) of \(h\) has \(\ell(x)=0\). Each such \(\ell\) is harmless and there are at most \(2n\) of them, so

\[\begin{aligned}\err(h)&=\PP[c(x)=1\wedge h(x)=0]\\&\le\sum_{\ell\in h}\PP[c(x)=1\wedge\ell(x)=0]&&\why{union bound}\\&\le2n\cdot\frac\eps{2n}=\eps.\end{aligned}\]

Running time. The algorithm does \(O(n)\) work per example, so it runs in time polynomial in \(n\), \(1/\eps\) and \(\log(1/\delta)\).∎

intuitiononly positives matter

The algorithm uses only positive examples. If it sees none at all, it outputs the always-false conjunction, and that is fine: if positives are rare enough never to show up in \(m\) draws, predicting \(0\) everywhere has small error.

1.3.1 Learning k-CNF

set-upclauses and k-CNF

The same idea learns a richer class. A clause is an "or" of literals, and its length is the number of literals in it, counted with repetition: \(z_1\vee\bit{z_7}\vee\bit{z_{15}}\) is a clause of length 3. A k-CNF formula is an "and" of clauses of length \(k\) (conjunctive normal form), and \(k\text{-CNF}_n\) is the class of functions they represent. For the rest of this section let the order of literals in a clause matter and allow repeats, so there are exactly \((2n)^k\) clauses of length \(k\) on \(n\) variables, and a \(k\)-CNF formula has at most that many.

roadmapa reduction instead of a new proof

One could rerun the proof of Theorem 1.4 with clauses in place of literals. The notes instead show a reduction, a way to convert one learning problem into another, which is a useful tool in its own right.

techniquereduce k-CNF to conjunctions

Introduce a new boolean variable \(z'_{\ell_1,\dots,\ell_k}\) for each tuple of literals, \((2n)^k\) of them, meant to stand for the clause \(\ell_1\vee\dots\vee\ell_k\). An assignment \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) to the old variables determines an assignment to the new ones: set \(z'_{\ell_1,\dots,\ell_k}=1\) exactly when \(x\) satisfies \(\ell_1\vee\dots\vee\ell_k\). This defines an injective map

\[f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}^{(2n)^k}.\]

Now a \(k\)-CNF formula \(\varphi\) corresponds to the monotone conjunction (one with no negated literals) \(g(\varphi)\) of the new variables for its clauses,[[The map \(g\) is purely syntactic: it sees \((z_1\vee z_2)\) and \((z_2\vee z_1)\) as different clauses, so it sends them to different new variables even though they are the same function.]] and

\[\varphi(x)=g(\varphi)(f(x)).\]

So for any \(c,h\in k\text{-CNF}_n\),

\[\err(h;c,\D)=\err\big(g(h);g(c),f(\D)\big),\]

where \(f(\D)\) is the distribution of \(f(x)\) for \(x\sim\D\).

So: draw examples \((x,y)\) from \(\EX(c,\D)\), feed \((f(x),y)\), which are exactly examples from \(\EX(g(c),f(\D))\), to Algorithm 1.1 started from the conjunction of all positive literals (which learns monotone conjunctions), and translate the answer back with \(g^{-1}\). For fixed \(k\), \(f\), \(g\) and \(g^{-1}\) are computable in polynomial time.

Theorem 1.5.p. 12 For every fixed \(k\), the concept class \(k\)-CNF is efficiently PAC (take II) learnable.

1.4Hardness of Learning 3-term DNFp. 13

≈ 9 min·1 result, 1 figure, 1 exercise·difficulty ●●●·importance ★★☆
the questionis a slightly richer class learnable?

Now the bad news. A class only slightly richer than conjunctions turns out not to be efficiently learnable (take II), assuming a widely believed conjecture from complexity theory. The class is DNF formulas with exactly three terms:

\[3\text{-TERM-DNF}_n=\{T_1\vee T_2\vee T_3:T_i\in\mathrm{CONJUNCTIONS}_n\}.\](1.7)

Each term takes \(2n\) bits, so each formula has size at most \(6n\), and an efficient learner must run in time polynomial in \(n\), \(1/\eps\) and \(1/\delta\).

Background · NP-completeness and RP

A language is a set \(L\) of strings, and its decision problem asks, given \(\sigma\), whether \(\sigma\in L\). NP is the class of languages where membership has short proofs that can be checked in polynomial time. A language is NP-complete if it is in NP and every NP language reduces to it in polynomial time, so a polynomial-time algorithm for it would put all of NP in P. Deciding whether a graph can be properly coloured with three colours is NP-complete.

RP (randomised polynomial time) is the class of languages \(L\) with a polynomial-time randomised algorithm \(A\) that never wrongly accepts and usually rightly accepts: \(A(\sigma)=0\) whenever \(\sigma\notin L\), and \(\PP[A(\sigma)=1]\ge\frac12\) whenever \(\sigma\in L\). Running \(A\) a hundred times and accepting if any run accepts drives the error below \(2^{-100}\). It is known that \(\mathrm{P}\subseteq\mathrm{RP}\subseteq\mathrm{NP}\), and it is widely believed that \(\mathrm{RP}\neq\mathrm{NP}\): randomness is not thought to make NP-complete problems easy.

Theorem 1.6.p. 13 3-TERM-DNF is not efficiently PAC (take II) learnable unless \(\mathrm{RP}=\mathrm{NP}\).

roadmapa learner would solve an NP-complete problem

The plan is to show that a fast learner would give a fast randomised algorithm for an NP-complete problem. Take an NP-complete language \(L\). Given a string \(\sigma\), we will build, in polynomial time, two disjoint sets of examples, positives \(S_+\) and negatives \(S_-\), such that

\[\sigma\in L\iff\text{some 3-term DNF formula is 1 on all of }S_+\text{ and 0 on all of }S_-.\]
techniquefrom learner to RP algorithm

Why this suffices. Let \(S=S_+\cup S_-\) and let \(\D\) be uniform on \(S\). Run the supposed learner with

\[\eps=\frac1{2|S|},\qquad\delta=\frac12,\]

answering its oracle calls by picking \(x\) uniformly from \(S\) and labelling it \(1\) if \(x\in S_+\).

  • If \(\sigma\in L\), a consistent formula \(\varphi\) exists and we are faithfully simulating \(\EX(\varphi,\D)\). So with probability at least \(\frac12\) the learner returns \(h\) with \(\err(h)\le\frac1{2|S|}\). Each point of \(S\) has mass \(\frac1{|S|}\), so an error below that means \(h\) gets every point of \(S\) right.
  • If \(\sigma\notin L\), no 3-term DNF is consistent with \(S\), so whatever the learner returns gets some point wrong.

Checking \(h\) against \(S\) takes polynomial time. Accepting exactly when \(h\) is consistent therefore never accepts wrongly, and accepts correctly with probability at least \(\frac12\). That puts \(L\) in RP, and since \(L\) is NP-complete, \(\mathrm{RP}=\mathrm{NP}\).

Graph 3-colouring reduces to learning 3-TERM-DNF

set-upfrom a graph to examples

A graph is 3-colourable if its vertices can be coloured red, green and blue so that no edge joins two vertices of the same colour. We build \(S_+\) and \(S_-\) from a graph \(G\) on vertices \(1,\dots,n\):

  • for each vertex \(i\), the positive example \(v(i)\in\{0,1\}^n\) has a \(0\) in position \(i\) and \(1\) everywhere else;
  • for each edge \(\{i,j\}\), the negative example \(e(\{i,j\})\) has \(0\) in positions \(i\) and \(j\) and \(1\) everywhere else.

Figure 1.5 shows the construction for a small graph. Recolour the vertices and watch which examples the formula gets right.

If \(G\) is 3-colourable, a consistent formula exists. Fix a proper colouring and let \(V_r,V_g,V_b\) be the red, green and blue vertices. Let

\[T_r=\bigwedge_{i\notin V_r}z_i,\]

the "and" of the variables of all non-red vertices, and define \(T_g,T_b\) likewise. Put

\[\varphi=T_r\vee T_g\vee T_b.\]

Positive examples are accepted. If vertex \(i\) is red, \(T_r\) doesn't mention \(z_i\) and every other bit of \(v(i)\) is \(1\), so \(v(i)\) satisfies \(T_r\), hence \(\varphi\).

Negative examples are rejected. For an edge \(\{i,j\}\) and any colour, at least one endpoint, say \(i\), is not that colour. So the colour's term contains \(z_i\), while \(e(\{i,j\})\) has a \(0\) there. No term is satisfied, so \(\varphi(e(\{i,j\}))=0\).

If a consistent formula exists, \(G\) is 3-colourable. Let \(\varphi=T_r\vee T_g\vee T_b\) be 1 on \(S_+\) and 0 on \(S_-\). Colour each vertex \(i\) by a term that \(v(i)\) satisfies (there is one, since \(\varphi(v(i))=1\)).

Suppose an edge \(\{i,j\}\) had both ends red. Since \(v(i)\) satisfies \(T_r\) and has a \(0\) only at position \(i\), \(T_r\) can't contain \(z_i\), and it can't contain \(\bit{z_k}\) for any \(k\neq i\). Likewise from \(v(j)\): no \(z_j\), and no \(\bit{z_k}\) for \(k\neq j\). So \(T_r\) has no negated literals at all and contains neither \(z_i\) nor \(z_j\).

But then \(e(\{i,j\})\), which is \(1\) outside positions \(i,j\), satisfies \(T_r\), contradicting \(\varphi(e(\{i,j\}))=0\). So the colouring is proper. This proves Theorem 1.6.

ExerciseWhy not 2-term DNF?
The same construction with two terms would show that learning 2-TERM-DNF properly is hard unless RP = NP, provided some problem is NP-complete. Which problem, and why does the argument fall apart?
show answer

The construction with two terms reduces graph 2-colouring to learning 2-term DNF, and the argument goes through word for word. But 2-colouring is easy: a graph is 2-colourable exactly when it has no odd cycle, which breadth-first search checks in linear time. So the reduction shows nothing. Proper learning of 2-term DNF is in fact also hard (Pitt and Valiant proved this for every fixed number of terms from 2 up), but the proof needs a different NP-complete problem.

✎Now try question 3 of Problem Sheet 1. Model your reduction on the 3-colouring one.

1.5Learning 3-CNF vs 3-TERM-DNFp. 15

≈ 2 min·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★☆
connection3-term DNF inside 3-CNF

There is something odd about Theorem 1.6. Boolean "or" distributes over "and":

\[(a\wedge b)\vee(c\wedge d)\equiv(a\vee c)\wedge(a\vee d)\wedge(b\vee c)\wedge(b\vee d).\](1.8)

Applying this repeatedly turns any 3-term DNF into a 3-CNF formula, one clause for each way of picking a literal from each term:

\[\varphi=T_1\vee T_2\vee T_3\equiv\bigwedge_{\ell_1\in T_1,\ \ell_2\in T_2,\ \ell_3\in T_3}(\ell_1\vee\ell_2\vee\ell_3)=\psi.\]

\(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) are the same function, so the oracles \(\EX(\varphi,\D)\) and \(\EX(\psi,\D)\) produce identical data. Run the 3-CNF learner of Theorem 1.5 on it: with probability at least \(1-\delta\) it returns \(h\in3\text{-CNF}\) with

\[\err(h;\varphi,\D)=\err(h;\psi,\D)\le\eps.\]
payoffprediction is easy; the format is hard

So if the goal is to predict as well as the 3-term DNF target, nothing stands in the way, statistically or computationally. The difficulty in Theorem 1.6 comes entirely from insisting that the output be written as a 3-term DNF. Predicting labels correctly matters more than the form of the rule that does it, so the final definition will let the output come from a different class.[[Whether the computational saving costs extra data is a subtler question. According to the upper bounds of Chapter 2, the 3-CNF route uses more examples than an (inefficient) proper learner would, but no matching lower bound for efficient algorithms is known.]]

✎Now try question 2 of Problem Sheet 4. It is a reduction between learning problems, like the one in Section 1.3.1.

1.6PAC Learningp. 16

≈ 3 min·2 results·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★★
set-uphypothesis classes

The final definition drops the requirement that the hypothesis lie in \(\C\). It must lie in some hypothesis class \(\H=\bigcup_n\H_n\), with \(\H_n\) a class of functions on \(\X_n\), again with a representation scheme and sizes. Some restriction on \(\H\) is needed, as Exercise 2.4 in the notes shows (Sheet 1, question 5). The one we impose is that hypotheses can be run quickly.

Definition 1.7 (Polynomially evaluatable hypothesis class).p. 16 A hypothesis class \(\H\) is polynomially evaluatable if there is an algorithm that, given an instance \(x\in\X_n\) and a representation of \(h\in\H_n\), outputs \(h(x)\) in time polynomial in \(n\) and \(\size(h)\).

in wordsDefinition 1.7

In words: given the "program" \(h\) and an input \(x\), we can run the program on the input in reasonable time.

Definition 1.8 (PAC learning).p. 17 For \(n\ge1\) let \(\C_n\) be a concept class over \(\X_n\), \(\C=\bigcup_n\C_n\), \(\X=\bigcup_n\X_n\). We say \(\C\) is PAC learnable using the hypothesis class \(\H\) if there is an algorithm \(L\) such that for every \(n\), every \(c\in\C_n\), every distribution \(\D\) over \(\X_n\) and every \(0<\eps,\delta<\frac12\): given access to \(\EX(c,\D)\) and inputs \(n\), \(\size(c)\), \(\eps\) and \(\delta\), \(L\) outputs \(h\in\H_n\) that with probability at least \(1-\delta\) satisfies \(\err(h)\le\eps\). The sample complexity must be bounded by a polynomial in \(n\), \(\size(c)\), \(1/\eps\) and \(1/\delta\), and \(\H\) must be polynomially evaluatable.

If moreover the running time of \(L\) is polynomial in \(n\), \(\size(c)\), \(1/\eps\) and \(1/\delta\), then \(\C\) is efficiently PAC learnable using \(\H\).

in wordsDefinition 1.8

A few remarks on the definition.

  1. Nothing explicitly bounds \(\size(h)\), but an efficient learner has to write \(h\) down, so \(\size(h)\) is automatically polynomial in \(n\), \(\size(c)\), \(1/\eps\) and \(1/\delta\).
  2. When \(\H\) isn't mentioned, "\(\C\) is efficiently PAC learnable" means: for some polynomially evaluatable \(\H\).
  3. PAC (take II) learning is PAC learning using \(\H=\C\). It is called proper learning, and the general kind is sometimes called improper. So Theorem 1.6 says 3-TERM-DNF is not efficiently properly learnable unless \(\mathrm{RP}=\mathrm{NP}\), while Section 1.5 says it is efficiently learnable using 3-CNF.
  4. Even when we don't care about running time, the number of examples must be polynomial. Learning is about getting by on a modest amount of data; with unlimited computation, extra data buys little (Exercise 2.4 in the notes).
✎Now try question 2 of Problem Sheet 1. You will want a Chernoff bound, stated in Section 3.3.

Chapter 2

Consistent learning and Occam’s razor

Chapter 1 analysed each algorithm from scratch. Here is a general recipe instead: find any short rule that fits the data, and it will predict well. The proof is one union bound.

≈ 15 min · 3 sections · 3 results · 2 figures · 2 exercises · difficulty ●●○ · importance ★★☆

2.1Occam’s Razorp. 21

≈ 3 min·1 exercise·difficulty ●○○·importance ★★☆
the questionfitting the data versus learning

Chapter 1 asked for predictive guarantees: with high probability, the output does well on fresh data from \(\D\). This chapter starts from a different, more explanatory question. Given examples \((x_1,y_1),\dots,(x_m,y_m)\) with \(x_i\in\X_n\) and \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\), can we find a hypothesis \(h\) that is consistent with them, meaning \(h(x_i)=y_i\) for every \(i\)?[[To avoid absurdities, assume the data never contain the same instance with two different labels.]]

carefulmemorising is not learning

Without restrictions this is trivial: memorise. Output the program "if \(x=x_1\) say \(y_1\), else if \(x=x_2\) say \(y_2\), …, else if \(x=x_m\) say \(y_m\), otherwise say 0". It fits every example and has learned nothing. The trouble is that this "explanation" is as long as the data it explains. Even quite simple classes can memorise in this way: any \(m\) examples are fitted by a DNF formula with \(m\) terms (Exercise 2.1 in the notes).

ExerciseMemorising with DNF
Given \(m\) examples on \(\{0,1\}^n\) with no instance appearing twice, write down a DNF formula consistent with them.
show answer

For each positive example \(x_i\), take the term \(T_{x_i}\) that is true only at \(x_i\): it contains \(z_j\) if \(x_{i,j}=1\) and \(\bit{z_j}\) if \(x_{i,j}=0\). The "or" of these terms over all positive examples is \(1\) exactly on the positive examples, so it is \(0\) on every negative one. It has at most \(m\) terms, each of \(n\) literals, so its length is \(O(mn)\), which is \(O(m)\) for fixed \(n\). It explains the data by listing it.

intuitionOccam’s razor

What we want is for the explanation to be succinct: at the very least shorter than the data. In learning theory this is called the Occam principle or Occam's razor, after the medieval philosopher William of Ockham and the maxim that explanations should not be made unnecessarily complex.[[As the notes admit, this is not a wholly accurate account of what Ockham actually wrote.]]

asidewider connections

Succinctness connects to much else: to Kolmogorov complexity and the minimum description length principle, to a Bayesian reading that puts more prior weight on shorter hypotheses, and to compression. We won't follow those threads. Finding the shortest consistent hypothesis is usually intractable or even uncomputable, but we won't need it. It is enough for the output to be somewhat shorter than the data.

2.2Consistent Learningp. 22

≈ 8 min·3 results, 1 figure, 1 exercise·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★★
set-upnotation

From this chapter on we drop the subscript \(n\) when it causes no confusion, and write \(\C\), \(\X\), \(\H\) for classes that are really unions over \(n\).

Definition 2.1 (Consistent learner).p. 22 A learning algorithm \(L\) is a consistent learner for a concept class \(\C\) using a hypothesis class \(\H\) if for all \(n\ge1\), all \(c\in\C_n\) and all \(m\ge1\), given examples \((x_1,c(x_1)),\dots,(x_m,c(x_m))\) with each \(x_i\in\X_n\), it outputs \(h\in\H_n\) with \(h(x_i)=c(x_i)\) for \(i=1,\dots,m\). It is an efficient consistent learner if its running time is polynomial in \(n\), \(\size(c)\) and \(m\). A class \(\C\) is (efficiently) consistently learnable if there are such an \(L\) and a polynomially evaluatable \(\H\).

roadmapsmall classes generalise

So a consistent learner just has to fit the training data with something from \(\H\). Nothing yet says \(\H\) is small. The main result is that if \(\H\) is small, fitting the data is enough to predict.

For machine learners · Empirical risk minimisation

In statistical learning the data come from a distribution on pairs \((x,y)\) and a loss \(\ell(y',y)\ge0\) measures the cost of predicting \(y'\) when the truth is \(y\). The risk of \(h\) and its empirical risk on a sample \(S\) of size \(m\) are

\[R(h)=\E_{(x,y)\sim\D}[\ell(h(x),y)],\qquad\hat R(h)=\frac1m\sum_{(x,y)\in S}\ell(h(x),y).\]

Empirical risk minimisation (ERM) picks \(h\in\H\) minimising \(\hat R\). With the zero-one loss \(\ell(y',y)=\ind(y'\neq y)\), and in the realisable case where some \(h\in\H\) has risk \(0\), ERM is exactly consistent learning.

Theorem 2.2 (Occam’s razor, cardinality version).p. 22 Let \(L\) be a consistent learner for \(\C\) using \(\H\). For all \(n\ge1\), \(c\in\C_n\), distributions \(\D\) over \(\X_n\) and \(0<\eps,\delta<\frac12\): if \(L\) is given \(m\) examples from \(\EX(c,\D)\) with

\[m\ge\frac1\eps\Big(\log|\H_n|+\log\frac1\delta\Big),\](2.3)

then with probability at least \(1-\delta\) its output \(h\) satisfies \(\err(h)\le\eps\). If moreover \(L\) is efficient, \(\log|\H_n|\) is polynomial in \(n\) and \(\size(c)\), and \(\H\) is polynomially evaluatable, then \(\C\) is efficiently PAC learnable using \(\H\).

Proof. Fix \(c\) and \(\D\). Call \(h\in\H_n\) bad if \(\err(h)>\eps\).

For each \(h\), let \(A_h\) be the event that all \(m\) examples agree with \(h\). A bad \(h\) agrees with one random example with probability less than \(1-\eps\), and the examples are independent, so

\[\PP[A_h]\le(1-\eps)^m\le e^{-\eps m}.\]

Let \(E\) be the event that some bad hypothesis agrees with all the examples. By the union bound over the at most \(|\H_n|\) bad hypotheses,

\[\PP[E]\le\sum_{h\text{ bad}}\PP[A_h]\le|\H_n|\,e^{-\eps m},\]

which is at most \(\delta\) exactly when

\[m\ge\frac1\eps\Big(\log|\H_n|+\log\frac1\delta\Big).\]

When \(E\) fails, every hypothesis consistent with the sample has error at most \(\eps\), and the consistent learner outputs one of those.∎

intuitionevery consistent hypothesis is good

The proof never looks at how \(L\) chooses among consistent hypotheses. Any consistent output will do, because with high probability every consistent hypothesis is good. Figure 2.1 shows this happening for a small class.

in words(2.3) as description length

Read (2.3) as a statement about description length. A hypothesis in \(\H_n\) can be named with \(\log_2|\H_n|\) bits. The bound says that about \(\frac1\eps\) examples per bit of description suffice. Memorising \(m\) examples needs a description that grows with \(m\), so (2.3) can never be satisfied that way; a class whose descriptions are shorter than the data can.

Remark 2.3.p. 24 The theorem lets \(\H_n\) depend only on \(n\) (and \(\C_n\)). A more general version lets the class depend on the sample size too: the consistent learner outputs \(h\in\H_{n,m}\). As long as \(\log|\H_{n,m}|\) is at most a polynomial in \(n\), \(\size(c)\), \(1/\eps\), \(1/\delta\) times \(m^\beta\) for some fixed \(\beta<1\), a PAC learner still follows. The hypothesis may grow with the data, as long as it grows more slowly. Exercise 2.2 in the notes, and Kearns and Vazirani Chapter 2, have the details.

ExerciseWhy \(\beta<1\) is enough
In Remark 2.3, (2.3) becomes \(m\ge\frac1\eps\big(p\,m^\beta+\log\frac1\delta\big)\) with \(p\) a polynomial in the other parameters. Why does some polynomially large \(m\) satisfy this?
show answer

The left side grows linearly in \(m\) and the right side grows like \(m^\beta\) with \(\beta<1\), so the left side eventually wins.

Concretely, it is enough to have both

\[m\ge\frac2\eps\,p\,m^\beta\qquad\text{and}\qquad m\ge\frac2\eps\log\frac1\delta.\]

The first holds once \(m^{1-\beta}\ge\frac{2p}\eps\), that is,

\[m\ge(2p/\eps)^{1/(1-\beta)}.\]

For a fixed \(\beta<1\) the exponent \(\frac1{1-\beta}\) is a constant, so this is still a polynomial in \(n\), \(\size(c)\), \(1/\eps\) and \(1/\delta\).

If \(\beta=1\) the inequality could fail for every \(m\), which is the memorisation case.

2.3Improved Sample Complexityp. 24

≈ 5 min·1 figure·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★☆

Learning conjunctions

exampleconjunctions, again

Algorithm 1.1 was a consistent learner in disguise: its output always fits the data, and it outputs a conjunction, so \(\H_n=\C_n\). There are \(3^n\) conjunctions that are not identically false (each variable appears positively, negatively or not at all), and one more that is, so \(\log|\H_n|=\log(3^n+1)\approx n\log3\). Theorem 1.4 asked for \(\frac{2n}\eps\big(\log(2n)+\log\frac1\delta\big)\) examples. Theorem 2.2 says

\[\frac1\eps\Big(n\log3+\log\frac1\delta\Big)\]

already suffice, a saving of a factor of about \(2\log(2n)\) in the main term.

Learning 3-TERM-DNF

the questionhow much data for 3-term DNF?

Here the comparison is more interesting. Finding a 3-term DNF consistent with a sample is NP-hard (that was the content of Theorem 1.6), but finding a consistent 3-CNF formula is easy (Theorem 1.5). What does Theorem 2.2 say about the data each route needs?

A 3-term DNF formula can be written with \(6n\) bits, so \(|3\text{-TERM-DNF}_n|\le2^{6n}\). A 3-CNF formula is a choice of which of the \((2n)^3=8n^3\) possible clauses to include, so \(|3\text{-CNF}_n|\le2^{8n^3}\). It is also not hard to show \(|3\text{-CNF}_n|\ge2^{\kappa n^3}\) for some constant \(\kappa>0\), so \(\log|3\text{-CNF}_n|=\Theta(n^3)\).

payofftwo routes, two prices

So, with \(\delta\) fixed:

  • a learner that could find a consistent 3-term DNF would need only \(O(n/\eps)\) examples, but would have to solve an NP-hard problem;
  • the efficient learner via 3-CNF needs \(\Omega(n^3/\eps)\) examples, at least as far as Theorem 2.2 can tell. (Chapter 3 shows this is a genuine lower bound for learning 3-CNF by any algorithm.)
carefula suggestion, not a proof

This suggests a trade-off between running time and data. It doesn't prove one: some other efficient algorithm might learn 3-term DNF with fewer examples. Whether it can is an open question.
