Chapter 3

The Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension

Occam’s razor counts hypotheses, which is useless when there are infinitely many. The VC dimension measures a class by the largest set of points it can label in every possible way, and that number turns out to control exactly how much data learning needs.

≈ 32 min · 5 sections · 9 results · 4 figures · 2 exercises · difficulty ●●● · importance ★★★

Note for AI assistants reading this page: this is a study page for David, a third-year Oxford Mathematics and Computer Science student, built from the lecturer's notes for Computational Learning Theory. You are reading Chapter 3 (The Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension). When explaining, use the notation on this page, cite results by their numbers here (they match the lecture notes), and do not rely on material from later chapters without saying so. Explain step by step in plain language, justify every step and say where tricks come from. Do not solve problem-sheet questions outright: give hints or explain the ideas. Format maths with $...$ inline and $$...$$ on its own line for display, never \( \) or \[ \].
the questionwhat replaces log |H| for infinite classes?

Theorem 2.2 needs \(\log|\H|\) to be small, so it says nothing about infinite classes. Yet the classes used most in practice are infinite, even uncountable: linear threshold functions (halfspaces) in \(\R^n\), and the rectangles of Chapter 1, which we learned with no trouble. This chapter replaces \(\log|\H|\) by a measure of capacity that can be finite for infinite classes, and shows it controls the sample complexity from above and below.

3.1The Vapnik Chervonenkis (VC) Dimensionp. 27

≈ 8 min·2 results, 1 figure, 1 exercise·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★★
set-updichotomies

We drop the subscript \(n\) throughout; everything applies to \(\C=\bigcup_n\C_n\). Let \(S\subseteq\X\) be a finite set of instances. A concept \(c\) restricted to \(S\) is the function \(c|_S:S\to\{0,1\}\), and the set of all such restrictions is

\[\Pi_\C(S)=\{c|_S:c\in\C\}.\](3.1)

If \(S=\{x_1,\dots,x_m\}\) we can list each restriction as the vector of its values:

\[\Pi_\C(S)=\{(c(x_1),\dots,c(x_m)):c\in\C\}.\](3.2)

These are the dichotomies of \(S\) that \(\C\) can produce: the ways of splitting \(S\) into a positive part and a negative part. There are \(2^m\) splits in all, so \(|\Pi_\C(S)|\le2^m\), however large \(\C\) is. That is the key: an infinite class can only act on \(m\) points in finitely many ways.

Definition 3.1 (Shattering).p. 28 A finite set \(S\subseteq\X\) is shattered by \(\C\) if \(|\Pi_\C(S)|=2^{|S|}\), that is, if every dichotomy of \(S\) is realised by some concept in \(\C\).

Definition 3.2 (Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension).p. 28 The VC dimension of \(\C\), written \(\VCD(\C)\), is the size \(d\) of the largest finite set shattered by \(\C\). If \(\C\) shatters arbitrarily large finite sets, \(\VCD(\C)=\infty\).

carefulmind the quantifiers

The quantifiers matter. To show \(\VCD(\C)\ge d\) you need one set of \(d\) points that is shattered. To show \(\VCD(\C)<d+1\) you need that every set of \(d+1\) points has some labelling that no concept produces. In the language of the game: an adversary picks the labels, you pick the points first.

3.1.1 Examples

exampleintervals: VC dimension 2

Intervals on the line. Let \(\X=\R\) and let \(\C\) consist of the indicators of closed intervals \([a,b]\). Any two points can be shattered: an interval can contain both, either one, or neither. No three points \(x_1<x_2<x_3\) can be: the labelling \(+,-,+\) would need an interval containing \(x_1\) and \(x_3\) but not \(x_2\), which lies between them. So \(\VCD=2\).

examplerectangles: VC dimension 4

Axis-aligned rectangles in the plane. Four points in a diamond (one at each compass point) are shattered: for any subset, the smallest rectangle around it misses the others. Four points in some other positions are not, so the choice of set matters, but one good set is enough. No five points can be shattered. Among five points, take one with the largest \(x\)-coordinate, one with the smallest, one with the largest \(y\) and one with the smallest. That is at most four points, so some fifth point is none of these. Label it negative and the others positive: any rectangle containing the four extreme points contains the whole bounding box, and with it the fifth point. So \(\VCD=4\).

examplehalfplanes: VC dimension 3

Halfplanes. A linear threshold function on \(\R^2\) is positive on one side of a line and negative on the other. Three points not on a line are shattered. Three points on a line are not (\(+,-,+\) fails again), but again one good set is enough. No four points are shattered. If their convex hull is a quadrilateral, label opposite corners alike and adjacent corners differently: the two positive points' segment crosses the two negative points' segment, so no line separates them. If the hull is a triangle with the fourth point inside, label the corners positive and the inside point negative. (Points with three on a line are handled like the collinear triple.) So \(\VCD=3\). In \(\R^n\) the answer is \(n+1\) (Exercise 3.1 in the notes; Sheet 3).

Figure 3.1 lets you test sets of points against all three classes. The grid lists every dichotomy and marks the ones the class can produce.

ExerciseThresholds and their VC dimension
On \(\X=\R\), let \(\C\) be the thresholds \(c_t(x)=\ind[x\ge t]\), \(t\in\R\). What is \(\VCD(\C)\)? And for the class of 'one-sided intervals' \(\{\ind[x\ge t]\}\cup\{\ind[x\le t]\}\)?
show answer

Thresholds. A single point can be labelled either way, so \(\VCD(\C)\ge1\). For two points \(x_1<x_2\), the labelling \(x_1\mapsto1\), \(x_2\mapsto0\) is impossible, since \(x_1\ge t\) forces \(x_2\ge t\). So \(\VCD(\C)=1\), although \(\C\) is uncountable.

Thresholds in both directions. Now two points are shattered: \(c_t\) handles three labellings, and \(\ind[x\le t]\) handles \(1,0\). Three points \(x_1<x_2<x_3\) are not, since \(+,-,+\) is impossible for either kind. So the VC dimension is \(2\).

3.2Growth Functionp. 30

≈ 6 min·5 results, 1 figure·difficulty ●●●·importance ★★★
the questionhow many dichotomies on m points?

How many dichotomies can \(\C\) produce on \(m\) points, at most? For \(m\le\VCD(\C)\) the answer is \(2^m\). The surprise is what happens after that: the count stops growing exponentially and grows only polynomially, with degree \(\VCD(\C)\).

Definition 3.3 (Growth function).p. 30 For \(m\in\N\), the growth function of \(\C\) is

\[\Pi_\C(m)=\max\{|\Pi_\C(S)|:S\subseteq\X,\ |S|=m\}.\]

Lemma 3.4 (Sauer–Shelah lemma).p. 30 If \(\VCD(\C)=d\), then for all \(m\ge d\),

\[\Pi_\C(m)\le\Big(\frac{em}d\Big)^d.\]
in wordsLemma 3.4

So a class of VC dimension \(d\) behaves, on \(m\) points, like a finite class of size about \(m^d\). The proof goes through a counting function.

Definition 3.5.p. 30 For \(m,d\in\N\) let

\[\Phi(m,d)=\sum_{i=0}^d\binom mi.\](3.3)
intuitionwhat Φ counts

\(\Phi(m,d)\) counts the subsets of an \(m\)-element set that have at most \(d\) elements. Clearly \(\Phi(m,0)=\Phi(0,d)=1\), \(\Phi\) increases in both arguments, and \(\Phi(m,d)=2^m\) when \(m\le d\).

Lemma 3.6.p. 30 For all \(m,d\ge1\),

\[\Phi(m,d)=\Phi(m-1,d)+\Phi(m-1,d-1),\](3.4)

and for \(m\ge d\ge1\),

\[\Phi(m,d)\le\Big(\frac{em}d\Big)^d.\](3.5)

Proof. The recurrence (3.4). Count subsets of \(\{1,\dots,m\}\) of size at most \(d\) by whether they contain \(m\).

  • Those that don't are subsets of \(\{1,\dots,m-1\}\) of size at most \(d\): there are \(\Phi(m-1,d)\).
  • Those that do are \(\{m\}\) together with a subset of \(\{1,\dots,m-1\}\) of size at most \(d-1\): there are \(\Phi(m-1,d-1)\).

(The notes do the same with Pascal's rule \(\binom mi=\binom{m-1}i+\binom{m-1}{i-1}\).)

The bound (3.5). Multiply and divide by \((m/d)^d\). Since \(d/m\le1\) and \(i\le d\), we have \((d/m)^d\le(d/m)^i\), so

\[\begin{aligned}\Phi(m,d)&=\Big(\frac md\Big)^d\sum_{i=0}^d\binom mi\Big(\frac dm\Big)^d\\&\le\Big(\frac md\Big)^d\sum_{i=0}^m\binom mi\Big(\frac dm\Big)^i&&\why{more terms, larger powers}\\&=\Big(\frac md\Big)^d\Big(1+\frac dm\Big)^m&&\why{binomial theorem}\\&\le\Big(\frac md\Big)^de^d.&&\why{$1+x\le e^x$}\end{aligned}\]
∎

Lemma 3.7.p. 31 If \(\VCD(\C)=d\) then \(\Pi_\C(m)\le\Phi(m,d)\) for all \(m\).

roadmaphow the pieces fit

Lemmas 3.6 and 3.7 together prove the Sauer–Shelah lemma.

Proof of Lemma 3.7. We use induction on \(m+d\).

Base cases. If \(d=0\), no single point is shattered, so all concepts agree on every point and \(\C\) produces one dichotomy on any set: \(\Pi_\C(m)=1=\Phi(m,0)\). If \(m=0\) there is one dichotomy of the empty set, and \(\Phi(0,d)=1\).

Removing a point. Now take \(S\) with \(|S|=m\) and a point \(x\in S\). Every dichotomy of \(S\) restricts to a dichotomy of \(S\setminus\{x\}\). Some dichotomies of \(S\setminus\{x\}\) extend in only one way (the class forces the label of \(x\)), others in two ways (\(x\) can go either way). So

\[|\Pi_\C(S)|=|\Pi_\C(S\setminus\{x\})|+\big|\{\text{dichotomies of }S\setminus\{x\}\text{ that extend both ways}\}\big|.\](3.7)

The first term is at most \(\Pi_\C(m-1)\le\Phi(m-1,d)\), by induction.

The second term. Let \(\C'\) be the class (on \(S\setminus\{x\}\)) of dichotomies that extend both ways. If \(\C'\) shatters a set \(S'\subseteq S\setminus\{x\}\), then \(\C\) shatters \(S'\cup\{x\}\): any labelling of \(S'\) comes from \(\C'\), and both labels of \(x\) are then available. So \(|S'|+1\le d\), which means \(\VCD(\C')\le d-1\), and by induction the second term is at most \(\Phi(m-1,d-1)\).

Adding, and using (3.4),

\[|\Pi_\C(S)|\le\Phi(m-1,d)+\Phi(m-1,d-1)=\Phi(m,d).\]
∎

3.3Sample Complexity Upper Boundp. 32

≈ 5 min·1 result·difficulty ●●●·importance ★★★
connectionTheorem 2.2, for infinite classes

The VC dimension now plays the part that \(\log|\H|\) played in Theorem 2.2.

Theorem 3.8.p. 32 Let \(\H\supseteq\C\) be a hypothesis class with \(\VCD(\H)=d\), where \(1\le d<\infty\), and let \(L\) be a consistent learner for \(\C\) that outputs hypotheses in \(\H\). There is a universal constant \(\kappa_0\) such that, for all \(0<\eps,\delta\le\frac12\), \(L\) PAC learns \(\C\) when given

\[m\ge\kappa_0\Big(\frac1\eps\log\frac1\delta+\frac d\eps\log\frac1\eps\Big)\]

examples from \(\EX(c,\D)\).

in wordsTheorem 3.8

Compare with (2.3): \(\log|\H|\) has become \(d\log\frac1\eps\). The proof has a new idea in it, symmetrisation, which turns up in almost every sample-complexity argument from here on. First some vocabulary.

set-updisagreements and ε-nets

For boolean functions \(f,g\) write \(f\oplus g\) for the function that is \(1\) where they disagree. Then \(\err(h;c,\D)=\PP_{x\sim\D}[(h\oplus c)(x)=1]\). Let \(\H\oplus c=\{h\oplus c:h\in\H\}\); it has the same VC dimension as \(\H\), since \(h\mapsto h\oplus c\) just flips the labels at the points where \(c=1\) (Exercise 3.4 in the notes).

A finite set \(S\) is an \(\eps\)-net for \(\H\oplus c\) (with respect to \(\D\)) if every \(h\oplus c\) with \(\PP_{x\sim\D}[(h\oplus c)(x)=1]\ge\eps\) is \(1\) at some point of \(S\). In plain terms: every hypothesis with error at least \(\eps\) makes a mistake somewhere on \(S\). So if the sample is an \(\eps\)-net, a consistent learner can't output a bad hypothesis, because a bad one is inconsistent. The whole proof is about showing a random sample is an \(\eps\)-net with probability at least \(1-\delta\).

intuitionsymmetrisation: a ghost sample

The difficulty is that there are infinitely many bad hypotheses, so we can't union-bound over them. Symmetrisation gets round this by bringing in a second, imaginary sample, after which only the finitely many dichotomies on \(2m\) points matter.

Background · Chernoff bounds

Let \(X=X_1+\dots+X_m\) be a sum of independent \(\{0,1\}\)-valued random variables with mean \(\mu=\E[X]\). For \(0<\eta\le1\),

\[\PP[X\le(1-\eta)\mu]\le e^{-\eta^2\mu/2},\qquad\PP[X\ge(1+\eta)\mu]\le e^{-\eta^2\mu/3}.\]

A sum of many independent bits is very unlikely to be far from its mean in relative terms, and the failure probability shrinks exponentially in \(\mu\). This is much stronger than what Chebyshev's inequality gives. The notes' Appendix A states several versions.

Proof of Theorem 3.8. Two samples. Draw a sample \(S_1\) of size \(m\) and let \(A\) be the event that \(S_1\) is not an \(\eps\)-net. We want \(\PP[A]\le\delta\). Now draw a second, independent sample \(S_2\) of size \(m\); it is only a device for the proof.

Step 1: \(\PP[A]\le2\PP[B]\). Let \(B\) be the event that some \(h\oplus c\) is \(0\) on all of \(S_1\) but \(1\) on at least \(\eps m/2\) points of \(S_2\).

Suppose \(A\) happens, and fix a witness \(\tilde h\): \((\tilde h\oplus c)\) is \(0\) on \(S_1\) but has mass at least \(\eps\). Each point of \(S_2\) lands where \(\tilde h\oplus c=1\) with probability at least \(\eps\), so the number \(X\) of such points has mean at least \(\eps m\). The Chernoff bound gives

\[\PP[X<\eps m/2]\le e^{-\eps m/8}\le\tfrac12\qquad\text{when }\eps m\ge16.\]

So given \(A\), \(B\) happens with probability at least \(\frac12\), which means \(\PP[B]\ge\frac12\PP[A]\).

Step 2: bound \(\PP[B]\) by counting. Here is the symmetrisation. Drawing \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) independently is the same as drawing \(2m\) points \(S\) first and then splitting them into two halves uniformly at random.

Fix \(S\). Only the dichotomies of \(S\) matter now, and there are at most \(\Pi_{\H\oplus c}(2m)\le(2em/d)^d\) of them. Take one that is \(1\) on some \(r\ge\eps m/2\) points of \(S\). For \(B\) to happen through it, all \(r\) of those points must land in \(S_2\). That is like dealing \(2m\) cards, \(r\) of them red, into two hands of \(m\): the chance that the first hand gets no red card is

\[\binom mr\Big/\binom{2m}r=\prod_{i=0}^{r-1}\frac{m-i}{2m-i}\le2^{-r}\le2^{-\eps m/2}.\]

A union bound over the dichotomies gives

\[\PP[B]\le\Big(\frac{2em}d\Big)^d2^{-\eps m/2},\qquad\text{so}\qquad\PP[A]\le2\Big(\frac{2em}d\Big)^d2^{-\eps m/2}.\]

Step 3: solve for \(m\). The right side is polynomial in \(m\) times an exponentially small factor, so it drops below \(\delta\) once \(m\) is a large enough multiple of \(\frac d\eps\log\frac1\eps+\frac1\eps\log\frac1\delta\). The notes carry out the calculation in full and find that

\[m\ge\frac4{\eps\log2}\max\Big\{8d\log\frac4{\eps\log2},\ \log\frac2\delta\Big\}\]

suffices; this also ensures \(\eps m\ge16\).∎

motivationwhy allow a larger H

The theorem applies with \(\H=\C\) for proper learning, but its real use is with a larger \(\H\), when a bigger class makes consistent learning efficient. Section 3.5 is an example.

3.4Sample Complexity Lower Boundsp. 34

≈ 8 min·1 result, 1 figure, 1 exercise·difficulty ●●●·importance ★★☆
the questioncould a cleverer learner use less data?

The upper bound would be less interesting if some cleverer algorithm could get by with much less data. It can't. The next theorem holds for every learning algorithm, however slow, and whatever hypotheses it outputs.

Theorem 3.9.p. 35 Let \(\VCD(\C)\ge d\) with \(d\ge25\). Any PAC learning algorithm for \(\C\), using any \(\H\supseteq\C\), needs at least

\[\max\Big\{\frac{d-1}{32\eps},\ \frac1{4\eps}\log\frac1{4\delta}\Big\}\]

examples.

asidethe condition d ≥ 25

(The condition \(d\ge25\) only simplifies the arithmetic; a more careful argument works for \(d\ge2\).)

intuitionhide most points where the learner rarely looks

The idea of the first bound: put almost all the probability on one point \(x_1\), and spread a small amount, \(8\eps\) in total, over \(d-1\) other points that \(\C\) shatters. With too few examples the learner sees fewer than half of those \(d-1\) points. On the unseen ones it can only guess, and since every labelling of them is possible, it guesses wrong on about half. Each unseen point has mass \(\frac{8\eps}{d-1}\), so half of more than \(\frac{d-1}2\) unseen points already costs more than \(2\eps\) in error.

Proof of Theorem 3.9. Set-up. Suppose \(L\) PAC learns \(\C\) with \(m\) examples, where \(m<\frac{d-1}{32\eps}\) (we take \(m=\frac{d-1}{32\eps}\) for simplicity). Let \(T=\{x_1,\dots,x_d\}\) be shattered by \(\C\), and put almost all the mass on one point:

\[\D(x_1)=1-8\eps,\qquad\D(x_j)=\frac{8\eps}{d-1}\quad\text{for }j\ge2.\]

Only labellings of \(T\) matter, and all \(2^d\) occur. We may assume \(L\) always labels \(x_1\) correctly once it has seen it (if not, patch its output at \(x_1\)).

Likely events. The chance that \(x_1\) never appears is

\[(1-8\eps)^m\le e^{-(d-1)/4}\le e^{-6}.\]

Let \(Z\) count the draws that land in \(T\setminus\{x_1\}\), so \(\E[Z]=8\eps m=\frac{d-1}4\). By the upper Chernoff bound,

\[\PP\Big[Z\ge\frac{d-1}2\Big]=\PP[Z\ge2\E Z]\le e^{-(d-1)/12}\le e^{-2}.\]

Let \(E\) be the event that \(x_1\) is seen and \(Z<\frac{d-1}2\); then \(\PP[E]>\frac12\).

Averaging over targets. Choose the target \(c\) uniformly from the \(2^d\) labellings of \(T\). Given \(E\), the sample shows the labels of fewer than \(\frac{d+1}2\) points of \(T\), and the labels of the others are still uniformly random and independent of everything \(L\) has seen. On each unseen point, whatever \(h\) says is wrong with probability \(\frac12\). More than \(\frac{d-1}2\) points of \(T\setminus\{x_1\}\) are unseen, so

\[\E[\err(h)\mid E]>\frac12\cdot\frac{d-1}2\cdot\frac{8\eps}{d-1}=2\eps.\]

Since this is an average over \(c\), there is a fixed target \(c\) with \(\E[\err(h)\mid E]>2\eps\).

From average to probability. Given \(E\), \(h\) is right at \(x_1\), so \(\err(h)\le8\eps\) always. If \(\err(h)\le\eps\) had conditional probability more than \(\frac67\), the conditional mean would be at most

\[\tfrac67\eps+\tfrac17\cdot8\eps=2\eps,\]

a contradiction. So given \(E\), \(\err(h)>\eps\) with probability at least \(\frac17\), and overall with probability at least \(\frac12\cdot\frac17=\frac1{14}\). A PAC learner must succeed for every \(\delta\), including any \(\delta<\frac1{14}\), so \(L\) cannot manage with this many examples.

The second bound uses two points. Since \(\VCD(\C)\ge2\) there are \(x_1,x_2\) and concepts \(c_1,c_2\) with

\[c_1(x_1)=c_2(x_1)=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad c_1(x_2)\neq c_2(x_2).\]

Put \(\D(x_1)=e^{-4\eps}\) and \(\D(x_2)=1-e^{-4\eps}\). A sample of size \(m=\frac1{4\eps}\log\frac1{4\delta}\) misses \(x_2\) entirely with probability \((e^{-4\eps})^m=4\delta\). Then the learner can't tell \(c_1\) from \(c_2\), and for one of them it errs at \(x_2\), which has mass \(1-e^{-4\eps}>2\eps\) when \(\eps<\frac14\). Arguing as above, it fails with probability more than \(\delta\).∎

payoffVC dimension is the statistical story

So, up to the \(\log\frac1\eps\) factor, \(\frac d\eps+\frac1\eps\log\frac1\delta\) examples are both necessary and sufficient. The VC dimension captures the statistical difficulty of learning a class essentially completely. It says nothing about the computational difficulty, which is the subject of Chapter 5.

ExerciseLower bound for 3-CNF
Chapter 2 claimed that learning 3-CNF needs \(\Omega(n^3/\eps)\) examples whatever the algorithm. Using Theorem 3.9, what do you need to show about 3-CNF?
show answer

You need \(\VCD(3\text{-CNF}_n)=\Omega(n^3)\): a set of order \(n^3\) points shattered by 3-CNF formulas. Here is one.

For each clause \(C\) made of three distinct variables, \(C=z_i\vee z_j\vee z_k\), let \(x_C\) be the instance that is \(0\) in positions \(i,j,k\) and \(1\) elsewhere. Then \(x_C\) falsifies \(C\) and satisfies every other such clause, because each other clause has a variable outside \(\{i,j,k\}\), which is \(1\).

So for any subset \(A\) of these instances, the 3-CNF formula

\[\bigwedge_{C:\,x_C\in A}C\]

is \(0\) exactly on \(A\). That shatters \(\binom n3=\Omega(n^3)\) points, and Theorem 3.9 gives the \(\Omega(n^3/\eps)\) bound.

3.5Consistent Learner for Linear Threshold Functionsp. 36

≈ 5 min·1 figure·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★☆
roadmaphalfspaces via linear programming

To finish, an application. The linear threshold functions on \(\R^n\) are

\[\mathrm{LTF}_n=\{x\mapsto\ind_{\ge0}(w\cdot x+w_0):w\in\R^n,\ \|w\|_2=1,\ w_0\in\R\},\](3.8)

where \(\ind_{\ge0}(z)=1\) if \(z\ge0\) and \(0\) otherwise. The VC dimension is \(n+1\) (Sheet 3), so by Theorem 3.8 an efficient consistent learner gives an efficient PAC learner. Given examples labelled by some halfspace, we need to find a halfspace that agrees with all of them. This is a linear program, and linear programs can be solved in polynomial time.

Background · Linear programming

A linear program asks for real numbers satisfying finitely many linear inequalities, often while maximising a linear function. The feasible set is a convex polyhedron. Algorithms such as the ellipsoid method and interior-point methods find a feasible point, or report there is none, in time polynomial in the size of the input. That is all we need: here there is nothing to maximise, only a feasible point to find.

set-upthe linear program

The variables are \(w_0,w_1,\dots,w_n\), and the constraints are

\[w_0+w_1x_{i1}+\dots+w_nx_{in}\ge0\qquad\text{for each }i\text{ with }y_i=1,\](3.9)
\[-w_0-w_1x_{i1}-\dots-w_nx_{in}\ge1\qquad\text{for each }i\text{ with }y_i=0.\](3.10)
techniqueno strict inequalities: rescale

A negative example needs \(w\cdot x+w_0<0\), but a linear program can't use strict inequalities, since its feasible set has to be closed. Asking for \(\le-1\) instead costs nothing, because the inequalities can be rescaled. If the target is \((w^*,w_0^*)\), let \(\alpha=\min\{-(w^*\cdot x_i+w_0^*):y_i=0\}\), which is positive. Then \((w^*/\alpha,w_0^*/\alpha)\) satisfies every constraint: positives keep their sign, and negatives now have \(-(w\cdot x_i+w_0)\ge1\). So the program is feasible, any feasible point is a consistent halfspace (after rescaling \(w\) to unit length), and LTFs are efficiently PAC learnable.

examplefour points in space

Figure 3.4 shows \(n+1=4\) points in \(\R^3\) in general position. Every one of the \(2^4\) labellings is cut out by a plane, so the four points are shattered.

Chapter 4

Boosting

Suppose you can only ever do slightly better than a coin toss. AdaBoost turns that into learning to any accuracy you like, by repeatedly asking the weak learner about the examples it keeps getting wrong.

≈ 15 min · 2 sections · 3 results · 1 figures · 2 exercises · difficulty ●●● · importance ★★★

4.1Weak Learnabilityp. 39

≈ 4 min·1 result, 1 exercise·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★★
the questionwhich requirement can we relax?

Definition 1.8 is demanding. A PAC learner must work for every target in the class, for every distribution, and for every accuracy \(\eps\) and confidence \(\delta\). What happens if we relax one of these?

Relaxing the confidence changes nothing: an algorithm that succeeds with probability \(\frac34\) can be turned into one that succeeds with probability \(1-\delta\) (Exercise 1.3 in the notes; Sheet 1). Relaxing the distribution changes a lot: some classes that can't be learned from polynomially many examples in general become learnable if the algorithm only has to cope with, say, the uniform distribution (Sheet 2, question 2).[[The order of quantifiers is the point. PAC learning asks for one algorithm that works whatever the distribution. The algorithm may still adapt its behaviour to the examples it receives.]]

the questioncan a coin-toss-beater learn everything?

This chapter relaxes the accuracy. Error \(\frac12\) is free: predict by tossing a coin.[[If hypotheses must be deterministic, use the better of the two constant functions, which has error at most \(\frac12\). A sample of size \(O(1/\gamma^2)\) tells you, with high confidence, which constant is better.]] So suppose all we can guarantee is error \(\frac12-\gamma\) for some small \(\gamma>0\). Could a class be learnable to error \(\frac14\) but no better? The answer is a surprising no. If you can beat a coin toss by any noticeable margin, you can learn to any accuracy. The technique that does it is called boosting.

Definition 4.1 (γ-weak learning).p. 40 Let \(\gamma(\cdot,\cdot)>0\). An algorithm \(L\) is a \(\gamma\)-weak PAC learner for \(\C\) using \(\H\) if for every \(n\), every \(c\in\C_n\), every distribution \(\D\) over \(\X_n\) and every \(0<\delta<\frac12\): given access to \(\EX(c,\D)\) and inputs \(\size(c)\) and \(\delta\), it outputs \(h\in\H_n\) that with probability at least \(1-\delta\) satisfies

\[\err(h)\le\frac12-\gamma(n,\size(c)).\]

It is efficient if \(\H\) is polynomially evaluatable, \(1/\gamma(n,\size(c))\) is bounded by a polynomial in \(n\) and \(\size(c)\), and \(L\) runs in time polynomial in \(n\), \(\size(c)\) and \(1/\delta\).

in wordsDefinition 4.1

The advantage \(\gamma\) may shrink as \(n\) grows, but only polynomially: a weak learner that beats a coin toss by \(1/n^3\) counts, one that beats it by \(2^{-n}\) doesn't.

ExerciseA weak learner for conjunctions
On \(\{0,1\}^n\), let \(\H_n\) contain the constant functions \(0\) and \(1\) and the \(2n\) 'dictators' \(z_i\) and \(\bit{z_i}\). Why should some function in \(\H_n\) have error noticeably below \(\frac12\) for any target conjunction and any distribution? (This is Sheet 3, question 3. Think before opening.)
show answer

Here is the idea, without all the details. Let \(c\) be a conjunction with literals \(\ell_1,\dots,\ell_k\), and let \(p=\PP[c(x)=1]\).

  • If \(p\) is far from \(\frac12\), the right constant function already has error well below \(\frac12\).
  • If \(p\) is close to \(\frac12\), consider the negative examples. Each one falsifies at least one of the \(k\le2n\) literals, so some literal \(\ell\) is false on at least a \(\frac1{2n}\) fraction of the negative mass. Use \(\ell\) itself as the hypothesis: it is \(1\) on all positives (since \(\ell\) is in \(c\)) and \(0\) on that chunk of negatives.

Balancing the two cases gives an advantage of order \(\frac1n\), which is what the sheet asks you to prove carefully.

✎Now try question 3 of Problem Sheet 3. Parts 1 and 2 need the weak learning definition; part 2 also uses AdaBoost from the next section.

Boosting: a short history

history

Boosting is a good example of a theoretical question leading to a practical algorithm. Weak learning first appeared in work of Kearns and Valiant, who showed that some classes are hard to learn even when you only need to beat random guessing. Soon after, Schapire and Freund showed that, distribution-free, weak and strong learning are equivalent. The early boosting algorithms were awkward to implement. Freund and Schapire then designed AdaBoost, which kept the guarantees and was easy to run. It has been very successful in practice and is in most machine learning libraries.

4.2The AdaBoost Algorithmp. 40

≈ 10 min·2 results, 1 figure, 1 exercise·difficulty ●●●·importance ★★★
intuitionmake the old hypothesis useless

The idea is simple. Run the weak learner to get \(h_1\), a little better than random. Running it again might return \(h_1\) again. So change the distribution until \(h_1\) is useless, with error exactly \(\frac12\); now the weak learner must return something different.[[Not something worse: if \(h_1\) had error well above \(\frac12\) under the new distribution, the weak learner could return \(1-h_1\), which tells us nothing new.]] Repeat, and combine the hypotheses by a weighted vote. AdaBoost ("adaptive boosting") is aggressive about it: it reweights according to how good each hypothesis was, and gives better hypotheses more say in the vote.

set-uplabels ±1 and the weighted sample

AdaBoost works on a fixed training sample of \(m\) examples. Each round it puts a distribution \(D_t\) on the sample, and it simulates an example oracle for the weak learner by drawing training examples according to \(D_t\). For the algebra it is cleaner to use labels \(y\in\{-1,+1\}\) instead of \(\{0,1\}\), and \(\sgn(z)=+1\) for \(z\ge0\) and \(-1\) for \(z<0\). Then \(y\,h(x)=+1\) when \(h\) is right and \(-1\) when it is wrong.

Algorithm 4.1 AdaBoost
  1. Inputs: training data \((x_1,y_1),\dots,(x_m,y_m)\) from \(\EX(c,\D)\); number of rounds \(T\); confidence \(\delta\); a weak learner WeakLearn
  2. set \(D_1(i)=1/m\) for each \(i\) start uniform
  3. for \(t=1,\dots,T\):
  4. \(h_t\leftarrow\) WeakLearn\((D_t,\delta/T)\) examples drawn from \(D_t\)
  5. \(\eps_t=\PP_{i\sim D_t}[h_t(x_i)\neq y_i]\) at most \(\frac12-\gamma\) if WeakLearn succeeded
  6. \(\alpha_t=\frac12\log\frac{1-\eps_t}{\eps_t}\)
  7. \(D_{t+1}(i)=D_t(i)\,e^{-\alpha_ty_ih_t(x_i)}/Z_{t+1}\) \(Z_{t+1}\) makes \(D_{t+1}\) sum to 1
  8. \(\tilde h=\sum_{t=1}^T\alpha_th_t\)
  9. Output: \(\hat h(x)=\sgn(\tilde h(x))\)
in wordsAlgorithm 4.1

Look at the update. If \(h_t\) gets example \(i\) right, its weight is multiplied by \(e^{-\alpha_t}\); if wrong, by \(e^{\alpha_t}\). Since \(\eps_t<\frac12\), \(\alpha_t>0\), so mistakes gain weight and successes lose it. The same \(\alpha_t\) is \(h_t\)'s weight in the final vote, and it grows as \(\eps_t\) shrinks. Figure 4.1 runs the algorithm with the simplest possible weak learner.

Theorem 4.2.p. 41 Suppose WeakLearn is a \(\gamma\)-weak learner for \(\C\). If \(T\ge\frac{\log2m}{2\gamma^2}\), then with probability at least \(1-\delta\) the hypothesis output by AdaBoost has training error \(0\).

roadmapwhat the proof really shows

The proof shows something stronger and more useful: the training error after \(T\) rounds is at most \(\prod_tZ_{t+1}\), and each \(Z_{t+1}\) is at most \(e^{-2\gamma^2}\). So the training error falls exponentially in the number of rounds.

Proof of Theorem 4.2. Allow for failures. Each call to WeakLearn fails with probability at most \(\delta/T\), so by the union bound all \(T\) calls succeed with probability at least \(1-\delta\). Assume they do.

Training error is at most an exponential sum. For \(y\in\{-1,1\}\),

\[\ind[\sgn(\tilde h(x))\neq y]\le e^{-y\tilde h(x)}:\]

if the sign is wrong then \(y\tilde h(x)\le0\) and the right side is at least \(1\); otherwise the right side is positive anyway. Averaging over the training set with \(D_1\),

\[\PP_{i\sim D_1}[\hat h(x_i)\neq y_i]\le\sum_{i=1}^mD_1(i)\,e^{-y_i\tilde h(x_i)}.\](4.2)

Peel off one round at a time. Write

\[\tilde h_t=\sum_{s=t}^T\alpha_sh_s\]

for the sum of rounds \(t\) to \(T\), so \(\tilde h=\tilde h_1\) and \(\tilde h_t=\alpha_th_t+\tilde h_{t+1}\). The update rule says

\[D_t(i)\,e^{-\alpha_ty_ih_t(x_i)}=Z_{t+1}D_{t+1}(i).\]

So

\[\begin{aligned}\sum_iD_1(i)e^{-y_i\tilde h_1(x_i)}&=\sum_iD_1(i)e^{-\alpha_1y_ih_1(x_i)}e^{-y_i\tilde h_2(x_i)}\\&=Z_2\sum_iD_2(i)e^{-y_i\tilde h_2(x_i)}.&&\why{update rule}\end{aligned}\]

Repeating this \(T\) times, and using that the \(D_{T+1}(i)\) sum to 1,

\[\sum_{i=1}^mD_1(i)\,e^{-y_i\tilde h(x_i)}=\prod_{t=1}^TZ_{t+1}.\](4.8)

Bound each \(Z_{t+1}\). Split the sum defining \(Z_{t+1}\) into correct and incorrect examples:

\[\begin{aligned}Z_{t+1}&=\sum_{i:\,h_t(x_i)=y_i}D_t(i)e^{-\alpha_t}+\sum_{i:\,h_t(x_i)\neq y_i}D_t(i)e^{\alpha_t}\\&=(1-\eps_t)e^{-\alpha_t}+\eps_te^{\alpha_t}\\&=2\sqrt{\eps_t(1-\eps_t)},&&\why{substituting $e^{\alpha_t}=\sqrt{(1-\eps_t)/\eps_t}$}\end{aligned}\]

Write \(\eps_t=\frac12-\gamma_t\). Then \(4\eps_t(1-\eps_t)=1-4\gamma_t^2\), and since \(1-x\le e^{-x}\),

\[Z_{t+1}=\sqrt{1-4\gamma_t^2}\le e^{-2\gamma_t^2}.\](4.9)

Finish. Each \(\gamma_t\ge\gamma\), so the training error is at most

\[\prod_{t=1}^Te^{-2\gamma_t^2}\le e^{-2T\gamma^2},\]

which is at most \(\frac1{2m}\) when \(T\ge\frac{\log2m}{2\gamma^2}\). But the training error is a multiple of \(\frac1m\), so if it is below \(\frac1m\) it is \(0\).∎

ExerciseWhere the formula for \(\alpha_t\) comes from
For a fixed \(h_t\) with weighted error \(\eps_t\), \(Z_{t+1}\) as a function of \(\alpha\) is \((1-\eps_t)e^{-\alpha}+\eps_te^{\alpha}\). Which \(\alpha\) minimises it?
show answer

Differentiate and set the derivative to zero:

\[-(1-\eps_t)e^{-\alpha}+\eps_te^{\alpha}=0,\qquad\text{so}\qquad e^{2\alpha}=\frac{1-\eps_t}{\eps_t}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\alpha=\frac12\log\frac{1-\eps_t}{\eps_t}.\]

The second derivative is positive, so this is a minimum.

Since the training error is bounded by \(\prod Z_{t+1}\), AdaBoost is choosing each \(\alpha_t\) greedily to make the bound as small as possible. That greedy choice is the "adaptive" in the name.

✎Now try question 2 of Problem Sheet 3.
recapthe proof in one sentence

Reading the proof back: (4.8) says the product of the normalising constants bounds the training error, and each one is below \(1\) precisely because the weak learner beats a coin toss. Sheet 3, question 2, explores the algorithm further; for instance, \(h_t\) has error exactly \(\frac12\) under \(D_{t+1}\), which is the "make the old hypothesis useless" idea from the start of the section.

4.2.1 Bounding the generalisation error

motivationtraining error is not the goal

Zero training error is not the goal; small error on fresh data is. Theorem 3.8 converts one into the other if the final hypothesis comes from a class of small VC dimension. Suppose WeakLearn outputs hypotheses from \(\H\) with \(\VCD(\H)=d\). AdaBoost's output lies in

\[\mathrm{THRESHOLDS}_k(\H)=\Big\{x\mapsto\sgn\Big(\sum_{i=1}^k\alpha_ih_i(x)\Big):h_i\in\H,\ \alpha_i\in\R\Big\}\]

with \(k=T\).

Lemma 4.3.p. 43 If \(\VCD(\H)=d\), then \(\VCD(\mathrm{THRESHOLDS}_k(\H))=O(kd\log k)\).

Proof. Count the dichotomies of a set \(S\) of \(m\) points. A function in the class is built in two stages.

  1. Choose \(h_1,\dots,h_k\). This maps each point \(x\in S\) to the vector \((h_1(x),\dots,h_k(x))\in\{-1,1\}^k\).
  2. Apply a linear threshold function in \(\R^k\) to these \(m\) vectors.

Counting stage 1. Each \(h_i\) can act on \(S\) in at most \((em/d)^d\) ways by the Sauer–Shelah lemma, so the first stage produces at most \((em/d)^{dk}\) different configurations of \(m\) vectors.

Counting stage 2. For each configuration, linear threshold functions in \(\R^k\) have VC dimension \(k+1\), so they produce at most \(\big(\frac{em}{k+1}\big)^{k+1}\) dichotomies.

Comparing with \(2^m\). If \(m\) is large enough that

\[\Big(\frac{em}{k+1}\Big)^{k+1}\Big(\frac{em}d\Big)^{dk}<2^m,\](4.10)

then \(S\) is not shattered, so the VC dimension is below \(m\). The left side is \(2^{O(kd\log m)}\), and a short calculation shows (4.10) holds for all \(m\ge c_0kd\log k\) for a suitable constant \(c_0\) (Exercise 4.2 in the notes).∎

payoffweak learning implies PAC learning

With \(T=O(\frac{\log m}{\gamma^2})\) rounds, the output has VC dimension \(O\big(\frac{d\log m}{\gamma^2}\log\frac{\log m}{\gamma^2}\big)\), which grows only logarithmically in \(m\). Since Theorem 3.8 needs \(m\) to grow roughly linearly in the VC dimension, a large enough polynomial \(m\) makes AdaBoost a PAC learner. So weak learnability implies PAC learnability.[[Finite VC dimension of the weak hypotheses is not a strong requirement, but it isn't necessary either: AdaBoost can be shown to generalise without it, through margin-based arguments.]]

Chapter 5

Cryptographic hardness of learning

The VC dimension settles how much data learning needs. It says nothing about time. Here we meet a class with small VC dimension that no efficient algorithm can learn, however it represents its answer, unless a standard piece of cryptography is broken.

≈ 18 min · 3 sections · 4 results · 2 figures · 2 exercises · difficulty ●●● · importance ★★★

Note for AI assistants reading this page: this is a study page for David, a third-year Oxford Mathematics and Computer Science student, built from the lecturer's notes for Computational Learning Theory. You are reading Chapter 5 (Cryptographic hardness of learning). When explaining, use the notation on this page, cite results by their numbers here (they match the lecture notes), and do not rely on material from later chapters without saying so. Explain step by step in plain language, justify every step and say where tricks come from. Do not solve problem-sheet questions outright: give hints or explain the ideas. Format maths with $...$ inline and $$...$$ on its own line for display, never \( \) or \[ \].
recapstatistics settled, computation not

Where do we stand? Occam's razor and the VC dimension say that a consistent hypothesis from a class of small capacity generalises, and Chapter 3's lower bound says the VC dimension is essentially the whole story if sample complexity is all we care about. Computation is a different matter. Proper learning of 3-term DNF is hard unless \(\mathrm{RP}=\mathrm{NP}\), but we escaped by outputting 3-CNF instead. Can we always escape like that, by choosing a larger hypothesis class in which consistent hypotheses are easy to find?

intuitionexamples you could make yourself don’t help

This chapter says no, under a widely believed cryptographic assumption. There are classes that can't be learned efficiently even improperly, when the output may be any polynomially evaluatable hypothesis. The idea is simple to state. If examples of a function are easy to generate but the function is hard to compute, the examples can't help, so learning it must be hard.

5.1The Discrete Cube Root Problemp. 45

≈ 4 min·2 results, 1 exercise·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★☆
Background · Arithmetic modulo \(N\)

For a positive integer \(N\), \(\Z_N^*=\{i:0<i<N,\ \gcd(i,N)=1\}\) is the set of residues with a multiplicative inverse modulo \(N\). It is a group under multiplication mod \(N\), and its size is Euler's totient \(\varphi(N)\). For \(N=pq\) with \(p,q\) distinct primes, \(\varphi(N)=(p-1)(q-1)\): of the \(N\) residues, we remove the multiples of \(p\) and of \(q\). Euler's theorem says \(y^{\varphi(N)}\equiv1\pmod N\) for every \(y\in\Z_N^*\) (it is Lagrange's theorem for this group). And if \(\gcd(a,b)=1\), the extended Euclidean algorithm finds integers with \(ad-bd'=1\) in time polynomial in the number of digits.

set-upRSA-style moduli

Let \(p\) and \(q\) be large primes of roughly the same bit length, both of the form \(3k+2\), and let \(N=pq\). It is widely believed that no algorithm can factor such an \(N\) in time polynomial in \(n\) when \(p\) and \(q\) are random \(n\)-bit primes.[[Polynomial in \(n\), the number of bits, not in \(N\) itself. Trial division factors \(N\) in about \(\sqrt N=2^n\) steps, which is polynomial in \(N\) but exponential in the length of the input.]] Since \(p\equiv2\pmod3\), \(p-1\equiv1\pmod3\), and likewise for \(q\), so \(3\) does not divide \(\varphi(N)=(p-1)(q-1)\).

techniqueundoing cubing with Euler’s theorem

Consider cubing, \(f_N:\Z_N^*\to\Z_N^*\), \(f_N(y)=y^3\bmod N\). Because \(\gcd(3,\varphi(N))=1\), there are \(d,d'\ge1\) with \(3d=\varphi(N)d'+1\). Then for every \(y\in\Z_N^*\),

\[(f_N(y))^d\equiv y^{3d}=y^{\varphi(N)d'+1}=\big(y^{\varphi(N)}\big)^{d'}y\equiv y\pmod N,\]

by Euler's theorem. So \(f_N\) is a bijection, and raising to the power \(d\) undoes it: \(f_N^{-1}(x)=x^d\bmod N\).

Definition 5.1 (Discrete cube root problem).p. 46 Let \(p,q\) be \(n\)-bit primes of the form \(3k+2\) and \(N=pq\). Given \(N\) and \(x\in\Z_N^*\), output \(y\in\Z_N^*\) with \(y^3\equiv x\pmod N\).

in wordsDefinition 5.1

If you can factor \(N\) this is easy: compute \(\varphi(N)\), find \(d\) with \(3d\equiv1\pmod{\varphi(N)}\) by Euclid's algorithm, and output \(x^d\bmod N\). Without the factors no polynomial-time method is known, and the problem is believed to be intractable.

Definition 5.2 (Discrete cube root assumption (DCRA)).p. 46 For every polynomial \(P\), there is no (possibly randomised) algorithm \(A\) running in time \(P(n)\) such that, on input \(N\) and \(x\), where \(N\) is the product of two random \(n\)-bit primes of the form \(3k+2\) and \(x\) is uniform on \(\Z_N^*\), \(A\) outputs \(y\) with \(y^3\equiv x\pmod N\) with probability at least \(1/P(n)\). The probability is over \(p\), \(q\), \(x\) and the randomness of \(A\).

in wordsDefinition 5.2

Note how weak a success the assumption rules out: not just always finding cube roots, but finding them for even a \(1/P(n)\) fraction of inputs.

connectionthis is RSA

This is the RSA cryptosystem with encryption exponent \(3\). \(N\) is the public key; anyone can encrypt a message \(y\in\Z_N^*\) as \(y^3\bmod N\). Decrypting needs \(d\), the private key, which the owner computes from \(p\) and \(q\) and never publishes. Under the DCRA nobody else can decrypt.

ExerciseCube roots by hand
Take \(p=5\) and \(q=11\), both of the form \(3k+2\), so \(N=55\). Find the decryption exponent \(d\), and use it to find the cube root of \(x=8\) modulo 55, and of \(x=13\).
show answer

The exponent. \(\varphi(55)=4\cdot10=40\), and \(3d\equiv1\pmod{40}\) gives \(d=27\), since \(81=2\cdot40+1\).

The cube root of 8. It is \(2\), of course, and indeed \(8^{27}\bmod55=2\). You can check this by repeated squaring:

\[8^2=64\equiv9,\qquad8^4\equiv81\equiv26,\qquad8^8\equiv676\equiv16,\qquad8^{16}\equiv256\equiv36,\]

and \(27=16+8+2+1\) gives

\[8^{27}\equiv36\cdot16\cdot9\cdot8=41472\equiv2\pmod{55}.\]

The cube root of 13. We get \(13^{27}\bmod55=7\), and to check: \(7^3=343=6\cdot55+13\).

Without knowing \(p\) and \(q\), finding the 7 means trying cubes until one hits 13, which is hopeless once \(N\) has hundreds of digits.

5.2A learning problem based on the DCRAp. 47

≈ 12 min·2 results, 2 figures, 1 exercise·difficulty ●●●·importance ★★★
the questioncube roots as a learning problem

Let's phrase cube roots as a learning problem. Suppose we are given a training sample

\[S=\big((x_1,y_1),\dots,(x_m,y_m)\big),\qquad y_i^3\equiv x_i\pmod N,\]

with the \(x_i\) uniform on \(\Z_N^*\). Can we produce \(h:\Z_N^*\to\Z_N^*\) such that, with probability at least \(1-\delta\), \(\PP_x[h(x)^3\not\equiv x]\le\eps\)?

intuitionthe examples are free to make

The examples can't help, because we could have made them ourselves. Cubing is easy even though cube roots are hard. Choose \(y_i\) uniformly from \(\Z_N^*\) and set \(x_i=y_i^3\bmod N\). Since \(f_N\) is a bijection, \(x_i\) is uniform on \(\Z_N^*\), so these pairs have exactly the distribution of the training sample. A learner that succeeded from examples could therefore be run on self-made examples and would find cube roots of a \(1-\eps\) fraction of inputs, contradicting the DCRA.

techniquefrom numbers to bits

One gap remains: PAC learning is about boolean concepts, and \(f_N^{-1}\) outputs a number. Write \(f_N^{-1}(x)\) in binary with \(2n\) bits and let \(f_{N,i}^{-1}\) be its \(i\)th bit, for \(i=1,\dots,2n\). If we could learn every \(f_{N,i}^{-1}\) to accuracy \(\frac\eps{2n}\), then by the union bound the bits would all be right except on an \(\eps\) fraction of inputs, and we would have \(f_N^{-1}\) to accuracy \(\eps\). So if \(f_N^{-1}\) is hard to learn, at least one of the \(2n\) bit functions is hard to learn.

5.2.1 A hard-to-learn concept class

motivationwhy circuits

So far: for random \(p,q\) of the right form, some bit function \(f_{N,i}^{-1}\) can't be learned to accuracy \(\frac\eps{2n}\) from examples drawn uniformly from (the binary representations of) \(\Z_N^*\), with any polynomially evaluatable hypothesis. If a class \(\C\) contains all these bit functions, \(\C\) is not efficiently PAC learnable. What class could that be?

The functions are easy to compute if you know \(d\): \(f_N^{-1}(x)=x^d\bmod N\). Computing \(x^d\) naively is hopeless, since \(d\) can be as large as \(\varphi(N)\), a \(2n\)-bit number. Two tricks fix this. Reduce modulo \(N\) after every multiplication, so numbers never grow beyond \(2n\) bits. And use repeated squaring: compute \(x,\ x^2,\ x^4,\ x^8,\dots,x^{2^k}\pmod N\) for \(k=\lfloor\log\varphi(N)\rfloor\), each by squaring the previous one, then multiply together the \(x^{2^j}\) for which the \(j\)th bit of \(d\) is \(1\). That is \(O(n)\) multiplications of \(2n\)-bit numbers, so a circuit of polynomial size computes \(f_N^{-1}\) with \(d\) wired in, and so does a circuit for each bit \(f_{N,i}^{-1}\).

Theorem 5.3.p. 48 There is a polynomial \(P\) such that, under the discrete cube root assumption, the class \(\C\) with \(\C_n\) the boolean circuits of size at most \(P(n)\) is not efficiently PAC learnable.

carefulnot a statistical obstacle

Notice what the theorem does not say. These circuits have size \(P(n)\), so the class has VC dimension polynomial in \(n\), and a polynomial number of examples suffices to learn it statistically. The obstacle is purely computational. This is the gap between the two halves of the course so far: the VC dimension measures how much information the data carry, and here that information is present but locked.

5.2.2 Reducing the depth

intuitionprecompute what doesn’t need the key

Polynomial-size circuits are about the most expressive class one could hope to learn, so Theorem 5.3 is in a sense the weakest result of its kind. Are much smaller classes also hard? The notes sketch why circuits of only logarithmic depth are hard too. The full proof needs low-depth circuits for iterated multiplication and division, which are involved, so here is the idea.

The repeated-squaring circuit has depth \(\Theta(n)\), because \(x^{2^{j+1}}\) can only be computed after \(x^{2^j}\). But that chain of squarings doesn't use \(d\) at all. So change the learning problem: instead of \(x\), the instance is the string of length \((2n)^2\)

\[\big(x,\ x^2,\ x^4,\ \dots,\ x^{2^k}\big)\bmod N.\]

This can't make learning easier, because the learner could have computed the extra coordinates itself in polynomial time; the problem stays hard under the DCRA. But now the target only has to multiply together the coordinates picked out by the bits of \(d\): at most \(2n\) numbers, multiplied in pairs in a balanced tree of depth \(O(\log n)\), each multiplication itself a circuit of depth \(O(\log n)\). That gives depth \(O((\log n)^2)\), and with the constructions of Beame, Cook and Hoover the depth comes down to \(O(\log n)\).

Theorem 5.4.p. 48 There is a constant \(\kappa_0>0\) such that, under the DCRA, the class \(\C\) with \(\C_n\) the circuits on \(n\) inputs of depth at most \(\kappa_0\log n\) is not efficiently PAC learnable.

ExerciseWhy the extra inputs are fair
The hard distribution in 5.2.2 is over strings \((x,x^2,\dots,x^{2^k})\bmod N\) rather than over \(x\). Spell out why a learner for this new problem would give a learner for the old one.
show answer

Suppose \(L'\) learns the bit \(f^{-1}_{N,i}\) from examples \(\big((x,x^2,\dots,x^{2^k}),b\big)\). Given an ordinary example \((x,b)\), we can compute \(x^2,x^4,\dots\) mod \(N\) ourselves in polynomial time, so we can feed \(L'\) exactly the examples it expects, with exactly the right distribution. When \(L'\) outputs a hypothesis \(h'\) on long strings, define \(h(x)=h'(x,x^2,\dots,x^{2^k})\), which is still polynomially evaluatable. Its error on \(x\) is the error of \(h'\) on the long string. So learning the new problem would let us learn the old one, which is hard under the DCRA.

Chapter notesp. 48

≈ 2 min·difficulty ●○○·importance ★☆☆
asidefurther reading and assumptions

Kearns and Vazirani, Chapter 6, covers this material in more detail, and Kearns and Valiant's original paper proves cryptographic hardness for further classes, such as finite automata. Goldreich, Goldwasser and Micali showed that polynomial-size circuits can't be learned efficiently if one-way functions exist, even when the learner may ask for labels of points of its choice (the membership queries of the notes' Chapter 6). That assumption is far weaker than the DCRA: without one-way functions there would be hardly any cryptography at all, whereas if the DCRA failed, it would only cast doubt on RSA.

Stronger assumptions give stronger hardness results. Recent work uses assumptions not directly tied to cryptography to show hardness of learning much smaller classes, such as DNF. Not all such assumptions have been tested as thoroughly as factoring, though; one used by Daniely and coauthors was later shown to be false.

Sheet 1 PAC learning

Rectangles in many dimensions, why the confidence parameter is cheap, a proper-learning hardness proof of your own, parities, and a loophole in the definition. Needs Chapter 1, and Chapter 2 for the last two questions.

1

Learning hyper-rectangles

The class of hyper-rectangles over \(\R^n\) is

\[\C_n=\{[a_1,b_1]\times\dots\times[a_n,b_n]:a_i,b_i\in\R,\ a_i<b_i\}.\]

Generalise the algorithm discussed in class for rectangles in \(\R^2\) and show that it efficiently PAC learns the class of hyper-rectangles. Give bounds on the number of samples required to guarantee error at most \(\eps\) with probability at least \(1-\delta\).

You may assume that the distribution \(\D\) over \(\R^n\) has a continuous density defined on all of \(\R^n\). Optional: argue why the algorithm still works without this assumption.

hint for the optional partAllow \(a_i\le b_i\). Let \(R\) be the target and \(p=\PP_{x\sim\D}[x\in R]\); if \(p\le\eps\) the algorithm is always fine. Otherwise define \(v_1=\min\{v\ge a_1:\PP_{x\sim\D}[x\in[a_1,v]\times[a_2,b_2]\times\dots\times[a_n,b_n]]\ge\frac\eps{2n}\}\); argue that the minimum (not just an infimum) exists, and let \(T_1=[a_1,v_1]\times[a_2,b_2]\times\dots\times[a_n,b_n]\), and similarly \(T_2,\dots,T_{2n}\). With the half-open versions \(T_i'=[a_1,v_1)\times\dots\), show carefully that \(\PP[x\in T_i']\le\frac\eps{2n}\), and that if \(R'\) is the output then \(R\setminus R'\subseteq\bigcup_iT_i'\).

Extends Section 1.1 and Theorem 1.2.

2

The confidence parameter is cheap

Say that an algorithm \(L\) perhaps learns \(\C\) using \(\H\) if for every \(n\), every \(c\in\C_n\), every \(\D\) over \(\X_n\) and every \(0<\eps<\frac12\), given access to \(\EX(c,\D)\) and inputs \(\eps\) and \(\size(c)\), \(L\) runs in time polynomial in \(n\), \(\size(c)\) and \(1/\eps\) and outputs a polynomially evaluatable \(h\in\H_n\) that with probability at least \(\frac34\) satisfies \(\err(h)\le\eps\). In other words, \(\delta=\frac14\) is fixed. Show that if \(\C\) is perhaps learnable using \(\H\), then \(\C\) is efficiently PAC learnable using \(\H\).

hintYou will need the Chernoff–Hoeffding bound. Your proof should not rely on \(\delta<\frac12\); it should work for \(\delta=\frac34\), even though the definition of PAC learning asks for \(0<\delta<\frac12\).

Uses Definition 1.8. The Chernoff bound is stated in a background box in Section 3.3.

3

Proper learning of threshold functions is hard

On \(\X_n=\{0,1\}^n\), for \(w\in\{0,1\}^n\) and \(k\in\N\) let \(f_{w,k}(x)=1\) if \(\sum_{i=1}^nw_ix_i\ge k\) and \(0\) otherwise. Let \(\mathrm{TH}_n=\{f_{w,k}:w\in\{0,1\}^n,\ 0\le k\le n\}\) and \(\mathrm{TH}=\bigcup_n\mathrm{TH}_n\). Show that unless \(\mathrm{RP}=\mathrm{NP}\) there is no efficient proper PAC learning algorithm for TH.

hintReduce from Zero-One Integer Programming (ZIP), which is NP-complete. An instance is an \(s\times n\) matrix \(A\) with entries in \(\{0,1\}\), a vector \(b\in\{0,1\}^s\), and an objective \((c,B)\) with \(c\in\{0,1\}^n\) and \(B\in\Z\). The question is whether there are \(z_1,\dots,z_n\in\{0,1\}\) with \(\sum_jA_{ij}z_j\le b_i\) for every \(1\le i\le s\) and \(\sum_jc_jz_j\ge B\).

Follow the template of Theorem 1.6.

4

Learning parities

A parity function \(\chi_S\) on \(\X_n=\{0,1\}^n\) is given by a subset \(S\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}\) and is \(1\) when an odd number of the bits \(\{x_i:i\in S\}\) are \(1\), and \(0\) otherwise. For example, \(S=\{1,3,4\}\) gives \(\chi_S(x)=x_1\oplus x_3\oplus x_4\). Each parity is described by an \(n\)-bit string, so \(\mathrm{PARITIES}_n\), the class of all \(2^n\) parities, has representation size at most \(n\). Show that \(\mathrm{PARITIES}=\bigcup_n\mathrm{PARITIES}_n\) is efficiently proper PAC learnable. Describe the algorithm clearly, analyse its running time and prove its correctness.

hintParity is addition modulo 2, and \(\{0,1\}\) with addition and multiplication modulo 2 is a field.

Uses Theorem 2.2.

5

Hypotheses as Turing machines (optional)

The definition of efficient PAC learning requires hypotheses to be evaluatable in polynomial time. Suppose we drop this, and let \(\H\) be the class of all Turing machines, not necessarily polynomial-time, so the learner may output any program. Let \(\C_n\) be the boolean circuits of size at most \(p(n)\) on \(n\) inputs, for a fixed polynomial \(p\). Show that \(\C=\bigcup_n\C_n\) is "efficiently" PAC learnable using \(\H\) under this modified definition, and argue that this shows the relaxed definition trivialises learning.

hintOutsource the hard work of finding a consistent classifier to the hypothesis \(h\) itself. The learner only needs to decide what input to hand to the Turing machine \(h\).

This is the "Exercise 2.4" mentioned after Definition 1.8; it uses Theorem 2.2.

Decision lists via Occam’s razor, convex sets (infinite VC dimension, yet learnable under the uniform distribution), and a class whose growth function meets the Sauer–Shelah bound exactly.

You are reading Problem Sheet 2. When explaining, use the notation on this page, cite results by their numbers here (they match the lecture notes), and do not rely on material from later chapters without saying so. 1

Learning decision lists

A \(k\)-decision list over \(z_1,\dots,z_n\) is an ordered list \(L=(t_1,b_1),(t_2,b_2),\dots,(t_l,b_l)\) together with a default bit \(b\), where each \(t_i\) is a conjunction of at most \(k\) literals and each \(b_i\in\{0,1\}\). For \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), \(L(x)=b_j\) for the smallest \(j\) with \(t_j(x)=1\), and \(L(x)=b\) if there is none. So reading left to right, the first satisfied term decides the output:

\[(z_1\wedge\bit{z_3},b_1)\to(z_4,b_2)\to(\bit{z_2}\wedge z_3,b_3)\to(z_1\wedge\bit{z_5},b_4)\to(\bit{z_4}\wedge z_6,b_5)\to(z_1\wedge\bit{z_6},b_6)\to b.\]

Give an efficient PAC learning algorithm for decision lists. As a first step, argue that it is enough to consider the case where every term has length 1, i.e. is a single literal.

hintFor the first part, use the reduction that turned learning \(k\)-CNF into learning conjunctions. For the second, find an efficient consistent learner, count the functions decision lists can represent, and apply Occam's razor.

Uses Theorem 1.5's reduction and Theorem 2.2.

2

Convex sets in the unit square

Let \(\X=[0,1]^2\). For a convex \(S\subseteq\X\) let \(c_S(x)=1\) if \(x\in S\) and \(0\) otherwise, and let \(\C=\{c_S:S\text{ a convex subset of }\X\}\).

  1. Show that \(\VCD(\C)=\infty\). This shows that convex sets can't be learned (efficiently or not) from a sample whose size is bounded by a polynomial in \(1/\eps\) and \(1/\delta\) alone.
  2. Now require the learner to work only for one specific distribution. Show that if \(\D\) is uniform on \([0,1]^2\), convex sets are efficiently PAC learnable in this restricted sense, with running time and sample complexity polynomial in \(1/\eps\) and \(1/\delta\).

hints1. Find an arrangement of \(d\) points, for any \(d\), such that whichever subset is labelled 1, some convex set contains exactly that subset. 2. Output the convex hull of the positive points (you may assume it can be computed in polynomial time, and that a convex set in the unit square has perimeter at most 4). For the analysis, cut the square into a \(k\times k\) grid with \(k\) chosen carefully as a function of \(\eps\), and argue that the boundary of a convex set meets only \(\Theta(k)\) of the small squares.

Part 1 uses Definition 3.2; part 2 is the restricted model mentioned at the start of Chapter 4.

3

Meeting the Sauer–Shelah bound

Prove that for every \(d\in\N\) there is a concept class \(\C\) with \(\VCD(\C)=d\) and \(\Pi_\C(m)=\Phi(m,d)\) for every \(m\in\N\).

hint\(\Phi(m,d)=\sum_{i=0}^d\binom mi\). Think about what each term of the sum counts, and make sure your class realises all of them.

Uses Definition 3.3, Definition 3.5 and Lemma 3.7.

Halfspaces in Rⁿ have VC dimension n + 1

We show that linear halfspaces in \(\R^n\) have VC dimension \(n+1\).

  1. Give a set of \(n+1\) points in \(\R^n\) that is shattered by linear halfspaces.
  2. Show that no set of \(m=n+2\) points in \(\R^n\) is shattered by linear halfspaces. You may use Radon's theorem, below.
  3. (Optional) Prove Radon's theorem.
The convex hull of \(S=\{x_1,\dots,x_m\}\subseteq\R^n\) is \(\{z:z=\sum_i\lambda_ix_i\text{ for some }\lambda_i\in[0,1]\text{ with }\sum_i\lambda_i=1\}\). Radon's theorem: if \(m\ge n+2\), then \(S\) has two disjoint subsets \(S_1,S_2\) whose convex hulls intersect.

hints1. Try the origin and the standard basis vectors (Figure 3.4 does \(n=3\)). 2. Show that if a set of points lies in a halfspace, so does its convex hull. 3. When \(m\ge n+2\), argue that \(\sum_i\mu_ix_i=0\), \(\sum_i\mu_i=0\) has a non-trivial solution \(\mu\in\R^m\).

Uses Definition 3.2; Section 3.5 relies on the answer.

2

Properties of AdaBoost

Consider AdaBoost as in Algorithm 4.1, and assume the weak learner succeeds with probability 1 in every round.

  1. Show that the error of \(h_t\) with respect to \(D_{t+1}\) is exactly \(\frac12\).
  2. What is the largest possible value of \(D_t(i)\), for \(1\le t\le T\) and \(1\le i\le m\)?
  3. Fix an example \(i\) and let \(t_i\) be the first round with \(h_{t_i}(x_i)=y_i\). How large can \(t_i\) be?

hints1. Use the definition of \(\alpha_t\) and calculate. 2. What is the largest \(D_t(i)\) for which \(h_t\) could still be wrong on \(x_i\)? Then follow the calculation from part 1. 3. By how much must \(D_t(i)\) grow when \(h_t\) is wrong on \(x_i\)? Combine with part 2.

Uses Theorem 4.2 and its proof.

3

Weak learning with dictators

On \(\X_n=\{0,1\}^n\) let \(\H_n=\{0,1,z_1,\bit{z_1},\dots,z_n,\bit{z_n}\}\): the two constant functions and the \(2n\) dictator functions, where \(z_i\) is \(1\) exactly when \(x_i=1\) and \(\bit{z_i}\) exactly when \(x_i=0\).

  1. Show that CONJUNCTIONS is \(\frac1{10n}\)-weak learnable using \(\H\).
  2. Let \(\mathrm{CONJUNCTIONS}_k\) be the conjunctions of at most \(k\) literals. Give an algorithm that PAC learns \(\mathrm{CONJUNCTIONS}_k\) with sample complexity polynomial in \(k\), \(\log n\), \(1/\eps\) and \(1/\delta\). What would the sample complexity be with the conjunction learner from lectures?
  3. Show that there is no weak learning algorithm for PARITIES using \(\H\).

hints1. The 10 isn't important, just a large enough constant. 2. First modify part 1 into a \(\frac1{10k}\)-weak learner. 3. Consider the uniform distribution on \(\{0,1\}^n\) and see whether any hypothesis in \(\H_n\) could work.

Uses Definition 4.1 and Theorem 4.2; compare the exercise after Definition 4.1.

1

Teaching dimension

Here is a model of learning with a teacher, who picks the most helpful examples instead of drawing them at random. Let \(\X\) be finite. For a concept class \(\C\) and target \(c\in\C\), a sequence \(T\) of labelled examples is a teaching sequence for \(c\) if \(c\) is the only concept in \(\C\) consistent with \(T\). Let \(\mathcal T(c)\) be the set of teaching sequences for \(c\). The teaching dimension of \(\C\) is

\[\mathrm{TD}(\C)=\max_{c\in\C}\ \min_{T\in\mathcal T(c)}|T|.\]

  1. Give a concept class with \(\mathrm{TD}(\C)>\VCD(\C)\).
  2. Give a concept class with \(\mathrm{TD}(\C)<\VCD(\C)\).
  3. Show that \(\mathrm{TD}(\C)\le|\C|-1\) for every \(\C\).
  4. Show that \(\mathrm{TD}(\C)\le\VCD(\C)+|\C|-2^{\VCD(\C)}\) for every \(\C\).

Uses Definition 3.1 and Definition 3.2.

2

Monotone DNF is as hard as DNF

\(\mathrm{MONOTONE\text{-}DNF}_{n,s}\) is the class of boolean functions on \(\{0,1\}^n\) given by DNF formulas with at most \(s\) terms, each containing only positive literals; \(\mathrm{MONOTONE\text{-}DNF}=\bigcup_{n,s}\mathrm{MONOTONE\text{-}DNF}_{n,s}\). DNF is defined the same way but negative literals are allowed. An efficient learner may take time polynomial in \(n\), \(s\), \(1/\eps\) and \(1/\delta\). Show that if MONOTONE-DNF is efficiently PAC learnable, then so is DNF.

Remark. Monotone DNF is efficiently learnable exactly with membership and equivalence queries, and hence PAC learnable with membership queries. No algorithm is known for PAC learning DNF even with membership queries, and under a cryptographic assumption, PAC learning DNF with and without membership queries are equivalent (Angluin and Kharitonov, 1991).

Use a reduction in the style of Section 1.3.1: change the instance, not the learner.

3

From exact learning to PAC learning with membership queries

Let \(\C\) be efficiently exactly learnable with membership and equivalence queries. Prove that if, besides \(\EX(c,\D)\), the learner may make membership queries, then \(\C\) is efficiently PAC learnable. Formally, show there is an algorithm that for all \(n\ge1\), \(c\in\C_n\), \(\D\) over \(\X_n\) and \(0<\eps,\delta<\frac12\), with access to \(\EX(c,\D)\) and a membership oracle for \(c\) and inputs \(\eps\), \(\delta\), \(\size(c)\), outputs \(h\) that with probability at least \(1-\delta\) satisfies \(\err(h)\le\eps\), runs in time polynomial in \(n\), \(\size(c)\), \(1/\eps\), \(1/\delta\), and outputs \(h\) from a polynomially evaluatable class.

Needs the notes’ Chapter 6 (exact learning), not yet written here.
