B8.4 · Information TheoryChapter 0 · notes pp. 5–6

Chapter 0

Two questions

Every phone call, zip file and streamed film rests on two questions: how much information is in a message, and how much of it can survive a noisy wire. This course answers the first and starts on the second.

≈ 11 min · 3 sections · 0 results · 2 figures · 1 exercises · difficulty ●○○ · importance ★★★

Note for AI assistants reading this page: this is a study page for David, a third-year Oxford Mathematics and Computer Science student, built from the lecturer's notes for Information Theory. You are reading Chapter 0 (Introduction). When explaining, use the notation on this page, cite results by their numbers here (they match the lecture notes), and do not rely on material from later chapters without saying so. Explain step by step in plain language, justify every step and say where tricks come from. Do not solve problem-sheet questions outright: give hints or explain the ideas. Format maths with $...$ inline and $$...$$ on its own line for display, never \( \) or \[ \].

0.1Two questionsp. 5

≈ 5 min·1 figure·difficulty ●○○·importance ★★★
the questionsource coding and channel coding

Communication theory is a young subject, and it shaped the digital age. Whenever you store a file, make a call or stream a film, algorithms based on this course are running. But the mathematics arises on its own as soon as one tries to think precisely about "information": what it is, how to write it down, and how to send it somewhere. A large part of the course is about two questions.

  1. How much information is contained in a message? If you want to store a text, how few bits can you get away with? This is source coding, or compression.
  2. What are the limits to sending information over a channel that is subject to noise? If some bits get flipped on the way, how fast can you still communicate reliably? This is channel coding.
roadmapwhat the chapters do

Both questions need new mathematical objects. Chapter 1 builds them: entropy, which measures how unpredictable a random variable is; divergence, which measures how different two distributions are; and mutual information, which measures how much one random variable tells you about another. Chapter 2 introduces codes and the key probabilistic fact behind compression, that long random sequences are almost all "typical". Chapter 3 puts the two together and proves Shannon's first theorem: a source can be compressed to its entropy, and no further. Chapter 4 turns to the second question: every noisy channel has a capacity, and Shannon's second theorem says any rate below it can be sent with vanishing error, and no rate above it can. Chapter 5 extends both theorems to sources with memory, such as Markov chains, shows that compressing and then channel coding loses nothing, and ends with two algorithms for decoding a hidden Markov signal.

0.2A first guess at measuring informationp. 5

≈ 6 min·1 figure, 1 exercise·difficulty ●○○·importance ★★★
intuitioninformation as the number of yes/no questions

Before any definitions, here is the idea that the whole course makes precise. I think of a number between 1 and 64, and you may ask yes/no questions. The best strategy halves the possibilities each time ("is it at most 32?"), and finds the number in exactly \(6=\log_264\) questions. With \(N\) equally likely possibilities you need about \(\log_2N\) questions. So a sensible first measure of the information in the answer is \(\log_2N\) bits: one bit is the answer to one well-chosen yes/no question.

the questionwhat if the outcomes are not equally likely?

Now suppose the possibilities are not equally likely. If I almost always pick 7, you should ask "is it 7?" first, and usually you are done after one question. On average you need fewer questions than \(\log_2N\), because the answer was less uncertain to begin with. Figure 0.2 lets you try this. Pick a distribution and see the best question tree: likely outcomes are reached with few questions, unlikely ones with more.

payoffthe number that appears

The average number of questions in the best tree is always close to one particular number computed from the probabilities,

\[H=-\sum_xp(x)\log_2p(x),\]

which is the entropy of the distribution. For the uniform distribution on \(N\) outcomes it is exactly \(\log_2N\). Chapter 1 defines entropy properly and studies it; Chapter 3 proves that the best average number of yes/no questions (equivalently, the best average length of a binary code) lies between \(H\) and \(H+1\).

ExerciseTwenty questions
In the game of twenty questions you may ask 20 yes/no questions. Roughly how many equally likely objects can a perfect player distinguish? And if the objects are not equally likely, could a clever player handle even more of them?
show answer

With 20 questions, each halving the possibilities, a perfect player can separate \(2^{20}=1{,}048{,}576\) equally likely objects, about a million. If the objects are not equally likely, the player can tolerate many more of them in the list, as long as the rare ones are rare enough: the question tree can give long paths to rare objects and short ones to common ones. What matters is the entropy of the distribution, not the number of objects. (Strictly, a game with a hard limit of 20 questions must still separate every object, so it is the average number of questions that drops, not the worst case.)

0.3Connections and booksp. 5

≈ 2 min·difficulty ●○○·importance ★☆☆
connectionwhere else entropy appears

Information theory gives new interpretations of results in probability, and it is closely tied to

  • physics: thermodynamics, statistical mechanics, quantum theory;
  • computer science: Kolmogorov complexity, data compression, error-correcting codes;
  • statistics and machine learning: the log-loss, cross-entropy and Kullback–Leibler divergence are all objects from Chapter 1;
  • large deviation theory;
  • economics, finance and gambling.
asidetextbooks

The course mostly follows the classic textbook by Cover and Thomas, Elements of Information Theory (2nd edition, 2006). MacKay's Information Theory, Inference and Learning Algorithms (2003) is more informal, full of applications, and free online. Csiszár and Körner's Information Theory: Coding Theorems for Discrete Memoryless Systems (2011) is a concise, theory-first treatment.

← ContentsITChapter 1 →Entropy, Divergence and Mutual Information
B8.4 · Information TheoryChapter 1 · notes pp. 7–18

Chapter 1

Entropy, divergence and mutual information

Three numbers, all built from one function, the logarithm of a probability. Entropy measures how unpredictable one random variable is, divergence how far apart two distributions are, and mutual information how much one variable tells you about another.

≈ 42 min · 3 sections · 22 results · 4 figures · 7 exercises · difficulty ●●○ · importance ★★★

Note for AI assistants reading this page: this is a study page for David, a third-year Oxford Mathematics and Computer Science student, built from the lecturer's notes for Information Theory. You are reading Chapter 1 (Entropy, Divergence and Mutual Information). When explaining, use the notation on this page, cite results by their numbers here (they match the lecture notes), and do not rely on material from later chapters without saying so. Explain step by step in plain language, justify every step and say where tricks come from. Do not solve problem-sheet questions outright: give hints or explain the ideas. Format maths with $...$ inline and $$...$$ on its own line for display, never \( \) or \[ \].
set-updiscrete random variables

Most of this course is about sequences that are not perfectly predictable: letters of a text, or noisy readings of a signal. We model the randomness with a probability space \((\Omega,\F,\PP)\), as in B8.1, and random variables on it. In fact we will hardly ever look at \(\Omega\). We work with discrete random variables, taking values in a finite or countable set \(\X\), and describe each one by its probability mass function (pmf)

\[p(x)=\PP(X=x),\qquad x\in\X.\]

When several random variables are around we write \(p_X\), \(p_Y\), \(p_{X,Y}\) for the pmfs of \(X\), \(Y\) and the pair \((X,Y)\).

From Prelims · Laws, and what depends only on them

The law (or distribution) of \(X\) is the probability measure \(\PP_X=\PP\circ X^{-1}\) on the values of \(X\): it says how likely each set of values is, and forgets everything else about \(\Omega\). For a discrete random variable the law is the same information as the pmf.

Many quantities depend only on the law. The expectation \(\E[X]=\sum_xx\,p(x)\) is one: two random variables with the same pmf have the same mean, even if they live on different probability spaces. Other properties need more. Whether \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent cannot be read off from \(p_X\) and \(p_Y\) separately; it depends on the joint law of \((X,Y)\), through \(p_{X,Y}(x,y)=p_X(x)p_Y(y)\) for all \(x,y\).

1.1Basic definitions in information theoryp. 7

≈ 22 min·11 results, 3 figures, 5 exercises·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★★
historywhere the word comes from

The first challenge is to define the "level of randomness" of a random variable. The notion we use, entropy, goes back to Boltzmann, Gibbs and Maxwell's work on the statistical mechanics of gases; the word was coined by Clausius in 1865, from the Greek for "in-turning". Claude Shannon adapted these ideas to random signals in the late 1940s, which founded information theory. Von Neumann reportedly suggested the name to Shannon, on the grounds that "no one knows what entropy really is", so he would always win an argument.[[Why the letter H? Boltzmann used E. Around 1900 Gibbs or Zermelo switched to a capital eta, which looks like H, for reasons nobody knows, and Shannon followed the usage of his day, which referred to Boltzmann's H-theorem.]]

motivationmeasuring surprise

We want \(H(X)\) to measure our average uncertainty about \(X\): the less sure we are of its value, the bigger \(H(X)\). One way in is to first measure the surprise \(s(A)\) of seeing the event \(\{X\in A\}\). It seems natural to ask that

  1. \(s(A)\) depends continuously on \(\PP(X\in A)\), and on nothing else;
  2. \(s(A)\) is decreasing in \(\PP(X\in A)\): rarer events are more surprising;
  3. surprises of independent events add: \(s(A\cap B)=s(A)+s(B)\) whenever \(\PP(X\in A\cap B)=\PP(X\in A)\PP(X\in B)\).

Writing \(s(A)=g(\PP(X\in A))\), the third condition says \(g(uv)=g(u)+g(v)\): \(g\) turns products into sums. The logarithm does this, and a classical result of Cauchy says that, among continuous functions, only multiples of the logarithm do. Decreasing forces a negative multiple, so

\[s(A)=-\log\PP(X\in A),\]

up to the choice of base. This is sometimes called the Shannon information content of the outcome. An event of probability \(\frac12\) carries one bit of surprise, an event of probability \(\frac18\) three bits, and a certain event none.

ExerciseWhy the logarithm is forced
Let \(g:(0,1]\to\R\) be continuous with \(g(uv)=g(u)+g(v)\). Show that \(g(u)=c\log u\) for some constant \(c\).
show answer

Put \(u=e^{-s}\) and \(f(s)=g(e^{-s})\) for \(s\ge0\). Then \(f\) is continuous and \(f(s+t)=f(s)+f(t)\). By induction \(f(ns)=nf(s)\), so \(f(m/n)=\frac mnf(1)\) for positive integers \(m,n\): \(f\) is linear on the positive rationals. By continuity \(f(s)=f(1)s\) for all \(s\ge0\). So \(g(u)=f(-\ln u)=-f(1)\ln u\), a multiple of the logarithm. If \(g\) is decreasing, then \(f(1)>0\) and the multiple is negative, as claimed.

intuitionentropy is average surprise

Entropy is the average surprise: weight the surprise \(-\log p(x)\) of each value by how often it happens.

Definition 1.1 (Entropy).p. 8 The entropy in base \(b\) of a discrete random variable \(X\) is

\[H_b(X)=-\sum_{x\in\X}\PP(X=x)\log_b\PP(X=x),\](1.1.1)

with the convention \(0\cdot\log_b0=0\). We usually work in base 2 and write \(H(X)\) for \(H_2(X)\) and \(\log\) for \(\log_2\).

in wordsDefinition 1.1

The convention \(0\log0=0\) says that values which never happen contribute nothing; it is also the limit of \(p\log p\) as \(p\downarrow0\). Some remarks on the definition:

  • The notation \(H(X)\) is a little misleading: \(H\) depends only on the law of \(X\), not on \(X\) itself. Two random variables with the same pmf have the same entropy, just as they have the same mean. So it is also natural to write \(H(p_X)\) or \(H(\PP_X)\).
  • As an expectation, \(H(X)=-\E[\log p(X)]\), where \(p=p_X\) is the pmf. Here \(p(X)\) is a random variable: first draw \(X\), then look up the probability of the value you drew.[[Careful with the notation: \(p_X:\X\to[0,1]\) is an ordinary, non-random function. Only once you plug in the random \(X\) do you get something random.]]
  • The base only changes the unit. Since \(\log_bx=\log_ax/\log_ab\), we have \(H_b(X)=H_a(X)/\log_ab\). In base 2 the unit is the bit, in base \(e\) the nat, in base 256 the byte.

Example 1.2.p. 9 If \(\X=\{H,T\}\) and \(\PP(X=H)=p\), then

\[H(X)=-p\log p-(1-p)\log(1-p).\](1.1.2)

If \(p\in\{0,1\}\) then \(H(X)=0\). Differentiating in \(p\) shows that \(H(X)\) increases on \((0,\frac12)\) and decreases on \((\frac12,1)\), so it is maximised at \(p=\frac12\), where \(H(X)=\log2=1\) bit. This case comes up so often that we also write

\[H(p)=-p\log p-(1-p)\log(1-p),\]

the binary entropy function. So \(H(X)=H(p)=H(p_X)=H(\PP_X)\), which is notation at its most confusing.

ExerciseA fair die
What is the entropy of a fair six-sided die? And of the number of sixes in two throws?
show answer

For a fair die, every face has surprise \(\log6\), so \(H=\log6\approx2.585\) bits. The number of sixes \(N\) in two throws takes the values \(0,1,2\) with probabilities \(\frac{25}{36},\frac{10}{36},\frac1{36}\), so

\[H(N)=\tfrac{25}{36}\log\tfrac{36}{25}+\tfrac{10}{36}\log\tfrac{36}{10}+\tfrac1{36}\log36\approx0.365+0.513+0.144=1.02\text{ bits}.\]

That is far less than \(\log3\approx1.585\), because the outcome is usually \(0\).

Example 1.3.p. 9 If \(X=(X_1,X_2)\) with \(X_i\in\X_i\), then

\[H(X)=H(X_1,X_2)=-\sum_{x_1\in\X_1,\,x_2\in\X_2}p_{X_1,X_2}(x_1,x_2)\log p_{X_1,X_2}(x_1,x_2).\](1.1.3)

If \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) are independent, so \(p_{X_1,X_2}(x_1,x_2)=p_{X_1}(x_1)p_{X_2}(x_2)\), then

\[H(X)=H(X_1)+H(X_2),\](1.1.4)

and if they are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.), then

\[H(X)=2H(X_1)=2H(X_2).\](1.1.5)
intuitionentropy as a storage bound

Here is a second reading of entropy, which the course will make rigorous. Suppose we want to store the results of \(n\) independent flips of the coin of Example 1.2, knowing \(p\). If \(p\in\{0,1\}\) the results are certain and need no storage at all, matching \(H(X)=0\). If \(p=\frac12\) every sequence of \(n\) flips is equally likely, and it is intuitive that we need \(n\) bits, matching \(nH(X)=n\). In between, Chapter 3 will show that about \(nH(p)\) bits are needed and suffice. So entropy is also a compression bound.

motivationcomparing two distributions

Entropy measures one distribution. The next quantity compares two pmfs \(p\) and \(q\) on the same set. It will tell us, for instance, how much we lose by designing a code for the wrong distribution (Proposition 3.6).

Definition 1.4 (Divergence).p. 9 Let \(p\) and \(q\) be pmfs on \(\X\). The divergence between \(p\) and \(q\) is

\[D(p\|q)=\sum_{x\in\X}p(x)\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)},\](1.1.6)

with the conventions \(0\log0=0\) (terms with \(p(x)=0\) contribute nothing) and \(D(p\|q)=\infty\) if there is an \(x\) with \(q(x)=0\) but \(p(x)>0\). It is also called Kullback–Leibler divergence, relative entropy or information divergence.

in wordsDefinition 1.4 as extra surprise

If \(X\sim p\) (meaning \(X\) has pmf \(p\)), then

\[\begin{aligned}D(p\|q)&=\E\Big[\log\frac{p(X)}{q(X)}\Big]\\&=\E\Big[\log\frac1{q(X)}\Big]-\E\Big[\log\frac1{p(X)}\Big]\\&=\E\Big[\log\frac1{q(X)}\Big]-H(X).\end{aligned}\]

In words: \(\E[\log\frac1{q(X)}]\) is the average surprise of someone who believes the pmf is \(q\) while the truth is \(p\), and \(D(p\|q)\) is how much more surprised they are, on average, than someone who knows the truth. We will show it is never negative. But it is not a metric: in general \(D(p\|q)\neq D(q\|p)\), and it can be infinite. The next example shows these are features, not bugs.

Example 1.5.p. 10 Let \(\X=\{0,1\}\), with \(p(0)=\frac12\) and \(q(0)=1\). We see independent samples from one of the two distributions, but don't know which. If we observe \(0000001\), we immediately know the source is \(p\), since \(q\) never produces a \(1\). If we observe \(0000000\), the source is probably \(q\), but we can't rule out \(p\). The divergence reflects this: \(D(p\|q)=\infty\), since \(q(1)=0<p(1)\), while \(D(q\|p)=1\cdot\log\frac1{1/2}=1\).

Example 1.6.p. 10 If \(q\) is the uniform distribution on a finite set \(\X\), then \(D(p\|q)=\log|\X|-H(X)\), where \(X\sim p\).

in wordsExample 1.6

Indeed \(\log\frac1{q(x)}=\log|\X|\) for every \(x\), so the first term in the identity above is \(\log|\X|\). So entropy is "\(\log|\X|\) minus the distance from uniform": the closer \(p\) is to uniform, the larger its entropy.

ExerciseDivergence between two coins
Compute \(D(p\|q)\) and \(D(q\|p)\) for coins with heads probability \(\frac12\) and \(\frac14\).
show answer

With \(p=(\frac12,\frac12)\) and \(q=(\frac14,\frac34)\),

\[D(p\|q)=\tfrac12\log\tfrac{1/2}{1/4}+\tfrac12\log\tfrac{1/2}{3/4}=\tfrac12-\tfrac12\log\tfrac32\approx0.5-0.292=0.208,\]
\[D(q\|p)=\tfrac14\log\tfrac{1/4}{1/2}+\tfrac34\log\tfrac{3/4}{1/2}=-\tfrac14+\tfrac34\log\tfrac32\approx-0.25+0.439=0.189.\]

Both positive, and different.

motivationhow much does Y tell us about X?

The third quantity measures dependence. If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, \(p_{X,Y}=p_Xp_Y\). So one natural measure of dependence is how far the joint pmf is from the product of its marginals, measured by divergence.

Definition 1.7 (Mutual information).p. 10 Let \(X,Y\) be discrete random variables taking values in \(\X\) and \(\mathcal Y\). The mutual information between \(X\) and \(Y\) is

\[I(X;Y)=\sum_{x\in\X}\sum_{y\in\mathcal Y}\PP(X=x,Y=y)\log\frac{\PP(X=x,Y=y)}{\PP(X=x)\PP(Y=y)}.\]
in wordsfour ways to see Definition 1.7
  • It is exactly the divergence described above: \(I(X;Y)=D(p_{X,Y}\|p_Xp_Y)\). So it measures how much dependence there is between \(X\) and \(Y\).
  • Unlike the covariance \(\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=\E[(X-\E X)(Y-\E Y)]\), which only sees linear (second-order) dependence, mutual information sees every kind of dependence. Exercise "Uncorrelated but dependent" below gives an example.
  • It is symmetric: \(I(X;Y)=I(Y;X)\), since the formula is.
  • In terms of entropies,
    \[\begin{aligned}I(X;Y)&=\E\Big[\log\frac{p_{X,Y}(X,Y)}{p_X(X)p_Y(Y)}\Big]\\&=\E\big[\log p_{X,Y}(X,Y)-\log p_X(X)-\log p_Y(Y)\big]\\&=H(X)+H(Y)-H(X,Y).\end{aligned}\]
    So \(I(X;Y)\) is the amount by which the entropies of \(X\) and \(Y\) "overlap".
ExerciseUncorrelated but dependent
Let \(X\) be uniform on \(\{-1,0,1\}\) and \(Y=X^2\). Show that \(\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=0\), but compute \(I(X;Y)\).
show answer

\(\E[X]=0\) and \(\E[XY]=\E[X^3]=0\), so \(\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=0\). But \(Y\) is a function of \(X\), so knowing \(X\) removes all uncertainty about \(Y\). Using the formula above, \(H(X,Y)=H(X)\) (the pair takes three values, each with probability \(\frac13\)), so

\[I(X;Y)=H(X)+H(Y)-H(X,Y)=H(Y)=H(\tfrac13)\approx0.918\text{ bits}.\]

1.1.1 Conditional entropy, divergence and mutual information

motivationconditioning on extra knowledge

Often we know something extra, such as the value of another random variable. So we want versions of entropy, divergence and mutual information that condition on it.

Definition 1.8 (Conditional entropy).p. 11 Let \(X,Y\) be discrete random variables taking values in \(\X\). The conditional entropy of \(Y\) given \(X\) is

\[\begin{aligned}H(Y|X)&=-\sum_{x\in\X}\sum_{y\in\X}\PP(X=x,Y=y)\log\PP(Y=y|X=x)\\&=-\sum_{x\in\X}\sum_{y\in\X}\PP(X=x,Y=y)\log\frac{\PP(Y=y,X=x)}{\PP(X=x)}.\end{aligned}\]
in wordsDefinition 1.8 as an average

Grouping the terms by the value of \(X\) shows it is an average of ordinary entropies:

\[\begin{aligned}H(Y|X)&=-\sum_{x}\PP(X=x)\sum_{y}\PP(Y=y|X=x)\log\PP(Y=y|X=x)\\&=\sum_{x}\PP(X=x)\,H(Y|X=x)\\&=-\E\big[\log p_{Y|X}(Y|X)\big].\end{aligned}\]

Here \(H(Y|X=x)\) is the entropy of the conditional pmf of \(Y\) given \(X=x\). So \(H(Y|X)\) is the surprise we still have about \(Y\) after seeing \(X\), averaged over what we see. If \(Y=X\) there is none left.

payoffthe chain rule

Writing \(\PP(Y=y|X=x)=\PP(X=x,Y=y)/\PP(X=x)\) inside the logarithm and splitting gives the chain rule for entropy:

\[H(Y|X)=H(X,Y)-H(X),\qquad\text{that is,}\qquad H(X,Y)=H(X)+H(Y|X).\]

The uncertainty in the pair is the uncertainty in \(X\), plus what remains about \(Y\) once \(X\) is known.

Definition 1.9 (Conditional divergence).p. 11 Let \(p_X\) be a pmf on a discrete space \(\X\), and for each \(x\in\X\) let \(p(\cdot|x)\) and \(q(\cdot|x)\) be pmfs. The conditional divergence of \(p(\cdot|X)\) from \(q(\cdot|X)\) given \(p_X\) is

\[D(p_{Y|X}\|q_{Y|X}\,|\,p_X)=\sum_{x\in\X}p_X(x)\,D\big(p(\cdot|x)\,\big\|\,q(\cdot|x)\big).\]
in wordsDefinition 1.9

So it compares the two conditional pmfs for each value \(x\), and averages the answers using the weights \(p_X(x)\). Note that the weights come from \(p_X\) only; there is no "\(q_X\)".

Definition 1.10 (Conditional divergence, with random variables).p. 11 Let \(X\) and \(Y_1,Y_2\) be discrete random variables, with joint pmfs \(p_{X,Y_i}\). The divergence between \(p_{Y_1}\) and \(p_{Y_2}\) conditioned on \(X\) is

\[D(p_{Y_1|X}\|p_{Y_2|X}\,|\,p_X)=\sum_{x\in\X}p_X(x)\,D(p_{Y_1|X=x}\|p_{Y_2|X=x})=\E\Big[D\big(p_{Y_1|X}(\cdot|X)\,\big\|\,p_{Y_2|X}(\cdot|X)\big)\Big].\]

Definition 1.11 (Conditional mutual information).p. 12 Let \(X,Y,Z\) be discrete random variables. The conditional mutual information between \(X\) and \(Y\) given \(Z\) is

\[I(X;Y|Z):=H(X|Z)-H(X|Y,Z).\]
in wordsDefinition 1.11

It is the reduction in uncertainty about \(X\) from learning \(Y\), when \(Z\) is known already. Expanding the entropies, as for \(I(X;Y)\),

\[I(X;Y|Z)=\E\Big[\log\frac{p_{X,Y|Z}(X,Y|Z)}{p_{X|Z}(X|Z)\,p_{Y|Z}(Y|Z)}\Big],\]

which shows that \(I(X;Y|Z)=I(Y;X|Z)\). It measures how dependent \(X\) and \(Y\) are once \(Z\) is known.

intuitiona picture of the relations

All the identities so far fit into one picture. Take the entropy \(H(X,Y)\) of the pair as a bar. It splits into three pieces: the part only \(X\) knows about, \(H(X|Y)\); the shared part, \(I(X;Y)\); and the part only \(Y\) knows about, \(H(Y|X)\). The entropy of \(X\) is the first two pieces, the entropy of \(Y\) the last two. Figure 1.3 draws this for a joint pmf you can change.

ExerciseA noisy bit
Let \(X\) be a fair bit, and let \(Y=X\) with probability \(1-f\) and \(Y=1-X\) with probability \(f\), independently of \(X\). Compute \(H(Y)\), \(H(Y|X)\) and \(I(X;Y)\).
show answer

\(Y\) is again a fair bit (by symmetry), so \(H(Y)=1\). Given \(X=x\), \(Y\) is \(x\) or \(1-x\) with probabilities \(1-f\) and \(f\), so \(H(Y|X=x)=H(f)\) for both \(x\), and \(H(Y|X)=H(f)\). Hence

\[I(X;Y)=H(Y)-H(Y|X)=1-H(f).\]

With \(f=0\) the channel is perfect and \(I=1\) bit; with \(f=\frac12\) the output is pure noise and \(I=0\). This quantity is the capacity of the binary symmetric channel, the star of Chapter 4.

1.2Basic properties and inequalitiesp. 12

≈ 13 min·9 results, 1 exercise·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★★
roadmapthree inequalities first

We now prove the basic properties of entropy, divergence and mutual information. Almost all of them come from three elementary inequalities: Jensen's, Gibbs' and the log sum inequality. All three are about convexity.

Definition 1.12 (Convex function).p. 12 Let \(I\subseteq\R\). A function \(f:I\to\R\) is convex if

\[f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\le\lambda f(x)+(1-\lambda)f(y)\]

for all \(x,y\in I\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\). It is strictly convex if the inequality is strict for all \(\lambda\in(0,1)\) whenever \(x\neq y\). A function \(f\) is concave if \(-f\) is convex.

in wordsDefinition 1.12

Geometrically: a convex function lies below each of its chords. The point \(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y\) is between \(x\) and \(y\), and the right side is the height of the chord at that point. The functions we meet most are \(-\log x\) and \(x\log x\) (strictly convex on \((0,\infty)\)), and \(\log x\) and \(-x\log x\) (strictly concave).

Lemma 1.13 (Jensen’s inequality).p. 12 If \(f\) is convex and \(X\) is a random variable taking values in \(\X\) with pmf \(p\), such that \(\E X=\sum_xxp(x)\) and \(\E f(X)=\sum_xf(x)p(x)\) exist, then

\[f\Big(\sum_{x\in\X}xp(x)\Big)=f(\E X)\le\E f(X)=\sum_{x\in\X}f(x)p(x).\]

If \(f\) is strictly convex, equality holds if and only if \(X\) is constant (with probability one).

Proof sketch. For a pmf on two points this is exactly the definition of convexity, with \(\lambda=p(x)\). For a pmf on finitely many points, induct on the number of points: split off one point and write the rest as a single weighted average. The countable case needs one more limiting step. The details are Problem Sheet 1, Question 3.∎

✎Now try question 3 of Problem Sheet 1. Jensen's inequality for discrete random variables, the induction above.

Lemma 1.14 (Gibbs’ inequality).p. 12 Let \(p\) and \(q\) be pmfs on \(\X\). Then

\[-\sum_{x\in\X}p(x)\log p(x)\le-\sum_{x\in\X}p(x)\log q(x),\]

with equality if and only if \(p\equiv q\).

in wordsLemma 1.14

In words: if you code your surprise using the wrong pmf \(q\), you are on average more surprised than with the true pmf \(p\). Equivalently, the map \(q\mapsto-\E[\log q(X)]\), with \(X\sim p\), is minimised exactly at \(q=p_X\), and the minimum value is \(H(X)\).

Proof of Lemma 1.14. Let \(X\) have pmf \(p\). Adding \(\sum_xp(x)\log p(x)\) to both sides, we must show that \(\sum_xp(x)\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\ge0\). The sums run over \(x\) with \(p(x)>0\), and if \(q(x)=0\) for one of those the left side is \(+\infty\), so assume not. Then

\[\begin{aligned}\sum_{x\in\X}p(x)\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}&=\E\Big[-\log\frac{q(X)}{p(X)}\Big]\\&\ge-\log\E\Big[\frac{q(X)}{p(X)}\Big]&&\why{Jensen, with $f=-\log$}\\&=-\log\Big(\sum_{x:\,p(x)>0}p(x)\frac{q(x)}{p(x)}\Big)\\&\ge-\log1=0.&&\why{the sum is at most $1$}\end{aligned}\]

For equality we need equality in both steps. Since \(-\log\) is strictly convex, the first is an equality only if \(q(X)/p(X)\) is constant, so \(q=cp\) on the support of \(p\). The second needs \(q\) to put all its mass on that support. Together these force \(c=1\) and \(q\equiv p\).∎

Lemma 1.15 (Log sum inequality).p. 13 Let \(a_1,\dots,a_n\) and \(b_1,\dots,b_n\) be non-negative. Then

\[\sum_{i=1}^na_i\log\frac{a_i}{b_i}\ge\Big(\sum_{i=1}^na_i\Big)\log\frac{\sum_{i=1}^na_i}{\sum_{i=1}^nb_i},\]

with equality if and only if \(a_i/b_i\) is constant.

in wordsLemma 1.15

The usual conventions apply: \(0\log\frac0b=0\), and \(a\log\frac a0=\infty\) for \(a>0\). The notes state this without proof; it is Gibbs' inequality in disguise.

Proof of Lemma 1.15. Write \(A=\sum_ia_i\) and \(B=\sum_ib_i\). If \(A=0\) both sides are \(0\); if \(B=0<A\) both sides are \(+\infty\). Otherwise \(a_i/A\) and \(b_i/B\) are pmfs on \(\{1,\dots,n\}\), and

\[\sum_ia_i\log\frac{a_i}{b_i}-A\log\frac AB=A\sum_i\frac{a_i}A\log\frac{a_i/A}{b_i/B}=A\,D\Big(\frac aA\,\Big\|\,\frac bB\Big)\ge0\]

by Gibbs' inequality, with equality iff \(a_i/A=b_i/B\) for all \(i\), that is, iff \(a_i/b_i=A/B\) is constant.∎

✎Now try question 1 of Problem Sheet 1. The "polling inequalities" are the log sum inequality with \(n=2\), read two ways.

1.2.1 Divergence properties

Theorem 1.16 (Divergence properties).p. 13 Let \((X,Y)\) and \((\tilde X,\tilde Y)\) be discrete random vectors taking values in \(\X\times\mathcal Y\). Then

  1. (Information inequality) \(D(p_X\|p_{\tilde X})\ge0\), with equality iff \(p_X=p_{\tilde X}\).
  2. (Chain rule) \(D(p_{X,Y}\|p_{\tilde X,\tilde Y})=D(p_{Y|X}\|p_{\tilde Y|\tilde X}\,|\,p_X)+D(p_X\|p_{\tilde X})\).
  3. \(D(p_{X,Y}\|p_{\tilde X,\tilde Y})\ge D(p_X\|p_{\tilde X})\).
  4. \(D(p_{Y|X}\|p_{\tilde Y|\tilde X}\,|\,p_X)=D(p_Xp_{Y|X}\,\|\,p_Xp_{\tilde Y|\tilde X})\).
  5. (Convexity) For pmfs \(p_1,p_2,q_1,q_2\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\),
    \[D\big(\lambda p_1+(1-\lambda)p_2\,\big\|\,\lambda q_1+(1-\lambda)q_2\big)\le\lambda D(p_1\|q_1)+(1-\lambda)D(p_2\|q_2).\]
in wordsTheorem 1.16

Part 2 says divergence between joint laws splits like entropy does: first compare the first coordinates, then compare the second coordinates given the first. Part 3 says comparing more coordinates can only reveal more difference. Part 5 says that mixing two pairs of distributions makes them harder to tell apart.

Proof of Theorem 1.16. Part 1 is Gibbs' inequality, rearranged.

Part 2. Factor each joint pmf as marginal times conditional, then split the logarithm:

\[\begin{aligned}D(p_{X,Y}\|p_{\tilde X,\tilde Y})&=\sum_{x,y}p_{X,Y}(x,y)\log\frac{p_X(x)\,p_{Y|X}(y|x)}{p_{\tilde X}(x)\,p_{\tilde Y|\tilde X}(y|x)}\\&=\sum_{x,y}p_{X,Y}(x,y)\log\frac{p_{Y|X}(y|x)}{p_{\tilde Y|\tilde X}(y|x)}+\sum_{x,y}p_{X,Y}(x,y)\log\frac{p_X(x)}{p_{\tilde X}(x)}\\&=\sum_xp_X(x)\sum_yp_{Y|X}(y|x)\log\frac{p_{Y|X}(y|x)}{p_{\tilde Y|\tilde X}(y|x)}+D(p_X\|p_{\tilde X})\\&=\sum_xp_X(x)\,D(p_{Y|X=x}\|p_{\tilde Y|\tilde X=x})+D(p_X\|p_{\tilde X})\\&=D(p_{Y|X}\|p_{\tilde Y|\tilde X}\,|\,p_X)+D(p_X\|p_{\tilde X}).\end{aligned}\]

In the third line, the second sum only depends on \(x\), so summing out \(y\) leaves \(\sum_xp_X(x)\log\frac{p_X(x)}{p_{\tilde X}(x)}\).

Part 3. The conditional divergence is an average of divergences, each \(\ge0\) by part 1, so it is \(\ge0\). Drop it from part 2.

Part 4. Both sides are the same expectation:

\[\begin{aligned}D(p_{Y|X}\|p_{\tilde Y|\tilde X}\,|\,p_X)&=\E\Big[\log\frac{p_{Y|X}(Y|X)}{p_{\tilde Y|\tilde X}(Y|X)}\Big]\\&=\E\Big[\log\frac{p_X(X)\,p_{Y|X}(Y|X)}{p_X(X)\,p_{\tilde Y|\tilde X}(Y|X)}\Big]=D(p_Xp_{Y|X}\,\|\,p_Xp_{\tilde Y|\tilde X}).\end{aligned}\]

Part 5. For each \(x\), apply the log sum inequality with \(n=2\) and

\[a_1=\lambda p_1(x),\quad a_2=(1-\lambda)p_2(x),\quad b_1=\lambda q_1(x),\quad b_2=(1-\lambda)q_2(x).\]

It gives

\[\big(\lambda p_1(x)+(1-\lambda)p_2(x)\big)\log\frac{\lambda p_1(x)+(1-\lambda)p_2(x)}{\lambda q_1(x)+(1-\lambda)q_2(x)}\le\lambda p_1(x)\log\frac{p_1(x)}{q_1(x)}+(1-\lambda)p_2(x)\log\frac{p_2(x)}{q_2(x)}.\]

Now sum over \(x\in\X\).∎

1.2.2 Mutual information properties

set-upconditional independence and Markov chains

The next theorem includes a chain rule and the data processing inequality. For those we need one more notion. \(X\) and \(Z\) are conditionally independent given \(Y\), written \((X\perp Z)\,|\,Y\), if

\[p_{(X,Z)|Y}(x,z|y)=p_{X|Y}(x|y)\,p_{Z|Y}(z|y)\qquad\text{for all }x,y,z.\]

This is the same as saying that \(X\to Y\to Z\) is a Markov chain with three time steps: \(p_{X,Y,Z}(x,y,z)=p(x)\,p(y|x)\,p(z|y)\). Once you know \(Y\), knowing \(X\) as well tells you nothing more about \(Z\).

Theorem 1.17 (Mutual information properties).p. 14

  1. \(I(X;Y)\ge0\), with equality iff \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent.
  2. \(I(X;Y)=I(Y;X)=H(X)-H(X|Y)=H(Y)-H(Y|X)\).
  3. (Information chain rule)
    \[I(X_1,\dots,X_n;Y)=\sum_{i=1}^nI(X_i;Y\,|\,X_{i-1},\dots,X_1).\]
  4. (Data processing inequality) If \((X\perp Z)\,|\,Y\), then \(I(X;Y)\ge I(X;Z)\).
  5. If \(f:\mathcal Y\to\mathcal Z\), then \(I(X;Y)\ge I(X;f(Y))\).

Proof. Part 1. \(I(X;Y)=D(p_{X,Y}\|p_Xp_Y)\ge0\) by the information inequality (Theorem 1.16), with equality iff \(p_{X,Y}=p_Xp_Y\), which is independence.

Part 2. The first equality holds because the definition is symmetric. For the others, we saw after Definition 1.7 that

\[I(X;Y)=\E\Big[\log\frac{p_{X,Y}(X,Y)}{p_X(X)p_Y(Y)}\Big]=H(X)+H(Y)-H(X,Y),\]

and the chain rule for entropy says

\[\begin{aligned}H(X,Y)&=-\sum_{x,y}\PP(X=x,Y=y)\log\PP(X=x,Y=y)\\&=-\sum_{x,y}\PP(X=x,Y=y)\big[\log\PP(Y=y|X=x)+\log\PP(X=x)\big]\\&=H(Y|X)+H(X).\end{aligned}\]

Substituting gives \(I(X;Y)=H(Y)-H(Y|X)\), and by symmetry \(I(X;Y)=H(X)-H(X|Y)\).

An aside: the chain rule for many variables. Applying the two-variable chain rule repeatedly, with \((X_1,\dots,X_{n-1})\) playing the part of \(X\),

\[H(X_1,\dots,X_n)=H(X_n|X_{n-1},\dots,X_1)+H(X_{n-1},\dots,X_1)=\sum_{i=1}^nH(X_i|X_{i-1},\dots,X_1),\]

with the convention \(H(X_1|X_0)=H(X_1)\). The same argument, conditioning everything on \(Y\), gives

\[H(X_1,\dots,X_n\,|\,Y)=\sum_{i=1}^nH(X_i|X_{i-1},\dots,X_1,Y).\]

Part 3. Subtract the two chain rules term by term:

\[\begin{aligned}I(X_1,\dots,X_n;Y)&=H(X_1,\dots,X_n)-H(X_1,\dots,X_n\,|\,Y)\\&=\sum_{i=1}^n\big\{H(X_i|X_{i-1},\dots,X_1)-H(X_i|X_{i-1},\dots,X_1,Y)\big\}\\&=\sum_{i=1}^nI(X_i;Y\,|\,X_{i-1},\dots,X_1),\end{aligned}\]

the last step by the definition of conditional mutual information.

Part 4. Expand \(I(Y,Z;X)\) with the chain rule in two orders. Conditioning on \(Y\) first,

\[I(Y,Z;X)=I(Y;X)+I(Z;X|Y)=I(Y;X),\]

because \(I(Z;X|Y)=0\) when \(X\) and \(Z\) are conditionally independent given \(Y\) (the conditional version of part 1). Conditioning on \(Z\) first,

\[I(Y,Z;X)=I(Z;X)+I(Y;X|Z)\ge I(Z;X).\]

Comparing the two gives \(I(X;Y)\ge I(X;Z)\).

Part 5. Take \(Z=f(Y)\) in part 4. Given \(Y\), \(Z\) is fixed, so it is certainly conditionally independent of \(X\).∎

Remark 1.18.p. 15

  • Part 2 with \(Y=X\) gives \(I(X;X)=H(X)\), which is why entropy is sometimes called self-information.
  • Part 2 also says \(I(X;Y)\) is the reduction in uncertainty about either variable from learning the other.
  • The data processing inequality formalises a simple but fundamental idea: post-processing cannot create information. If \(Z\) depends on \(X\) only through \(Y\), then \(Z\) cannot know more about \(X\) than \(Y\) does. No clever computation on your data can tell you more about the world than the data itself.
  • In statistics, a statistic \(T(X)\) is sufficient for a parameter \(\theta\) if, given \(T(X)\), the law of \(X\) does not depend on \(\theta\). This is equivalent to \(I(\theta;X)=I(\theta;T(X))\) for every prior on \(\theta\): the statistic keeps all the information the data have about the parameter, so the data processing inequality is an equality.

1.2.3 Entropy properties

Theorem 1.19 (Entropy properties).p. 16 Let \(X,Y\) be discrete random variables taking values in \(\X\), and write \(|\X|\) for the number of elements of \(\X\).

  1. \(0\le H(X)\le\log|\X|\). The upper bound is attained iff \(X\) is uniform on \(\X\); the lower bound iff \(X\) is constant with probability one.
  2. \(0\le H(X|Y)\le H(X)\). \(H(X|Y)=H(X)\) iff \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, and \(H(X|Y)=0\) iff \(X=f(Y)\) for some function \(f\).
  3. (Chain rule) \(H(X_1,\dots,X_n)=\sum_{i=1}^nH(X_i|X_{i-1},\dots,X_1)\le\sum_{i=1}^nH(X_i)\), with equality iff the \(X_i\) are independent.
  4. For \(f:\X\to\mathcal Y\), \(H(f(X))\le H(X)\), with equality iff \(f\) is injective on the values \(X\) takes.
  5. If \(X\) and \(Y\) are i.i.d., then \(\PP(X=Y)\ge2^{-H(X)}\), with equality iff \(X\) is uniform on the set of values it takes.
  6. \(H(X)\) is a concave function of \(p_X\).
in wordsTheorem 1.19

Each part is a piece of common sense about "average surprise". Part 1: you can't be less than certain, and the most uncertain you can be about \(|\X|\) possibilities is when they are equally likely. Part 2: on average, extra information can only help ("information can't hurt"). Part 3: the uncertainty of a list is at most the sum of the uncertainties of its entries. Part 4: relabelling outcomes does not change entropy, and merging outcomes can only reduce it. Part 5: low entropy makes collisions likely. Part 6: mixing distributions increases uncertainty.

Proof of Theorem 1.19. Part 1. Every term \(-p(x)\log p(x)\) is \(\ge0\), since \(\log p(x)\le0\), so \(H(X)\ge0\); and it is \(0\) only if \(p(x)\in\{0,1\}\). Since the \(p(x)\) sum to \(1\), all terms vanish iff exactly one \(x\) has \(p(x)=1\), that is, iff \(X\) is constant. For the upper bound, apply Gibbs' inequality with the uniform pmf \(q(x)=|\X|^{-1}\):

\[H(X)\le-\sum_{x\in\X}p(x)\log q(x)=\log|\X|,\]

with equality iff \(p_X=q\), that is, iff \(X\) is uniform.

Part 2. By Theorem 1.17, \(0\le I(X;Y)=H(X)-H(X|Y)\), which gives the upper bound, with equality iff \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent. For the lower bound, by definition

\[H(X|Y)=\sum_{y}p_Y(y)\,H(X|Y=y),\qquad H(X|Y=y)=-\sum_xp_{X|Y}(x|y)\log p_{X|Y}(x|y),\]

and each \(H(X|Y=y)\ge0\) by part 1. So \(H(X|Y)=0\) iff \(H(X|Y=y)=0\) for every \(y\) that \(Y\) takes. By part 1 that happens iff, for each such \(y\), \(\PP(X=x|Y=y)=1\) for a single value \(x=f(y)\). That is exactly \(X=f(Y)\) almost surely.

Part 3. The equality is the chain rule from the proof of Theorem 1.17. For the inequality, each \(H(X_i|X_{i-1},\dots,X_1)\le H(X_i)\) by part 2, with equality iff \(X_i\) is independent of \((X_{i-1},\dots,X_1)\); this holds for all \(i\) iff the \(X_i\) are independent.

Part 4. Expand \(H(X,f(X))\) with the chain rule in two orders. First,

\[H(X,f(X))=H(X)+H(f(X)|X)=H(X),\]

since \(f(X)\) is a function of \(X\) and part 2 gives \(H(f(X)|X)=0\). Second,

\[H(X,f(X))=H(f(X))+H(X|f(X))\ge H(f(X)).\]

So \(H(f(X))\le H(X)\), with equality iff \(H(X|f(X))=0\), that is, iff \(X\) can be recovered from \(f(X)\): \(f\) is injective on the values \(X\) takes.

Part 5. The function \(t\mapsto2^t\) is convex, so by Jensen's inequality

\[2^{-H(X)}=2^{\E[\log p_X(X)]}\le\E\big[2^{\log p_X(X)}\big]=\E[p_X(X)]=\sum_xp_X(x)^2=\PP(X=Y).\]

The last step uses independence: \(\PP(X=Y)=\sum_x\PP(X=x)\PP(Y=x)\). Since \(2^t\) is strictly convex, equality holds iff \(p_X(X)\) is constant, that is, iff \(X\) is uniform on the values it takes.

Part 6. \(H(p)=\sum_xg(p(x))\) with \(g(t)=-t\log t\), which is concave on \([0,1]\). A sum of concave functions of the coordinates is concave.∎

Remark 1.20.p. 17 Part 1 is intuitive if entropy is average surprise; part 2 formalises "more information is better"; part 4 shows that entropy is unchanged by relabelling the values.

ExerciseIs entropy just a property of the values?
True or false: \(H(X)=H(2X)\), \(H(X)=H(X^2)\), \(H(X|Y)\ge H(X|Y,Z)\). Think before opening, then compare with Sheet 1, Question 4.
show answer

\(H(X)=H(2X)\) is true: \(x\mapsto2x\) is injective, so part 4 gives equality. \(H(X)=H(X^2)\) can fail: if \(X\) is uniform on \(\{-1,1\}\) then \(H(X)=1\) but \(X^2=1\) is constant, so \(H(X^2)=0\). It holds when \(X\) takes only non-negative values (or more generally when \(x\mapsto x^2\) is injective on the values of \(X\)). \(H(X|Y)\ge H(X|Y,Z)\) is true: it is part 2 applied conditionally on \(Y\) ("conditioning reduces entropy"), or equivalently \(I(X;Z|Y)\ge0\).

✎Now try questions 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 of Problem Sheet 1. Questions 4 to 9 are all about the properties in this section. Question 7 is the maximum entropy principle, a constrained version of part 1 of Theorem 1.19.
✎Now try questions 6, 9 of Problem Sheet 2. Question 6 is a "grouping" identity for mixtures. Question 9 extends entropy to densities; its hint is Gibbs' inequality for densities.
✎Now try question 10 of Problem Sheet 3. Betting on horses: the best long-run growth rate of wealth is an entropy, and the cost of betting with the wrong probabilities is a divergence.

1.3Fano’s inequalityp. 17

≈ 6 min·2 results, 1 figure, 1 exercise·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★☆
the questionguessing X from Y

A common situation: we observe \(Y\) and use it to guess the value of \(X\). If the guess is always right, \(\PP(X\neq Y)=0\), then \(X\) is a function of \(Y\) and \(H(X|Y)=0\) by part 2 of Theorem 1.19. We should expect that if the guess is usually right, \(H(X|Y)\) is small. Fano's inequality makes this precise.

Theorem 1.21 (Fano’s inequality, 1966).p. 17 Let \(X,Y\) be discrete random variables taking values in \(\X\). Then

\[H(X|Y)\le H(\ind_{X\neq Y})+\PP(X\neq Y)\log(|\X|-1).\]
in wordsTheorem 1.21

Read the right side as a two-stage description of \(X\) for someone who already knows \(Y\). First say whether the guess \(Y\) was right: that costs at most \(H(\ind_{X\neq Y})\) bits. If it was right you are done. If it was wrong (probability \(\PP(X\neq Y)\)), say which of the other \(|\X|-1\) values \(X\) took, at most \(\log(|\X|-1)\) bits. Turned around, the inequality is a lower bound on the error probability: if \(H(X|Y)\) is large, no way of guessing \(X\) from \(Y\) can be reliable. This is how it will be used for noisy channels.

Proof of Theorem 1.21. Let \(Z=\ind_{X\neq Y}\) be the indicator of an error. Given both \(X\) and \(Y\), \(Z\) is determined, so \(H(Z|X,Y)=0\). Then

\[\begin{aligned}H(X|Y)&=H(X|Y)+H(Z|X,Y)\\&=H(X,Z|Y)&&\why{chain rule, given $Y$}\\&=H(Z|Y)+H(X|Y,Z)&&\why{chain rule the other way}\\&\le H(Z)+H(X|Y,Z).&&\why{conditioning reduces entropy}\end{aligned}\]

Now split the last term according to the values of \(Y\) and \(Z\):

\[H(X|Y,Z)=\sum_{y\in\X}\Big[\PP(Y=y,Z=0)\,H(X|Y=y,Z=0)+\PP(Y=y,Z=1)\,H(X|Y=y,Z=1)\Big].\]

  • On \(\{Y=y,Z=0\}\) the guess was right, so \(X=y\), and \(H(X|Y=y,Z=0)=0\).
  • On \(\{Y=y,Z=1\}\) the guess was wrong, so \(X\in\X\setminus\{y\}\), a set of \(|\X|-1\) elements. By part 1 of Theorem 1.19, \(H(X|Y=y,Z=1)\le\log(|\X|-1)\).
Therefore

\[H(X|Y)\le H(Z)+\sum_{y\in\X}\PP(Y=y,Z=1)\log(|\X|-1)=H(Z)+\PP(Z=1)\log(|\X|-1).\]
∎

Corollary 1.22.p. 18 \(H(X|Y)\le1+\PP(X\neq Y)\log(|\X|-1)\).

in wordsCorollary 1.22

This follows because \(Z\) takes two values, so \(H(Z)\le\log2=1\) by part 1 of Theorem 1.19. Rearranged, it gives a clean lower bound on the error probability:

\[\PP(X\neq Y)\ge\frac{H(X|Y)-1}{\log(|\X|-1)}.\]

Figure 1.4 shows the exact region that Fano's inequality allows.

ExerciseFano for a noisy bit
In Exercise 'A noisy bit' above, guess \(X\) by \(Y\) itself. What does Fano's inequality say, and is it tight?
show answer

Here \(|\X|=2\), so \(\log(|\X|-1)=0\) and Fano reads \(H(X|Y)\le H(\ind_{X\neq Y})=H(f)\), since the guess is wrong with probability \(f\). By symmetry \(H(X|Y)=H(Y|X)=H(f)\) (both equal \(H(X,Y)-1\)). So Fano holds with equality: for binary variables the inequality is tight whenever errors are independent of the guess.

Chapter 2

Codes and sequences

Two separate ideas that Chapter 3 will marry. First, which codeword lengths a decodable code can have: the Kraft–McMillan inequality. Second, the law of large numbers in disguise: a long random sequence is almost certainly "typical", and there are only about 2 to the nH typical sequences.

≈ 24 min · 4 sections · 15 results · 2 figures · 3 exercises · difficulty ●●○ · importance ★★★

Symbol codesp. 19

≈ 4 min·4 results, 1 exercise·difficulty ●○○·importance ★★★
the questionwriting a message in bits

Suppose we receive a sequence of symbols from a set \(\X\), say letters of the Latin alphabet, and want to store it on a computer as a sequence of 0s and 1s. We need a rule for turning symbols into bits, and back again.

Definition 2.1 (Strings and symbol codes).p. 19 For a finite set \(\X\), let \(\X^*\) be the set of finite sequences, or strings, of elements of \(\X\). For \(x=x_1\cdots x_n\in\X^*\) with each \(x_i\in\X\), call \(|x|=n\) the length of \(x\). Given finite sets \(\X\) and \(\mathcal Y\), a symbol code is a function \(c:\X\to\mathcal Y^*\), and \(c(x)\) is the codeword of \(x\). The code is \(d\)-ary if \(|\mathcal Y|=d\).

in wordsDefinition 2.1

To encode a whole message we simply concatenate the codewords: \(x_1\cdots x_n\mapsto c(x_1)\cdots c(x_n)\). To get the message back we certainly need \(c\) to be injective. That is not enough.

Example 2.2.p. 19 Let \(\X=\{1,\dots,6\}\) and let \(c(x)\) be the binary expansion of \(x\), so the codewords are \(1,10,11,100,101,110\). Then \(c\) is injective, but we cannot always recover the message: \(110\) could be \(x_1=6\) or \(x_1x_2=12\) (that is, \(1\) followed by \(2\)).

motivationwhat we want from a code

Ideally a code lets us recover the message, is easy to decode, and compresses as much as possible. A second aim is that the encoding rule should be simple to build and store. To make this precise we name three classes of codes.

Definition 2.3 (Unambiguous, uniquely decodable and prefix codes).p. 19 Let \(c:\X\to\mathcal Y^*\) be a symbol code, and let \(c^*:\X^*\to\mathcal Y^*\) be its extension, \(c^*(x_1\cdots x_n)=c(x_1)\cdots c(x_n)\). Then \(c\) is

  1. unambiguous (or nonsingular) if \(c\) is injective: different symbols get different codewords;
  2. uniquely decodable if \(c^*\) is injective: different strings give different bit sequences, even though the codewords are run together with no separators;
  3. a prefix code (or instantaneous code) if no codeword is a prefix of another: there are no \(x_1\neq x_2\) in \(\X\) and \(y\in\mathcal Y^*\) with \(c(x_1)y=c(x_2)\).
in wordsDefinition 2.3

Clearly

\[\{\text{prefix codes}\}\subseteq\{\text{uniquely decodable codes}\}\subseteq\{\text{unambiguous codes}\}.\]

Prefix codes are the easy ones to decode, and that is where the name "instantaneous" comes from. Read the bits from the left; the moment the bits read so far form a codeword, that must be the first symbol, because no other codeword starts the same way. Then start again. For a general uniquely decodable code you may have to read far ahead before knowing even the first symbol. It is not even easy to check whether a given code is uniquely decodable.

Example 2.4.p. 20 Take \(\X=\{A,B,C,D\}\), \(\mathcal Y=\{0,1\}\) and \(c(A)=0\), \(c(B)=01\), \(c(C)=011\), \(c(D)=111\). This code is uniquely decodable, though that is not obvious, and describing a decoding algorithm is not easy either. What leads to \(011\,111\,01\)? What about \(011\,111\,11\)?

ExerciseDecode from the right
Decode \(01111101\) and \(01111111\) in the code of Example 2.4. (Hint: look at the codewords written backwards.)
show answer

Written backwards the codewords are \(0,10,110,111\), and that is a prefix code. So decode by reading from the right end. The string \(01111101\) read backwards is \(10111110\), which splits as \(10\,|\,111\,|\,110\), that is \(B,D,C\) backwards. So the message was \(CDB\). Similarly \(01111111\) backwards is \(11111110=111\,|\,111\,|\,10\), so the message was \(BDD\): \(01\,111\,111\). Notice that the two strings agree in their first six bits but begin with different symbols, which is exactly why a left-to-right decoder can't commit early. A code whose reversal is a prefix code is called a suffix code; it is always uniquely decodable.

2.1The Kraft–McMillan Theoremp. 20

≈ 9 min·4 results, 1 figure, 1 exercise·difficulty ●●●·importance ★★★
the questionwhich lengths are possible?

Short codewords are what compression is about, but they can't all be short: there are only two codewords of length 1, four of length 2, and so on, and a prefix code can't use both \(0\) and \(01\). The question is which lists of codeword lengths are possible at all. The surprising answer is that uniquely decodable codes are no better than prefix codes in this respect, so we may as well design prefix codes.

Theorem 2.5 (Kraft–McMillan Theorem).p. 20

  1. Let \(c:\X\to\mathcal Y^*\) be uniquely decodable, and set \(l_x=|c(x)|\). Then
    \[\sum_{x\in\X}|\mathcal Y|^{-l_x}\le1.\](2.1.1)
  2. Conversely, given lengths \((l_x)_{x\in\X}\subseteq\N\) and a finite set \(\mathcal Y\) such that (2.1.1) holds, there is a prefix code \(c:\X\to\mathcal Y^*\) with \(|c(x)|=l_x\) for each \(x\in\X\).
intuitiona budget of 1

Think of (2.1.1) as a budget. With \(d=|\mathcal Y|\) letters, a codeword of length \(l\) costs \(d^{-l}\), and the total spend may not exceed \(1\). A short codeword is expensive. For a prefix code this is easy to see: a codeword of length \(l\) rules out every string that starts with it, which is a fraction \(d^{-l}\) of all long strings, and different codewords rule out disjoint sets. McMillan's surprise is that unique decodability alone forces the same budget. Figure 2.1 lets you choose lengths and see the budget and the code.

Proof of Theorem 2.5. Part 1. Set \(d=|\mathcal Y|\) and \(l_{\max}=\max_x|c(x)|\). The trick is to look at strings of \(n\) source symbols at once. Expanding the \(n\)-th power of the sum,

\[\Big(\sum_{x\in\X}d^{-l_x}\Big)^n=\sum_{x_1,\dots,x_n\in\X}d^{-l_{x_1}}d^{-l_{x_2}}\cdots d^{-l_{x_n}}=\sum_{x_1,\dots,x_n\in\X}d^{-\sum_{i=1}^nl_{x_i}}.\]

The exponent \(k=\sum_il_{x_i}\) is the length of the encoded string \(c(x_1)\cdots c(x_n)\), which lies between \(1\) and \(nl_{\max}\). Group the terms by \(k\), and let \(a(k)\) be the number of source strings of length \(n\) whose encoding has length \(k\). Then

\[\Big(\sum_{x\in\X}d^{-l_x}\Big)^n=\sum_{k=1}^{nl_{\max}}a(k)\,d^{-k}.\]

Now use unique decodability. Different source strings have different encodings, and there are only \(d^k\) strings of length \(k\) over \(\mathcal Y\), so by the pigeonhole principle \(a(k)\le d^k\). Each term of the sum is at most \(1\), so

\[\Big(\sum_{x\in\X}d^{-l_x}\Big)^n\le nl_{\max},\qquad\text{that is,}\qquad\sum_{x\in\X}d^{-l_x}\le(nl_{\max})^{1/n}.\]

This holds for every \(n\), and \((nl_{\max})^{1/n}\to1\) as \(n\to\infty\). That gives (2.1.1). (If the sum were bigger than \(1\), its \(n\)-th power would grow exponentially, faster than the linear bound allows.)

Part 2. Let \((l_x)\) satisfy (2.1.1). Relabel so that \(\X=\{1,\dots,|\X|\}\) and \(l_1\le l_2\le\dots\le l_{|\X|}\): shortest codewords first. Define running totals of the budget,

\[r_m:=\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}d^{-l_i},\qquad m=1,\dots,|\X|,\]

so \(r_1=0\) and every \(r_m<1\) by assumption. Let \(c(m)\) be the first \(l_m\) digits of the \(d\)-ary expansion of \(r_m\):[[With the usual convention that the expansion ends in zeros rather than in \((d-1)\)s, so \(\frac12\) in binary is \(0.1000\ldots\) and not \(0.0111\ldots\).]]

\[c(m):=y_1\cdots y_{l_m},\qquad\text{where }r_m=\sum_{i\ge1}y_id^{-i}.\]

In other words, cut \([0,1)\) into consecutive pieces of lengths \(d^{-l_1},d^{-l_2},\dots\), and name each piece by the first \(l_m\) digits of its left end.

We check this is a prefix code. Since \(l_i\le l_m\) for \(i<m\), each term \(d^{-l_i}\) of \(r_m\) is a multiple of \(d^{-l_m}\), so \(r_m\) is too: its expansion stops within the first \(l_m\) digits, and \(c(m)\) records \(r_m\) exactly. Suppose \(c(m)\) were a prefix of \(c(n)\) with \(m<n\). Then \(r_n\) starts with the same \(l_m\) digits as \(r_m\), so it lies in the interval \([r_m,r_m+d^{-l_m})\) of numbers with that start, and

\[r_n-r_m<d^{-l_m}.\]

But by definition

\[r_n-r_m=\sum_{i=m}^{n-1}d^{-l_i}\ge d^{-l_m},\]

a contradiction. And \(c(n)\) can't be a prefix of \(c(m)\) with \(m<n\) either: \(l_n\ge l_m\), so that would need \(c(n)=c(m)\), which is the same contradiction.∎

Remark 2.6.p. 21 The inequality (2.1.1) is called the Kraft–McMillan inequality. Kraft proved Theorem 2.5 for prefix codes, where part 1 has a nice proof using trees (Problem Sheet 2, Question 10). The version for uniquely decodable codes is McMillan's, building on Kraft's work.

Remark 2.7.p. 21 The construction in part 2, reading codewords off the expansions of cumulative sums, will come back many times: Shannon's code, Elias' code and arithmetic codes in Chapter 3 are all variations on it.

Corollary 2.8.p. 21 For any uniquely decodable code there is a prefix code with the same codeword lengths.

payoffCorollary 2.8

Part 1 of the theorem says the lengths of a uniquely decodable code satisfy (2.1.1); part 2 builds a prefix code with those lengths. Since compression only cares about lengths, from now on we can restrict attention to prefix codes, which are the easy ones to decode.

ExerciseIs there a code with these lengths?
Is there a binary uniquely decodable code with codeword lengths \(1,2,3,3,3\)? With \(1,2,3,3\)? With \(2,2,2,3,3\)? Build a prefix code when there is one.
show answer

The Kraft sums are \(\frac12+\frac14+\frac38=\frac98>1\), so no code exists for \(1,2,3,3,3\). For \(1,2,3,3\) the sum is exactly \(1\), and the construction gives \(r=0,\frac12,\frac34,\frac78\), so the codewords \(0,10,110,111\). For \(2,2,2,3,3\) the sum is \(\frac34+\frac14=1\), giving \(r=0,\frac14,\frac12,\frac34,\frac78\) and codewords \(00,01,10,110,111\).

✎Now try question 10 of Problem Sheet 2. Kraft's theorem through code trees: part 1 of Theorem 2.5 for prefix codes, and part 2 by growing a tree.

2.2The Asymptotic Equipartition Propertyp. 21

≈ 10 min·5 results, 1 figure, 1 exercise·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★★
the questionone sample tells you little; many tell you a lot

Given a distribution, what can we say about one sample from it? Not much. Shannon's elementary but far-reaching insight is that this changes completely for long sequences of samples, because of the law of large numbers. Since we will encode sequences, this is just what we need.

Example 2.9.p. 21 Let \(X\) take values in \(\X=\{0,1\}\), and let \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) be i.i.d. copies of \(X\). A particular sequence \((x_1,\dots,x_n)\in\{0,1\}^n\) occurs with probability

\[\PP\big((X_1,\dots,X_n)=(x_1,\dots,x_n)\big)=p^{\alpha(x_1,\dots,x_n)}q^{\beta(x_1,\dots,x_n)},\](2.2.1)

where \(p=\PP(X=0)\), \(q=1-p\), and \(\alpha=\sum_i\ind_{x_i=0}\), \(\beta=\sum_i\ind_{x_i=1}\) count the zeros and ones. For a "typical" sequence the law of large numbers says \(\alpha\approx np\) and \(\beta\approx nq\). Hence

\[\PP\big((X_1,\dots,X_n)=(x_1,\dots,x_n)\big)\approx p^{np}q^{nq},\]

and taking logarithms,

\[-\log\PP\big((X_1,\dots,X_n)=(x_1,\dots,x_n)\big)\approx-np\log p-nq\log q=nH(X).\]

So every typical sequence has probability about \(2^{-nH(X)}\). Since together they carry almost all the probability, there must be about \(2^{nH(X)}\) of them. Note \(2^{nH(X)}\le2^n\), and the difference can be enormous.

intuitionequipartition

The informal calculation suggests splitting \(\X^n\) into two sets:

  • typical sequences: relatively few, but carrying almost all the probability, and each roughly equally likely (hence "equipartition");
  • atypical sequences: everything else, which together are unlikely.

For a coin with \(p=0.1\) and \(n=100\) there are \(2^{100}\approx10^{30}\) sequences, but the typical ones number about \(2^{100H(0.1)}\approx2^{47}\). Figure 2.2 shows how the probability concentrates as \(n\) grows. We now make this rigorous.

From Prelims and B8.1 · The weak law of large numbers

If \(Z_1,Z_2,\dots\) are i.i.d. with finite mean \(\mu\), then \(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nZ_i\to\mu\) in probability: for every \(\eps>0\),

\[\PP\Big(\Big|\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nZ_i-\mu\Big|>\eps\Big)\to0\qquad\text{as }n\to\infty.\]

With a finite variance \(\sigma^2\) this is one line from Chebyshev's inequality, since the average has variance \(\sigma^2/n\); that is Problem Sheet 1, Question 2. Without a variance it is still true, and the strong law even gives almost sure convergence (B8.1, Chapter 7).

Theorem 2.10 (Weak AEP 1).p. 22 Let \(X\) be a discrete random variable and \((X_i)_{i\ge1}\) i.i.d. copies of \(X\). Then

\[-\frac1n\log p_{X_1,\dots,X_n}(X_1,\dots,X_n)\xrightarrow{\text{in prob.}}H(X)\qquad\text{as }n\to\infty.\](2.2.2)
in wordsTheorem 2.10

The left side is the surprise of the sequence you actually drew, per symbol. It is random, but for long sequences it is almost certainly close to the entropy.

Proof of Theorem 2.10. By independence the joint pmf is a product, so its logarithm is a sum:

\[-\log p_{X_1,\dots,X_n}(X_1,\dots,X_n)=-\sum_{i=1}^n\log p_X(X_i).\]

The terms \(-\log p_X(X_i)\) are i.i.d., with mean \(\E[-\log p_X(X)]=H(X)\). The weak law of large numbers finishes the proof.∎

Definition 2.11 (Typical set).p. 22 For \(n\in\N\) and \(\eps>0\), the set of (weakly) typical sequences of length \(n\) with error \(\eps\) is

\[T_n^\eps:=\Big\{(x_1,\dots,x_n)\in\X^n:\Big|-\frac1n\log p_{X_1,\dots,X_n}(x_1,\dots,x_n)-H(X)\Big|\le\eps\Big\}.\]
in wordsDefinition 2.11

A sequence is typical if its surprise per symbol is within \(\eps\) of the entropy. Equivalently, its probability lies between \(2^{-n(H(X)+\eps)}\) and \(2^{-n(H(X)-\eps)}\). Notice the definition says nothing about counting symbols: it only asks about the probability of the sequence.

Theorem 2.12 (Weak AEP 2, Shannon 1948).p. 22 For every \(\eps>0\) there is an \(n_0\in\N\) such that for every \(n>n_0\):

  1. \(p_{X_1,\dots,X_n}(x_1,\dots,x_n)\in\big[2^{-n(H(X)+\eps)},2^{-n(H(X)-\eps)}\big]\) for every \((x_1,\dots,x_n)\in T_n^\eps\);
  2. \(\PP\big((X_1,\dots,X_n)\in T_n^\eps\big)\ge1-\eps\);
  3. \(|T_n^\eps|\in\big[(1-\eps)2^{n(H(X)-\eps)},\,2^{n(H(X)+\eps)}\big]\).

For part 1 one can take \(n_0=0\).

in wordsTheorem 2.12

The three parts are the three features of the informal picture, now with error bars: typical sequences are roughly equally likely (part 1), they carry almost all the probability (part 2), and there are roughly \(2^{nH(X)}\) of them (part 3).

Proof of Theorem 2.12. Part 1 is Definition 2.11, rearranged: multiply the inequality by \(-n\) and exponentiate. It holds for every \(n\).

Part 2. By Theorem 2.10, for every \(\eps>0\),

\[\PP\big((X_1,\dots,X_n)\notin T_n^\eps\big)=\PP\Big(\Big|-\frac1n\log p_{X_1,\dots,X_n}(X_1,\dots,X_n)-H(X)\Big|>\eps\Big)\to0\]

as \(n\to\infty\). So it is at most \(\eps\) once \(n\) is large.

Part 3, upper bound. The total probability is \(1\), and each typical sequence has probability at least \(2^{-n(H(X)+\eps)}\) by part 1:

\[1=\sum_{x\in\X^n}p(x)\ge\sum_{x\in T_n^\eps}p(x)\ge\sum_{x\in T_n^\eps}2^{-n(H(X)+\eps)}=2^{-n(H(X)+\eps)}\,|T_n^\eps|.\]

Part 3, lower bound. For \(n\) large, part 2 says the typical set has probability at least \(1-\eps\), and each typical sequence has probability at most \(2^{-n(H(X)-\eps)}\):

\[1-\eps\le\PP\big((X_1,\dots,X_n)\in T_n^\eps\big)\le\sum_{x\in T_n^\eps}2^{-n(H(X)-\eps)}=2^{-n(H(X)-\eps)}\,|T_n^\eps|.\]

Rearranging gives the lower bound.∎

Remark 2.13.p. 23

  • For large \(n\), it is reasonable to think of \((X_1,\dots,X_n)\) as drawn uniformly from \(T_n^\eps\), each typical sequence having probability about \(2^{-nH(X)}\).
  • Theorem 2.12 does not say that most sequences are typical. The typical set is tiny compared with \(\X^n\):
    \[\frac{|T_n^\eps|}{|\X^n|}\approx\frac{2^{nH(X)}}{2^{n\log|\X|}}=2^{-n(\log|\X|-H(X))},\]
    which tends to \(0\) unless \(H(X)=\log|\X|\), that is, unless \(X\) is uniform (Theorem 1.19). What is true is that the typical set carries most of the probability (part 2).
  • So we can prove a property for typical sequences and conclude that it holds for the random sequence with high probability.
  • The single most likely sequence is in general not typical. Take \(\X=\{0,1\}\) and \(\PP(X=1)=0.9\). The most likely sequence is \((1,\dots,1)\), but its surprise per symbol is \(-\log0.9\approx0.15\), while \(H(X)=-0.1\log0.1-0.9\log0.9\approx0.47\).[[The notes give \(0.11\) here, which is \(-\ln0.9\), the value in nats; in bits it is \(0.152\).]] As \(n\to\infty\) the probability of every individual sequence, including the most likely one, tends to \(0\).
ExerciseMost likely is not typical
For the coin with \(\PP(X=1)=0.9\) and \(n=100\), how many ones does a typical sequence have, and how does the probability of \((1,\dots,1)\) compare with that of one typical sequence?
show answer

A typical sequence has about \(90\) ones and \(10\) zeros, with probability about \(0.9^{90}0.1^{10}=2^{-100\cdot0.469}\approx2^{-46.9}\). The all-ones sequence has probability \(0.9^{100}=2^{-15.2}\), about \(2^{31.7}\) times more likely. But there is only one of it, whereas there are \(\binom{100}{10}\approx1.7\times10^{13}\approx2^{44}\) sequences with exactly ten zeros. Being likely individually and being likely as a class are different things.

✎Now try questions 2, 10 of Problem Sheet 1. Question 2 is the weak law of large numbers used above. Question 10 is an almost sure version of the AEP in disguise.
✎Now try questions 1, 2, 4 of Problem Sheet 2. Question 1 is the AEP with the wrong pmf (the answer involves Definition 1.4). Question 2 counts sequences with a given number of ones, the exact version of Example 2.9.

2.3Strong typicalityp. 23

≈ 2 min·2 results·difficulty ●●●·importance ★☆☆
the questionis there a smaller set that does the job?

The last point of Remark 2.13 suggests a question. The typical set leaves out the most likely sequences. Is there a set with fewer elements than \(T_n^\eps\) that still carries most of the probability?

Definition 2.14 (Smallest high-probability set).p. 23 Let \(S_n^\eps\) be the smallest subset of \(\X^n\) such that

\[\PP\big((X_1,\dots,X_n)\in S_n^\eps\big)\ge1-\eps.\]
in wordsDefinition 2.14

To build it, order the sequences by probability, most likely first, and add them one at a time until the total reaches \(1-\eps\). By construction no set with probability \(\ge1-\eps\) is smaller.

Proposition 2.15.p. 23 Let \((\eps_m)_m\) be a sequence of positive numbers with \(\eps_m\to0\). Then

\[\lim_{m\to\infty}\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\log\frac{|S_n^{\eps_m}|}{|T_n^{\eps_m}|}=0.\]

Proof sketch. Write \(\eps\) for \(\eps_m\) and \(H\) for \(H(X)\). Since \(S_n^\eps\) is the smallest set with probability \(\ge1-\eps\), and \(T_n^\eps\) is such a set for large \(n\), we have \(|S_n^\eps|\le|T_n^\eps|\). For the other direction, both sets have probability at least \(1-\eps\), so their intersection has probability at least \(1-2\eps\) (a union bound on the complements). Every element of \(T_n^\eps\) has probability at most \(2^{-n(H-\eps)}\). So

\[1-2\eps\le\PP\big(S_n^\eps\cap T_n^\eps\big)\le|S_n^\eps|\,2^{-n(H-\eps)}\le\frac{|S_n^\eps|}{|T_n^\eps|}\,2^{2n\eps},\]

using \(|T_n^\eps|\le2^{n(H+\eps)}\) in the last step. Taking \(\frac1n\log\) and letting \(n\to\infty\) gives a limit between \(-2\eps\) and \(0\); then let \(\eps=\eps_m\to0\). The details are Problem Sheet 2, Question 3.∎

payoffwhy we keep the typical set

So the strong and weak typical sets have the same size to first order in the exponent: both are about \(2^{nH(X)}\). Nothing is gained by working with \(S_n^\eps\), even though its construction looks more efficient. One might still prefer \(S_n^\eps\) because its definition is simpler. But every argument that uses typical sequences needs to count them, and counting \(T_n^\eps\) is trivial because its elements are all about equally likely, while counting \(S_n^\eps\) is hard.

✎Now try question 3 of Problem Sheet 2. Bounds on the size of the smallest high-probability set, completing the proof above.

B8.4 · Information TheoryChapter 3 · notes pp. 25–36

Chapter 3

Optimal codes and Shannon’s first theorem

No uniquely decodable code beats the entropy on average, and long blocks get you arbitrarily close to it. Then the practical question: how to actually build good codes. Shannon’s, Fano’s, Huffman’s (which is optimal), Elias’, arithmetic coding, and Tunstall’s code, which turns the problem around.

≈ 46 min · 8 sections · 14 results · 4 figures · 3 exercises · difficulty ●●○ · importance ★★☆
