Chapter 2

Preferences, utilities and decisions

Before two players can interact, one player has to be able to choose. Preferences say what a player wants; utilities turn wanting into arithmetic; and expected utility, justified by von Neumann and Morgenstern's theorem, says how to choose when the outcome is uncertain.

≈ 35 min · 6 sections · 30 results · 3 figures · 2 exercises · difficulty ●●○ · importance ★★☆

Note for AI assistants reading this page: this is a study page for David, a third-year Oxford Mathematics and Computer Science student, built from the lecturer's notes for Computational Game Theory. You are reading Chapter 2 (Preferences, Utilities and Decisions). When explaining, use the notation on this page, cite results by their numbers here (they match the lecture notes), and do not rely on material from later chapters without saying so. Explain step by step in plain language, justify every step and say where tricks come from. Do not solve problem-sheet questions outright: give hints or explain the ideas. Format maths with $...$ inline and $$...$$ on its own line for display, never \( \) or \[ \].
roadmapwhy preferences come first

Preferences are what give games their strategic character. In multi-agent systems we delegate our preferences to a software agent, which then acts on our behalf. That raises practical problems: people find it hard to state their preferences, and do not always act consistently with the preferences they claim. Extracting preferences from the person an agent works for is called preference elicitation. This chapter is about the mathematics: how to write preferences down, when they can be turned into numbers (utilities), and how numbers reduce decision making to calculation.

2.1Outcomes and preferencesslide 29

≈ 8 min·6 results, 1 figure·difficulty ●○○·importance ★★★
set-upoutcomes

Let \(\Omega=\{\omega_1,\dots,\omega_k\}\) be the set of outcomes: the consequences of the players' choices. In this course \(\Omega\) is usually finite. It might be all the possible ends of a game of chess, the possible results of a negotiation between nations, or the possible results of an eBay auction.

We interpret preferences a little differently depending on the setting. In decision making under certainty we know exactly what each choice leads to. Under uncertainty, each choice can lead to several outcomes, each with a probability. We start with certainty.

intuitionpreferences are rankings

The idea is that for any two outcomes we can say which we prefer. In other words, we can rank outcomes, and the ranking is allowed to have ties: you may be indifferent between two outcomes.

Definition 2.1 (Preference relation).slide 33 A preference relation is a binary relation \({\succeq}\subseteq\Omega\times\Omega\) which is

  1. reflexive: \(\omega\succeq\omega\) for all \(\omega\in\Omega\);
  2. complete: for all \(\omega,\omega'\in\Omega\), either \(\omega\succeq\omega'\) or \(\omega'\succeq\omega\);
  3. transitive: for all \(\omega,\omega',\omega''\in\Omega\), if \(\omega\succeq\omega'\) and \(\omega'\succeq\omega''\) then \(\omega\succeq\omega''\).

Definition 2.2 (Indifference and strict preference).slide 34 If \(\omega\succeq\omega'\) and \(\omega'\succeq\omega\), you are indifferent between \(\omega\) and \(\omega'\), written \(\omega\sim\omega'\). If \(\omega\succeq\omega'\) but not \(\omega'\succeq\omega\), you strictly prefer \(\omega\) to \(\omega'\), written \(\omega\succ\omega'\).

carefulwhat preferences mean (important)

Two points that prevent many arguments.

  • Revealed preference. Preferences are not observable; choices are. So \(\omega\succ\omega'\) means: if you have a choice between \(\omega\) and \(\omega'\) you will choose \(\omega\), and more generally, if one option leads to \(\omega\) and another to \(\omega'\), you choose the first.
  • Rational choice doesn't make you Scrooge. A preference relation must include everything that influences your decision. If you care about other people, that is part of your preferences. The theory copes equally well with angels and devils: "self-interested" means acting on your own preferences, whatever they are, not acting selfishly.
motivationnumbers are easier than relations

It is convenient to attach numbers to outcomes, higher numbers for more preferred outcomes. These numbers are called utilities (or utility values, or payoffs).

Definition 2.3 (Utility function).slide 38 A function \(u:\Omega\to\R\) represents a preference relation \(\succeq\) if, for all \(\omega,\omega'\in\Omega\),

\[u(\omega)\ge u(\omega')\iff\omega\succeq\omega'.\]

Theorem 2.4.slide 38 If \(\Omega\) is finite, then every preference relation \({\succeq}\subseteq\Omega\times\Omega\) is represented by some utility function \(u:\Omega\to\R\).

Proof (added here; the slides leave it as an exercise). Score each outcome by how many outcomes it is at least as good as:

\[u(\omega)=\big|\{\omega'\in\Omega:\omega\succeq\omega'\}\big|.\]

If \(\omega\succeq\omega'\) then \(u(\omega)\ge u(\omega')\). Every \(\omega''\) counted for \(\omega'\) satisfies \(\omega'\succeq\omega''\), so \(\omega\succeq\omega''\) by transitivity, and it is counted for \(\omega\) too.

If \(u(\omega)\ge u(\omega')\) then \(\omega\succeq\omega'\). Suppose not. By completeness \(\omega'\succeq\omega\), and \(\omega'\not\sim\omega\), so \(\omega'\succ\omega\). By the first part every outcome counted for \(\omega\) is counted for \(\omega'\). Also \(\omega'\) is counted for \(\omega'\) (reflexivity) but not for \(\omega\) (since \(\omega\not\succeq\omega'\)). So \(u(\omega')>u(\omega)\), a contradiction.∎

✎Now try questions 1, 2 of Problem Sheet 1. Question 1 builds a utility function for lexicographic preferences (Section 2.4). Question 2 shows that on an infinite set a preference relation need not have one.
carefulwhat utility is and isn't

Utilities are chosen to represent preferences, which is what makes rational choice a calculation. Three warnings.

  • It is a fallacy to say you choose \(\omega\) over \(\omega'\) because \(u(\omega)>u(\omega')\). You choose it because \(\omega\succ\omega'\); the numbers were picked to reflect that. But if the numbers are right, you behave as though you were maximising utility.
  • Under certainty, utilities are ordinal: they record the ranking, not its intensity. Any increasing transformation of \(u\) represents the same preferences.
  • Interpersonal comparisons are difficult. There is no Celsius scale for utility: one "util" for me is not one util for you.

And utility is not money. Much misunderstanding, including the idea that game theory is about greed, comes from reading utility as money. Money is often a useful analogy, but the typical relationship is concave (Figure 2.1): each extra pound matters less than the last.

Definition 2.5 (Outcome function).slide 41 Let \(\Sigma\) be the set of strategies (choices, actions, alternatives) available to a decision maker. An outcome function is a map \(g:\Sigma\to\Omega\). The feasible outcomes are those in its range \(\operatorname{ran}g\); if \(\operatorname{ran}g\subsetneq\Omega\), some outcomes are not feasible.

Definition 2.6 (Decision making under certainty).slide 42 A problem of decision making under certainty is a quadruple \(\langle\Omega,\;u:\Omega\to\R,\;\Sigma,\;g:\Sigma\to\Omega\rangle\). The task is to select a strategy that leads to an outcome of maximal utility:

\[\sigma^*\in\arg\max_{\sigma\in\Sigma}u(g(\sigma)).\]
in wordsDefinition 2.6

This is just an optimisation problem. (\(\arg\max\) is the set of maximisers, which is why we write \(\sigma^*\in\).) The interesting cases are when the outcome is uncertain, or when it also depends on other players' choices.

2.2Decision making under uncertaintyslide 43

≈ 11 min·9 results, 1 figure·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★★
the questionchoosing between gambles

In most settings we don't know exactly which outcome a strategy will produce: each strategy leads to a range of outcomes, with different probabilities. Preferences over outcomes are then not enough. We need preferences over lotteries.

Example 2.7.slide 45 A robot sits at \((2,2)\) on a \(4\times4\) grid, and wants to reach the cell marked with money at \((2,0)\), two steps north. Its motors are unreliable. Each move succeeds with probability \(0.6\), and otherwise slips to one of two neighbouring cells with probability \(0.2\) each:

  • north gives \((2,1)\) with probability \(0.6\), \((1,2)\) with \(0.2\) and \((3,2)\) with \(0.2\);
  • west gives \((1,2)\) with probability \(0.6\), \((2,1)\) with \(0.2\) and \((2,3)\) with \(0.2\);
  • east gives \((3,2)\) with probability \(0.6\), \((2,1)\) with \(0.2\) and \((2,3)\) with \(0.2\).

Each action induces a lottery over cells, and choosing the best action means choosing the most preferred lottery. Figure 2.2 lets you put utilities on the cells and compare.

From Prelims · Probability distributions on a finite set

A probability distribution over a non-empty finite set \(S\) is a function \(f:S\to[0,1]\) with \(\sum_{s\in S}f(s)=1\); \(f(s)\) is the probability of \(s\). Write \(\Delta(S)\) for the set of all of them, and \(P(s,f)\) for \(f(s)\) when that is clearer.

Definition 2.8 (Lottery).slide 52 A lottery over \(\Omega\) is a probability distribution over \(\Omega\). Write \(\ell,\ell',\ell_1,\ldots\) for lotteries and \(\operatorname{lott}(\Omega)\) for the set of them. We write a lottery as a weighted sum, leaving out outcomes of probability \(0\); for example, with \(\Omega=\{\text{whisky},\text{gin},\text{brandy},\text{rum}\}\),

\[\ell_1=\tfrac1{10}\,\text{whisky}+\tfrac2{10}\,\text{gin}+\tfrac7{10}\,\text{brandy}\]

gives whisky with probability \(0.1\), gin \(0.2\), brandy \(0.7\) and rum \(0\). The support of a lottery is the set of outcomes with strictly positive probability. A lottery with a single outcome in its support, such as \(\ell_2=\text{brandy}\), is degenerate: brandy with certainty.

Definition 2.9 (Compound lotteries).slide 54 A compound lottery is a lottery whose prizes are themselves lotteries. Define \(\operatorname{lott}^0(\Omega)=\operatorname{lott}(\Omega)\) and

\[\operatorname{lott}^k(\Omega)=\operatorname{lott}\big(\operatorname{lott}^{k-1}(\Omega)\big)\cup\operatorname{lott}^{k-1}(\Omega)\quad(k\ge1),\qquad\operatorname{Lott}(\Omega)=\bigcup_{k\in\N}\operatorname{lott}^k(\Omega).\]

Every compound lottery can be reduced to a simple one, an element of \(\operatorname{lott}(\Omega)\), by multiplying out the probabilities. We work with preference relations on \(\operatorname{Lott}(\Omega)\).

exampleDefinition 2.9

With \(\ell_1=\frac1{10}\text{gin}+\frac9{10}\text{brandy}\) and \(\ell_2=\text{brandy}\), the compound lottery \(\ell_3=\frac9{10}\ell_1+\frac1{10}\ell_2\) first picks \(\ell_1\) or \(\ell_2\), then runs it. Multiplying out, gin has probability \(\frac9{10}\cdot\frac1{10}=\frac9{100}\) and brandy the rest, so \(\ell_3\) reduces to \(\frac9{100}\text{gin}+\frac{91}{100}\text{brandy}\).

Definition 2.10 (Expected utility).slide 56 Given a utility function \(u:\Omega\to\R\), the expected utility of a lottery \(\ell\) is

\[EU(\ell)=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}u(\omega)\,P(\omega,\ell),\]

the average utility the lottery gives, weighted by probability (for a compound lottery, use the probabilities after reducing it).

the questionwhen do utilities exist for lotteries?

Now the main question. Suppose I give you a preference relation \({\succeq}\subseteq\operatorname{Lott}(\Omega)\times\operatorname{Lott}(\Omega)\). Is there a utility function \(u:\Omega\to\R\) on outcomes such that

\[\ell_1\succeq\ell_2\iff EU(\ell_1)\ge EU(\ell_2)?\]

The answer is yes exactly when the preferences satisfy a few extra axioms, due to von Neumann and Morgenstern. Important: utilities under uncertainty must capture the intensity of preferences, not just the ranking. Whether you prefer a sure \(\omega_2\) to a coin flip between \(\omega_1\) and \(\omega_3\) depends on how much better \(\omega_1\) is than \(\omega_2\).

Theorem 2.11 (Win-lose lotteries).slide 59 Let \(\Omega=\{W,L\}\) with \(W\succ L\), and suppose \({\succeq}\) on \(\operatorname{Lott}(\{W,L\})\) is reflexive, complete and transitive, and monotone: \(\ell_1\succeq\ell_2\) iff \(P(W,\ell_1)\ge P(W,\ell_2)\). Then there is a utility function \(u:\{W,L\}\to\R\) with \(\ell_1\succeq\ell_2\) iff \(EU(\ell_1)\ge EU(\ell_2)\).

Proof (added here). Take \(u(W)=1\) and \(u(L)=0\). Then \(EU(\ell)=P(W,\ell)\), and monotonicity says exactly that \(\ell_1\succeq\ell_2\) iff \(P(W,\ell_1)\ge P(W,\ell_2)\).∎

Definition 2.12 (Von Neumann–Morgenstern axioms).slide 60 In addition to reflexivity, completeness and transitivity, a preference relation on \(\operatorname{Lott}(\Omega)\) may satisfy:

  1. Reduction of compound lotteries. Only the final distribution over outcomes matters: if \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_2\) reduce to the same simple lottery, then \(\ell_1\sim\ell_2\).
  2. Monotonicity. If \(\ell_1\succ\ell_2\), then for \(p,q\in[0,1]\),
    \[p>q\iff p\ell_1+(1-p)\ell_2\succ q\ell_1+(1-q)\ell_2:\]
    you prefer the bigger chance of the better lottery.
  3. Continuity (or the Archimedean axiom). If \(\ell_1\succeq\ell_2\succeq\ell_3\), there is a \(p\in[0,1]\) with
    \[\ell_2\sim p\ell_1+(1-p)\ell_3.\]
  4. Independence (or substitution). For all lotteries \(\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3\) and \(p\in(0,1)\),
    \[\ell_1\succeq\ell_2\iff p\ell_1+(1-p)\ell_3\succeq p\ell_2+(1-p)\ell_3.\]
in wordsDefinition 2.12

Continuity says preferences can be quantified: anything between two lotteries is equivalent to some mixture of them. Independence says we can freely substitute lotteries we are indifferent between, like equal terms in algebra: mixing both sides with the same third lottery, in the same proportion, doesn't change the comparison. Reduction says the "story" of how a lottery is run doesn't matter, only the odds.

Definition 2.13 (Representing preferences over lotteries).slide 65 A utility function \(u:\Omega\to\R\) represents a preference relation \({\succeq}\subseteq\operatorname{Lott}(\Omega)\times\operatorname{Lott}(\Omega)\) if, for all \(\ell_1,\ell_2\in\operatorname{Lott}(\Omega)\),

\[\ell_1\succeq\ell_2\iff EU(\ell_1)\ge EU(\ell_2).\]

Theorem 2.14 (Von Neumann and Morgenstern).slide 66 A preference relation \({\succeq}\subseteq\operatorname{Lott}(\Omega)\times\operatorname{Lott}(\Omega)\) satisfies the von Neumann–Morgenstern axioms if and only if some utility function \(u:\Omega\to\R\) represents it.

Proof of the forward direction. The plan: find the best and worst outcomes, call them \(W\) and \(L\); use them as the ends of a scale with \(L\) at \(0\) and \(W\) at \(1\); and use continuity to place every other outcome on the scale.

Step 1: the trivial case. If all outcomes are indifferent, \(\omega_1\sim\dots\sim\omega_k\), then by reduction every lottery is indifferent to every other, and \(u\equiv1\) works.

Step 2: a scale from worst to best. Otherwise, by completeness and transitivity we can order the outcomes. Let \(L\) be a worst one and \(W\) a best one, so \(W\succeq\omega\succeq L\) for every \(\omega\) and \(W\succ L\). Set \(u(L)=0\) and \(u(W)=1\). For \(p\in[0,1]\) write

\[\ell^*(p)=pW+(1-p)L\]

for the lottery that wins with probability \(p\).

Step 3: place each outcome. Since \(W\succeq\omega\succeq L\), continuity gives some \(p_\omega\in[0,1]\) with \(\omega\sim\ell^*(p_\omega)\). Define \(u(\omega)=p_\omega\). (By monotonicity this \(p_\omega\) is unique, so \(u\) is well defined; and \(u(W)=1\), \(u(L)=0\) agree with step 2.)

Step 4: rewrite lotteries in terms of \(W\) and \(L\). Take any lottery, which by reduction we may assume simple: \(\ell=p_1\omega_1+\dots+p_k\omega_k\). Replace each \(\omega_i\) by the equivalent \(\ell^*(u(\omega_i))\), one at a time, using independence each time. Then multiply out using reduction:

\[\begin{aligned}\ell&\sim p_1\ell^*(u(\omega_1))+\dots+p_k\ell^*(u(\omega_k))&&\why{independence, $k$ times}\\&\sim\Big(\sum_{i=1}^kp_iu(\omega_i)\Big)W+\Big(1-\sum_{i=1}^kp_iu(\omega_i)\Big)L&&\why{reduction}\\&=\ell^*\big(EU(\ell)\big).\end{aligned}\]

So every lottery is equivalent to "win with probability equal to its expected utility".

Step 5: compare. For two lotteries, \(\ell_1\sim\ell^*(EU(\ell_1))\) and \(\ell_2\sim\ell^*(EU(\ell_2))\). Since \(W\succ L\), monotonicity says \(\ell^*(a)\succeq\ell^*(b)\) iff \(a\ge b\). So

\[\ell_1\succeq\ell_2\iff\ell^*(EU(\ell_1))\succeq\ell^*(EU(\ell_2))\iff EU(\ell_1)\ge EU(\ell_2).\]

(Step 2 of the slides assumes the order is strict, with no ties. The argument above doesn't need that; ties just give equal values of \(u\).)∎

in wordswhat the theorem buys

The utility function is unique up to a positive affine change \(u\mapsto au+b\) with \(a>0\): that changes every expected utility in the same way and so represents the same preferences. Under uncertainty, utility is no longer just a ranking; the differences between utilities matter.

Definition 2.15 (Decision making under uncertainty).slide 75 A problem of decision making under uncertainty is a quadruple \(\langle\Omega,\;u:\Omega\to\R,\;\Sigma,\;g:\Sigma\to\operatorname{Lott}(\Omega)\rangle\). The task is to select a strategy that maximises expected utility:

\[\sigma^*\in\arg\max_{\sigma\in\Sigma}EU(g(\sigma))=\arg\max_{\sigma\in\Sigma}\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}u(\omega)\,P(\omega,g(\sigma)).\]
connectionthe most important single definition in AI

This maximum expected utility (MEU) principle is probably the most important single definition underpinning contemporary AI: a rational agent is often defined as one that maximises expected utility.

✎Now try questions 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 of Problem Sheet 1. Question 3 is a decision under uncertainty (like Figure 2.2). Questions 4 to 7 exercise the axioms directly.

2.3Paradoxes of expected utilityslide 76

≈ 6 min·4 results, 1 figure·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★☆
the questiondoes anyone actually behave like this?

The MEU paradigm is so entrenched that rational agents are commonly defined as expected utility maximisers. But it is not hard to find examples where maximising expected utility seems wrong, or where the theory's advice runs against strong intuitions.

Example 2.16.slide 77 Compare \(\ell_1=\$50\) for certain with \(\ell_2=\frac12\$101+\frac12\$0\). The second has higher expected money (\(\$50.50\)), but many people prefer the certain \(\$50\). That is risk aversion, and it shows that expected monetary reward is not expected utility. With a concave utility of money (Figure 2.1) it is perfectly consistent with the theory.

Example 2.17 (The Allais paradox).slide 78 Consider the lotteries

\[\ell_A=\$2\text{m},\qquad\ell_B=\tfrac{89}{100}\$2\text{m}+\tfrac{10}{100}\$10\text{m}+\tfrac1{100}\$0,\]
\[\ell_C=\tfrac{11}{100}\$2\text{m}+\tfrac{89}{100}\$0,\qquad\ell_D=\tfrac{10}{100}\$10\text{m}+\tfrac{90}{100}\$0.\]

Most people prefer \(\ell_A\) to \(\ell_B\) (why risk anything when \(\$2\)m is certain?), and \(\ell_D\) to \(\ell_C\) (the chances are similar, so go for the bigger prize).

Lemma 2.18.slide 80 Anyone with preferences \(\ell_A\succ\ell_B\) and \(\ell_D\succ\ell_C\) does not satisfy the von Neumann–Morgenstern axioms.

Proof. Suppose \(u\) represents \(\succeq\), and write \(x=u(\$0)\), \(y=u(\$2\text{m})\), \(z=u(\$10\text{m})\). The two preferences say

\[\begin{aligned}EU(\ell_A)>EU(\ell_B):&\qquad y>0.1z+0.89y+0.01x,\\EU(\ell_D)>EU(\ell_C):&\qquad0.1z+0.9x>0.11y+0.89x.\end{aligned}\]

Add \(0.89(x-y)\) to both sides of the first inequality:

\[0.11y+0.89x>0.1z+0.9x,\]

which says \(EU(\ell_C)>EU(\ell_D)\), contradicting the second. So no \(u\) represents these preferences, and by Theorem 2.14 the axioms fail.∎

intuitionthe common consequence

Here is why. All four lotteries share a common piece. \(\ell_A\) and \(\ell_B\) both give \(\$2\)m with probability \(0.89\); \(\ell_C\) and \(\ell_D\) both give \(\$0\) with probability \(0.89\). On the remaining \(0.11\) of probability, \(A\) and \(C\) are identical (\(\$2\)m for sure), and so are \(B\) and \(D\) (\(\frac{10}{11}\) chance of \(\$10\)m, \(\frac1{11}\) of \(\$0\)). The independence axiom says the common \(0.89\) shouldn't matter, so you must rank \(A\) against \(B\) the same way as \(C\) against \(D\). Figure 2.3 shows the four lotteries as bars.

Example 2.19 (Framing effects).slide 82 (Tversky and Kahneman, 1981.) A disease is expected to kill 600 people, and there are two treatments.

  • (A) 200 people will be saved.
  • (B) With probability \(\frac13\), 600 will be saved; with probability \(\frac23\), nobody will be saved.

72% of subjects chose A. A second group was offered:

  • (C) 400 people will die.
  • (D) With probability \(\frac13\) nobody will die; with probability \(\frac23\), 600 will die.

78% chose D. But A and C describe the same lottery, as do B and D.

in wordsExample 2.19

People are affected by how a decision problem is framed: described in terms of lives saved, we are risk-averse; described in terms of deaths, risk-seeking. The study of how people actually make economic decisions is behavioural economics (Ariely's Predictably Irrational is a fun introduction). None of this refutes the theory as a normative account, but it limits the descriptive one.

✎Now try questions 8, 9 of Problem Sheet 1. Question 8 is the St Petersburg paradox; Question 9 a story about bomber pilots whose preferences seem to break the axioms.

2.4Preferences with structureslide 83

≈ 3 min·3 results, 1 exercise·difficulty ●○○·importance ★★☆
set-upthree common shapes

Preference relations often have structure. Three important classes are single-peaked, dichotomous and lexicographic preferences.

Definition 2.20 (Single-peaked preferences).slide 86 Fix an ordering \(\omega_1>\omega_2>\dots>\omega_k\) of the alternatives, called the axis. A preference relation \(\succeq\) is single-peaked with respect to it if

  1. there is a unique most preferred alternative \(\omega^*\), and
  2. of any two alternatives on the same side of \(\omega^*\), the one closer to \(\omega^*\) is strictly preferred: if \(\omega'>\omega>\omega^*\) then \(\omega\succ\omega'\), and if \(\omega^*>\omega>\omega'\) then \(\omega\succ\omega'\).
exampleDefinition 2.20

Order election candidates from left-wing to right-wing. It is natural to have a personal ideal point on that axis and to prefer candidates closer to it. A bar chart of utilities in axis order is then a mountain with a single peak. Single-peaked preferences matter in social choice theory, where they are the hypothesis of the median voter theorem.

Definition 2.21 (Dichotomous preferences).slide 87 A preference relation is dichotomous if it splits all outcomes into wins and losses: there are \(W,L\subseteq\Omega\) with \(W\cup L=\Omega\) and \(W\cap L=\emptyset\), such that \(\omega_1\sim\omega_2\) whenever both are in \(W\) or both are in \(L\), and \(\omega_1\succ\omega_2\) whenever \(\omega_1\in W\) and \(\omega_2\in L\).

in wordsDefinition 2.21

The set \(W\) can be thought of as a goal. Dichotomous preferences are naturally specified by logical formulae, as in Section 2.5, and they are the preferences of the Boolean games of Chapter 3 and the win-lose games of Chapter 7.

Definition 2.22 (Lexicographic preferences).slide 88 Suppose outcomes are described by attributes \(a_1,\dots,a_m\) in decreasing order of importance. Each attribute \(a_j\) has a set of values \(D_j\) with a strict ranking \(\succ_j\), and \(\omega[a_j]\in D_j\) is the value of \(\omega\) on attribute \(a_j\). A preference relation is lexicographic if, for all \(\omega,\omega'\), \(\omega\succ\omega'\) iff there is an attribute \(a_j\) with

\[\omega[a_j]\succ_j\omega'[a_j]\qquad\text{and}\qquad\omega[a_k]=\omega'[a_k]\text{ for all }k<j.\]
exampleDefinition 2.22

The name comes from the dictionary: all words starting with "a" before all words starting with "b", and among those starting with "a", all "aa" words before all "ab" words. For cars, someone might rank by colour first, then engine, then nationality:

\[\text{red}\succ\text{blue}\succ\text{green};\qquad\text{electric}\succ\text{petrol}\succ\text{diesel};\qquad\text{German}\succ\text{French}\succ\text{UK}.\]

Then every red car beats every non-red car, every red electric car beats every red petrol car, and so on. No amount of a lower attribute compensates for a higher one.

ExerciseA utility for lexicographic cars
Give a utility function for the car preferences above without listing all 27 cars. (This is Sheet 1, Question 1.)
show answer

Score each attribute \(0\), \(1\) or \(2\) from worst to best, and read the three scores as the digits of a number in base \(3\):

\[u(\text{car})=9\,s_{\text{colour}}+3\,s_{\text{engine}}+s_{\text{nationality}}.\]

A better colour adds at least \(9\), while the other two attributes together can add at most \(3\cdot2+2=8\), so colour always wins; similarly engine beats nationality. This is exactly the lexicographic order. (Any base larger than the number of values per attribute works.)

2.5Compact representationsslide 92

≈ 4 min·5 results, 1 exercise·difficulty ●●●·importance ★★☆
the questionwhen there are too many outcomes to list

Often \(\Omega\) is too large to list a preference relation explicitly. If you must form a team with some subset of \(n\) classmates, your preferences have to order \(2^n\) possible teams. We need compact and tractable representations. But compactness has a price: decision problems start to get hard. Finding representations that are both is a major research area.

set-upBoolean domains

Many domains are described by a finite set of Boolean variables \(\Phi=\{x_1,\dots,x_l\}\), each true (\(\top\)) or false (\(\bot\)). In the team example, take a variable \(x_i\) for each classmate \(i\in N=\{1,\dots,n\}\), meaning "\(i\) is in the team". Every valuation \(v:\Phi\to\{\top,\bot\}\) then describes a team. Dichotomous preferences over teams can be given by a propositional formula \(\gamma\): the winning teams are its satisfying valuations, and

\[u(v)=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }v\models\gamma,\\0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}\]
ExerciseThe Fab Four
Which teams satisfy \(\gamma=(\text{John}\vee\text{Paul})\wedge(\text{George}\wedge\text{Ringo})\wedge\neg(\text{John}\wedge\text{Paul})\)?
show answer

George and Ringo must both be in, and exactly one of John and Paul. So the winning teams among the four are \(\{\text{John},\text{George},\text{Ringo}\}\) and \(\{\text{Paul},\text{George},\text{Ringo}\}\) (together with anyone else from the class, if \(N\) is bigger, since \(\gamma\) doesn't mention them).

Theorem 2.23.slide 97 Let the naive representation of dichotomous Boolean preferences list all winning sets \(W\subseteq2^N\) explicitly.

  1. The propositional formula representation is complete: every dichotomous Boolean preference relation is given by some formula.
  2. It can be exponentially more compact than the naive representation.
  3. Some dichotomous preference relations have no formula smaller than exponential in \(|N|\), so in the worst case it is no better than the naive representation.
in wordsTheorem 2.23

Completeness: take the disjunction, over all winning valuations, of the conjunction describing that valuation exactly. Compactness: the formula \(x_1\) alone describes \(2^{n-1}\) winning teams. The worst case is a counting argument: there are \(2^{2^n}\) dichotomous preference relations, but far fewer short formulas.

Definition 2.24 (Weighted formula representation).slide 98 A weighted formula (or rule) is a pair \((\varphi,x)\) of a propositional formula \(\varphi\) and a number \(x\in\R\), sometimes written \(\varphi\to x\). A rule base \(R=\{(\varphi_1,x_1),\dots,(\varphi_k,x_k)\}\) defines the utility function

\[u_R(v)=\sum_{(\varphi_i,x_i)\in R,\;v\models\varphi_i}x_i,\]

the sum of the weights of the rules that \(v\) satisfies.

Theorem 2.25.slide 99 The weighted formula representation is complete for utility functions \(u:2^N\to\R\); it can be exponentially more compact than the naive representation (listing all \(2^{|N|}\) input/output pairs); and some utility functions need exponentially many rules.

set-upassumption on the weights

From now on the weights are natural numbers written in binary. Then the largest possible utility,

\[S=\sum_{i=1}^kx_i,\]

is at most exponential in the input size, so its binary length is polynomial.

Theorem 2.26.slide 102 Given a rule base \(R\) and a target \(t\in\N\), deciding whether some valuation \(v\) has \(u_R(v)\ge t\) (the problem \(\text{AT-LEAST}(t)\)) is NP-complete.

Proof. In NP. A certificate is a valuation \(v\): we can evaluate every \(\varphi_i\) on \(v\) in polynomial time, add up the weights, and compare with \(t\).

NP-hard. Reduce SAT. Given a formula \(\varphi\), take the rule base \(R=\{(\varphi,1)\}\) and \(t=1\). Some valuation has utility at least \(1\) iff \(\varphi\) is satisfiable.∎

Theorem 2.27.slide 101 Finding an optimal valuation \(v^*\in\arg\max_vu_R(v)\) is in \(\mathrm{FP}^{\mathrm{NP}}\): it can be done in polynomial time with polynomially many calls to an NP oracle.

Proof. Find the optimal value by binary search. Keep an interval \([L,U]\) that always contains the optimum \(\mathrm{OPT}\), starting with \(L=0\) and \(U=S\). While \(L<U\), ask the oracle about the upper midpoint \(m=\lfloor(L+U+1)/2\rfloor\):

  1. if \(\text{AT-LEAST}(m)\) says yes, then \(\mathrm{OPT}\ge m\), so set \(L\leftarrow m\);
  2. if it says no, then \(\mathrm{OPT}<m\), so set \(U\leftarrow m-1\).

The interval halves each time, so this takes about \(\log_2S\) queries, polynomial in the input size, and returns \(L=\mathrm{OPT}\). (The upper midpoint is what guarantees progress when \(U=L+1\).)

Then find a valuation achieving it. Fix the variables one at a time. For \(x_1\), ask whether value \(\mathrm{OPT}\) is still achievable with \(x_1\) forced true (replace \(x_1\) by \(\top\) in every rule). If so, keep \(x_1=\top\), otherwise set \(x_1=\bot\). Continue with \(x_2,\dots,x_l\). That is \(l\) more queries.∎

2.6Preferences for combinatorial auctionsslide 105

≈ 2 min·3 results·difficulty ●●○·importance ★☆☆
examplebundles of goods

In a combinatorial auction, bidders buy bundles of goods. Spectrum licences are the classic case: a licence for the 1.7–1.72 GHz band in Brooklyn is far more useful together with the same band in Manhattan, Queens and Staten Island. Licences for the same band are most valuable together, but a licence for a different band is still better than none. Preferences over bundles are complicated.

Definition 2.28 (Valuation function).slide 107 Let \(\mathcal Z=\{z_1,\dots,z_m\}\) be the items for sale. Bidder \(i\)'s preferences are a valuation function \(u_i:2^{\mathcal Z}\to\R\), giving for every bundle \(Z\subseteq\mathcal Z\) what it is worth to \(i\). It is normalised if \(u_i(\emptyset)=0\), and satisfies free disposal if \(Z_1\subseteq Z_2\) implies \(u_i(Z_1)\le u_i(Z_2)\): more stuff never hurts.

Definition 2.29 (Atomic and XOR bids).slide 110 An atomic bid is a pair \((Z,p)\) with \(Z\subseteq\mathcal Z\) and \(p\in\R_+\). A bundle \(Z'\) satisfies it if \(Z\subseteq Z'\): it contains at least the items asked for. An atomic bid defines the valuation \(u(Z')=p\) if \(Z'\) satisfies \((Z,p)\), and \(0\) otherwise. An XOR bid

\[\beta=(Z_1,p_1)\;\text{XOR}\;\cdots\;\text{XOR}\;(Z_k,p_k)\]

defines the valuation

\[u_\beta(Z')=\begin{cases}0&\text{if }Z'\text{ satisfies no }(Z_i,p_i),\\\max\{p_i:Z_i\subseteq Z'\}&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}\]
exampleDefinition 2.29

"XOR" because the bidder pays for at most one of the atomic bids. For \(\beta_1=(\{a,b\},3)\;\text{XOR}\;(\{c,d\},5)\):

\[u_{\beta_1}(\{a\})=u_{\beta_1}(\{b\})=0,\quad u_{\beta_1}(\{a,b\})=3,\quad u_{\beta_1}(\{c,d\})=5,\quad u_{\beta_1}(\{a,b,c,d\})=5.\]

The last one is \(5\), not \(8\): having both bundles is worth only the better of the two.

Proposition 2.30.slide 114 XOR bids are fully expressive: they can express any normalised valuation function with free disposal. Doing so may need exponentially many atomic bids. But given an XOR bid, the value of any bundle can be computed in polynomial time.

in wordsProposition 2.30

For expressiveness, bid \((Z,u(Z))\) for every bundle \(Z\); free disposal makes the maximum over contained bundles equal to \(u(Z')\). That is \(2^m\) atomic bids. Evaluation is easy: check each atomic bid for \(Z_i\subseteq Z'\) and take the largest price.

Chapter 3

Normal form games and Nash equilibrium

Several players choose at once, and each one's payoff depends on everybody's choice. Best responses, dominant strategies and Nash equilibrium say what rational play looks like; social welfare says whether it is any good; and a gallery of famous games shows how often the two disagree.

≈ 41 min · 8 sections · 31 results · 4 figures · 0 exercises · difficulty ●●○ · importance ★★☆

Format maths with $...$ inline and $$...$$ on its own line for display, never \( \) or \[ \].

3.1Game forms and gamesslide 116

≈ 2 min·3 results·difficulty ●○○·importance ★★★
set-upsimultaneous, independent choices

This chapter studies strategic form (or normal form) non-cooperative games, the best-known class of games. Each player makes one choice, all at the same time, and players act alone: joint decisions are not possible.

Definition 3.1 (Game form).slide 118 Let \(N=\{1,\dots,n\}\) be the set of players. Each player \(i\) simultaneously chooses a pure strategy from a set \(\Sigma_i\). The combination of choices produces an outcome in \(\Omega\), given by an outcome function

\[g:\Sigma_1\times\dots\times\Sigma_n\to\Omega.\]

A game form is the structure \(\langle N,\Omega,\Sigma_1,\dots,\Sigma_n,g\rangle\).

set-updropping the outcomes

Now give each player \(i\) a utility function. It is convenient to skip the outcomes and put utilities directly on combinations of choices: instead of \(u_i:\Omega\to\R\) we write

\[u_i:\Sigma_1\times\dots\times\Sigma_n\to\R,\]

with \(u_i(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)\) short for \(u_i(g(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n))\).

Definition 3.2 (Normal form game).slide 120 A normal form game is a structure \(\langle N,\Sigma_1,\dots,\Sigma_n,u_1,\dots,u_n\rangle\), where \(N=\{1,\dots,n\}\) is the set of players, \(\Sigma_i\) is the set of pure strategies of player \(i\), and \(u_i:\Sigma_1\times\dots\times\Sigma_n\to\R\) is player \(i\)'s utility function.

in wordsDefinition 3.2

The utility player \(i\) gets depends not only on her own choice but on everybody else's, and the same goes for every other player. That interdependence is the whole subject.

set-uppayoff matrices

A two-player game fits in a payoff matrix (two-player games are also called bimatrix games). Player 1, the row player, chooses a row; player 2, the column player, chooses a column. Each cell holds both players' utilities for that pair of choices. On these pages the row player's utility sits at the bottom left of the cell, in brick red, and the column player's at the top right, in slate blue.

Example 3.3.slide 122 Take \(N=\{1,2\}\), \(\Sigma_1=\{T,B\}\), \(\Sigma_2=\{l,r\}\) and

\[u_1(T,l)=u_1(T,r)=1,\quad u_1(B,l)=u_1(B,r)=0,\qquad u_2(T,l)=u_2(B,r)=1,\quad u_2(T,r)=u_2(B,l)=0.\]

As a payoff matrix:

21lr
T1101
B0010
If you were player 1, what would you do?

3.2Best responses and dominanceslide 123

≈ 3 min·4 results·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★★
the questionwhat is rational when outcomes depend on others?

If players act rationally, what will happen? Solution concepts answer this; for strategic games the main ones are dominant strategies, Nash equilibrium and iterated elimination of dominated strategies. All of them are built from one idea, the best response.

Definition 3.4 (Strategy profile).slide 125 A strategy profile is a tuple \(\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)\in\Sigma_1\times\dots\times\Sigma_n\), one strategy for each player. Write \((\sigma_{-i},\sigma_i')\) for the profile obtained from \(\sigma\) by replacing player \(i\)'s strategy with \(\sigma_i'\):

\[(\sigma_{-i},\sigma_i')=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_{i-1},\sigma_i',\sigma_{i+1},\dots,\sigma_n),\]

and \(\Sigma_{-i}\) for the set of choices of all players except \(i\).

Definition 3.5 (Best response).slide 127 Player \(i\)'s best response function \(BR_i:\Sigma_1\times\dots\times\Sigma_n\to2^{\Sigma_i}\) is

\[BR_i(\sigma)=\arg\max_{\sigma_i'\in\Sigma_i}u_i(\sigma_{-i},\sigma_i'),\]

the set of choices that would give \(i\) the highest utility if the others kept to \(\sigma\). The game's best response function is \(BR(\sigma)=BR_1(\sigma)\times\dots\times BR_n(\sigma)\).

in wordsDefinition 3.5

\(BR_i(\sigma)\) ignores \(\sigma_i\) itself; it only looks at the others. It is never empty (for finite \(\Sigma_i\)), but it can have several elements when there are ties. In the running example, \(BR_1(l)=BR_1(r)=\{T\}\), \(BR_2(T)=\{l\}\) and \(BR_2(B)=\{r\}\).

techniqueboxing best responses

A convention that will pay off: in each column, box the row player's best responses; in each row, box the column player's best responses. Here is the running example boxed:

21lr
T1101
B0010

motivationa strategy that is always a best response

Suppose one of your strategies has the property that, whatever the others choose, it is a best response. Then choosing it is never a mistake. That is a very compelling argument for choosing it.

Definition 3.6 (Dominant strategies).slide 131 A strategy \(\sigma_i\in\Sigma_i\) is

  1. dominant if for every profile \(\sigma\) and every \(\sigma_i'\in\Sigma_i\), \(u_i(\sigma_{-i},\sigma_i)\ge u_i(\sigma_{-i},\sigma_i')\);
  2. weakly dominant if it is dominant and, for every other \(\sigma_i'\neq\sigma_i\), there is some profile \(\sigma\) with \(u_i(\sigma_{-i},\sigma_i)>u_i(\sigma_{-i},\sigma_i')\);
  3. strictly dominant if for every profile \(\sigma\) and every \(\sigma_i'\neq\sigma_i\), \(u_i(\sigma_{-i},\sigma_i)>u_i(\sigma_{-i},\sigma_i')\).
carefulthree definitions in the literature

Computer science books tend to use the first definition, often vaguely; traditional game theory books use the second. Unless stated otherwise, "dominant" means the first. With a weakly dominant strategy you are never worse off and sometimes strictly better off than with any other; with a strictly dominant one you are always strictly better off. (The slides state the weak version with "for some \(\sigma\), \(u_i(\sigma_{-i},\sigma_i)>u_i(\sigma_{-i},\sigma_i')\) for all \(\sigma_i'\)"; the standard version above lets the profile depend on the alternative \(\sigma_i'\).)

examplethe running example

In the running example, \(T\) is strictly dominant for player 1: it is boxed in every column. Player 2 has no dominant strategy: against \(T\) the best response is \(l\), against \(B\) it is \(r\).

Definition 3.7 (Dominant strategy equilibrium).slide 136 A dominant strategy equilibrium is a strategy profile in which every player plays a dominant strategy.

in wordsDefinition 3.7

A very strong solution concept, but most games have no dominant strategy equilibrium, because most players have no dominant strategy.

3.3Nash equilibriumslide 137

≈ 2 min·3 results·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★★
motivationrelax the requirement

A dominant strategy must be a best response to everything the others might do. Nash equilibrium asks only that each strategy be a best response to what the others actually do.

Definition 3.8 (Pure strategy Nash equilibrium).slide 137 A strategy profile \(\sigma\) is a (pure strategy) Nash equilibrium if no player \(i\in N\) has a strategy \(\sigma_i'\in\Sigma_i\) with

\[u_i(\sigma_{-i},\sigma_i')>u_i(\sigma).\]

Write \(NE(G)\) for the set of Nash equilibria of \(G\).

in wordsDefinition 3.8

Nobody can benefit by deviating alone from a Nash equilibrium, assuming everyone else sticks to it. In a payoff matrix, the pure Nash equilibria are exactly the cells where both payoffs are boxed. In the running example \((T,l)\) is the unique Nash equilibrium (shaded below); from every other cell someone has a beneficial deviation, for instance from \((B,r)\) player 1 would switch to \(T\).

21lr
T1101
B0010

carefulthree problems

Nash equilibrium has three problems, which much of the course is about.

  • Not every game has a pure Nash equilibrium (Matching Pennies, Section 3.5). Chapter 4 fixes this with mixed strategies.
  • Some games have several, which raises the equilibrium selection problem.
  • Some Nash equilibria are bad: they have undesirable social properties (the Prisoner's Dilemma).

Lemma 3.9.slide 140 \(\sigma\in NE(G)\) if and only if \(\sigma\in BR(\sigma)\). In other words,

\[NE(G)=\{\sigma\in\Sigma_1\times\dots\times\Sigma_n:\sigma\in BR(\sigma)\}.\]
in wordsLemma 3.9

For a function \(f:S\to S\), a fixed point is an \(s\) with \(f(s)=s\); for a set-valued \(f:S\to2^S\) it is an \(s\) with \(s\in f(s)\). So the lemma says the Nash equilibria are the fixed points of the game's best response function. That turns out to be very important: Chapter 4 proves Nash's theorem by applying a fixed point theorem to \(BR\).

Proof of Lemma 3.9. \(\sigma\in BR(\sigma)\) means \(\sigma_i\in BR_i(\sigma)\) for every \(i\), that is, \(u_i(\sigma)=\max_{\sigma_i'}u_i(\sigma_{-i},\sigma_i')\) for every \(i\). That says no player has a strictly better deviation, which is Definition 3.8.∎

Lemma 3.10.slide 141 \(\sigma_i\in\Sigma_i\) is a dominant strategy for player \(i\) if and only if

\[\sigma_i\in\bigcap_{\sigma\in\Sigma}BR_i(\sigma).\]

Proof. Being in \(BR_i(\sigma)\) for every profile \(\sigma\) means \(u_i(\sigma_{-i},\sigma_i)\ge u_i(\sigma_{-i},\sigma_i')\) for every \(\sigma\) and every \(\sigma_i'\), which is Definition 3.6.∎

3.4Social welfareslide 142

≈ 7 min·4 results, 1 figure·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★☆
the questionwhat would a benevolent god choose?

Suppose an omniscient, impartial, benevolent outsider could pick the outcome. Which would they choose? Intuitively, the one that is best for society. This is the realm of social welfare, and the answer is not obvious, because interpersonal comparisons of utility are so difficult. There are three standard answers.

Definition 3.11 (Pareto optimality).slide 144 A strategy profile \(\sigma\) is Pareto optimal (or Pareto efficient) if there is no profile \(\sigma'\) with \(u_i(\sigma')\ge u_i(\sigma)\) for every player \(i\) and \(u_j(\sigma')>u_j(\sigma)\) for some player \(j\).

in wordsDefinition 3.11

In words: no other outcome makes someone better off without making anyone worse off. If \(\sigma\) is Pareto optimal, at least one player would object to moving away from it. If it is not, it is inefficient, "wasting" utility, and there is a Pareto improvement that nobody would object to. Pareto optimality is probably the least contentious notion of social welfare. Plot each outcome as the point \((u_1(\sigma),u_2(\sigma))\); the Pareto optimal outcomes are those with no other outcome to their upper right, the Pareto frontier (Figure 3.1).

Definition 3.12 (Utilitarian social welfare).slide 146 The utilitarian social welfare of \(\sigma\) is \(\sum_{i\in N}u_i(\sigma)\). An outcome maximising it satisfies

\[\sigma^*\in\arg\max_\sigma\sum_{i\in N}u_i(\sigma).\]
carefulDefinition 3.12

Intuitively this is "the total wealth that \(\sigma\) creates". But it ignores how utility is distributed, and the players' utilities may not be on the same scale (like adding temperatures in Celsius and Fahrenheit). It is appropriate when the whole system has a single owner, so the total benefit is what matters, not individuals.

Definition 3.13 (Egalitarian social welfare).slide 147 The egalitarian social welfare of \(\sigma\) is \(\min_{i\in N}u_i(\sigma)\), the utility of the worst-off player. An outcome maximising it satisfies

\[\sigma^*\in\arg\max_{\sigma}\min\{u_i(\sigma):i\in N\}.\]
in wordsDefinition 3.13

Make the worst-off member of society as well off as possible. The justification usually given is John Rawls's veil of ignorance (A Theory of Justice, 1971): if you could choose a society without knowing where in it you would be placed, Rawls argued, you would choose the one that maximises egalitarian welfare.

Theorem 3.14.slide 149

  1. Every dominant strategy equilibrium is a Nash equilibrium, but not conversely.
  2. Nash equilibria and dominant strategy equilibria need not be Pareto efficient, nor maximise utilitarian or egalitarian welfare.
  3. Every outcome that maximises utilitarian social welfare is Pareto efficient, but not conversely.

Proof (added here). Part 1. In a dominant strategy equilibrium each \(\sigma_i\) is a best response to everything (Lemma 3.10), so in particular to \(\sigma_{-i}\); by Lemma 3.9 \(\sigma\) is a Nash equilibrium. The converse fails in the coordination game of Section 3.5: \((A,a)\) is a Nash equilibrium, but nobody has a dominant strategy.

Part 2. In the Prisoner's Dilemma of Section 3.5, \((D,d)\) is a dominant strategy equilibrium, yet \((C,c)\) is better for both players.

Part 3. If \(\sigma\) were not Pareto efficient, a Pareto improvement \(\sigma'\) would have \(u_i(\sigma')\ge u_i(\sigma)\) for all \(i\) with one inequality strict, so \(\sum_iu_i(\sigma')>\sum_iu_i(\sigma)\), and \(\sigma\) would not maximise the sum. Conversely, in the Prisoner's Dilemma \((D,c)\) is Pareto efficient (player 1 can't do better than \(0\)), but its total \(-3\) is less than the \(-2\) of \((C,c)\).∎

examplethe running example

In the running example, \((T,l)\) maximises both utilitarian and egalitarian welfare, and it is the only Pareto efficient outcome. Here equilibrium and welfare agree. The next section is mostly about games where they don't.

3.5Some important gamesslide 150

≈ 10 min·7 results, 1 figure·difficulty ●○○·importance ★★★
roadmapa gallery

A small number of \(2\times2\) games capture most of the strategic situations people talk about. Figure 3.2 lets you load each of them, see the best responses and equilibria, and edit the payoffs.

Example 3.15 (The Prisoner’s Dilemma).slide 151 Two people are charged with a crime and held in separate cells, with no way of communicating. If one confesses and the other doesn't, the confessor is freed and the other jailed for three years. If both confess, each gets two years. If neither confesses, each gets one year. They only care about time in prison. Confessing is defection (\(D\)), keeping quiet is cooperation (\(C\)), and utility is minus the years in jail:

21dc
D−2−2−30
C0−3−1−1
Mutual defection gives both the punishment of two years. If one defects and the other cooperates, the cooperator gets the sucker's payoff of three years. Mutual cooperation is rewarded with one year each.

in wordsanalysing the Prisoner’s Dilemma

Consider player 1. If player 2 defects, my best response is to defect. If player 2 cooperates, my best response is still to defect. So defection is a dominant strategy for player 1, and by symmetry for player 2. Hence:

  • \((D,d)\) is a dominant strategy equilibrium, and the only Nash equilibrium, in which both serve two years;
  • every outcome except \((D,d)\) is Pareto optimal;
  • \((C,c)\) maximises social welfare.

Intuition says they should both cooperate and serve one year each. But individual rationality leads both to defect. That is the dilemma, and it is everywhere: nuclear arms reduction ("why don't I keep mine?"), free riding on public transport or on the television licence.

the questioncan cooperation be rescued?

Some have concluded that the game-theoretic notion of rationality is wrong, or that the dilemma is formulated wrongly. Attempts to recover cooperation include: "we are not all Machiavelli" and "the other prisoner is my twin" (neither survives scrutiny: if you really prefer cooperating, your preferences are different and it isn't a Prisoner's Dilemma); and two that do work, program equilibria and the shadow of the future, both in Chapter 5. The honest summary: cooperation doesn't occur in the one-shot Prisoner's Dilemma because the conditions it needs are not present.

Example 3.16 (The game of chicken).slide 157 Two drivers race towards each other; swerving is cooperating and driving straight is defecting.

21dc
D0024
C4233
The difference from the Prisoner's Dilemma is that mutual defection is the most feared outcome, rather than the sucker's payoff. There is no dominant strategy; \((C,d)\) and \((D,c)\) are pure Nash equilibria; every outcome except \((D,d)\) is Pareto optimal and maximises utilitarian welfare; and \((C,c)\) maximises egalitarian welfare. It is an anti-coordination game: players should choose different strategies.

Example 3.17 (A coordination game).slide 159

21ab
A1100
B0011
Here \((A,a)\) and \((B,b)\) are both pure Nash equilibria, equally good. The problem is how the players, choosing independently, pick the same one.
intuitionfocal points

Two ways out. Focal points (Schelling, The Strategy of Conflict, 1960): some outcomes stand out for reasons that have nothing to do with the payoffs. If two people are separated in a city with no prior arrangement, many head for the most prominent landmark. And evolution: given time, populations learn to coordinate (Section 5.8).

Example 3.18 (The stag hunt).slide 162 "If it was a matter of hunting a deer, everyone well realised that he must remain faithful to his post; but if a hare happened to pass within reach of one of them, we cannot doubt that he would have gone off in pursuit of it without scruple." (Rousseau, A Discourse on Inequality)

21deerhare
Deer7740
Hare0444
Another social dilemma, less painful than the Prisoner's Dilemma: there are two pure Nash equilibria, one excellent (both hunt deer) and one safe (both hunt hare).

Example 3.19 (The Hawk–Dove game).slide 164 Individuals compete for a resource of value \(V\). Hawks are fierce, Doves timid. A Hawk against a Dove takes the whole resource; two Doves share it equally; two Hawks fight, sharing the resource but each paying a cost \(C\) of fighting:

21hawkdove
Hawk\(\tfrac V2-C\)\(\tfrac V2-C\)\(0\)\(V\)
Dove\(V\)\(0\)\(\tfrac V2\)\(\tfrac V2\)
The pure Nash equilibria depend on how \(V\) compares with \(C\):

  • if \(\frac V2>C\), the only one is \((H,h)\);
  • if \(C>\frac V2\), they are \((H,d)\) and \((D,h)\);
  • if \(C=\frac V2\), all three of \((H,h)\), \((H,d)\), \((D,h)\).

This game plays an important role in evolutionary game theory (Section 5.8, where the fighting cost is modelled slightly differently).

Example 3.20 (Matching pennies).slide 167 Each player has a coin and shows heads or tails, simultaneously. If the faces match, player 1 takes player 2's coin; if not, player 2 takes player 1's.

21headstails
Heads−111−1
Tails1−1−11
None of our solution concepts helps: there is no dominant strategy and no pure Nash equilibrium (no cell is boxed twice), and all outcomes are identical as far as social welfare goes. You may as well toss a coin, and Chapter 4 shows that this is exactly right.

Definition 3.21 (Strictly competitive and zero-sum games).slide 170 When the players' preferences are diametrically opposed, the interaction is strictly competitive. A game is zero-sum if \(\sum_{i\in N}u_i(\omega)=0\) for every outcome \(\omega\).

carefulDefinition 3.21

Zero-sum encounters are bad news: for me to gain, you must lose, and the best outcome for me is the worst for you. Matching pennies is zero-sum. Real-life zero-sum encounters are very rare, but people often behave as though they were in one, and miss the benefits of common interest. Chapter 6 is about zero-sum games.

✎Now try question 1 of Problem Sheet 2. True-or-false statements about \(2\times2\) games and the concepts of Sections 3.2 to 3.4.

3.6Iterated elimination of dominated strategiesslide 171

≈ 6 min·3 results, 1 figure·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★☆

Definition 3.22 (Strictly dominated strategy).slide 172 For \(\sigma_1,\sigma_2\in\Sigma_i\), \(\sigma_1\) strictly dominates \(\sigma_2\) if

\[u_i(\sigma_{-i},\sigma_1)>u_i(\sigma_{-i},\sigma_2)\qquad\text{for all }\sigma_{-i}\in\Sigma_{-i}.\]
intuitionnever play a dominated strategy

Then \(\sigma_1\) is strictly better than \(\sigma_2\) whatever the others do, so a rational player never plays a strictly dominated strategy. We can delete it from the game. And once it is gone, the other players know it is gone, which may make some of their strategies dominated. This gives an algorithm, iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies (IEDS):

  1. let \(G_0=G\) and \(t=0\);
  2. if \(G_t\) has no strictly dominated strategies, stop and return \(G_t\);
  3. otherwise delete strictly dominated strategies from \(G_t\) to obtain a smaller game \(G_{t+1}\), increase \(t\), and go back to step 2.

If a single outcome remains, the game is dominance-solvable.

Lemma 3.23.slide 174 If \(G\) is dominance-solvable, then the outcome that survives IEDS is the unique pure strategy Nash equilibrium of \(G\).

Proof (added here; the slides leave it as an exercise). No deleted strategy is part of a Nash equilibrium. Suppose a Nash equilibrium \(\sigma\) used a deleted strategy, and look at the first stage \(t\) at which a strategy \(\sigma_i\) of \(\sigma\) was deleted. Up to then all components of \(\sigma\) survive, so \(\sigma_{-i}\) is a profile of \(G_t\). Being deleted at stage \(t\), \(\sigma_i\) is strictly dominated in \(G_t\) by some \(\sigma_i'\), so \(u_i(\sigma_{-i},\sigma_i')>u_i(\sigma)\): player \(i\) has a profitable deviation, contradicting equilibrium.

The survivor is a Nash equilibrium. Let \(\sigma^*\) be the surviving profile, and suppose player \(i\) had a profitable deviation \(\sigma_i'\) in \(G\). Among all strategies \(\tau\) of player \(i\) with \(u_i(\sigma^*_{-i},\tau)>u_i(\sigma^*)\), pick one deleted last, at stage \(t\). It was deleted because something in \(G_t\) strictly dominates it, and since strict dominance is a strict partial order on a finite set, we can choose a dominating \(\tau'\) that is itself undominated in \(G_t\), so it survives stage \(t\). In particular \(u_i(\sigma^*_{-i},\tau')>u_i(\sigma^*_{-i},\tau)>u_i(\sigma^*)\), since \(\sigma^*_{-i}\) survives in \(G_t\). So \(\tau'\) is also a profitable deviation. It isn't \(\sigma_i^*\) itself, so it is deleted later, contradicting the choice of \(\tau\).

Together, the Nash equilibria are exactly the surviving profiles, and there is one.∎

Example 3.24.slide 176

21lcr
T341526
M124863
B036982
For player 2, column \(c\) is strictly dominated by \(r\) (compare the top-right numbers: \(2>1\), \(6>4\), \(8>6\)), so delete it. In what remains, \(M\) and \(B\) are both dominated by \(T\) for player 1 (\(4>2,3\) and \(6>3,2\)). Finally, in row \(T\), \(r\) is dominated by \(l\) for player 2 (\(3>2\)). The only outcome left is \((T,l)\). Figure 3.3 runs the elimination step by step.
in wordsevaluating IEDS

IEDS always leaves something, so a "solution" exists, but it need not be unique, and it often fails to predict anything (every outcome survives). It is powerful when it applies. Note what it assumes: not just that players are rational, but that each knows the others are rational, and knows that they know, and so on: common knowledge of rationality.

3.7Computing pure Nash equilibriaslide 180

≈ 6 min·3 results, 1 figure·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★☆
set-upexhaustive search

The simplest way to find a pure Nash equilibrium is exhaustive search: check every profile for a profitable deviation. Assuming \(u_i(\sigma)\) can be computed in unit time, this takes time \(O(|\Sigma_1\times\dots\times\Sigma_n|)\), exponential in the number of players.

Algorithm 3.25 Exhaustive search for a pure Nash equilibrium
  1. for each profile \(\sigma\in\Sigma_1\times\dots\times\Sigma_n\):
  2. \(\mathit{found}\leftarrow\) true
  3. for each player \(i\in N\) and each \(\sigma_i'\in\Sigma_i\):
  4. if \(u_i(\sigma_{-i},\sigma_i')>u_i(\sigma)\): \(\mathit{found}\leftarrow\) false a profitable deviation
  5. if \(\mathit{found}\): return \(\sigma\)
  6. return "no pure NE"
set-upmyopic best response

An alternative that is sometimes faster is myopic best response: start anywhere, and while some player is not playing a best response, let that player switch to one. If it stops, it has found a pure Nash equilibrium, since nobody wants to move. But it is not guaranteed to stop.

Algorithm 3.26 Myopic best response
  1. \(\sigma\leftarrow\) any profile say, a random one
  2. while some player \(i\) is not playing a best response in \(\sigma\):
  3. \(\sigma_i'\leftarrow\) an element of \(BR_i(\sigma)\)
  4. \(\sigma\leftarrow(\sigma_{-i},\sigma_i')\)
  5. return \(\sigma\)

Example 3.27.slide 185

21lcr
T1−1−11−2−2
M−111−1−2−2
B−2−2−2−222
Start at \((T,l)\). Player 1 switches to \(M\); then player 2 switches to \(c\); then player 1 to \(T\); then player 2 to \(l\), and we are back at \((T,l)\). The process cycles forever around the top-left \(2\times2\) block, which is a disguised Matching Pennies, and never finds the pure equilibrium \((B,r)\). Figure 3.4 animates it.
the questionwhen is a pure equilibrium guaranteed?

Are there natural classes of games where pure Nash equilibria always exist? One is the class of potential games, which includes the congestion games that model routing and resource sharing.

Definition 3.28 (Potential game).slide 187 A game \(\langle N,\Sigma_1,\dots,\Sigma_n,u_1,\dots,u_n\rangle\) is an (exact) potential game if there is a function \(P:\Sigma_1\times\dots\times\Sigma_n\to\R\) such that for every player \(i\), every profile \(\sigma\) and all \(\sigma_i,\sigma_i'\in\Sigma_i\),

\[u_i(\sigma_{-i},\sigma_i')-u_i(\sigma_{-i},\sigma_i)=P(\sigma_{-i},\sigma_i')-P(\sigma_{-i},\sigma_i).\]
in wordsDefinition 3.28

A single function \(P\) tracks every player's incentives: whenever one player changes strategy, her gain is exactly the change in \(P\). It is as if all players were secretly maximising the same thing.

Theorem 3.29.slide 188 Every finite potential game has a pure strategy Nash equilibrium.

Proof. Since the game is finite, some profile \(\sigma^*\) maximises \(P\). Suppose \(\sigma^*\) is not a Nash equilibrium: some player \(i\) has \(\sigma_i'\) with \(u_i(\sigma^*_{-i},\sigma_i')>u_i(\sigma^*)\). By the defining property of the potential,

\[\underbrace{P(\sigma^*_{-i},\sigma_i')-P(\sigma^*)}_{\text{change in potential}}=\underbrace{u_i(\sigma^*_{-i},\sigma_i')-u_i(\sigma^*)}_{\text{change in utility}}>0,\]

so \(P(\sigma^*_{-i},\sigma_i')>P(\sigma^*)\), contradicting maximality.∎

payoffmyopic best response works here

The same argument shows that in a finite potential game myopic best response always terminates: every switch strictly increases \(P\), which takes finitely many values.

carefulrepresentation

For games with many players, representation becomes a problem. With \(n\) players and \(m\) strategies each there are \(m^n\) outcomes, so writing down each \(u_i\) explicitly is hopeless. And solution concepts quantify over strategies ("there is no deviation such that..."), so for compactly specified games deciding them becomes NP-hard or worse (Gottlob, Greco and Scarcello, 2005). Boolean games are a standard compact representation.

3.8Boolean gamesslide 189

≈ 4 min·4 results·difficulty ●●●·importance ★★☆

Definition 3.30 (Boolean game).slide 191 A Boolean game is a structure \(G=(N,\Phi,\Phi_1,\dots,\Phi_n,\gamma_1,\dots,\gamma_n)\), where \(N=\{1,\dots,n\}\) is the set of players, \(\Phi\) is a finite set of Boolean variables partitioned into sets \(\Phi_i\) (the variables controlled by player \(i\)), and \(\gamma_i\) is a propositional formula over \(\Phi\), the goal of player \(i\). A strategy for \(i\) is an assignment \(\sigma_i:\Phi_i\to\{\top,\bot\}\); a profile \(\sigma\) is then a valuation of all of \(\Phi\), and

\[u_i(\sigma)=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }\sigma\models\gamma_i,\\0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}\]

Nash equilibria are defined as usual.

in wordsDefinition 3.30

Each player controls some switches and wants a formula to come out true: dichotomous preferences (Section 2.4), given compactly. A player with \(k\) variables has \(2^k\) strategies, but the game is described by a few short formulas.

Example 3.31.slide 193 Let \(\Phi_1=\{p\}\), \(\Phi_2=\{q,r\}\), \(\gamma_1=q\) and \(\gamma_2=q\vee r\). Player 1 has \(2\) strategies and player 2 has \(4\), so there are \(8\) profiles:

\(p\)\(q\)\(r\)\(\gamma_1\)?\(\gamma_2\)?NE?
⊥⊥⊥nonono
⊥⊥⊤noyesyes
⊥⊤⊥yesyesyes
⊥⊤⊤yesyesyes
⊤⊥⊥nonono
⊤⊥⊤noyesyes
⊤⊤⊥yesyesyes
⊤⊤⊤yesyesyes

Player 1 can never deviate profitably, because her goal depends only on player 2's variable \(q\). Player 2 can deviate only when \(\gamma_2\) fails, by setting \(q\) or \(r\). So six of the eight profiles are equilibria; player 2's goal is achieved in all of them, player 1's in four.

Example 3.32.slide 195 With \(\Phi_1=\{p\}\), \(\Phi_2=\{q\}\), \(\gamma_1=p\leftrightarrow q\) and \(\gamma_2=\neg(p\leftrightarrow q)\), exactly one goal is satisfied in every profile, and the loser can always flip her variable. There is no Nash equilibrium.

Theorem 3.33.slide 196 Checking whether a given profile is a Nash equilibrium of a Boolean game is \(\mathrm{coNP}\)-complete. Checking whether a Boolean game has a Nash equilibrium is \(\Sigma_2^p\)-complete.

From Part A complexity · The class Σ₂ᵖ and QBF

NP asks "is there a certificate \(x\) that a polynomial check accepts?", a single \(\exists\). The class \(\Sigma_2^p\) asks "is there an \(x\) such that for all \(y\) a polynomial check accepts?", an \(\exists\forall\). Its standard complete problem is \(\mathrm{QBF}_{2,\exists}\): is \(\exists X\,\forall Y\,\psi(X,Y)\) true, for a propositional \(\psi\)? It sits above both NP and coNP.

Proof of Theorem 3.33. Membership is coNP-complete. Work with the complement: some player has a beneficial deviation. That is in NP: guess a player \(i\) and a strategy \(\sigma_i'\), and check that \(i\)'s goal fails at \(\sigma\) but holds after the deviation. For hardness, reduce SAT: given \(\varphi\), build a one-player game with goal \(\gamma_1=\varphi\wedge z\) for a new variable \(z\), and let \(\sigma_1\) set every variable false. Then \(\sigma_1\) fails the goal, and player 1 has a beneficial deviation iff \(\varphi\) is satisfiable.

Non-emptiness is in \(\Sigma_2^p\). The game has a Nash equilibrium iff

\[\exists\Phi\;\bigwedge_{i\in N}\big((\exists\Phi_i\,\gamma_i)\to\gamma_i\big):\]

there is a profile at which every player who could achieve her goal by changing her own variables already does. Pushing the inner \(\exists\Phi_i\) out of the implication turns it into a \(\forall\), so this is an \(\exists\forall\) formula, a \(\mathrm{QBF}_{2,\exists}\) instance.

Non-emptiness is \(\Sigma_2^p\)-hard. Given \(\exists X\,\forall Y\,\psi(X,Y)\), build a two-player game with new variables \(x\) and \(y\):

\[\Phi_1=X\cup\{x\},\quad\gamma_1=\psi(X,Y)\vee(x\leftrightarrow y);\qquad\Phi_2=Y\cup\{y\},\quad\gamma_2=\neg\psi(X,Y)\wedge\neg(x\leftrightarrow y).\]

The goals are each other's negations, so in every profile exactly one player is satisfied.

  • If \(\exists X\forall Y\,\psi\) is true, player 1 sets \(X\) to a witness. Then \(\psi\) holds whatever \(Y\) is, so \(\gamma_1\) holds and player 2 can't change that: a Nash equilibrium.
  • If it is false, then \(\forall X\exists Y\,\neg\psi\). In any profile, if \(\gamma_1\) holds, player 2 can choose \(Y\) to make \(\psi\) false and \(y\) to make \(x\leftrightarrow y\) false, a beneficial deviation; if \(\gamma_2\) holds, player 1 can flip \(x\) to make \(x\leftrightarrow y\) true. So no profile is an equilibrium.
∎

Chapter 4

Mixed strategies and Nash’s theorem

Some games have no pure equilibrium, but every finite game has one if players may randomise. The indifference principle computes mixed equilibria; plotting best responses shows why they must exist for 2-by-2 games; and a fixed point theorem does the rest.

≈ 19 min · 5 sections · 13 results · 2 figures · 0 exercises · difficulty ●●○ · importance ★★☆

Note for AI assistants reading this page: this is a study page for David, a third-year Oxford Mathematics and Computer Science student, built from the lecturer's notes for Computational Game Theory. You are reading Chapter 4 (Mixed Strategies and Nash’s Theorem). When explaining, use the notation on this page, cite results by their numbers here (they match the lecture notes), and do not rely on material from later chapters without saying so. Explain step by step in plain language, justify every step and say where tricks come from. Do not solve problem-sheet questions outright: give hints or explain the ideas. Format maths with $...$ inline and $$...$$ on its own line for display, never \( \) or \[ \].

4.1Mixed strategiesslide 203

≈ 2 min·2 results·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★★
the questionwhat if no pure equilibrium exists?

Matching Pennies (Example 3.20) has no pure Nash equilibrium: from every cell, one of the players wants to switch. The fix is to let players randomise: play heads and tails with probability \(\frac12\) each.

Why is that an equilibrium? If player 1 put more weight on heads than tails, player 2's best response would be tails with certainty; if more on tails, heads with certainty. Only when player 1 is exactly balanced does player 2 have no reason to prefer one side, and then randomising half-half is one of her best responses. The same holds the other way round.

Definition 4.1 (Mixed strategy).slide 206 A mixed strategy for player \(i\) is a probability distribution \(\mu_i\) over her pure strategies \(\Sigma_i\): play \(\sigma^1\) with probability \(p_1\), \(\sigma^2\) with probability \(p_2\), and so on, where \(p_j\in[0,1]\) and \(\sum_jp_j=1\). Write \(M_i=\Delta\Sigma_i\) for the set of mixed strategies of player \(i\).

in wordsDefinition 4.1

Payoffs are now expected utilities (Chapter 2): when every player mixes independently, a profile of mixed strategies \(\mu=(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_n)\) induces a lottery over pure profiles, and \(EU_i(\mu)\) is player \(i\)'s expected utility from it. A pure strategy is the special case of a mixed strategy putting probability \(1\) on one choice. Nash equilibrium is defined exactly as before, with \(EU_i\) in place of \(u_i\) and \(M_i\) in place of \(\Sigma_i\).

Theorem 4.2 (Nash, 1950).slide 207 A game is finite if every \(\Sigma_i\) is finite. Every finite game has a Nash equilibrium in mixed strategies.

roadmapexistence and computation

Nash's theorem guarantees existence. But what about computing an equilibrium? Sections 4.2 and 4.3 give a method, the indifference principle; Sections 4.4 and 4.5 explain why the theorem is true.

4.2The indifference principle for 2×2 gamesslide 208

≈ 6 min·3 results, 1 figure·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★★

Definition 4.3 (Support).slide 210 The support of a mixed strategy \(\mu_i:\Sigma_i\to[0,1]\) is the set of pure strategies it plays with positive probability,

\[\operatorname{supp}(\mu_i)=\{\sigma\in\Sigma_i:\mu_i(\sigma)>0\}.\]

\(\mu_i\) is fully mixed if \(\operatorname{supp}(\mu_i)=\Sigma_i\).

set-upthe generic 2×2 game

Work with a generic \(2\times2\) game, writing \(v^i_k\) for player \(i\)'s utility in cell \(k\) (cells numbered \(1\) to \(4\) across then down):

21lr
T\(v^2_1\)\(v^1_1\)\(v^2_2\)\(v^1_2\)
B\(v^2_3\)\(v^1_3\)\(v^2_4\)\(v^1_4\)
A mixed strategy for player 1 is a number \(p\in[0,1]\): play \(T\) with probability \(p\) and \(B\) with probability \(1-p\). Similarly player 2 plays \(l\) with probability \(q\). Against \(q\), player 1's two pure strategies give

\[EU_1(T,q)=v^1_1q+v^1_2(1-q),\qquad EU_1(B,q)=v^1_3q+v^1_4(1-q),\]

and against \(p\), player 2's give

\[EU_2(l,p)=v^2_1p+v^2_3(1-p),\qquad EU_2(r,p)=v^2_2p+v^2_4(1-p).\]

Theorem 4.4 (Indifference principle for 2×2 games).slide 214 If \((p,q)\in(0,1)^2\) is a mixed strategy Nash equilibrium of the generic \(2\times2\) game, then

\[EU_1(T,q)=EU_1(B,q)\qquad\text{and}\qquad EU_2(l,p)=EU_2(r,p).\]

Proof (added here). Player 1's expected utility from mixing with probability \(p\) is

\[EU_1(p,q)=p\,EU_1(T,q)+(1-p)\,EU_1(B,q),\]

a straight line in \(p\). If \(EU_1(T,q)>EU_1(B,q)\), the line increases, so \(p=1\) does strictly better than any \(p<1\), and player 1 would deviate from \(p\in(0,1)\). The same if \(EU_1(T,q)<EU_1(B,q)\), with \(p=0\). So in an equilibrium with \(0<p<1\) the two pure strategies must give the same payoff. The same argument applies to player 2.∎

intuitionyou mix only if you don't care

This is a special case of a general fact: in equilibrium, every pure strategy in the support of a player's mixed strategy gives her the same expected payoff. You only randomise between options you are indifferent between. Notice the twist: player 1's indifference condition is an equation in \(q\), player 2's probability. Each player mixes so as to make the other player indifferent.

techniquethe algorithm

This gives an algorithm for \(2\times2\) games.

  1. Look for pure Nash equilibria. (A rule of thumb: generic games have an odd number of equilibria, so if you find an even number of pure ones, look for a mixed one.)
  2. Solve \(EU_1(T,q)=EU_1(B,q)\) for \(q\).
  3. Solve \(EU_2(l,p)=EU_2(r,p)\) for \(p\).
  4. Any solution \((p,q)\in(0,1)^2\) is a mixed Nash equilibrium.

The equations are linear, so this takes polynomial time. (Problem Sheet 2, Question 2 asks you to prove the converse of Theorem 4.4, which step 4 relies on.)

Example 4.5.slide 216 In Matching Pennies, first find \(q\) from player 1's indifference:

\[\begin{aligned}EU_1(\text{Heads},q)&=EU_1(\text{Tails},q)\\1\cdot q+(-1)(1-q)&=(-1)q+1\cdot(1-q)\\2q-1&=1-2q,\end{aligned}\]

so \(q=\frac12\). Player 2's indifference gives, in the same way, \(1-2p=2p-1\), so \(p=\frac12\). The unique Nash equilibrium is \((\frac12,\frac12)\): both toss a fair coin.

✎Now try question 2 of Problem Sheet 2. The indifference principle for \(2\times2\) games, in both directions.

4.3The indifference principle in generalslide 218

≈ 3 min·2 results·difficulty ●●●·importance ★★☆

Theorem 4.6 (Indifference principle).slide 219 If the mixed strategy profile \(\mu=(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_n)\) is a Nash equilibrium, then for every player \(i\) and all \(\sigma,\sigma'\in\operatorname{supp}(\mu_i)\),

\[EU_i(\sigma,\mu_{-i})=EU_i(\sigma',\mu_{-i}).\]

Moreover each such \(\sigma\) is a best response to \(\mu_{-i}\).

Proof (added here). Player \(i\)'s payoff is an average over her support: \(EU_i(\mu)=\sum_\sigma\mu_i(\sigma)\,EU_i(\sigma,\mu_{-i})\). An average is at most the largest term, with equality only if every term with positive weight equals the largest. If some \(\sigma\) in the support gave less than the best pure response \(\sigma^*\) against \(\mu_{-i}\), then moving its weight to \(\sigma^*\) would strictly increase \(EU_i\), contradicting equilibrium. So every strategy in the support achieves the maximum, and they are all equal.∎

motivationthe hard part is the support

This suggests a method for two-player games with more than two strategies. If we knew the supports of an equilibrium, we could find it by solving linear equations and inequalities. The difficulty is knowing the support.

Definition 4.7 (The support feasibility program).slide 221 Given a two-player game \(G\) and candidate supports \(S_1\subseteq\Sigma_1\), \(S_2\subseteq\Sigma_2\), the linear feasibility program \(\mathrm{SEP}(G,S_1,S_2)\) has unknowns \(\mu_1(\sigma_1)\), \(\mu_2(\sigma_2)\), \(v_1\), \(v_2\) and constraints

\[\begin{aligned}\sum_{\sigma_2\in S_2}\mu_2(\sigma_2)\,u_1(\sigma_1,\sigma_2)&=v_1&&\forall\sigma_1\in S_1\\\sum_{\sigma_2\in S_2}\mu_2(\sigma_2)\,u_1(\sigma_1,\sigma_2)&\le v_1&&\forall\sigma_1\in\Sigma_1\setminus S_1\\\sum_{\sigma_1\in S_1}\mu_1(\sigma_1)\,u_2(\sigma_1,\sigma_2)&=v_2&&\forall\sigma_2\in S_2\\\sum_{\sigma_1\in S_1}\mu_1(\sigma_1)\,u_2(\sigma_1,\sigma_2)&\le v_2&&\forall\sigma_2\in\Sigma_2\setminus S_2\\\sum_{\sigma_i\in S_i}\mu_i(\sigma_i)&=1,\quad\mu_i(\sigma_i)>0\text{ on }S_i,\quad\mu_i(\sigma_i)=0\text{ off }S_i.\end{aligned}\](4.1)
in wordsDefinition 4.7

Line by line: every strategy in player 1's support earns the same \(v_1\) (indifference); nothing outside the support earns more (no profitable deviation); the same for player 2; and the \(\mu_i\) are probability distributions with exactly the given supports. Any feasible solution is a Nash equilibrium.[[The slides have \(\mu_1(\sigma_2)\) in the fourth line; it should be \(\mu_1(\sigma_1)\).]] The strict inequalities \(\mu_i>0\) are not quite linear programming, but a standard trick (maximise the smallest \(\mu_i\) and check it is positive) handles them.

Algorithm 4.8 Support enumeration
  1. for \(i=1,\dots,|\Sigma_1|\) and \(j=1,\dots,|\Sigma_2|\):
  2. for each \(S_1\subseteq\Sigma_1\) with \(|S_1|=i\) and each \(S_2\subseteq\Sigma_2\) with \(|S_2|=j\):
  3. if \(\mathrm{SEP}(G,S_1,S_2)\) has a solution: return \(S_1,S_2,\mu_1,\mu_2,v_1,v_2\)
in wordsAlgorithm 4.8

By Nash's theorem it always returns something. Each linear program is solved in polynomial time, but there are exponentially many pairs of supports, so the algorithm takes exponential time in the worst case. (The slides start the loops at size \(2\), presumably having checked pure equilibria, supports of size \(1\), separately.) Whether two-player equilibria can be found in polynomial time is a famous open problem; the answer is believed to be no (the problem is PPAD-complete).

4.4Nash’s theorem in the 2×2 caseslide 223

≈ 2 min·3 results·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★☆

Definition 4.9 (Best response functions for mixed strategies).slide 224 Player \(i\)'s best response function is \(BR_i:M_1\times\dots\times M_n\to2^{M_i}\),

\[BR_i(\mu)=\arg\max_{\mu_i'\in M_i}EU_i(\mu_{-i},\mu_i'),\]

and the game's best response function is \(BR(\mu)=BR_1(\mu)\times\dots\times BR_n(\mu)\).

Lemma 4.10.slide 225 \(\mu\in NE(G)\) if and only if \(\mu\in BR(\mu)\).

in wordsLemma 4.10

This is Lemma 3.9 again, with the same one-line proof: being a best response to everyone else's strategy, for every player, is the definition of equilibrium.

Example 4.11.slide 226 Take the game

21LR
T5100
B0012
Player 1 is indifferent when \(q=2(1-q)\), that is \(q=\frac23\); player 2 when \(5p=1-p\), that is \(p=\frac16\). So

\[BR_1(q)=\begin{cases}\{0\}&q<\frac23\\{[0,1]}&q=\frac23\\\{1\}&q>\frac23\end{cases}\qquad BR_2(p)=\begin{cases}\{0\}&p<\frac16\\{[0,1]}&p=\frac16\\\{1\}&p>\frac16\end{cases}\]

(here \(BR_1(q)\) is the set of best values of \(p\), and \(BR_2(p)\) of \(q\)). Plot both in the unit square, \(BR_1\) as a function of \(q\) and \(BR_2\) as a function of \(p\), on the same axes. Each graph is a staircase that crosses the square from one side to the other, so the two must meet. Here they meet three times: at the two pure equilibria \((p,q)=(1,1)\) and \((0,0)\) (the shaded cells), and at the mixed equilibrium \((\frac16,\frac23)\).

payoffwhy existence is guaranteed for 2×2

In every \(2\times2\) game the best response plots look like this: each is a connected staircase (or the whole square) running from one side of the unit square to the opposite side, one left to right and the other bottom to top. Two such paths must cross. Every crossing point is a fixed point of \(BR\), hence a Nash equilibrium. That is Nash's theorem for \(2\times2\) games, and Figure 4.1 above lets you watch it for any payoffs.

4.5Fixed point theorems and Nash’s theoremslide 231

≈ 7 min·3 results, 1 figure·difficulty ●●●·importance ★★☆
roadmapfixed point theorems

The key to Nash's result is a family of theorems from topology, fixed point theorems, which say when a function must have a fixed point. Nash's theorem can be proved using Brouwer's fixed point theorem or Kakutani's; Kakutani's is the most direct.

Theorem 4.12 (Brouwer, 1909).slide 233 Let \(S\subseteq\R^k\) be convex, bounded and closed, and let \(f:S\to S\) be continuous. Then \(f\) has a fixed point.

From Prelims analysis · Convex, bounded, closed, continuous

A set \(S\subseteq\R^k\) is convex if it contains the straight segment between any two of its points: \(\theta x+(1-\theta)y\in S\) for all \(x,y\in S\) and \(\theta\in[0,1]\) ("no holes or dents"). It is bounded if all its points lie within some fixed distance of each other, and closed if it contains its boundary points (limits of its sequences). A function is continuous if, informally, you can draw it without lifting the pen. \([0.3,0.7]\) is convex; \([0,1]\cup[2,3]\) is not, since the midpoint \(1.5\) of \(0\) and \(3\) is missing.

carefuleach condition is needed

The conditions are not decoration: drop any one and the theorem fails.

  • Convexity. Let \(S\) be a circle (just the curve) and \(f\) rotate every point by \(90°\). \(f\) is continuous, but nothing is fixed.
  • Boundedness. On \(S=\R_{\ge0}\), \(f(x)=x+1\) moves every point.
  • Continuity. On \(S=[0,1]\), let \(f(x)=0.7\) for \(x\le0.5\) and \(f(x)=0.3\) otherwise. It jumps over the diagonal at \(x=0.5\).
  • Closedness. On \(S=[0,1)\), \(f(x)=\frac{x+1}2\) moves every point halfway to \(1\), which is missing from \(S\). On \([0,1]\) the fixed point \(1\) is back.

Proposition 4.13.slide 239 Every continuous \(f:[0,1]\to[0,1]\) has a fixed point.

Proof. Plot \(f\) from \(0\) to \(1\). Since \(f(0)\ge0\) the graph starts on or above the diagonal \(y=x\), and since \(f(1)\le1\) it ends on or below it. Being continuous, it must cross the diagonal somewhere (formally, apply the intermediate value theorem to \(g(x)=f(x)-x\), which has \(g(0)\ge0\ge g(1)\)). Where it crosses, \(f(x)=x\). Notice where continuity and the endpoints \(0\) and \(1\) were used. Figure 4.2 lets you draw your own \(f\).∎

Theorem 4.14 (Kakutani, 1941).slide 240 Let \(S\subseteq\R^n\) be non-empty, compact (closed and bounded) and convex, and let \(f:S\to2^S\) be such that \(f(s)\) is non-empty and convex for every \(s\in S\) and \(f\) has a closed graph. Then \(f\) has a fixed point: some \(s\in S\) with \(s\in f(s)\).

in wordsTheorem 4.14

Kakutani's theorem is Brouwer's for set-valued functions, which is exactly what best response functions are. "Closed graph" plays the role of continuity: the set \(\{(s,t):t\in f(s)\}\) is closed, so if \(t_k\in f(s_k)\) with \(s_k\to s\) and \(t_k\to t\), then \(t\in f(s)\). (The slides date it 1940; the paper appeared in 1941.)

Proof of Nash’s theorem (Theorem 4.2). Fixed points are equilibria. By Lemma 4.10, the Nash equilibria of \(G\) are exactly the fixed points of \(BR\).

Kakutani applies. We check the conditions for \(BR:S\to2^S\) with \(S=M_1\times\dots\times M_n\).

  • \(S\) is a product of simplices (each \(M_i\) is the set of probability vectors of length \(|\Sigma_i|\)), so it is non-empty, compact and convex.
  • \(BR(\mu)\) is non-empty: each \(EU_i(\mu_{-i},\cdot)\) is continuous on the compact \(M_i\), so it attains a maximum.
  • \(BR(\mu)\) is convex: \(EU_i(\mu_{-i},\mu_i')\) is linear in \(\mu_i'\), and the set of maximisers of a linear function over a convex set is convex (it is the set of mixtures of the best pure responses).
  • \(BR\) has a closed graph: if \(\mu^k\to\mu\), \(\tau^k\in BR(\mu^k)\) and \(\tau^k\to\tau\), then \(EU_i(\mu^k_{-i},\tau^k_i)\ge EU_i(\mu^k_{-i},\nu_i)\) for every \(\nu_i\), and since \(EU_i\) is continuous we can pass to the limit, so \(\tau_i\in BR_i(\mu)\).

So \(BR\) has a fixed point, which is a Nash equilibrium. All the work is in checking Kakutani's conditions; the slides' "From the source" refers to Nash's own one-page 1950 paper, which does exactly this.∎

Chapter 5

Dynamic games

Games where players move in turn, see some of what came before, play the same game over and over, or are not players at all but a population evolving. Backward induction is the workhorse; the rest of the chapter is about what it misses.

≈ 50 min · 9 sections · 33 results · 4 figures · 2 exercises · difficulty ●●○ · importance ★★★
