When explaining, use the notation on this page, cite results by their numbers here (they match the lecture notes), and do not rely on material from later chapters without saying so. 5.1Extensive form gamesslide 244

≈ 4 min·3 results·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★★
the questionwhat if players move in turn?

Strategic form games assume each player makes a single choice, in ignorance of the choices of the others. "Simultaneous moves" is really an assumption about information, not about time: it doesn't matter when you move, only what you know when you do. Many settings have a much richer structure: several moves each, with some knowledge of what has happened so far. This chapter studies three kinds of dynamic game: extensive form games (game trees), iterated games (the same game played repeatedly), and evolutionary games (where strategies are not chosen but selected).

set-upthree kinds of knowledge

Extensive form games come in increasing order of ignorance.

  • Perfect information: players know exactly how the current state of the game was reached. Chess is the standard example.
  • Imperfect information: players may be uncertain about earlier moves, and so about which state they are in. Card games where you can't see the other hands are like this.
  • Imperfect recall: players may forget things they once knew, even their own earlier moves.

We assume throughout that there are no chance moves: every move is made by a player.

From Prelims · Trees

A tree \(T=(V,E,v_0)\) is a directed graph with vertices \(V\) and edges \(E\subseteq V\times V\) such that

  1. exactly one vertex has no incoming edges, the root \(v_0\);
  2. there is a path from the root to every other vertex;
  3. every other vertex has exactly one incoming edge.

The children of \(v\) are \(\mathrm{children}(v)=\{v':(v,v')\in E\}\). Vertices with no children are leaves; the others are interior vertices. Because each vertex has one parent, there is exactly one path from the root to any vertex, so a vertex "remembers" the whole history of how it was reached.

Definition 5.1 (Extensive form game of perfect information).slide 252 An extensive form game of perfect information is a structure

\[G=(N,(V,E,v_0),\mathit{owner},a,u_1,\dots,u_n)\]

where

  • \(N=\{1,\dots,n\}\) is the set of players;
  • \((V,E,v_0)\) is a finite tree;
  • \(\mathit{owner}:\mathrm{interior}(V,E)\to N\) says which player moves at each decision node;
  • \(a:E\to A\) labels each edge with an action; the actions available at \(v\) are \(A(v)=\{a(v,v'):(v,v')\in E\}\), and we require that \(a(v,v')=a(v,v'')\) implies \(v'=v''\);
  • \(u_i:\mathrm{leaves}(V,E)\to\R\) is player \(i\)'s utility function.
in wordsDefinition 5.1

The game is played by starting at the root and letting the owner of the current node pick an edge, until a leaf is reached; the leaf's labels are the payoffs. The condition on \(a\) says that different edges out of the same node carry different actions, so naming an action at a node determines where you go. Write \(V_i=\{v:\mathit{owner}(v)=i\}\) for player \(i\)'s decision nodes and \(A_i=\bigcup_{v\in V_i}A(v)\) for all the actions she ever has.

Definition 5.2 (Strategy in an extensive form game).slide 253 A (pure) strategy for player \(i\) is a function \(\sigma_i:V_i\to A_i\) with \(\sigma_i(v)\in A(v)\) for every \(v\in V_i\). Strategy profiles, Nash equilibria and so on are defined as for strategic form games.

carefula strategy is a complete plan

A strategy chooses an action at every one of the player's nodes, including nodes that the strategy itself (or the other players' strategies) will never reach. It is a complete contingency plan, like instructions left for a deputy who might find themselves anywhere in the tree. Every profile \(\sigma\) traces a unique path from the root to a leaf \(v(\sigma)\), the outcome; if \(\sigma\) is an equilibrium this is the equilibrium path.

Example 5.3.slide 254 Player 1 moves first, choosing \(L\) or \(R\). Player 2 sees the choice and then chooses \(l\) or \(r\). The four leaves pay

\[(L,l)\mapsto(4,1),\qquad(L,r)\mapsto(0,2),\qquad(R,l)\mapsto(3,1),\qquad(R,r)\mapsto(1,2).\]

Player 1 has one decision node, so two pure strategies, \(L\) and \(R\). Player 2 has two decision nodes \(v_1\) (after \(L\)) and \(v_2\) (after \(R\)), and a strategy picks an action at each, so she has four: \(ll\), \(lr\), \(rl\), \(rr\), where \(lr\) means "\(l\) at \(v_1\), \(r\) at \(v_2\)". Figure 5.1 draws the tree.

5.2Backward inductionslide 257

≈ 6 min·2 results, 1 figure·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★★
intuitionsolve from the leaves up

Use dynamic programming. A node whose children are all leaves is easy: its owner picks the child that is best for her. Replace the node by that child's payoffs, and repeat. Eventually the root is labelled with the payoffs that rational play produces, and the choices made along the way form a strategy profile.

Algorithm 5.4 Backward induction
  1. \(\mathit{done}\gets\mathrm{leaves}(V,E)\)
  2. while \(\mathit{done}\ne V\):
  3. \(\mathit{next}\gets\{v\in V\setminus\mathit{done}:\mathrm{children}(v)\subseteq\mathit{done}\}\)
  4. for \(v\in\mathit{next}\):
  5. \(i\gets\mathit{owner}(v)\); \(\ O\gets\arg\max_{v'\in\mathrm{children}(v)}u_i(v')\) (the optimal choices)
  6. \(v''\gets\) any element of \(O\)
  7. for \(j\in N\): \(u_j(v)\gets u_j(v'')\) (back the utilities up)
  8. \(\mathit{done}\gets\mathit{done}\cup\{v\}\)
historythe name

It is sometimes called Zermelo's algorithm, after Ernst Zermelo's 1913 paper on chess, though he didn't invent it. It is one of the most useful algorithms in computer science: the same idea computes CTL model checking and optimal policies in Markov decision processes ("value iteration").

Example 5.5.slide 259 At \(v_1\) (after \(L\)), player 2 chooses between payoffs \(1\) (from \(l\)) and \(2\) (from \(r\)), so she picks \(r\), and \(v_1\) is labelled \((0,2)\). At \(v_2\) (after \(R\)), she again picks \(r\), labelling \(v_2\) with \((1,2)\). Now player 1 chooses between \(0\) (from \(L\)) and \(1\) (from \(R\)), so she picks \(R\). The root is labelled \((1,2)\). We write the equilibrium by listing each player's actions: \((R,rr)\), or just \((R,r)\) along the path.

Theorem 5.6.slide 264 In an extensive form game with perfect information and no chance moves:

  1. backward induction terminates in time polynomial in the size of the tree, labelling the root with the payoff profile of a Nash equilibrium (in fact, of a subgame perfect equilibrium, Section 5.3);
  2. in particular, every such game has a Nash equilibrium in pure strategies.

Proof sketch. Each node is processed once, and processing it takes time proportional to its number of children, so the total is linear in the size of the tree. For correctness, show by induction from the leaves up that the strategies chosen below any node \(v\) form a Nash equilibrium of the game starting at \(v\). At a node \(v\) owned by \(i\), the other players' choices below \(v\) are fixed, and \(i\) picks the child whose backed-up value is best for her; any deviation, at \(v\) or below it, can only lead to a child value that is no better, by the induction hypothesis.∎

carefuluniqueness

The slides add a third part: "if no two leaves have the same utility for any player, the Nash equilibrium is unique". That is true of the subgame perfect equilibrium of Section 5.3 (backward induction then never has to break a tie), but not of Nash equilibria in general.[[A counterexample: player 1 chooses Out, paying \((1,3)\), or In; after In, player 2 chooses Fight \((0,0)\) or Accommodate \((2,1)\). All payoffs of each player are distinct. Backward induction gives (In, Accommodate), but (Out, Fight) is also a Nash equilibrium: given Fight, Out is best for player 1, and given Out, player 2 gets \(3\) whatever she plans.]]

5.3Subgame perfect equilibriumslide 266

≈ 4 min·4 results·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★★

Example 5.7.slide 267 Player 1 chooses \(L\), which ends the game with \((0,0)\), or \(R\), after which player 2 chooses \(l\), giving \((0,0)\), or \(r\), giving \((2,2)\). Backward induction gives \((R,r)\), which makes sense. But \((L,l)\) is also a Nash equilibrium.

  • If player 1 plays \(L\), player 2 gets \(0\) whatever she does, so \(l\) is a best response to \(L\).
  • If player 2 plays \(l\), player 1 gets \(0\) from \(L\) and \(0\) from \(R\), so \(L\) is a best response to \(l\).
in wordsExample 5.7

In \((L,l)\), player 2 is threatening to play \(l\). But the threat is not credible: if she is ever actually called on to move, choosing \(l\) would be irrational. Nash equilibrium can't see this, because it only checks deviations from the equilibrium path's point of view, and player 2's node is off the path. We need a refinement, due to Reinhard Selten.

Definition 5.8 (Subgame perfect Nash equilibrium).slide 273 The subgames of an extensive form game \(G\) are the games starting at each decision node of \(G\), with strategies and utilities restricted accordingly. (\(G\) is a subgame of itself.) A strategy profile \(\sigma\) is a subgame perfect Nash equilibrium (SPNE) if it is a Nash equilibrium of every subgame of \(G\).

exampleDefinition 5.8

The game of Example 5.7 has two subgames: itself, and the one starting at player 2's node. \((L,l)\) is not subgame perfect, because in the second subgame \(l\) is not a Nash equilibrium (it is a one-player game, where \(r\) is strictly better). \((R,r)\) is subgame perfect.

Theorem 5.9.slide 274 Every extensive form game of perfect information with no chance moves has a subgame perfect equilibrium, and one can be computed in polynomial time by backward induction. If no player has the same utility at two different leaves, the SPNE is unique.

in wordsTheorem 5.9

Backward induction solves every subgame on the way up, which is exactly the SPNE condition. With no ties, every choice it makes is forced, which gives uniqueness.

Example 5.10 (The centipede game).slide 275 Players \(1\) and \(2\) alternately choose Right (end the game) or Down (continue). Ending at the four decision nodes pays \((1,1)\), \((0,3)\), \((2,2)\) and \((1,4)\) respectively; if everyone continues, the game ends at \((3,3)\). Backward induction: at the last node player 2 prefers \(4\) to \(3\), so ends it. Knowing that, player 1 at the third node prefers \(2\) to \(1\), so ends it. And so on back to the root: player 1 ends the game immediately, with \((1,1)\).

carefula poor outcome

Both players would be better off at \((3,3)\), and in experiments people do continue for a few rounds before someone ends it. The SPNE is an equilibrium with poor social welfare, and arguably a poor prediction. Load the centipede game into Figure 5.1 to watch the unravelling.

techniqueback to strategic form

Any extensive form game can be turned into a strategic form game: the strategies are the extensive form strategies, and \(u_i(\sigma)=u_i(v(\sigma))\) (an abuse of notation). For the running example:

21lllrrlrr
L14142020
R13211321
The shaded cell is the unique pure Nash equilibrium, \((R,rr)\). Note the exponential blowup: a player with \(k\) binary decision nodes has \(2^k\) strategies, so the matrix can be exponentially larger than the tree.

5.4Imperfect informationslide 279

≈ 7 min·5 results, 1 figure·difficulty ●●●·importance ★★☆
the questionwhat if you can't see the other move?

Try to write Matching Pennies as a tree: player 1 shows \(H\) or \(T\), then player 2 shows \(h\) or \(t\). This doesn't work, because when player 2 moves she knows what player 1 did, and the strategy "\(t\) after \(H\), \(h\) after \(T\)" wins every time. We need a way of saying that player 2 can't tell the two nodes apart.

Definition 5.11 (Information sets).slide 282 Partition each player's decision nodes into information sets; let \(I_i\) be player \(i\)'s information sets, and \([v]\) the one containing \(v\). If \([v]=[v']\), the player cannot distinguish \(v\) from \(v'\). We require \(A(v)=A(v')\) whenever \([v]=[v']\). A strategy now assigns an action to each information set,

\[\sigma_i:I_i\to A_i.\]
in wordsDefinition 5.11

The requirement \(A(v)=A(v')\) is forced: if the available actions differed, the player could tell the nodes apart by looking at them. In pictures, nodes in the same information set are joined by a dotted line (singletons aren't drawn). Matching Pennies is the tree above with \(I_2=\{\{v_1,v_2\}\}\): player 2 must choose \(h\) or \(t\) without knowing which node she is at, which is the same as moving simultaneously.

Definition 5.12 (Mixed and behavioural strategies).slide 285 In an extensive form game, a player can randomise in two ways.

  • A mixed strategy is a probability distribution over pure strategies, as before: \(M_i=\Delta\Sigma_i\). The player rolls one die at the start and then follows the chosen plan.
  • A behavioural strategy randomises separately at each information set: \(\beta_i:I_i\to\Delta A_i\) with \(\operatorname{supp}(\beta_i(I))\subseteq A(I)\). The player rolls a fresh die each time she has to move.

Definition 5.13 (Perfect recall).slide 289 A game has perfect recall if, along every play, each player always remembers all of her own information sets reached so far and all of her own earlier actions. Games of perfect information have perfect recall.

Theorem 5.14 (Kuhn).slide 290 In extensive form games with perfect recall, for every mixed strategy there is a behavioural strategy giving the same probability distribution over outcomes, and vice versa.

in wordsTheorem 5.14

So with perfect recall, it doesn't matter which kind of randomisation we use. Without it, the two can come apart, and the next example shows behavioural strategies doing strictly better.

Example 5.15 (The forgetful driver).slide 291 An absent-minded professor drives home in fog. The road has two exits, \(A\) then \(B\). Exiting at \(A\) means a long drive on poor country roads: utility \(0\). Exiting at \(B\) is best, straight home on good roads: utility \(4\). Missing both exits means a fair detour: utility \(1\). In the fog she can't tell which exit she is at: both decision nodes are in one information set, and she has to make the same choice at both.

payoffrandomising each time helps

A pure strategy says "exit" (and she exits at \(A\): utility \(0\)) or "straight" (and she misses both: utility \(1\)). A mixed strategy is a lottery over these two plans, so it also gets at most \(1\). The only way to have any chance of the prize \(4\) is to randomise at each node: a behavioural strategy that goes straight with some probability \(s\) reaches exit \(B\) with probability \(s\) and exits there with probability \(1-s\). Figure 5.2 plots the expected utility; its peak is above \(1\). (Problem Sheet 3, Question 4 asks you to find it.) The game has imperfect recall, since at the second exit she has forgotten that she has already passed one, so Kuhn's theorem doesn't apply.

✎Now try questions 1, 2, 3, 4 of Problem Sheet 3. Question 1 formulates a tree and finds its equilibria; Questions 2 to 4 are about information sets and recall.

5.5Iterated gamesslide 294

≈ 12 min·8 results, 1 figure, 1 exercise·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★★
the questiondoes repetition help cooperation?

In the Prisoner's Dilemma (Example 3.15) mutual defection is the unique dominant strategy equilibrium, although it fails every test of a socially reasonable outcome. One natural answer: play the game more than once. If you know you will meet your opponent again, perhaps the incentive to defect evaporates?

Theorem 5.16.slide 297 If the Prisoner's Dilemma is played for a fixed, finite number \(n\) of rounds that both players know in advance, then in every subgame perfect equilibrium both players defect in every round.

Proof. Backward induction on rounds. In round \(n\) nothing that happens can affect the future, so it is a one-shot Prisoner's Dilemma, and both defect. So in round \(n-1\), play in round \(n\) is mutual defection whatever happens now, and round \(n-1\) is also effectively one-shot: both defect. Continue back to round \(1\).∎

carefulnot a dominant strategy

The slides call all-defection a "dominant strategy equilibrium". It isn't one: always defecting is not dominant in the repeated game.[[Against an opponent playing Tit-for-Tat (Section 5.5) for \(3\) rounds, always defecting earns \(0-2-2=-4\), while cooperating twice and then defecting earns \(-1-1+0=-2\). What is true is that every Nash equilibrium has mutual defection on its path, and the SPNE is all-defection.]] The unravelling argument needs the number of rounds to be known: with an unknown or infinite horizon, there is no last round to start from.

the questioninfinitely many rounds

With infinitely many rounds there are two issues. How do we measure utility over an infinite play? Summing gives infinity. And how do we represent strategies? A strategy must now respond to arbitrarily long histories.

Definition 5.17 (Limit of means).slide 299 The value to player \(i\) of an infinite play \(\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3,\dots\) of stage-game outcomes is

\[\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^Tu_i(\omega_t),\]

the long-run average payoff.

carefulDefinition 5.17

For a general sequence this limit need not exist (the running average can oscillate forever). It does exist when the players use the finite automata below.

Definition 5.18 (Automaton strategies).slide 300 An automaton strategy is a finite state machine with output (a Moore machine, or transducer). Each state is labelled with the action it plays; each state has one outgoing arrow per action of the opponent, saying which state to move to after the opponent plays that action; one state is initial.

examplefive strategies

For the iterated Prisoner's Dilemma:

  • ALLD has one state, playing \(D\): always defect.
  • ALLC has one state, playing \(C\): always cooperate.
  • GRIM starts in a \(C\) state and stays there while the opponent cooperates; the first time the opponent defects it moves to a \(D\) state, which it never leaves.
  • TIT-FOR-TAT cooperates first, then copies the opponent's last move.
  • TAT-FOR-TIT starts with \(D\), then plays \(C\) if both players did the same thing last round and \(D\) otherwise.

Theorem 5.19.slide 302 When two finite automaton strategies play each other, the play has the form

\[\underbrace{\omega_0\,\omega_1\cdots\omega_k}_{\text{non-repeating prefix}}\ \underbrace{\omega_{k+1}\cdots\omega_l}_{\text{repeated forever}}.\]

So the limit of means is the average utility over the repeating block \(\omega_{k+1},\dots,\omega_l\).

Proof. The pair (state of machine 1, state of machine 2) determines everything that happens next. There are finitely many pairs, so some pair occurs twice; from then on the play repeats. The prefix contributes a fixed finite amount, which vanishes when divided by \(T\to\infty\).∎

Example 5.20.slide 303 With Prisoner's Dilemma payoffs (\(-1\) each for mutual cooperation, \(-2\) for mutual defection, \(0\) and \(-3\) when one defects on the other):

  • ALLC against ALLC: \(CC\) forever, utility \(-1\) each. Not a Nash equilibrium, since either player would rather switch to ALLD.
  • ALLC against ALLD: \(-3\) and \(0\). Not an equilibrium.
  • ALLD against ALLD: \(-2\) each. An equilibrium, much as in the one-shot game, and not a desirable one.
  • GRIM against ALLD: GRIM cooperates once, then defects forever. Both get \(-2\) in the limit. Not an equilibrium: ALLD could switch to GRIM and get \(-1\).
  • GRIM against GRIM: \(CC\) forever, \(-1\) each, and this is a Nash equilibrium. Deviating means defecting at some point, after which the other player defects forever, giving at best \(-2\) in the limit.

Cooperation is rationally sustained: the threat of punishment keeps players in line. Figure 5.3 runs any pair.

Theorem 5.21 (Nash folk theorem).slide 308 In an infinitely repeated game with limit-of-means utilities, every outcome in which every player gets at least her security value can be sustained as a Nash equilibrium.

in wordsTheorem 5.21

Player \(i\)'s security value is what she can be held down to: the other players choose the action that minimises her best response payoff. With two players, write

\[\bar u_i(\sigma_j)=\max_{\sigma_i\in\Sigma_i}u_i(\sigma_i,\sigma_j)\]

for the most \(i\) can get if \(j\) plays \(\sigma_j\). Then \(i\)'s security value is \(\min_{\sigma_j}\bar u_i(\sigma_j)\), a "minmax".[[The slides describe it in words as "the best utility it can guarantee for itself, no matter what the others do", which is the maximin of Chapter 6, but compute the minmax; the minmax is what the theorem needs, since it is the punishment the others can inflict. In pure strategies the two can differ, as below.]] The proof uses GRIM-like strategies: everyone plays their part of the target outcome every round, and if anyone deviates, the others switch to punishing her forever, holding her to her security value, which by assumption is no better than what she gets by complying. In the Prisoner's Dilemma, the security value is \(-2\), so mutual cooperation (\(-1\) each) can be sustained.

Example 5.22.slide 309 Consider the stage game

21lr
T−3−101
M−1210
B111−2
For player 1: \(\bar u_1(l)=\max\{-1,2,1\}=2\) and \(\bar u_1(r)=\max\{1,0,-2\}=1\), so player 2 punishes her with \(r\), and her security value is \(1\). For player 2: \(\bar u_2(T)=\max\{-3,0\}=0\), \(\bar u_2(M)=1\), \(\bar u_2(B)=1\), so player 1 punishes with \(T\), and the security value is \(0\). The outcomes giving at least \((1,0)\) are \((T,r)\), paying \((1,0)\), and \((B,l)\), paying \((1,1)\). Both can be sustained in the repeated game.

carefulmaximin would differ

Player 1's maximin here is \(0\) (row \(M\) guarantees \(\min\{2,0\}=0\)), lower than her minmax of \(1\). Using it would wrongly admit \((M,r)\), paying \((0,1)\): but in \((M,r)\) player 1 could deviate to \(T\) for \(1\), and the worst punishment player 2 can impose still leaves her \(1>0\).

ExerciseSustaining (B,l)
Draw finite state machines for both players that sustain \((B,l)\) as a Nash equilibrium of the repeated game in Example 5.22.
show answer

Player 1: a state playing \(B\), which she stays in as long as player 2 plays \(l\); if player 2 ever plays \(r\), move to a state playing \(T\) forever (holding player 2 to at most \(0\)). Player 2: a state playing \(l\), kept while player 1 plays \(B\); on anything else, move to a state playing \(r\) forever (holding player 1 to at most \(1\)). On the path both get \((1,1)\) every round. A deviation by player 1 gains at most \(2\) once, then she gets at most \(1\) forever, so her limit average is at most \(1\): no gain. A deviation by player 2 gains nothing even in the round she deviates (\(u_2(B,r)=1\)), and then she gets at most \(0\).

Definition 5.23 (Discounted sum).slide 314 With a discount factor \(0<\delta<1\), the value of the infinite play \(\omega_0,\omega_1,\omega_2,\dots\) to player \(i\) is

\[\sum_{t=0}^\infty\delta^t\,u_i(\omega_t)=u_i(\omega_0)+\delta\,u_i(\omega_1)+\delta^2u_i(\omega_2)+\cdots.\]
techniquethe geometric series

The key identity is the geometric series,

\[\sum_{t=0}^\infty\delta^t=\frac1{1-\delta}.\]

(The slides start the sum at \(t=1\), which gives \(\frac\delta{1-\delta}\).) For instance, GRIM against GRIM in the Prisoner's Dilemma is worth \(\frac{-1}{1-\delta}\); defecting once against GRIM is worth \(0+\frac{-2\delta}{1-\delta}\), which is worse exactly when \(\delta>\frac12\). Discounting rewards the future less, so cooperation needs players patient enough.

✎Now try questions 5, 6 of Problem Sheet 3. Automata for the iterated Prisoner's Dilemma. Figure 5.3 lets you check your runs.

5.6Rational verificationslide 315

≈ 7 min·5 results, 1 exercise·difficulty ●●●·importance ★☆☆
the questionis the system correct?

Model checking is the most successful approach to proving programs correct. View the state transition graph of a program \(P\) as a model \(M_P\) of a temporal logic, express the correctness condition as a formula \(\varphi\), and check \(M_P\models\varphi\). Tools such as SPIN, SMV, PRISM and MCMAS do this at industrial scale, and the most widely used specification language is LTL.

Definition 5.24 (Linear temporal logic).slide 318 LTL formulas are built from \(\top\), primitive propositions \(p\in\Phi\), \(\neg\), \(\vee\) and the temporal operators

  • \(\mathbf X\varphi\): \(\varphi\) holds in the next state;
  • \(\mathbf F\varphi\): \(\varphi\) holds at some future state (eventually);
  • \(\mathbf G\varphi\): \(\varphi\) holds globally (always from now on);
  • \(\varphi\,\mathbf U\,\psi\): \(\varphi\) holds until \(\psi\) does (and \(\psi\) eventually does).

Formulas are evaluated on infinite sequences of states.

examplereading LTL

\(\mathbf F\neg\mathit{jetlag}\): eventually I won't have jetlag (a liveness property). \(\mathbf G\neg\mathit{crash}\): the plane never crashes (a safety property). \(\mathbf G\mathbf F\,\mathit{drinkBeer}\): I drink beer infinitely often. \(\mathbf F\mathbf G\,\mathit{dead}\): eventually I am dead forever after. \((\neg\mathit{friends})\,\mathbf U\,\mathit{youApologise}\): we are not friends until you apologise.

LTL model checking is PSPACE-complete (with the state graph given explicitly). The basic questions are reachability (is there a computation on which \(\varphi\) eventually holds?) and invariance (does \(\varphi\) hold on all computations?).

motivationcorrectness without a judge

Classical verification assumes an absolute standard of correctness and a specifier in a privileged position, able to say "correct" or "not correct". For many systems that makes no sense: it is meaningless to ask whether the internet is "correct". Instead, interpret the system as a game and its components as rational players.

Definition 5.25 (LTL synthesis).slide 327 Two players \(E\) and \(A\) control disjoint sets of variables \(\Phi_E\) and \(\Phi_A\). In each of infinitely many rounds both simultaneously choose values for their variables; the play is an infinite word, an LTL model, and \(E\) wins if it satisfies a given LTL formula \(\gamma\). LTL synthesis asks: is there a strategy \(\sigma_E\) such that for all \(\sigma_A\), the play \(\rho(\sigma_E,\sigma_A)\models\gamma\)?

in wordsDefinition 5.25

These games are determined (one player has a winning strategy), and LTL synthesis is 2EXPTIME-complete (Pnueli and Rosner, 1989): hard, because we quantify over strategies for LTL goals. But win-or-lose is a very narrow, 1920s view of games. Picture two robots each needing to pass through a narrow corridor: neither can guarantee reaching its goal, so neither has a winning strategy, but both succeed if each reasons about the other as rational. That is the reasoning of equilibrium.

Definition 5.26 (Rational verification).slide 332 In rational verification we are given a system, the players' preferences (as temporal logic goals), and a property \(\varphi\), and ask whether \(\varphi\) holds on some Nash equilibrium of the game ("Nash reachability", E-NASH) or on all of them ("Nash invariance", A-NASH).

in wordsDefinition 5.26

Reachability and invariance over all computations are the wrong questions here: some computations will never arise, because they involve irrational play. We want the properties that hold assuming rational action.

Definition 5.27 (Iterated Boolean game).slide 336 An iterated Boolean game (iBG) is \(G=(N,\Phi,\Phi_1,\dots,\Phi_n,\gamma_1,\dots,\gamma_n)\): players \(N\), a finite set \(\Phi\) of Boolean variables partitioned into the sets \(\Phi_i\) that each player controls, and an LTL goal \(\gamma_i\) for each player. In each round every player sets her variables; the infinite sequence of valuations is a run \(\rho\), and player \(i\) is satisfied if \(\rho\models\gamma_i\). Strategies are machine strategies \(\sigma_i=(Q_i,q_i^0,\delta_i,\tau_i)\): finite states, an initial state, a transition function \(\delta_i:Q_i\times V\to Q_i\) reading the whole valuation, and an output \(\tau_i:Q_i\to V_i\) choosing values for \(\Phi_i\).

in wordsDefinition 5.27

This is a Boolean game (Definition 3.30) played forever, with temporal goals. Machine strategies are deterministic, so a profile \(\sigma\) induces a unique run \(\rho(\sigma)\). A profile is a Nash equilibrium if no player whose goal fails could make it hold by changing her own machine: for every \(i\) with \(\rho(\sigma)\not\models\gamma_i\), and every \(\sigma_i'\), \(\rho(\sigma_{-i},\sigma_i')\not\models\gamma_i\).

ExerciseAn iBG equilibrium
Player 1 controls \(p\) and has goal \(\mathbf G\mathbf F(p\leftrightarrow q)\); player 2 controls \(q\) and has goal \(\mathbf G\mathbf F\neg(p\leftrightarrow q)\). Find a pair of machine strategies forming a Nash equilibrium.
show answer

Let player 1 set \(p\) true forever (one state), and player 2 alternate \(q\) true, false, true, … (two states). Then \(p\leftrightarrow q\) holds in every other round, and fails in the rounds between, so both \(\mathbf G\mathbf F(p\leftrightarrow q)\) and \(\mathbf G\mathbf F\neg(p\leftrightarrow q)\) hold. Both players are satisfied, so neither can gain by deviating: a Nash equilibrium. (Matching Pennies played once has no pure equilibrium; played forever with "infinitely often" goals, it does.)

Theorem 5.28.slide 343 For iterated Boolean games:

  • MODEL CHECKING (given \(G\), \(\sigma\) and \(\varphi\), does \(\rho(\sigma)\models\varphi\)?) and MEMBERSHIP (is \(\sigma\in NE(G)\)?) are PSPACE-complete;
  • E-NASH (is there \(\sigma\in NE(G)\) with \(\rho(\sigma)\models\varphi\)?), A-NASH (do all \(\sigma\in NE(G)\) have \(\rho(\sigma)\models\varphi\)?) and NON-EMPTINESS (is \(NE(G)\ne\emptyset\)?) are 2EXPTIME-complete.
in wordsTheorem 5.28

The first pair follow because machine strategies can be encoded as LTL formulas; the hardness of the second three comes from LTL synthesis. There is also a folk theorem: if every player has a safety goal and every player is "punishable", then for every satisfiable \(\psi\) there is a Nash equilibrium whose run satisfies \(\psi\).

asidereactive modules and EVE

Reactive module games describe the system in a guarded-command language (reactive modules, Alur and Henzinger 1999, used in MOCHA and PRISM). Each agent is a module controlling some variables, with `init` and `update` commands such as \(\texttt{[] x -> x' := false}\). An arena \(\langle N,\Phi,m_1,\dots,m_n\rangle\) lists the modules (choices, but no preferences); adding LTL goals \(\gamma_i\) gives a game. NE-MEMBERSHIP is PSPACE-complete, and NON-EMPTINESS, E-NASH and A-NASH are 2EXPTIME-complete, even though the choices are much more restricted. Oxford's EVE tool solves E-NASH and A-NASH for these games with automata-theoretic methods.

5.7Program equilibriaslide 355

≈ 2 min·1 result·difficulty ●●○·importance ★☆☆
intuitioncooperate if she will

The strategy you really want to play in the one-shot Prisoner's Dilemma is "I'll cooperate if she will". Program equilibria (Tennenholtz) make this possible: each player submits a program to a mediator, which runs them all, and crucially a program can read the other programs' text. Consider

\[\texttt{IF HisProgram == ThisProgram THEN DO(C) ELSE DO(D)}\]

where \(\texttt{==}\) compares program texts. The best response to this program is to submit the same program, giving \((C,C)\); submitting anything else gets \(D\) played against you. Compare GRIM in the iterated game.

Theorem 5.29 (Tennenholtz’s folk theorem for program equilibria).slide 357 In any one-shot game, every outcome in which every player gets at least her security value can be obtained as the outcome of a program equilibrium. In particular, mutual cooperation in the Prisoner's Dilemma can.

5.8Axelrod’s tournamentsslide 358

≈ 3 min·1 result·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★★
the questionwhich strategy wins a tournament?

Suppose you play the iterated Prisoner's Dilemma against a whole range of opponents. Which strategy maximises your total? Robert Axelrod (The Evolution of Cooperation, 1984) ran a computer tournament to find out. Of the 63 strategies entered, including ALLD, TESTER (defect first; if the opponent retaliates, play Tit-for-Tat, otherwise mix in defections) and JOSS (Tit-for-Tat with occasional defections), the winner was TIT-FOR-TAT.

Proposition 5.30.slide 361 In any finitely repeated Prisoner's Dilemma, in a head-to-head match TIT-FOR-TAT's total payoff is at most its opponent's total.

carefulProposition 5.30

The slides phrase this as "TIT-FOR-TAT does no better (and possibly worse) than all other strategies", which overstates it. TIT-FOR-TAT does not do worse than every strategy in absolute terms; it never beats the opponent it is playing.

Proof of Proposition 5.30. Let the opponent play \(a_1,\dots,a_n\). Tit-for-Tat plays \(b_1=C\) and \(b_{t+1}=a_t\). Rounds where both play the same are symmetric. A round with \((b_t,a_t)=(C,D)\), where Tit-for-Tat is exploited, needs \(a_t=D\) and \(a_{t-1}=C\) (reading \(a_0=C\)): a switch from \(C\) to \(D\) in the sequence \(a_0,a_1,\dots,a_n\). A round with \((D,C)\) is a switch from \(D\) to \(C\). Switches alternate, and the sequence starts at \(C\), so

\[\#(C\to D)-\#(D\to C)=\begin{cases}1&a_n=D\\0&a_n=C.\end{cases}\]

Each exploited round gives the opponent \(3\) more than Tit-for-Tat, and each round the other way gives Tit-for-Tat \(3\) more, so the opponent's total minus Tit-for-Tat's is \(0\) or \(3\).∎

payoffso why does it win?

Because the tournament isn't head-to-head. Tit-for-Tat would suffer in a population of ALLD, but it isn't in one: it plays many cooperative strategies, and when cooperative strategies meet they share the benefit of mutual cooperation, while strategies that defect get bogged down in conflict. Axelrod's advice for success: don't be envious (don't play as if it were zero-sum); be nice (start by cooperating, and reciprocate cooperation); retaliate appropriately (punish defection immediately but in measure); don't hold grudges (reciprocate cooperation immediately). This is not mathematically robust advice, and it is somewhat controversial among game theorists.

historythe evolutionary tournament

Axelrod then treated tournament score as evolutionary fitness, and repeated the tournament over hundreds of generations, with strategies that scored well making up more of the next generation's population. How well a strategy does depends on which strategies are present. Again Tit-for-Tat did very well. In his words: "At first, a rule that is successful with all sorts of rules will proliferate, but later as the unsuccessful rules disappear, success requires success with other successful rules."

5.9Evolutionary gamesslide 366

≈ 7 min·4 results, 1 figure·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★★
intuitionfitness is utility

The exciting thing, for Axelrod, was that cooperation could arise through blind evolution, with no "thinking" about what strategy to choose. In evolutionary game theory (John Maynard Smith, Evolution and the Theory of Games, 1982) strategies are chosen by natural selection, and evolutionary fitness plays the role of utility.

Example 5.31 (The Hawk-Dove game).slide 367 This is Example 3.19 in evolutionary dress. A very large population contains two variants, Hawks and Doves, which play the role of strategies. Individuals don't decide what to be: the variants are hardwired, and individuals reproduce asexually, producing offspring of their own type. An individual's fitness measures how likely it is to reproduce. Individuals compete in pairs for a resource worth \(V\) (the fitness gained by getting it); \(C\) is the cost of injury.

  • Hawk meets Hawk: they fight, each equally likely to gain \(V\) or lose \(C\), so on average each gains \(\frac{V-C}2\).
  • Dove meets Dove: they share, each gaining \(\frac V2\).
  • Hawk meets Dove: the Hawk takes everything, \(V\), and the Dove gets \(0\).
21HawkDove
Hawk\(\frac{V-C}2\)\(\frac{V-C}2\)\(0\)\(V\)
Dove\(V\)\(0\)\(\frac V2\)\(\frac V2\)
(Example 3.19 charged each Hawk the full cost, giving \(\frac V2-C\) for a fight; here a fight is a fair gamble between winning \(V\) and losing \(C\). The story is the same.)

Definition 5.32 (Average fitness).slide 371 If a proportion \(p\) of the population are Hawks, a Hawk meets a Hawk with probability \(p\) and a Dove with probability \(1-p\), so the average fitnesses of Hawks and Doves are

\[F_H=p\cdot\frac{V-C}2+(1-p)V,\qquad F_D=(1-p)\frac V2.\]
in wordsDefinition 5.32

These are the expected utilities of being a Hawk or a Dove, against an opponent drawn at random from the population. Crucially, the fitness of each type depends on the population makeup: how well you do depends on who else is around.

Definition 5.33 (Replicator dynamics).slide 373 Let \(A=pF_H+(1-p)F_D\) be the average fitness of the whole population. The proportion of Hawks in the next generation is

\[p'=p\cdot\frac{F_H}{A}.\]

So Hawks increase when \(F_H>A\), that is when they are fitter than average, and decrease when \(F_H<A\).

carefulnegative fitness

When \(C>V\), a Hawk–Hawk fight has negative average payoff, and with enough Hawks \(F_H\) and even \(A\) can be negative or zero, making \(p'\) meaningless. The standard fix, presumably used for the slides' plots with \(C=10\) and \(C=100\), is to add a baseline fitness \(F_0\) to every payoff, large enough that everything stays positive. It changes the speed of the dynamics but not where they go.

payoffwhere the population settles

Hawks and Doves do equally well when

\[F_H=F_D\iff p\,\frac{V-C}2+(1-p)\frac V2=0\iff p=\frac VC.\]

If \(C\le V\), Hawks are always at least as fit as Doves, and they take over (slowly when \(C=V\)). If \(C>V\), the population settles at a mixture with a proportion \(\frac VC\) of Hawks: high costs of conflict keep the Hawks rare. Figure 5.4 runs the dynamics for the slides' values \(V=4\) and \(C\in\{2,3,4,10,100\}\), and any others.

Definition 5.34 (Evolutionarily stable strategy).slide 379 A strategy \(\sigma\) is an evolutionarily stable strategy (ESS) if

  1. it is a best response to itself, \(u(\sigma,\sigma)\ge u(\sigma',\sigma)\) for all \(\sigma'\); and
  2. for any \(\sigma'\ne\sigma\) that does as well against \(\sigma\) as \(\sigma\) does, \(\sigma\) does better against \(\sigma'\) than \(\sigma'\) does against itself: if \(u(\sigma',\sigma)=u(\sigma,\sigma)\) then \(u(\sigma,\sigma')>u(\sigma',\sigma')\).
in wordsDefinition 5.34

Here \(u(\sigma,\tau)\) is the payoff of \(\sigma\) against \(\tau\). Condition 1 says \((\sigma,\sigma)\) is a symmetric Nash equilibrium. Condition 2 handles a small invading group of mutants \(\sigma'\): if they do as well against the natives as the natives do, they can't benefit from meeting each other either. In Hawk-Dove with \(C>V\), the mixed strategy "Hawk with probability \(\frac VC\)" is an ESS, matching where the replicator dynamics settle; with \(C\le V\), pure Hawk is.

Chapter 6

Zero-sum games

When one player's gain is exactly the other's loss, pessimism is rational. Maximin and minimax values, saddle points, von Neumann's minimax theorem, and the linear programs that compute optimal mixed strategies in polynomial time.

≈ 16 min · 4 sections · 9 results · 2 figures · 1 exercises · difficulty ●●○ · importance ★★★

You are reading Chapter 6 (Zero-Sum Games). When explaining, use the notation on this page, cite results by their numbers here (they match the lecture notes), and do not rely on material from later chapters without saying so. Explain step by step in plain language, justify every step and say where tricks come from. Do not solve problem-sheet questions outright: give hints or explain the ideas. Format maths with $...$ inline and $$...$$ on its own line for display, never \( \) or \[ \].

6.1Strictly competitive gamesslide 381

≈ 2 min·difficulty ●○○·importance ★★★
the questionwhat is special about zero-sum?

Recall (Definition 3.21) that a game is zero-sum if \(\sum_{i\in N}u_i(\omega)=0\) for every outcome \(\omega\). With two players this means \(u_2=-u_1\): the players' preferences are exactly opposed,

\[\text{best outcome for me}\equiv\text{worst outcome for you},\qquad\text{best outcome for you}\equiv\text{worst outcome for me}.\]

Such games are strictly competitive. A zero-sum game is just a strategic form game, and everything from Chapters 3 and 4 still works (including mixed strategies). But the symmetry of preferences makes simpler, and computationally better, techniques available.

set-upone number per cell

Since \(u_2=-u_1\), we list only the row player's utilities. Player 1 wants the number large; player 2 wants it small. Here is the running example:

21XYZrow min
A25132
B65.610.55.6
C64.511
D103−2−2
col max105.613
The extra row and column, and the shading, are explained in Section 6.2.

6.2Maximin, minimax and saddle pointsslide 382

≈ 7 min·5 results, 1 figure·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★★
intuitionmove first and assume the worst

Imagine you are the row player and must choose first, after which the column player responds. Whichever row you choose, the column player will pick the column giving you the smallest number in that row. So you should choose the row whose minimum is largest.

Definition 6.1 (Maximin value).slide 384 The maximin value of a two-player zero-sum game is

\[\underline v=\max_{\sigma_1\in\Sigma_1}\ \min_{\sigma_2\in\Sigma_2}u_1(\sigma_1,\sigma_2).\]

A strategy achieving it is a safety strategy (or maximin strategy), and \(\underline v\) is player 1's safety level or reservation value.

exampleDefinition 6.1

The row minima are \(2\), \(5.6\), \(1\) and \(-2\), so \(\underline v=5.6\), and \(B\) is the safety strategy: whatever the column player does, choosing \(B\) guarantees at least \(5.6\).[[The slides write \(\bar v\) for the maximin and \(v\) for the minimax here, then swap to the opposite (standard) convention in the worked example of Section 6.4. These notes use \(\underline v\) (lower value, maximin) and \(\bar v\) (upper value, minimax) throughout.]]

carefullife is not zero-sum

Safety strategies are "worst case scenario" thinking. Is that ever justified? In a zero-sum game it is: the worst case for you is precisely what your opponent is trying to bring about. But zero-sum games are rare, and maximin play perhaps makes sense otherwise only against irrational players. In practice people often behave as though they were in a zero-sum game, and miss out on the benefits of common interest.

Definition 6.2 (Minimax value).slide 386 The minimax value is

\[\bar v=\min_{\sigma_2\in\Sigma_2}\ \max_{\sigma_1\in\Sigma_1}u_1(\sigma_1,\sigma_2).\]
in wordsDefinition 6.2

Now player 2 moves first: for each column, player 1 will take the largest entry, so player 2 picks the column whose maximum is smallest. In the running example the column maxima are \(10\), \(5.6\) and \(13\), so \(\bar v=5.6\). \(\bar v\) is the least that player 2 must concede.

Lemma 6.3.slide 386 In every two-player zero-sum game, \(\underline v\le\bar v\).

Proof (added here). Let \(\sigma_1^*\) achieve the maximin and \(\sigma_2^*\) the minimax. Then

\[\begin{aligned}\underline v&=\min_{\sigma_2}u_1(\sigma_1^*,\sigma_2)\\&\le u_1(\sigma_1^*,\sigma_2^*)&&\text{a minimum is at most any one term}\\&\le\max_{\sigma_1}u_1(\sigma_1,\sigma_2^*)&&\text{a maximum is at least any one term}\\&=\bar v.\end{aligned}\]
∎

Definition 6.4 (Saddle point).slide 387 An outcome that is the smallest in its row and the largest in its column is a saddle point.

in wordsDefinition 6.4

In the running example \((B,Y)\), with value \(5.6\), is a saddle point. The name comes from the shape of a horse's saddle: along one direction the point is a minimum, along the other a maximum, like the surface \(z=x^2-y^2\) at the origin. A saddle point is exactly a pure Nash equilibrium of the zero-sum game: player 1 can't gain by changing row (it is the largest in its column), and player 2 can't gain by changing column (it is the smallest in its row, and player 2 wants small numbers). Figure 6.1 computes row minima, column maxima and saddle points for any matrix.

Theorem 6.5 (Minimax theorem for pure strategies).slide 389 Suppose a finite two-player zero-sum game has a Nash equilibrium \((\sigma_1,\sigma_2)\) in pure strategies. Then

\[u_1(\sigma_1,\sigma_2)=\underline v=\bar v.\]

So Nash equilibria and saddle points coincide, and every equilibrium has the same payoff. This common number is the value of the game, \(v^*\); player 2 gets \(-v^*\).

Proof (added here). Since \((\sigma_1,\sigma_2)\) is an equilibrium, \(\sigma_1\) is a best response for player 1 and \(\sigma_2\) for player 2 (who minimises \(u_1\)), so

\[\max_{\tau_1}u_1(\tau_1,\sigma_2)=u_1(\sigma_1,\sigma_2)=\min_{\tau_2}u_1(\sigma_1,\tau_2).\]

Then

\[\bar v\le\max_{\tau_1}u_1(\tau_1,\sigma_2)=u_1(\sigma_1,\sigma_2)=\min_{\tau_2}u_1(\sigma_1,\tau_2)\le\underline v,\]

using the definitions of \(\bar v\) (a minimum over columns, at most the value at \(\sigma_2\)) and \(\underline v\) (a maximum over rows, at least the value at \(\sigma_1\)). With Lemma 6.3, all of these are equal.∎

payoffinterchangeable equilibria

A consequence: in a zero-sum game, equilibrium strategies are interchangeable. If \((\sigma_1,\sigma_2)\) and \((\tau_1,\tau_2)\) are both equilibria, so is \((\sigma_1,\tau_2)\), since each player's equilibrium strategy is just a safety strategy, and doesn't depend on which equilibrium the other has in mind. There is no coordination problem of the kind we saw in the coordination game of Example 3.17.

6.3Mixed strategies and the minimax theoremslide 390

≈ 5 min·1 result, 1 figure·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★★
the questionwhat if there is no saddle point?

Matching Pennies has \(\underline v=-1<1=\bar v\), and no saddle point. As in Chapter 4 the answer is to mix. Define the mixed maximin and minimax by letting each player choose a mixed strategy, with expected utility in place of utility:

\[\underline v=\max_{\mu_1\in M_1}\min_{\mu_2\in M_2}EU_1(\mu_1,\mu_2),\qquad\bar v=\min_{\mu_2\in M_2}\max_{\mu_1\in M_1}EU_1(\mu_1,\mu_2).\]

Theorem 6.6 (von Neumann’s minimax theorem, 1928). In every finite two-player zero-sum game, with mixed strategies,

\[\max_{\mu_1}\min_{\mu_2}EU_1(\mu_1,\mu_2)=\min_{\mu_2}\max_{\mu_1}EU_1(\mu_1,\mu_2)=v^*.\]

The mixed Nash equilibria are exactly the pairs of a maximin strategy for player 1 and a minimax strategy for player 2.

in wordsTheorem 6.6

Existence of an equilibrium is Nash's theorem (Theorem 4.2), and then the argument of Theorem 6.5 applies word for word to mixed strategies. Historically it went the other way: von Neumann's theorem came first (Chapter 1), and it can also be proved directly from linear programming duality, which is what the next section uses.

techniqueagainst a mixed strategy, pure replies suffice

For fixed \(\mu_1\), the function \(\mu_2\mapsto EU_1(\mu_1,\mu_2)\) is linear, so its minimum over \(M_2\) is attained at a pure strategy:

\[\min_{\mu_2}EU_1(\mu_1,\mu_2)=\min_{\sigma_2\in\Sigma_2}\sum_{\sigma_1}\mu_1(\sigma_1)\,u_1(\sigma_1,\sigma_2).\]

This is what makes the problem a linear program: player 1 only needs to guard against each column.

examplethe picture for two rows

When player 1 has two rows \(T\) and \(B\), a mixed strategy is a single number \(p\) (the probability of \(T\)), and each column \(\sigma_2\) gives a straight line \(p\mapsto p\,u_1(T,\sigma_2)+(1-p)u_1(B,\sigma_2)\). Player 1's guaranteed payoff is the lower envelope of these lines, and the maximin strategy is its highest point. Figure 6.2 draws it. For Matching Pennies the two lines are \(2p-1\) and \(1-2p\), crossing at \(p=\frac12\) with value \(0\).

6.4Computing optimal strategies by linear programmingslide 391

≈ 3 min·3 results, 1 exercise·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★★
motivationpolynomial time

The symmetry of two-player zero-sum games makes computing a mixed equilibrium an optimisation problem, which can be solved by linear programming. So mixed equilibria of two-player zero-sum games can be found in polynomial time, in contrast with the best known algorithms for general-sum games (support enumeration, Algorithm 4.8, is exponential).

Definition 6.7 (The maximin program for player 1).slide 391 With unknowns \(v\) and \(\mu_1(\sigma_1)\) for \(\sigma_1\in\Sigma_1\):

\[\begin{aligned}\text{maximise }&v\\\text{subject to }&\sum_{\sigma_1\in\Sigma_1}u_1(\sigma_1,\sigma_2)\,\mu_1(\sigma_1)\ge v&&\text{for all }\sigma_2\in\Sigma_2\\&\sum_{\sigma_1\in\Sigma_1}\mu_1(\sigma_1)=1,\qquad\mu_1(\sigma_1)\ge0&&\text{for all }\sigma_1\in\Sigma_1.\end{aligned}\]
in wordsDefinition 6.7

Player 1 chooses a probability distribution \(\mu_1\) so as to maximise the payoff \(v\) she can guarantee: each constraint says that against column \(\sigma_2\) she gets at least \(v\). By the previous section, guarding against every pure column is enough.

Definition 6.8 (The minimax program for player 2).slide 392

\[\begin{aligned}\text{minimise }&\bar v\\\text{subject to }&\sum_{\sigma_2\in\Sigma_2}u_1(\sigma_1,\sigma_2)\,\mu_2(\sigma_2)\le\bar v&&\text{for all }\sigma_1\in\Sigma_1\\&\sum_{\sigma_2\in\Sigma_2}\mu_2(\sigma_2)=1,\qquad\mu_2(\sigma_2)\ge0&&\text{for all }\sigma_2\in\Sigma_2.\end{aligned}\]
in wordsDefinition 6.8

Player 2 chooses \(\mu_2\) to minimise the payoff she must concede. The two programs are linear programming duals of each other, and LP duality says their optimal values are equal: that is the minimax theorem.

Example 6.9.slide 393 Take the zero-sum game

21LMRrow min
T3−21−2
C−132−1
B21−3−3
col max332
The row minima are \(-2,-1,-3\), so the pure maximin is \(-1\); the column maxima are \(3,3,2\), so the pure minimax is \(2\). They differ, so there is no saddle point, mixed strategies are required, and the value satisfies \(-1\le v^*\le2\). Player 1's program is

\[\begin{aligned}\text{maximise }v^*\text{ subject to }\quad3\mu_1(T)-\mu_1(C)+2\mu_1(B)&\ge v^*&&(\text{column }L)\\-2\mu_1(T)+3\mu_1(C)+\mu_1(B)&\ge v^*&&(\text{column }M)\\\mu_1(T)+2\mu_1(C)-3\mu_1(B)&\ge v^*&&(\text{column }R)\\\mu_1(T)+\mu_1(C)+\mu_1(B)&=1,\quad\mu_1\ge0,\end{aligned}\]

and player 2's is

\[\begin{aligned}\text{minimise }v^*\text{ subject to }\quad3\mu_2(L)-2\mu_2(M)+\mu_2(R)&\le v^*&&(\text{row }T)\\-\mu_2(L)+3\mu_2(M)+2\mu_2(R)&\le v^*&&(\text{row }C)\\2\mu_2(L)+\mu_2(M)-3\mu_2(R)&\le v^*&&(\text{row }B)\\\mu_2(L)+\mu_2(M)+\mu_2(R)&=1,\quad\mu_2\ge0.\end{aligned}\]
examplesolving it (added here)

The slides stop at the programs. Guess that every strategy is used (all supports full); then by the indifference principle every constraint is tight, giving three linear equations plus the normalisation for each player. Solving,

\[\mu_1=\Big(\frac{17}{47},\frac{23}{47},\frac7{47}\Big),\qquad\mu_2=\Big(\frac{23}{47},\frac{17}{47},\frac7{47}\Big),\qquad v^*=\frac{42}{47}\approx0.89.\]

All the probabilities are positive, so the guess was right, and since each player's strategy holds the other to exactly \(\frac{42}{47}\), both are optimal. As a check, \(3\cdot17-23+2\cdot7=42\), \(-2\cdot17+3\cdot23+7=42\), and \(17+2\cdot23-3\cdot7=42\). The value lies between \(-1\) and \(2\), as it must.

ExerciseIs it fair?
Two players each show one or two fingers. If the total is even, player 2 pays player 1 that many pounds; if odd, player 1 pays player 2 that many. (\(u_1\): \((1,1)\mapsto2\), \((1,2)\mapsto-3\), \((2,1)\mapsto-3\), \((2,2)\mapsto4\).) Who should want to play?
show answer

There is no saddle point (row minima \(-3,-3\); column maxima \(2,4\)). Player 1's indifference against player 2's mix \(q\) on "one": \(2q-3(1-q)=-3q+4(1-q)\), so \(5q-3=4-7q\), \(q=\frac7{12}\). By symmetry player 1 plays "one" with probability \(\frac7{12}\) too. The value is \(2\cdot\frac7{12}-3\cdot\frac5{12}=-\frac1{12}\). So player 2 wins about 8p per round on average: the game, which looks symmetric, favours player 2.

Chapter 7

Win-lose games and complexity

Two players, one wins, one loses. Backward induction solves such games, but when the game is described compactly the tree explodes, and the difficulty of deciding who wins climbs the complexity hierarchy from P through PSPACE and EXPTIME to EXPSPACE.

≈ 22 min · 5 sections · 17 results · 2 figures · 1 exercises · difficulty ●●○ · importance ★★★

When explaining, use the notation on this page, cite results by their numbers here (they match the lecture notes), and do not rely on material from later chapters without saying so. Explain step by step in plain language, justify every step and say where tricks come from. Do not solve problem-sheet questions outright: give hints or explain the ideas. 7.1Extensive form win-lose gamesslide 398

≈ 3 min·4 results·difficulty ●○○·importance ★★★
set-upthe simplest strictly competitive games

We now focus on two-player, strictly competitive extensive form games, with players called \(E\) and \(A\) (think "there Exists a move" and "for All moves"). Every leaf is labelled \(1\) or \(-1\), the payoff to \(E\):

  • payoff \(1\) means "\(E\) wins";
  • payoff \(-1\) means "\(E\) loses", that is, \(A\) wins.

As in any zero-sum game, we list only one player's payoff.

intuitionforcing a win

The key question is whether the game is determined: whether some player can force a win. You force a win if you have a strategy such that every outcome consistent with it is a win for you:

\[\text{there is a move for you such that for all replies there is a move for you such that for all replies}\ \cdots\ \text{you win.}\]

Such a strategy is a winning strategy.

Definition 7.1 (α-ability).slide 400 Player 1 has a winning strategy, or is \(\alpha\)-able to win, if

\[\exists\sigma_1\in\Sigma_1\ \ \forall\sigma_2\in\Sigma_2:\quad u_1(\sigma_1,\sigma_2)=1.\]
in wordsDefinition 7.1

Player 1 commits to \(\sigma_1\) without needing to know anything about player 2's strategy.

Definition 7.2 (β-ability).slide 401 Player 1 is \(\beta\)-able to win if

\[\forall\sigma_2\in\Sigma_2\ \ \exists\sigma_1\in\Sigma_1:\quad u_1(\sigma_1,\sigma_2)=1.\]
in wordsDefinition 7.2

Look at the order of the quantifiers. \(\beta\)-ability says player 1 can always win if she knows player 2's strategy. \(\alpha\)-ability implies \(\beta\)-ability (use the same \(\sigma_1\) for every \(\sigma_2\)), but not conversely: in Matching Pennies, read as a win-lose game, player 1 is \(\beta\)-able (match whatever player 2 shows) but not \(\alpha\)-able.

Example 7.3.slide 402 \(E\) chooses \(L\) or \(R\); then \(A\) chooses \(l\) or \(r\). The leaves are \((L,l)\mapsto1\), \((L,r)\mapsto1\), \((R,l)\mapsto1\), \((R,r)\mapsto-1\). Backward induction: after \(L\), both of \(A\)'s moves lose for \(A\), so the node is worth \(1\); after \(R\), \(A\) plays \(r\), so it is worth \(-1\). \(E\) forces a win by choosing \(L\).

Theorem 7.4.slide 404 In extensive form win-lose games, backward induction determines which player can force a win, and the strategies it computes are optimal for both players; in particular they include a winning strategy for the winner. Winning strategies can be computed in time polynomial in the size of the tree. Consequently, finite extensive form win-lose games are determined: one of the players can force a win.

in wordsTheorem 7.4

Backward induction labels every node \(1\) or \(-1\). A node owned by \(E\) is labelled \(1\) iff some child is labelled \(1\); a node owned by \(A\) is labelled \(1\) iff every child is. If the root gets \(1\), \(E\)'s choices form a winning strategy; if \(-1\), \(A\)'s do. There is no third option: that is determinacy. (Zermelo's 1913 theorem on chess is the same statement: either White can force a win, or Black can, or both can force a draw.)

7.2Compact games and complexityslide 405

≈ 2 min·1 result·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★☆
motivationdecision problems as games

Two-player win-lose games have a special role in computer science, though game-theoretically they are simple. Many decision problems can be phrased as a game:

\[x\text{ is a positive instance of problem }\Pi\iff\text{player 1 can force a win in the game }G_{(\Pi,x)}.\]

Different kinds of game then characterise different complexity classes.

carefulthe catch is the input size

Backward induction is polynomial in the size of the tree, but that assumes the whole tree is the input. In practice games are given compactly: the rules of chess fit on a page, while its tree has more nodes than there are atoms in the universe. With compact representations we should expect the complexity to rise, and it does.

Theorem 7.5.slide 407 Typically, deciding who can force a win is

  1. P-complete for explicitly represented games (the game tree, or game graph, is the input);
  2. PSPACE-complete for compact games guaranteed to end after a polynomial number of moves;
  3. EXPTIME-complete for compact games that can go on for exponentially many moves;
  4. EXPSPACE-complete for games that can go on for a long time and require memory of the history;
  5. of even higher complexity for games that go on for ever (recall LTL synthesis, 2EXPTIME-complete, in Section 5.6).
roadmapone example per rung

The rest of the chapter gives a representative for each rung: graph games for P, the formula game and Geography for PSPACE, and PEEK-G4 and its no-repetition variant for EXPTIME and EXPSPACE.

From Part A Computational Complexity · P, PSPACE, EXPTIME, EXPSPACE

P is the class of decision problems solvable in time polynomial in the input size; PSPACE, solvable using polynomial space (any amount of time); EXPTIME, solvable in time \(2^{\text{poly}(n)}\); EXPSPACE, in space \(2^{\text{poly}(n)}\). Known: \(\mathrm P\subseteq\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{PSPACE}\subseteq\mathrm{EXPTIME}\subseteq\mathrm{EXPSPACE}\), with \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{EXPTIME}\) and \(\mathrm{PSPACE}\ne\mathrm{EXPSPACE}\). A problem is complete for a class if it is in the class and every problem in the class reduces to it (for P-completeness, with logarithmic-space reductions). The canonical PSPACE-complete problem is QBF: is a fully quantified Boolean formula \(\exists x_1\forall y_1\exists x_2\cdots\varphi\) true?

7.3Simple graph gamesslide 408

≈ 7 min·3 results, 1 figure·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★★

Definition 7.6 (Simple graph game).slide 408 A simple graph game is played on a finite directed graph \((V,E,v_0)\) with \(E\subseteq V\times V\), whose vertices are split between the players: \(V_1\) for player 1, \(V_2\) for player 2, with \(v_0\in V_1\) (player 1 moves first), and every edge going from one player's vertex to the other's. A set \(W_0\subseteq V\) of winning positions for player 1 is given. Player 1 picks an edge out of \(v_0\), then player 2 an edge out of the new vertex, and so on. Player 1 wins if the play reaches a position in \(W_0\).

in wordsDefinition 7.6

GRAPH GAME is the problem: given such a game, can player 1 force a win? Unlike a tree, the graph can have cycles, so the play could go on forever, in which case player 1 hasn't reached \(W_0\) and loses.

techniqueunfolding versus working on the graph

One approach: unfold the graph into a game tree and apply backward induction. That shows simple graph games are determined, modulo some fiddly technicalities (cycles make the unfolding infinite, so it must be cut off). But we can apply the idea of backward induction directly to the graph.

Definition 7.7 (Winning positions).slide 411 Let \(W\subseteq V\) be the smallest set such that

  1. \(W_0\subseteq W\) (the initial winning positions are winning);
  2. if \(v\in V_1\) and some edge \((v,v')\in E\) has \(v'\in W\), then \(v\in W\) (player 1 can move into \(W\));
  3. if \(v\in V_2\) and every edge \((v,v')\in E\) has \(v'\in W\), then \(v\in W\) (player 2 can't avoid moving into \(W\)).

Theorem 7.8.slide 412 Player 1 can force a win in the simple graph game iff \(v_0\in W\).

Proof sketch (added here). Build \(W\) in rounds, as the algorithm below does, and give each vertex its rank: the round in which it was added (\(0\) for \(W_0\)).

If \(v_0\in W\), player 1 wins. At a vertex of \(V_1\) in \(W\) of rank \(k>0\), rule 2 put it there because of an edge into \(W\) of smaller rank; player 1 follows such an edge. At a vertex of \(V_2\) in \(W\) of rank \(k>0\), every edge leads into \(W\) to rank smaller than \(k\). So along the play the rank strictly decreases until it reaches \(0\), a position in \(W_0\).

If \(v_0\notin W\), player 2 can stop her. At \(v\in V_1\setminus W\), rule 2 failed, so every edge leads outside \(W\). At \(v\in V_2\setminus W\), rule 3 failed, so some edge leads outside \(W\), and player 2 takes it. The play never enters \(W\supseteq W_0\), so player 1 never wins.∎

Algorithm 7.9 Backward induction for simple graph games
  1. \(W\gets W_0\); \(\ \mathit{old}\gets\emptyset\)
  2. while \(\mathit{old}\ne W\):
  3. \(\mathit{old}\gets W\)
  4. for \(v\in V\setminus W\):
  5. if \(v\in V_1\) and some \((v,v')\in E\) has \(v'\in W\): \(W\gets W\cup\{v\}\)
  6. else if \(v\in V_2\) and every \((v,v')\in E\) has \(v'\in W\): \(W\gets W\cup\{v\}\)
  7. if \(v_0\in W\): return "player 1 can force a win" else return "player 2 can force a win"
in wordsAlgorithm 7.9

Each pass of the while loop adds at least one vertex or stops, so there are at most \(|V|\) passes, each taking polynomial time: the whole thing is polynomial. (With some care, linear in \(|V|+|E|\).) Figure 7.1 runs it. In fact GRAPH GAME is P-complete (Greenlaw, Hoover and Ruzzo, Limits to Parallel Computation, 1995): it is as hard as anything in P, so probably can't be solved fast in parallel. As a corollary of Theorem 7.8, simple graph games are determined.

7.4The formula game and Geographyslide 414

≈ 7 min·6 results, 1 figure·difficulty ●●○·importance ★★★
set-upgames with few moves

The second rung: games given compactly, but guaranteed to end after a small (polynomial) number of moves.

Definition 7.10 (The formula game).slide 415 The formula game is given by variables \(x=x_1,\dots,x_k\) and \(y=y_1,\dots,y_k\) and a propositional formula \(\varphi(x,y)\). Player 1 picks a value (\(\top\) or \(\bot\)) for \(x_1\), then player 2 for \(y_1\), then player 1 for \(x_2\), and so on, until every variable has a value. Player 1 wins if \(\varphi\) is true under the resulting valuation.

in wordsDefinition 7.10

It is a compactly specified extensive form game with only \(k\) moves per player. We could unfold it into a tree and apply backward induction, but the tree has \(2^{2k}\) leaves: exponential in the number of variables.

Example 7.11.slide 416 Two moves, \(x_1\) for player 1 and then \(x_2\) for player 2 (the slides name both variables \(x\)), with goal \(x_2\to x_1\). If player 1 sets \(x_1=\top\), the goal is true whatever player 2 does: a win. If she sets \(x_1=\bot\), player 2 sets \(x_2=\top\) and the goal is false. So player 1 wins by choosing \(x_1=\top\).

Theorem 7.12.slide 417 Player 1 can force a win in the formula game iff the quantified Boolean formula

\[\exists x_1\,\forall y_1\,\exists x_2\,\forall y_2\cdots\exists x_k\,\forall y_k\ \ \varphi(x,y)\]

is true. So deciding whether player 1 can force a win is PSPACE-complete.

in wordsTheorem 7.12

"There is a move for me such that for all your replies there is a move for me such that…" is just the quantifier prefix. The good news: formula games are determined, and winning strategies can be found by unfolding and backward induction. The bad news: the tree is exponentially large compared with the formula. Unfolding isn't practical: use a QBF solver instead.

Example 7.13 (Geography).slide 419 The cities are Peoria, Austin, Nashville, Albany, Amherst, Tucson, Oakland, Tokyo and Oxford.[[The slides spell it "Tuscon".]] The game starts at Peoria. Then the players take turns, player 1 first, to name a city whose name starts with the last letter of the previous city; no city may be named twice. A player who can't move loses.

in wordsExample 7.13

Peoria ends in \(a\), so player 1 can say Austin, Albany or Amherst. Albany ends in \(y\), and no city starts with \(y\), so it wins at once: player 2 is stuck. Austin lets player 2 reply Nashville, which ends in \(e\), a dead end for player 1. Amherst (\(t\)) leaves player 2 the choice of Tucson or Tokyo; after Tucson, player 1 says Nashville and wins; after Tokyo (\(o\)), player 1 says Oakland or Oxford, both ending in the dead letter \(d\), and wins. So player 1 can force a win, with Albany or Amherst. Unfolding the tree and applying backward induction settles any such game, at the cost of another exponential blowup. Figure 7.2 lets you play it against a perfect opponent.

Theorem 7.14.slide 421 Deciding whether player 1 can force a win in (generalised) Geography, played on an arbitrary directed graph, is PSPACE-complete.

Theorem 7.15.slide 422 Suppose a compactly specified win-lose game satisfies

  1. the length of every legal sequence of moves is bounded by a polynomial in the size of the input; and
  2. given a position, there is a polynomial space algorithm that lists all next moves and positions, or decides who has won.

Then who wins can be decided in polynomial space.

Proof sketch (added here). Run backward induction as a depth-first search of the game tree, keeping only the current path in memory. The path has polynomial length, and each position on it takes polynomial space, so the stack is polynomial. Each node's value is computed from its children one at a time (an "or" over children for player 1, an "and" for player 2) and the children's subtrees are discarded once evaluated. The time is exponential, but the space is polynomial.∎

7.5Games with exponentially many movesslide 423

≈ 3 min·3 results, 1 exercise·difficulty ●●●·importance ★★☆

Definition 7.16 (PEEK-G4).slide 424 An instance of PEEK-G4 is \(\langle\Phi_1,\Phi_2,\Phi_3,\gamma\rangle\), where

  • \(\Phi_1\) and \(\Phi_2\) are disjoint finite sets of Boolean variables, controlled by players 1 and 2;
  • \(\Phi_3\subseteq\Phi_1\cup\Phi_2\) is the set of variables true in the initial state;
  • \(\gamma\) is a propositional formula over \(\Phi_1\cup\Phi_2\), the winning condition.

Starting from the valuation \(\Phi_3\), the players alternate (player 1 first), each move setting the value of one of their own variables (passing is allowed). A player wins if her move makes \(\gamma\) true.

Theorem 7.17.slide 424 Deciding whether a given player has a winning strategy in an instance of PEEK-G4 is EXPTIME-complete.

ExerciseWhy exponentially many moves?
If a player can win at PEEK-G4, why can she do so in \(O(2^{|\Phi|})\) moves?
show answer

A position is a valuation of the \(|\Phi|\) variables plus whose turn it is: \(2^{|\Phi|+1}\) positions. The game is determined by the position (the history doesn't matter), so a winning strategy never needs to pass through the same position twice: if it did, cut out the loop and the strategy still wins, sooner. So some winning play visits each position at most once, and takes at most \(2^{|\Phi|+1}\) moves.

techniqueunfold the states, not the tree

First idea: unfold into a game tree and apply backward induction. That doesn't work: a tree with branching factor \(b\) and depth \(d\) has \(b^d\) leaves; here \(b\) is about \(|\Phi_i|\) and \(d\) about \(2^{|\Phi|}\), so the tree has around \(|\Phi_i|^{2^{|\Phi|}}\) nodes, and we get a 2EXPTIME algorithm. With care, backward induction still gives a "merely" exponential algorithm. Define a state as a valuation of \(\Phi\) together with whose turn it is: \(2^{|\Phi|+1}\) states. Make these the vertices of a simple graph game, with an edge for each legal move, and \(W_0\) the states reached by a move making \(\gamma\) true (for the player in question). Then run Algorithm 7.9, which is polynomial in the size of this exponentially large graph: exponential time overall.

Theorem 7.18.slide 427 PEEK-G4 in which no valuation of the variables may be repeated is EXPSPACE-complete.

in wordsTheorem 7.18

Forbidding repetition means the position now includes every previous configuration: you have to remember them all, and there are no shortcuts. The state-graph trick no longer works, because the "state" is the whole history. That is the fourth rung of the ladder.

Preferences and utility functions

1

A utility function for lexicographic preferences

Recall the lexicographic preferences of Definition 2.22. The attributes are colour, engine type and nationality, ranked

\[\text{colour}>\text{engine}>\text{nationality},\]

and within each attribute

  • colour: red \(\succ\) blue \(\succ\) green;
  • engine type: electric \(\succ\) petrol \(\succ\) diesel;
  • nationality: German \(\succ\) French \(\succ\) UK.

Define a utility function taking the three attributes as input and returning a real number, which represents this preference ordering. Don't do it by enumerating all \(27\) cases! Argue that your function is correct.

hintScore each attribute \(0\), \(1\) or \(2\), and combine the scores with weights chosen so that a one-step improvement in a more important attribute outweighs the largest possible change in all the less important ones together. Writing numbers in base \(3\) is one way to think about it.

Uses Definitions 2.2 and 2.22.

2

Preferences no utility function can represent

In the lectures \(\Omega\) was finite. Now let \(\Omega=\R^+\times\R^+\), where \(\R^+\) is the positive reals, and define

\[(x_1,x_2)\succeq(y_1,y_2)\iff x_1>y_1\ \text{ or }\ \big(x_1=y_1\text{ and }x_2\ge y_2\big).\]
  1. Prove that \(\succeq\) is a preference relation.
  2. Prove that no utility function \(u:\Omega\to\R\) represents \(\succeq\).

Between any two distinct real numbers lies a rational number.

hintFor part 2, suppose \(u\) exists. For each \(x_1\), the two points \((x_1,1)\prec(x_1,2)\) give an open interval \(\big(u(x_1,1),u(x_1,2)\big)\). Show that the intervals for different \(x_1\) are disjoint, pick a rational in each, and count.

Contrasts with Theorem 2.4, where finiteness of \(\Omega\) was what made the construction work.

Decisions under uncertainty

3

Football, pub or rowing

You can go to football, the pub, or rowing. Your utility depends on whether it rains:

activityutility if rainutility if no rain
football12
pub30
rowing01

Let \(p_{\text{rain}}\) be the probability of rain.

  1. Formulate this as a problem of decision making under uncertainty.
  2. Is there an alternative you would never choose, whatever \(p_{\text{rain}}\) is?
  3. Write down a rule saying what is best as a function of \(p_{\text{rain}}\), of the form "if \(p_{\text{rain}}\in[X,Y]\) then do \(Z\), else if…".
hintEach activity's expected utility is a straight line in \(p_{\text{rain}}\). Draw the three lines on \([0,1]\); the answer to part 3 is read off the upper envelope, as in Figure 2.2's comparison of lotteries.

Uses Definitions 2.8 and 2.10 (lotteries and expected utility).

The von Neumann–Morgenstern axioms

4

A mixture with something better is better

Suppose \(\Omega=\{A,B\}\) and \(A\succ B\). Show that if \(\succ\) satisfies the von Neumann–Morgenstern axioms, then for every \(p\in(0,1]\),

\[[pA+(1-p)B]\succ B.\]

Say which axioms you use.

hintWrite \(B\) itself as the degenerate lottery \([pB+(1-p)B]\) and compare the two lotteries using the axiom that lets you replace part of a lottery by something preferred.

Uses Definition 2.12.

5

Inconsistent choices about money

Consider the four lotteries

\[\ell_1=\Big[\tfrac12\,£100+\tfrac12\,£0\Big],\qquad\ell_2=£50,\qquad\ell_3=\Big[\tfrac1{20}\,£100+\tfrac{19}{20}\,£0\Big],\qquad\ell_4=\Big[\tfrac1{10}\,£50+\tfrac9{10}\,£0\Big].\]

Suppose I say \(\ell_2\succ\ell_1\) and \(\ell_3\succ\ell_4\). Show that my preferences don't satisfy the von Neumann–Morgenstern axioms.

hintNotice that \(\ell_3\) and \(\ell_4\) are \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_2\), each played with probability \(\frac1{10}\) and otherwise replaced by \(£0\). Either use independence directly, or argue as in Lemma 2.18 with \(u(£0)\), \(u(£50)\), \(u(£100)\).

The Allais paradox of Example 2.17 in miniature.

6

Ranking two compound lotteries

Let \(\Omega=\{A,B,C,D\}\) and

\[\ell_1=\Big[\tfrac35A+\tfrac25D\Big],\quad\ell_2=\Big[\tfrac34A+\tfrac14C\Big],\quad\ell_3=\Big[\tfrac25A+\tfrac15B+\tfrac15C+\tfrac15D\Big],\quad\ell_4=\Big[\tfrac25A+\tfrac35C\Big].\]

A von Neumann–Morgenstern preference relation satisfies \(C\sim\ell_1\), \(B\sim\ell_2\) and \(A\succ D\). How are \(\ell_3\) and \(\ell_4\) ranked?

hintBy Theorem 2.14 there is an expected utility representation, and you may normalise \(u(A)=1\), \(u(D)=0\). Then \(C\sim\ell_1\) and \(B\sim\ell_2\) pin down \(u(C)\) and \(u(B)\).

Uses Theorem 2.14.

7

Mixing preferred lotteries

Someone whose preferences satisfy the von Neumann–Morgenstern axioms says \(\ell_1\succeq\ell_2\) and \(\ell_3\succeq\ell_4\). Should it follow that for all \(p\in[0,1]\),

\[p\ell_1+(1-p)\ell_3\ \succeq\ p\ell_2+(1-p)\ell_4\,?\]

If so, give an argument from the axioms.

hintGo via the intermediate lottery \(p\ell_2+(1-p)\ell_3\), using independence twice, then transitivity. Alternatively use the linearity of expected utility.

Uses Definition 2.12 and Theorem 2.14.

Beyond the axioms

8

The St Petersburg game

Toss a fair coin until the first head appears. If that takes \(k\) tosses, you are paid \(£2^k\) (so \(H\) pays \(£2\), and \(TTH\) pays \(£8\)).

  1. Express this as a lottery with infinitely many outcomes.
  2. If utility is expected money, compute the expected utility.
  3. Now suppose \(u(£n)=\log_2n\). Show that the expected utility is bounded above.
  4. By giving examples, argue that an agent with this logarithmic utility is risk-averse.
hintPart 3: the series \(\sum_kk/2^k\) converges (compare with a geometric series, or differentiate \(\sum x^k\)). Part 4: compare a fair gamble with its expected value for certain, as in Figure 2.1.

Uses Definition 2.10 and Example 2.16 on risk aversion.

9

The bomber pilots

In the Second World War, a US bomber squadron was based 3000km from its target, too far for fighter escorts. Planes carried few bombs so that they had fuel to return. Pilots flew 30 missions before going home, but on average only half survived all 30. Logistics experts proposed that each plane carry a much heavier load but fuel for one way only: every mission a suicide mission, but so many fewer missions needed that 75% of pilots, chosen at random, would return home, while the 25% who flew would face certain death. Every pilot rejected the proposal in favour of the status quo.

  1. Formulate both scenarios as lotteries over two outcomes, \(\mathit{live}\succ\mathit{die}\). Show that the pilots' choice violates the von Neumann–Morgenstern axioms. Which axiom?
  2. Now use three outcomes, \(\mathit{live\ with\ honour}\succ\mathit{die\ with\ honour}\succ\mathit{live\ without\ honour}\) (flying and surviving; flying and being killed; living because someone else flew to certain death). Reformulate the scenarios. Do the pilots now violate the axioms?
  3. Are the airmen's preferences lexicographic? If so, give the attributes and their ranking.
  4. What factors do you think influenced the pilots?
hintPart 1 is a comparison of \([\frac12\mathit{live}+\frac12\mathit{die}]\) with \([\frac34\mathit{live}+\frac14\mathit{die}]\); think about which axiom says more probability on the better outcome is better. Part 2: what outcome does a pilot who is not selected now get?

Uses Definitions 2.12 and 2.22; compare the framing effects of Example 2.19.
